title: Slice2Mesh: 3D Surface Reconstruction From Sparse Slices of Images for the Left Ventricle
abstract: Cine MRI is a widely used technique to evaluate left ventricular function and motion, as it captures temporal information. However, due to the limited spatial resolution, cine MRI only provides a few sparse scans at regular positions and orientations, which poses challenges for reconstructing dense 3D cardiac structures, which is essential for better understanding the cardiac structure and motion in a dynamic 3D manner. In this study, we propose a novel learning-based 3D cardiac surface reconstruction method, Slice2Mesh, which directly predicts accurate and high-fidelity 3D meshes from sparse slices of cine MRI images under partial supervision of sparse contour points. Slice2Mesh leverages a 2D UNet to extract image features and a graph convolutional network to predict deformations from an initial template to various 3D surfaces, which enables it to produce topology-consistent meshes that can better characterize and analyze cardiac movement. We also introduce As Rigid As Possible energy in the deformation loss to preserve the intrinsic structure of the predefined template and produce realistic left ventricular shapes. We evaluated our method on 150 clinical test samples and achieved an average chamfer distance of 3.621 mm, outperforming traditional methods by approximately 2.5 mm. We also applied our method to produce 4D surface meshes from cine MRI sequences and utilized a simple SVM model on these 4D heart meshes to identify subjects with myocardial infarction, and achieved a classification sensitivity of 91.8% on 99 test subjects, including 49 abnormal patients, which implies great potential of our method for clinical use.

title: MorphiNet: A Graph Subdivision Network for Adaptive Bi-Ventricle Surface Reconstruction
abstract: Cardiac Magnetic Resonance (CMR) imaging is widely used to personalize heart models for cardiac digital twin analysis because of its ability to visualize soft tissues and capture dynamic functions. However, CMR images have an anisotropic nature, characterized by large inter-slice distances and misalignments from cardiac motion. These limitations result in data loss and measurement inaccuracies, hindering the capture of detailed anatomical structures. In this work, we introduce MorphiNet, a novel network that reproduces heart anatomy learned from high-resolution Computed Tomography (CT) images, unpaired with CMR images. MorphiNet encodes the anatomical structure as gradient fields, deforming template meshes into patient-specific geometries. A multilayer graph subdivision network refines these geometries while maintaining dense point correspondence, suitable for downstream computational analysis. MorphiNet achieved the strongest overall trade-off in bi-ventricular myocardium reconstruction on CMR patients with tetralogy of Fallot, with 0.3 higher Dice score and 2.6 lower Hausdorff distance compared to the best existing template-based methods, while achieving comparable geometric accuracy to neural implicit function methods on CT data at $50\times $ faster inference. Cross-dataset validation on the Automated Cardiac Diagnosis Challenge confirmed robust generalization, achieving a 0.7 Dice score with 30% improvement over previous template-based approaches. We validate our anatomical learning approach through the successful restoration of missing cardiac structures and demonstrate significant improvement over standard Loop subdivision. Motion tracking experiments further confirm MorphiNet's capability for cardiac function analysis, including ejection-fraction estimates that correctly identify myocardial dysfunction in tetralogy of Fallot patients. Code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/MalikTeng/MorphiNetV2.

title: How to use routine LGE-CMR and fluoroscopic roadmapping to guide targeted endomyocardial biopsy in focal inflammatory cardiomyopathy
abstract: Endomyocardial biopsy (EMB) remains a key diagnostic tool when myocardial tissue characterization is expected to alter management, particularly in suspected inflammatory cardiomyopathy or isolated cardiac sarcoidosis.1 Its value is especially high when histological confirmation may support immunosuppressive treatment or clarify the diagnosis in the setting of persistent troponin elevation, ventricular dysfunction, or unexplained arrhythmias. However, conventional EMB has an important limitation: diagnostic yield may be low when myocardial abnormalities are focal, patchy, or remote from standard biopsy sites.2 In such situations, the challenge is not only to identify the diseased substrate before the procedure, but also to translate this information into an actionable roadmap in the catheterization laboratory. We describe a workflow based on routine late gadolinium enhancement cardiovascular magnetic resonance (LGE-CMR), patient-specific three-dimensional modelling, and fluoroscopic roadmapping. The principle is to transform routine clinical LGE images into a patient-specific model that contains the predefined target and can be displayed in fluoroscopic working views during biopsy. This strategy is intended to improve spatial targeting rather than replace procedural expertise. It is especially useful when multimodality imaging reveals a focal myocardial abnormality and when tissue confirmation is likely to influence treatment. In our experience, the method is applicable not only to conspicuous septal lesions but also to smaller substrates that may be difficult to reach using fluoroscopy alone.3 An important practical point is that the workflow does not require a dedicated high-resolution 3D LGE acquisition. The planning model is generated from routine clinical LGE-CMR data. This matters because routine LGE datasets are frequently anisotropic and have limited through-plane resolution, which restricts their direct volumetric use. The segmentation strategy was therefore developed specifically to recover meaningful three-dimensional information from standard clinical acquisitions.4 In the present implementation, the LGE-positive target remains manually delineated, since the workflow is not yet a fully automated bedside tool. At this stage, manual delineation remains the most robust way to ensure that the final target truly corresponds to the abnormal substrate identified on LGE-CMR.3,4 Its innovative aspect lies in the segmentation strategy used to extract clinically meaningful three-dimensional information from routine LGE datasets. Rather than relying on a simple binary myocardial mask, the method first generates a probability map of healthy myocardium using a dedicated 2D MultiResUnet. This probability map is then concatenated with the original LGE dataset and processed by a transformer-based 3D U-Net architecture.4 An adapted contour-aware loss function is used to improve myocardial boundary delineation. This design addresses a major limitation of routine LGE-CMR, namely, substantial slice thickness and anisotropy. The probability map enriches the input of the second network, while the transformer-based 3D stage helps preserve spatial relationships despite limited z-axis resolution. The result is a patient-specific three-dimensional myocardial model that integrates ventricular geometry and the predefined LGE target.3,4 Once generated, the patient-specific 3D model is displayed using the same or closely matched oblique projections as those used during the biopsy procedure. The goal is not strict real-time fusion but a practical visual correspondence between fluoroscopic anatomy and the pre-identified CMR lesion. This step helps determine whether a right- or left-sided biopsy approach is more appropriate and increases operator confidence in catheter and bioptome positioning.1 A key procedural point is that targeted EMB should not rely on a single standard setup. Instead, the access route and support system should be adapted to the location of the imaging-defined target. For right ventricular targets, especially septal lesions, we favour a transfemoral venous approach using an Agilis™ NxT Steerable Introducer (Abbott) to improve directional control and contact stability. In this setting, the steerable sheath provides a stable and highly manoeuvrable platform for precise sampling. Biopsy is then performed using a 110-cm endomyocardial bioptome (BD2C, ab medica SAS, France). This configuration is particularly useful for septal targets, where subtle angulation differences may determine whether the bioptome reaches the intended lesion or only a neighbouring normal region. For left ventricular biopsy, we use a 7-F guiding catheter through either femoral or radial arterial access, depending on target location, vascular anatomy, and patient size. A JR4 90-cm guiding catheter is preferred for septal, inferior, posterior, lateral, and apical targets, whereas an AL1 90-cm guiding catheter is preferred for anterior targets. A rotating haemostatic Y-adapter is systematically used to allow flushing, pressure monitoring, and careful air management throughout the procedure. For left and right ventricular access, the ventricle is first entered with a pigtail catheter. A guidewire exchange is then performed, and the pigtail is replaced by the guiding catheter selected according to the target location. Before tissue acquisition, ventriculography is repeated in RAO and LAO views to recapitulate the fluoroscopic roadmapping projections and confirm target orientation relative to the catheter trajectory. In practice, both right- and left-sided procedures include ventriculography in matched projections to reproduce the same chamber shape and working incidences as the 3D model, thereby facilitating concordance between the roadmap and live fluoroscopy.1 During biopsy, the pre-procedural 3D model is displayed in matching views while EMB is performed under standard fluoroscopy. The objective is to reduce the mismatch between the biopsy site and the imaging-defined lesion. This is most valuable when the substrate is focal, patchy, or poorly represented by fluoroscopic landmarks alone. The roadmap may also support multimodality integration: when another imaging modality, such as FDG-PET, shows concordant abnormality in the same region, this overlap may further strengthen the targeting strategy in suspected inflammatory cardiomyopathy or cardiac sarcoidosis.3 Systemic anticoagulation is achieved with 5000 IU of unfractionated heparin during left ventricular EMB. Biopsy sampling is performed only after confirmation of an activated clotting time of approximately 250 s. This is particularly important because thromboembolic risk must be minimized, although the same careful anticoagulation monitoring is applied to targeted biopsy procedures in general. At the end of the procedure, transthoracic echocardiography is performed systematically as an immediate safety check. After right ventricular biopsy, echocardiography is used primarily to exclude pericardial effusion. After left ventricular biopsy, it is used to exclude both pericardial effusion and new or worsening mitral regurgitation. When transfemoral access is used, vascular closure is performed with a FemoSeal™ vascular closure device (Terumo) according to local practice. A representative case is that of a 74-year-old woman presenting with heart failure, severely reduced left ventricular ejection fraction, and persistent troponin elevation in a clinical context suggestive of overlap between systemic sclerosis and inflammatory cardiomyopathy. Cardiac magnetic resonance showed focal septal late gadolinium enhancement, increased T2 signal, and elevated extracellular volume, consistent with active inflammatory myocardial involvement. To optimize diagnostic yield, a patient-specific three-dimensional ventricular model was generated from the routine CMR dataset and displayed in fluoroscopic working views to define the most appropriate projections and biopsy approach. A targeted EMB was then performed under fluoroscopic guidance with simultaneous display of the CMR-derived roadmap. Histopathological analysis showed a moderate interstitial inflammatory infiltrate predominantly composed of lymphocytes and histiocytes, without myocyte necrosis, thereby supporting the diagnosis of inflammatory cardiomyopathy. Histological confirmation had a direct therapeutic consequence, leading to immunosuppressive treatment and subsequent clinical improvement (Figure 1). Targeted myocardial biopsy guided by CMR-based 3D roadmapping. (A) Cardiac magnetic resonance late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) short-axis view showing focal septal myocardial hyperenhancement, consistent with inflammatory myocardial involvement. (B) Right ventriculography in right anterior oblique (RAO) 60° projection. (C) Patient-specific three-dimensional cardiac model reconstructed from CMR data, with the targeted myocardial region highlighted in red. (D) Fusion of live fluoroscopic imaging during endomyocardial biopsy with the CMR-derived 3D model, demonstrating accurate positioning of the biopsy forceps within the targeted myocardial region. (E) Histopathological examination (haematoxylin–eosin–saffron staining) showing preserved myocardial architecture with a moderate interstitial inflammatory infiltrate predominantly composed of lymphocytes and histiocytes. This workflow has several practical strengths. First, it is based on routine LGE-CMR rather than a dedicated 3D high-resolution sequence, which supports broader clinical applicability. Second, it provides a tangible way to translate tissue characterization into procedural guidance. Third, it can help the operator choose not only where to biopsy, but also how to biopsy, by adapting the access route and support material to the target location. Finally, it may renew interest in advanced LGE-based targeting of EMB in focal inflammatory cardiomyopathies and related entities, where non-targeted biopsy is expected to have limited sensitivity.2 Several limitations should nevertheless be acknowledged. This workflow is currently best suited to expert centres familiar with advanced CMR, post-processing, and EMB. The present implementation still includes manual delineation of the LGE-positive target, which means that the workflow is not yet fully automated. Lesion accessibility also varies according to substrate distribution: some septal lesions are relatively straightforward to target, whereas smaller, more lateral, or less extensive lesions may remain technically challenging despite roadmapping. In addition, the current report illustrates a practical workflow rather than a standardized, prospectively validated targeting platform. It should therefore be regarded as a clinically useful proof of concept rather than a universally established method. Routine LGE-CMR can be transformed into a patient-specific three-dimensional roadmap for targeted EMB without requiring a dedicated 3D high-resolution acquisition. By combining routine clinical imaging, dedicated segmentation, fluoroscopic recapitulation, and target-adapted procedural material, this workflow may improve targeting of focal myocardial abnormalities and support histological diagnosis in selected patients. Beyond lesion visualization alone, its practical contribution is to bridge the gap between pre-procedural tissue characterization and the technical reality of biopsy in the catheterization laboratory. Benoit Caullery [Conceptualization, Writing—original draft (lead)], Celine Fouard [Resources (equal)], Mireille Garreau [Resources (equal)], Antoine Simon [Resources (equal)], and Gilles Barone-Rochette (Conceptualization [equal], Writing—review & editing [lead]) None. The data underlying this study are not publicly available due to intellectual property restrictions and software-related confidentiality constraints. Access to the data is therefore limited, as the proprietary software used for data processing and analysis is not publicly accessible for patent and confidentiality reasons.

title: Development and Clinical Validation of Cross-Modality, Time Resolved Finite Element Models for Ventricular Geometry and Deformation
abstract: Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) and multiphase cardiac computed tomography (CCT) provide imaging datasets capable of supporting four-dimensional (4D; 3D + time) patient-specific representations of cardiovascular physiology, encoding substantially richer information than is currently leveraged in routine clinical interpretation. Beyond conventional measures of chamber size and global function, these datasets capture spatially and temporally resolved patterns of myocardial architecture, deformation, and inter-chamber coupling that reflect more precise myocardial biology and disease-specific remodeling. Systematic extraction and standardized representation of these features creates an opportunity to define granular, mechanism-informed cardiovascular phenotypes—enabling the development of cardiac digital twins to improve disease detection, risk stratification, and patient-specific modeling of disease progression. To date, cardiac digital twin development has relied primarily on either CMR or CCT, each offering complementary strengths in temporal resolution, tissue characterization, and spatial fidelity. However, modality-specific solutions for representing spatiotemporal features limit cross-modal standardization and harbor efforts for multi-modal phenotyping and prediction modelling. The objective of this thesis was to develop and validate a fully automated 4D digital modeling pipeline for the left ventricle (LV) that bridges multiphase CMR and CCT, establishing a common foundation for interoperable cross-modality cardiac digital-twin construction. The first study developed and validated a novel post-processing method for quantitative 3D + t cardiac reconstructions across routine CMR and CCT imaging. In contrast to conventional pixel-based feature tracking, the novel approach applied shape registrations of machine-learning–derived cardiac chamber segmentations for the extraction of multimodal 4D left ventricle phenotypes. In ten prospectively recruited patients with aortic stenosis undergoing both cine CMR and multiphase CCT imaging, robust agreement of patient-specific 4D cardiac digital twin models was demonstrated across left ventricular chamber volumes, maximum wall thickness, regional 3D strain, and ejection and filling rates. Following measurement validation of the novel method, the third chapter used 4D left ventricle reconstructions for the prediction of clinical outcomes in 194 patients with structural heart disease. Patients with severe aortic stenosis undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) were retrospectively identified and followed for the composite outcome of heart failure hospitalization or death over a median of 4.2 years after intervention. Our novel 4D cardiac digital twin post-processing method was successfully executed on all pre-operative multiphase CCT datasets and high dimensional left ventricle phenotypes were subsequently transformed to interpretable, regionally encoded strain maps for patient specific risk prediction. Non-inferior predictive performance for the composite outcome was observed versus previously published approaches following adjustment for relevant baseline characteristics. Chapter 4 outlines future aims to expand 4D cardiac digital twin technology to biventricular phenotypes, noting the prognostic importance of right-heart functional markers available from multimodal cine imaging. The 4D GEOpath Biventricular Deformation Model is introduced, which extends the novel proof-of-concept method introduced by this thesis aimed at resolving limitations of test-re-test variability and registration drift for real-time construction of 4D biventricular phenotypes from both clinical CMR and CCT. A privileged-learning framework incorporating supplemental imaging is proposed to impose physiologic constraints and enhance model fidelity. This chapter concludes by proposing large-scale deployment of deformable 4D meshes to support multimodal cardiac phenomics foundation models using transformer architectures.

title: Electrophysiological Remodeling and Arrhythmogenic Substrate Characterization in Post-Myocardial Infarction Scar Tissue: A Combined High-Density Electroanatomical Mapping, Late Gadolinium Enhancement Magnetic Resonance Imaging, and Computational Modeling Study
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Authors: (Fictional for this example) Camilo Fernández¹, Elena Rossi², Marco Lombardi³, Sophia Chen⁴ ¹Department of Cardiology, Federal University of Bahia, Salvador, Brazil ²Electrophysiology Unit, San Raffaele Hospital, Milan, Italy ³Cardiac Imaging Center, University Hospital Zurich, Switzerland ⁴Computational Cardiology Laboratory, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, USA Corresponding author: Camilo Fernández (camilofb@email.com) Abstract Background: Post-myocardial infarction (post-MI) ventricular tachycardia (VT) arises from complex electrophysiological remodeling within heterogeneous scar tissue. This study integrates high-density electroanatomical mapping (HD-EAM), late gadolinium enhancement cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (LGE-CMR), and patient-specific computational modeling to characterize the arrhythmogenic substrate in healed infarcts. Methods: Twenty-eight patients with prior MI and documented VT underwent pre-procedural LGE-CMR followed by HD-EAM (using multipolar catheters with ≥1,000 points/cm² density in scar regions) during sinus rhythm and programmed stimulation. Scar borders, conduction velocity (CV), electrogram fractionation, and late potentials were quantified. Three-dimensional myocardial models were reconstructed by fusing LGE-CMR geometry with EAM data and simulated using monodomain/bidomain frameworks with heterogeneous fiber orientation and ionic remodeling. Results: LGE-CMR identified core scar (intensity >5 SD above remote myocardium) occupying 18.4 ± 7.2% of LV mass, with heterogeneous border zones (gray zone) comprising 12.1 ± 4.8%. HD-EAM revealed slowed CV (<0.3 m/s) in 68% of border-zone points, with fractionated/late potentials prevalent in channels connecting islands of viable myocardium within scar. Computational simulations reproduced reentrant circuits in 82% of cases where clinical VT morphologies matched induced VTs, identifying isthmuses characterized by CV gradients >40% and fibrosis anisotropy. The interface area between core scar and gray zone (>3.5 cm²) strongly predicted inducible sustained monomorphic VT (AUC 0.89, p<0.001). Conclusions: Multimodal integration of HD-EAM, LGE-CMR, and computational modeling provides unprecedented characterization of post-MI arrhythmogenic substrate, highlighting slow-conducting channels and fibrotic anisotropy as key determinants of reentry. This approach may refine substrate-based ablation strategies and improve risk stratification. Keywords: Myocardial infarction, ventricular tachycardia, arrhythmogenic substrate, high-density mapping, late gadolinium enhancement, computational modeling, reentry Introduction Myocardial infarction triggers a cascade of structural and electrophysiological remodeling that creates a substrate conducive to reentrant ventricular arrhythmias. Scar tissue consists of dense collagenous core zones surrounded by heterogeneous border zones containing surviving myocytes interspersed with fibrosis. These border zones facilitate slow conduction, unidirectional block, and reentry circuits underlying monomorphic VT. Traditional voltage-based electroanatomical mapping identifies low-voltage areas but often underestimates functional heterogeneity. High-density mapping overcomes this limitation by providing detailed characterization of local electrograms. Meanwhile, LGE-CMR non-invasively delineates scar extent, core vs. border zone, and 3D architecture. Computational models incorporating patient-specific geometry, fibrosis distribution, and ionic/current remodeling enable in silico reproduction and prediction of arrhythmogenesis. This study aimed to: (1) quantify electrophysiological remodeling using HD-EAM, (2) correlate findings with LGE-CMR-derived scar architecture, and (3) employ personalized computational simulations to elucidate mechanisms of VT maintenance in post-MI patients. Methods Patient Population Prospective enrollment of 28 patients (mean age 64 ± 9 years, 82% male) with ischemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 32 ± 8%), prior MI (>6 months), and at least one documented VT episode. Exclusion criteria included acute MI (<3 months), severe renal impairment, or contraindications to MRI. Imaging Protocol LGE-CMR was performed on a 1.5T or 3T scanner using phase-sensitive inversion recovery sequences 10–15 min post-gadolinium (0.2 mmol/kg). Scar was segmented semi-automatically (core: >5 SD; gray zone: 2–5 SD above remote). 3D scar meshes were exported with fiber orientation estimated via rule-based methods. Electrophysiological Study and Mapping Procedures were conducted under conscious sedation. HD-EAM used a 64-pole basket or grid catheter (Rhythmia or CARTO) during sinus rhythm and right ventricular pacing. Points were acquired at >1,000/cm² density in scar regions. Bipolar voltage thresholds: dense scar <0.5 mV, border zone 0.5–1.5 mV. Conduction velocity vectors were calculated using triangulation methods. Late potentials defined as electrograms after QRS end >50 ms. Computational Modeling Patient-specific biventricular models were generated by registering LGE-CMR scar meshes to EAM geometry using landmark-based affine transformation. Myocardium was discretized into tetrahedral elements (~300,000–500,000). Ten Tusscher-Panfilov ionic model was used with modifications for post-MI remodeling (reduced I_Na, altered gap junctions in border zone). Monodomain simulations employed CARPentry or OpenCARP solvers. Reentry induction was tested via programmed stimulation protocols mirroring clinical protocols. Statistical Analysis Continuous variables are presented as mean ± SD. Comparisons used paired t-tests or Wilcoxon tests. ROC analysis assessed predictive performance. P<0.05 was considered significant. Results Scar Quantification by LGE-CMR Mean scar mass 28.6 ± 11.4 g (18.4 ± 7.2% LV). Gray zone represented 38 ± 12% of total scar volume. Border-zone channels (≥2 mm width, connecting viable regions) were identified in 21/28 patients. High-Density Electroanatomical Findings A total of 18,420 ± 6,850 points per patient were collected in scar regions. Bipolar voltage <0.5 mV covered 72 ± 14% of mapped scar. Conduction velocity in dense scar averaged 0.18 ± 0.09 m/s vs. 0.62 ± 0.21 m/s in remote myocardium (p<0.001). Fractionated electrograms (>4 deflections) and late potentials occurred in 64% and 51% of border-zone points, respectively, predominantly along narrow isthmuses. Correlation Between Modalities Good spatial concordance existed between low-voltage areas and LGE core scar (Dice coefficient 0.78 ± 0.09). Gray-zone regions exhibited intermediate voltage (0.8 ± 0.4 mV) and slowest CV (0.29 ± 0.12 m/s). Channels detected by LGE-CMR colocalized with late potential sites in 79% of cases. Computational Simulations Reentrant VT circuits were inducible in 23/28 models (82%). Simulated circuits traversed border-zone channels with CV gradients of 45–70% across fibrosis interfaces. Core scar acted as anatomical barriers, forcing wavefronts into narrow isthmuses. Simulated VT cycle lengths (285 ± 42 ms) closely matched clinical/induced VTs (difference <35 ms in 19 cases). Larger scar-gray zone interface area (>3.5 cm²) predicted inducibility with sensitivity 91% and specificity 86%. Discussion This multimodal approach reveals that post-MI arrhythmogenic substrate is not merely anatomical but highly functional, with slow conduction and late activation critically dependent on heterogeneous fibrosis distribution. HD-EAM provides functional detail missed by voltage mapping alone, while LGE-CMR offers non-invasive 3D scar architecture. Computational modeling bridges these datasets, allowing mechanistic insight into reentry without inducing potentially unstable VT. These findings align with prior reports emphasizing border-zone heterogeneity and channel anatomy in VT maintenance. Personalized digital twins may enable pre-procedural planning of ablation targets, potentially reducing procedure time and improving outcomes. Limitations include selection bias toward inducible patients, computational assumptions regarding ionic remodeling, and registration errors between modalities. Conclusion Integration of HD-EAM, LGE-CMR, and patient-specific computational modeling offers a powerful framework for characterizing post-MI arrhythmogenic substrate. This approach identifies critical isthmuses and fibrosis interfaces driving reentry, with potential to advance precision ablation and risk prediction in scar-related VT. Acknowledgments None. Funding None

title: Personalized external aortic root support (PEARS): A narrative review
venue: Journal of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery
abstract: Central MessagePEARS is an operation to prevent dilatation and to maintain aortic valve function in Marfan and other aortic root aneurysms.PerspectiveAs the result of patient and family awareness and access to echocardiography and radiologic imaging, individuals with genetically triggered aortopathy with root aneurysm present earlier. For them, PEARS complements root replacement surgery.See Commentary on page XXX. PEARS is an operation to prevent dilatation and to maintain aortic valve function in Marfan and other aortic root aneurysms. As the result of patient and family awareness and access to echocardiography and radiologic imaging, individuals with genetically triggered aortopathy with root aneurysm present earlier. For them, PEARS complements root replacement surgery. See Commentary on page XXX. We review the development and present status of personalized external aortic root support (PEARS) in a chronological narrative. PEARS was first proposed to the UK Marfan Association in 2000 by Tal Golesworthy, a developmental engineer with Marfan syndrome. His aortic diameter had increased from 44 mm to 49 mm over 12 years. He questioned what had been told by his cardiologist—that he should have his ascending aorta and aortic valve replaced, followed by lifelong anticoagulation. He had heard Tom Treasure's annual lecture to families with Marfan syndrome, which included timing of surgery with reference to correspondence with Vincent Gott in the New England Journal of Medicine.1Treasure T. He envisaged the application of modern science to revisit the then 30-year-old idea of externally supporting an aortic aneurysm.2Robicsek F. Daugherty H.K. Mullen D.C. External grafting of aortic aneurysms.J Thorac Cardiovasc Surg. 1971; 61: 131-134Google Scholar He foresaw computer modeling, with data from digital images being used to generate a physical replica of the individual's aorta by 3-dimensional printing. Golesworthy came to the operating theaters to see what was entailed in total root replacement. Together, they went to Robert Anderson to take a focused look at the morphology of the aortic root. Golesworthy collaborated with Michael Lampérth and Warren Thornton of Imperial College London to develop computer-aided design modeling for rapid prototyping, now known as 3-dimensional printing. title: Anatomy-Aligned Surface Field Learning for Myocardial Reconstruction from Sparse Short-Axis Cine MRI
abstract: Patient-specific 4D myocardial reconstruction from cine MRI supports quantitative functional assessment, regional motion analysis, and simulation-based modeling. However, routinely acquired short-axis (SAX) cine MRI is sparsely sampled along the through-plane direction, making dense and anatomically consistent surface reconstruction challenging. In this study, we propose an anatomy-aligned surface learning framework that parameterizes the epicardial and endocardial surfaces on a shared circumferential-longitudinal UV domain. This formulation converts irregular 3D reconstruction into structured coordinate-field completion with explicit correspondence across subjects and cardiac phases. Sparse SAX contours are encoded as UV observation fields, coverage-aware sampling improves robustness to incomplete slice coverage, and topology- and distortion-aware learning preserves circumferential continuity and local surface quality. Experiments on three public cine MRI datasets showed that the proposed method consistently outperformed representative mesh-based and implicit reconstruction approaches, achieving overall Chamfer distances of $2.887$~mm on ACDC, $2.641$~mm on M\&Ms, and $2.810$~mm on M\&Ms-2. The reconstructed sequences also preserved ventricular function, with end-diastolic volume and ejection fraction errors of $3.3$~mL and $1.1 \%$, respectively. These results demonstrate that anatomy-aligned UV learning provides an accurate, efficient, and correspondence-aware representation for sparse cine MRI reconstruction and myocardial modeling. The source code will be available at https://github.com/yuan-xiaohan/SAX2MyoSurf.

title: Validation of an imageless electrocardiographic imaging technique for the non-invasive mapping of regular atrial tachyarrhythmias
abstract: Regular atrial tachyarrhythmias, including atypical atrial flutter (AFL) and focal atrial tachycardia (AT), are common,1 particularly following ablation of atrial fibrillation (AF). While typical AFL can often be identified on a 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG), determining the mechanism and location of other atrial arrhythmias remains challenging.2 Electroanatomical mapping (EAM) is the gold standard but is invasive and requires sustained arrhythmia.3 Classical electrocardiographic imaging (ECGi) offers a promising non-invasive alternative,4 though its reliance on pre-acquired cardiac imaging5 [computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)], lengthy setup, and limited inverse reconstruction restricts its use.6,7 Recently, an imageless ECGi system enabling non-invasive mapping without prior imaging has been introduced,8,9 but its clinical performance in atrial tachyarrhythmias has not been systematically evaluated. This study assessed the anatomical accuracy and diagnostic value of imageless ECGi compared with classical ECGi and EAM. A total of 68 patients with focal AT or AFL were prospectively enrolled (mean age 61 years; 63% male; 49% prior ablation; mean left atrium area 30 cm2). Patients were assigned either to a comparison cohort (n = 25) with available CT/MRI for comparison of classical and imageless ECGi or to a validation cohort (n = 43) for independent assessment. The study was approved by the local ethics committee, and all patients provided informed consent. All patients underwent simultaneous 12-lead ECG, non-invasive ECGi (ACORYS, Corify Care SL), and EAM during the clinical procedure. Following electrode placement, a 3D torso scan was acquired.9 When atrial activity was not identifiable, vagal manoeuvres were performed to increase the R-R interval. In the imageless ECGi workflow, the torso scan was fitted to a statistical shape model (SSM) trained on a large CT/MRI database capturing torso–atria variability.8,10 The algorithm iteratively aligned the scan to the most probable SSM torso-atria geometry, minimizing surface mismatch. In classical ECGi, patient-specific CT/MRI images were segmented (ADAS3D Medical SL) and co-registered to the torso scan using an iterative closest-point algorithm. In both methods, body-surface potentials were inverted to reconstruct atrial electrograms (EGMs) and compute local activation time (LAT) maps as previously described.10 Anatomical accuracy of imageless ECGi was quantified in the comparison cohort establishing vertex correspondence between meshes with consistent surface points and anatomical atrial landmarks to assess mean atrial surface distance between estimated and true geometries. Electrophysiological differences between classical and imageless ECGi maps were computed using correlation coefficient (CC) for EGMs morphology and mean absolute error (MAE), expressed in milliseconds, for LAT values. Clinical accuracy was assessed against invasive EAM for three predefined endpoints: (i) arrhythmia chamber, (ii) mechanism (focal or macro-re-entry), and (iii) ablation target (earliest activation or critical isthmus). Analyses were performed blinded to both surface ECG and EAM. A total of 79 arrhythmias were analysed: 30 (38.0%) in the comparison cohort and 49 (62.0%) in the validation cohort. The diagnosis based on EAM included 44 atypical AFL, 23 typical AFL, and 12 focal AT. Three cases were excluded from the analysis due to poor signal quality or unsuccessful manoeuvres failure that prevented acquisition of a complete atrial activation window. Figure 1A shows representative examples from the comparison cohort of complex AFL using the imageless and classical ECGi approaches compared to EAM. The technical performance of imageless ECGi is shown in Figure 1B, which illustrates a representative atrial geometry estimation compared with the MRI-based geometry. Additionally, the panel shows the relationship between geometric accuracy, the CC of EGM morphology, and the MAE of LATs. Overall, the mean surface distance between the estimated and personalized geometries was 15.3 ± 10.2 mm. The average CC for EGM morphology was 0.8 ± 0.1, and the average MAE for LATs was 20.0 ± 10.5 ms. The variability in surface distance had a moderate impact on these electrophysiological parameters. For the comparison cohort, both imageless and classical ECGi demonstrated comparable diagnostic accuracy as shown in Figure 1C; this included the identification of the cavity involved (93.3% vs. 86.7%, P = 0.7), the arrhythmia mechanism (96.7% vs. 96.7%, P = 1.0), and the ablation target (86.7% vs. 80.0%, P = 0.2). Imageless ECGi for the non-invasive mapping of regular atrial tachyarrhythmias. (A) Clinical cases of a left-sided (top) and right-sided (bottom) atrial flutters comparing imageless and classical ECGi approaches with the gold-standard EAM. Representative inverse atrial EGMs around the re-entrant circuits are displayed for both methods. (B) Technical evaluation of imageless ECGi. Left side: representative example of typical scenarios showing personalized and estimated atria meshes. Right side: relationship between atrial surface distance (x-axis), EGM morphology cross-correlation (left y-axis), and LAT mean absolute error in milliseconds (right y-axis) compared to classical ECGi solutions for all maps evaluated in the comparison cohort. (C) Diagnostic capacities of imageless ECGi compared to classical ECGi and traditional 12-lead ECG regarding the characterization of complex atrial arrhythmia for the comparison (continuous line) and validation (dashed line) cohorts. AFL, atrial flutter ; CS, coronary sinus; EAM, electroanatomical mapping; ECGi, electrocardiographic imaging; EGMs, electrograms; EP, endpoint, IVC, inferior vena cava; LATs, local activation times; LIPV, left inferior pulmonary vein; LSPV, left superior pulmonary vein; MV, mitral valve; RSPV, right superior pulmonary vein; SVC, superior vena cava; TV, tricuspid valve. In the validation cohort, imageless ECGi maintained a clinical diagnostic accuracy comparable to EAM and significantly outperformed 12-lead ECG in identifying the involved cavity (91.8% vs. 61.2%, P < 0.001), arrhythmia mechanism (89.8% vs. 71.4%, P < 0.05), and ablation target (83.7% vs. 42.9%, P < 0.001), as shown in Figure 1C. Specifically, in the detection of re-entry mechanisms, Imageless ECGi demonstrated higher diagnostic performance compared to 12-lead ECG, with 94.6% vs. 73.7% sensitivity and 100% vs. 87.5% specificity, respectively. The diagnostic accuracy of imageless ECGi remained consistent for non-counterclockwise typical AFL (n = 38) and in patients with prior ablation (n = 27), with 12-lead ECG significantly less accurate for chamber and target localization. Additionally, accurate pre-procedural identification of the right atrium as the involved cavity could have avoided six transseptal punctures, accounting for 24% of the 25 transseptal approaches. This study demonstrates that accurate non-invasive ECGi of regular atrial tachyarrhythmias can be achieved without cardiac imaging. Despite introducing measurable geometric differences, imageless ECGi maintained diagnostic accuracy and clinical interpretability comparable to classical ECGi. The mean atrial surface distance (∼15 mm) between imageless and CT-/MRI-derived geometries lies within the physiological range of atrial displacement during the cardiac cycle. Consequently, imageless ECGi preserves sufficient spatial fidelity to generate meaningful inverse solutions and LAT maps, enabling reliable arrhythmia characterization. These findings indicate that absolute anatomical precision relative to a static pre-procedural image is not required for accurate functional mapping. High CC for EGMs and moderate MAE for LATs were maintained even in patients with surface distances exceeding 30 mm. These discrepancies likely reflect physiological phenomena, such as respiratory motion and cardiac contraction, which are inherently present both when performing rigid registration to a static CT/MRI scan and in ‘imageless’ torso-to-heart approaches. The diagnostic disagreement observed is more plausibly explained by physiological motion or complex substrate characteristics rather than geometric factors. By eliminating the need for CT/MRI, imageless ECGi reduces preparation time, cost, and radiation exposure while minimizing dependence on imaging infrastructure. The acquisition requires only a torso scan that can be completed within minutes, allowing both pre-procedural and intra-procedural non-invasive mapping. Compared with the standard ECG, imageless ECGi provided superior diagnostic precision, particularly for chamber and ablation-target prediction. Its ability to identify right atrial tachyarrhythmias prior to mapping suggests potential to streamline procedural strategy and avoid unnecessary transseptal puncture. Furthermore, the imaging-free setup enables single-beat mapping of transient or non-sustained arrhythmias, a frequent scenario during ablation of persistent AF where conversion to AFL often occurs before sinus rhythm. This study validates the clinical performance of an imageless ECGi system for the characterization of regular atrial tachyarrhythmias. Its ability to provide rapid, full-chamber activation maps from a single beat may make it a potential solution for mapping transient arrhythmias or rhythm changes during ablation procedures. title: A Geometric Feature Tracking Approach for Noninvasive Patient-Specific Estimation of Leaflet Strain from 3D Images of Heart Valves
abstract: Abstract Purpose: Valvular heart disease is prevalent and a major contributor to heart failure. Valve leaflet strain is a promising metric for evaluating the mechanics underlying the initiation and progression of valvular pathology. However, generalizable methods for noninvasively quantifying valvular strain from clinically acquired patient images remain limited. This study aims to develop a robust feature tracking framework that enables accurate shape matching across variable valve morphologies and quantification of in vivo atrioventricular leaflet strain from three-dimensional echocardiographic (3DE) images in pediatric and adult patients. Methods We developed a geometric feature tracking framework to quantify in vivo leaflet strain from 3DE images and to assess anatomical deformation across the cardiac cycle. Our approach integrates a cohort-derived geometric reference atlas to establish geometric correspondence and introduces a novel distance-weighted coherent point drift algorithm within a Gaussian mixture model framework for non-rigid registration. We evaluated performance against a finite element benchmark model and compared the approach with conventional point-based tracking methods. The framework was applied to pediatric and adult patient datasets (N = 31) to assess robustness across variable valve morphologies. Results The proposed method demonstrated greater accuracy in quantifying anatomical alignment and leaflet strain than conventional point-based approaches. Validation against the finite element benchmark confirmed improved strain estimation. The framework achieved reliable inter-phase tracking of valve deformation across diverse morphologies in pediatric and adult patients. Analysis identified a consistent distribution pattern of the $$1^{\text {st}}$$ 1 st principal strain associated with leaflet billow (prolapse). Conclusion This feature tracking framework provides a generalizable method for noninvasive quantification of atrioventricular valve leaflet strain from clinical 3DE images. Characterization of biomechanical strain patterns may improve prognostic assessment and support longitudinal evaluation of valvular heart disease. Further investigation of the biomechanical signatures of heart valve disease has the potential to enhance prognostic assessment and longitudinal evaluation of valvular heart disease.

title: Desmond Julian Award Winner 2025: Hans Gustav Hørsted Thyregod
abstract: All correspondence relating to this paper should be sent to: [email protected] Danish researcher Hans Gustav Hørsted Thyregod has won the 5th annual Desmond Julian Award with a clinical trial comparing two procedures for treating aortic valve stenosis. The award celebrates the legacy of the pioneering British cardiologist by recognizing research that significantly advances understanding of cardiovascular disease. Dr Hørsted Thyregod’s 10 year follow-up of the NOTION (Nordic Aortic Valve Intervention) trial1, has earned recognition as the most outstanding paper published in the European Heart Journal in 2024. Accepting the accolade, Dr Hørsted Thyregod said he and his team were excited to receive the award. ‘Coming from the European Heart Journal, this is a great honour and recognition for all the work we have done in this trial which we have been working on since 2008. It’s been a pleasure and a privilege to have important results published in good-quality journals and to know the results have informed the guidelines for treating aortic valve stenosis. It is also personally rewarding to work with the patients on this trial because transcatheter treatment was new at that time and the patients were going into unchartered territory. They were very brave, and they knew the results would mean something for patients in the future’ (Figure 1A). (A) Winner of the 2025 Desmond Julian Award Dr Hans Gustav Hørsted Thyregod. (B) Professor Lars Søndergaard of the Heart Centre and the University of Copenhagen Dr Hørsted Thyregod graduated from medical school in Copenhagen in 2006. He had a keen early interest in surgery from understanding his father’s work as an orthopaedic surgeon and from carrying out dissections and teaching fellow students anatomy at university. He says: ‘The craftsmanship and technical aspects of surgery have always appealed to me and since I developed an interest in cardiac medicine at medical school, joining the two together seemed like a good career choice’. He is currently Consultant Adult and Paediatric Cardiac Surgeon at the Heart Centre of Copenhagen University Hospital in Denmark and has been there since September 2008. He undertook a research fellowship during medical school at the University of California San Francisco (UCSF), USA, learning trial methodology and investigating clinical pain and also spent a year in London, UK, training in paediatric cardiothoracic surgery at Great Ormond Street Hospital for Children. The research fellowship at UCSF, although not cardiology-related, convinced him to pursue a PhD, and when he started at the Heart Centre in Copenhagen, he consulted supervisors Daniel Steinbruchel and Lars Søndergaard to choose a suitable research topic. At that time in the early 2010s, transcatheter treatment of aortic valve disease was in its early clinical stages and was a hot topic in Denmark, where cardiologist Henning Rud Andersen had developed the first transcatheter aortic valve prosthesis and implanted it into pigs. He says: ‘The design and setup of the investigation, which would go on to become the NOTION trial, began to take shape many years before industry started their large-scale trials. We were different because we were the first to include mainly low surgical risk patients. Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) was quite new at that time and uncharted by trials or long follow-up studies. We didn’t know what outcomes to expect and designing the trial and finding out the relevant outcome measures was difficult’. The Danish Heart Foundation got behind the project with funding and support aiming to involve the whole of Denmark and the greater Nordic region. The trial enrolled almost 300 patients with severe aortic valve stenosis and randomized them to TAVI or surgery, and the 10-year follow-up published in 2024, showed no significant difference in all-cause mortality, stroke, or myocardial infarction between the two groups. He said: ‘There were some differences in hemodynamic measurements. The opening area of the prosthesis was larger with the transcatheter valves compared to the surgical valves and the corresponding pressure gradient between the left ventricle and the aorta is a little bit lower with the transcatheter valves. Surgical valves, on the other hand, had less paravalvular leak but that did not lead to significant differences in myocardial recovery and function. Besides differences in immediate post-procedure complications, the two groups were the same when looking at long-term clinical outcomes, and the prostheses had no differences in structural integrity or failure rates. That’s particularly important new knowledge, as the transcatheter valves are now the choice of treatment for most patients with aortic valve stenosis’. Since the NOTION trial started, there has been much development in transcatheter valves to treat issues such as paravalvular leakage, coronary access, and conduction abnormalities. The NOTION 2 trial is investigating different types of transcatheter valves, and specifically whether bicuspid valve patients can be treated as effectively with TAVI as with surgery. He says: ‘Since transcatheter valves are increasingly used in younger patients, who will live with their prosthesis for many years, it is reassuring, that the NOTION trial did not find any signs of compromised durability or any unexpected long-term complications. Although patients may prefer the minimally invasive transcatheter procedure, we need to know if all types of patients can be treated as effectively with TAVI as with surgery. For some patients with a specific patho anatomy, it might be a better idea to implant a surgical valve in the first place’. Commenting on what the paper means for the future, Lars Søndergaard Professor of Cardiology at the Heart Centre of the University of Copenhagen said: ‘When TAVI was commercially introduced into Europe in 2007, there was scepticism about procedural safety and valve durability. To test this, we launched the NOTION trial to compare TAVI and surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR). It is important to remember that the trial started in 2009 using first generation CoreValve prosthesis without the external sealing skirt to mitigate paravalvular leakage, and no possibility for re-positioning the valve. Furthermore, computer-assisted tomography was not available for pre-procedural planning and there was little or no experience with endovascular treatment of vascular complications. Despite this we demonstrated that TAVI was non-inferior to SAVR for the primary composite endpoint of mortality, stroke, and myocardial infarction at the one-year mark. The NOTION trial got attention when presented at the American College of Cardiology meeting in 2015, and interestingly the study has become even more important as longer-term outcomes have successively been reported (Figure 1B). ‘The 10-year outcome demonstrates sustained non-inferiority in clinical outcomes and valve durability. The data on reported long-term durability is unique, and high-quality, only made possible by performing many of the echocardiographic evaluations in the homes of these now elderly patients. ‘The NOTION trial has helped both in setting the stage for larger company sponsored trials on patients at low or intermediate surgical risk, and in building confidence among patients and health care professionals that TAVI is an important alternative to SAVR in selected patients. It is also interesting to follow new trials aiming for more evidence and expansion of the indication for TAVI. In addition to our NOTION 2 trial in younger, low-risk patients, the recently presented EARLY-TAVR may lead to upstream treatment of patients with severe aortic stenosis who are still asymptomatic. I am looking forward to following this field in the coming years – being proud of our own contribution in the early days of TAVI’. Nothing to declare.

title: Local2Mesh: Spatially Localized Contour-to-Mesh for Left Ventricular Reconstruction from Sparse 2D Cardiac MRI
abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) left ventricular (LV) reconstruction from sparse cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging remains challenging due to inter-slice misalignment and insufficient local spatial information between slices. Global aggregation of contour features may obscure local contour-to-surface relationships. We propose Local2Mesh, a spatially localized contour-to-mesh framework that deforms a template mesh to reconstruct 3D LV geometry from sparse 2D contours without 3D mesh annotations. The framework introduces geometry-aware alignment to correct inter-slice misalignment and a plane-aware Local Router that routes contour features to template vertices using vertex-to-plane distances. Local and global contour features then jointly guide graph-based template deformation for 3D LV reconstruction. Experiments on two public datasets, M\&Ms-2 and ACDC, demonstrate superior geometric reconstruction and functional estimation over existing methods. Zero-shot transfer from M\&Ms-2 to ACDC demonstrates strong cross-dataset generalization. Reconstructed meshes also improve disease classification over sparse contours, supporting their utility for downstream cardiac analysis. These results demonstrate that combining geometry-aware alignment with local contour-to-vertex modeling improves LV reconstruction from sparse 2D contours and supports downstream cardiac analysis. The code is available at https://github.com/hwu918945-alt/loca2mesh.

title: Reconstruction of 3D Whole Heart Mesh from 2D Cardiac Images
abstract: Standard echocardiography and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) typically provide only a limited number of 2D views rather than complete 3D volumes, restricting comprehensive analysis of the complex cardiac anatomy. In this work, we present an approach for mesh-based 3D whole-heart reconstruction from sparse 2D cardiac views. We employ a neural network that combines a U-Net with a graph neural network for template mesh deformation, and we systematically evaluate how the number and orientation of input views—including long-axis and short-axis configurations—affect reconstruction accuracy. We validate our method on the publicly available ImageCAS dataset to demonstrate the feasibility. Our results show that reconstruction performance, measured by Dice score, mean surface distance, and Hausdorff distance, consistently improves with an increasing number of views. Notably, even a single view achieves a Dice score of approximately 0.8, compared to 0.88 for the full 3D baseline. Furthermore, accuracy is highest for structures directly visible in the respective input configuration. These findings highlight the strong potential of mesh-based 3D cardiac reconstruction from sparse inputs and motivate future transfer to real world application.

title: 3D Spatiotemporal cardiac reconstruction for predicting MACE in acute myocardial infarction
abstract: Artificial intelligence has made significant strides in predicting major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI) following percutaneous coronary intervention. However, most existing methods rely solely on tabular variables derived from clinical data and cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), without fully leveraging the predictive potential of the CMR imaging modality itself. Moreover, these approaches often overlook the synergistic benefits of multimodal integration between imaging and tabular data. In addition, current models primarily focus on short-term MACE risk assessment (e.g., within 6 months or 1 year), limiting their applicability for long-term prognostication. To address these limitations, we first developed ReconSeg3D, a model that reconstructs short-axis cine CMR stacks into temporally-resolved 3D bi-ventricular volumes, capturing fine-grained cardiac anatomy and dynamic motion. These bi-ventricular sequences were then integrated with 45 clinical and CMR-derived variables using spatiotemporal decomposition and cross-attention mechanisms to construct a multimodal MACE prediction model-HeartTTable. HeartTTable achieved a 5-year time-dependent AUC of 0.934 (95% CI 0.907-0.959) and a Harrell's C-index of 0.897 for predicting MACE risk, significantly outperforming models based solely on clinical and CMR-derived tabular features, and demonstrated strong capabilities in postoperative risk stratification. Our study contributes to improved long-term postoperative management for AMI patients by offering clinicians an objective, data-driven decision-support tool.

title: Structural prior and stability-guided uncertainty for RoMa-based cross-modality cardiac MRI registration
abstract: Cross-modality registration between cine and late gadolinium enhancement cardiac MRI is challenging due to large appearance discrepancies and unreliable intensity correspondences. We propose a RoMa-based cine-to-LGE registration framework that integrates structural priors and stability-guided uncertainty. First, slice-wise preprocessing and random perspective perturbations are applied to the CARE2025\_MyoPS dataset to construct supervised registration pairs. An anatomical reliability prior derived from segmentation masks emphasizes structurally stable myocardial regions during training. Stability-guided uncertainty is estimated via multiple perturbation-based forward passes and fused with RoMa's native certainty during correspondence filtering and homography estimation, improving matching reliability. Experiments on CenterC show the method substantially outperforms SIFT+RANSAC and a VoxelMorph-style dense baseline, achieving a Dice score of 0.9585 and HD95 of 0.5341. These results demonstrate that combining dense matching with structural priors and stability-guided uncertainty is effective for cross-modality cardiac MRI registration.

title: Tricuspid valve prosthesis dysfunction revisited
abstract: According with the current recommendation, the majority of valve dysfunction are corrected by repairing instead of replacement. Particularly, in the case of tricuspid valve (TV), mostly TV replacement are performed at the time of left heart surgery. However, almost 90% of TV procedures are repaired in the United States.1 In isolated TV procedures, replacements continue to predominate. In the few cases of TV replacement, mostly are bioprostheses. Besides homografts or autografts (which are rare), surgical bioprosthetic valves are mostly xenografts (with porcine or bovine pericardial tissue; stented or stentless bioprostheses). Stentless bioprostheses and those with externally mounted leaflets have larger valve areas and lower transvalvular gradients, which means better hemodynamics.1 Pannus formation (defined as host tissue overgrowth) and structural valve deterioration are important causes of prosthesis dysfunction (which includes both stenosis and/or regurgitation). In younger patients, there are high rates of early structural valve dysfunction.1 Prosthetic TV dysfunction is associated with a high mortality rate, which underscores the importance of an appropriate TV prosthesis assessment. Because of the anterior position of the TV and the position of this valve relative to the esophagus (anterior and medial), transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) is more useful and easier than transesophageal echocardiography (TEE). Both imaging methods bring complementary data for prosthetic TV assessment. However, any prosthesis evaluation can be a challenge even for an experimented imager. The recent retrospective study published by Xin Zhang et al. analyzed which are the transthoracic Doppler parameters for the assessment of bioprosthesis TV dysfunction.2 They compared the echocardiographic parameters of 61 TV prostheses with normal function with 39 TV structural dysfunction (24 regurgitant and 15 stenotic TV bioprostheses). In this study, all stenotic and regurgitant TV prostheses received a diagnosis through TEE. Because for bioprosthetic valves, effective orifice area (EOA) by the pressure half time (PHT) calculation overestimates TV area compared with continuity equation–derived methods,1, 3 the authors evaluated the EOA of TV bioprosthesis by the continuity equation. EOA was defined as the ratio of stroke volume and prosthetic valve velocity-time integral (VTI). However, they found PHT (and not EOA by PHT) as the most effective parameter in detecting bioprosthesis TV stenosis (for a cutoff value of > 218.0 ms; sensitivity of 93.3%, and specificity of 87.1%). In the regurgitation group, none of the parameters exhibited a good area under the curve value (> 0.80). EOA and Doppler velocity index (DVI or VTI ratio assessed as the ratio of TV VTI and left ventricular outflow tract VTI) were the best predictors of TV bioprosthesis dysfunction. The VTI ratio > 2.8 and EOA ≤1.1 cm2, can detect this dysfunction with a sensitivity and specificity of 84.6% and 90.2%, respectively, 87.2% and 82.0%.2 Therefore, this study brings new elements for the evaluation of tricuspid bioprosthesis dysfunction, especially for tricuspid bioprosthesis stenosis. Prosthetic valve dysfunction (both bioprosthesis and mechanic prosthesis) includes the following causes: structural valve dysfunction, nonstructural valve dysfunction, endocarditis, and thrombus. Structural failure (either prosthetic stenosis or regurgitation) is more common in bio prosthetics than mechanical prostheses. When prosthetic valve dysfunction is suspected, analyzing the opening and closing of leaflets or occlude, the presence of leaflet thickening, calcifications, or abnormal echo densities on the various components of the prosthesis or adjacent to the prosthesis is essential. However, it is not sufficient for bioprosthetic valve dysfunction diagnosis. Besides morphology valve assessment by zoom imaging in multiple views, Doppler parameters can confirm the presence of prosthetic valve dysfunction and evaluate the severity. Color Doppler is useful by analyzing: (1) the regurgitant jet location (central, eccentric, or paravalvular); (2) the proximal flow convergence location and radius; (3) the regurgitant jet vena contracta; and (4) the regurgitant jet area. According to the brand new published guidelines,1 the following echocardiographic Doppler parameters are required for appropriate prosthetic TV assessment: (1) peak and mean diastolic gradient; (2) peak and mean diastolic gradient; (3) PHT; (4) DVI or VTI ratio; (5) EOA; (6) peak tricuspid regurgitation velocity; and (7) tricuspid regurgitation contour and density. However, transthoracic Doppler is less sensitive for detection of valvular regurgitation in the tricuspid prosthesis. Comparison of the above parameters with previous postoperative studies is particularly helpful in suspected prosthetic valvular dysfunction. Normal transvalvular velocities and gradients are flow dependent. The type, position, and size of a prosthetic valve influence its hemodynamic profile and rate of complications.1 For example, a smaller valve and high output states can significantly affect the mean gradient in the absence of prosthetic valve dysfunction.1 In a wide variety of bioprosthesis, a normal TV bioprosthetic function, is suggested by a mean gradient value < 6 mmHg.1 According to 2024 prosthetic guidelines, the cut off value of Doppler parameters suggestive of TV prosthetic stenosis are1: peak E velocity ≥2.1 m/s (in the absence of tachycardia); mean gradient ≥9 mm Hg; PHT ≥200 ms; EOA < 1.5 cm2 and VTI ratio or DVI≥3.3. In TV prosthetic regurgitation, not all echocardiographic parameters are yet validated. In color Doppler, a vena contracta width more than 7 mm (most accurate being the assessment by 3D planimetry) or a large central jet (area > 10 cm2) are suggestive of severe TV regurgitation. In addition, a significant TV regurgitation is associated with the dilatation of the inferior vena cava and holosystolic flow reversal in the hepatic vein. In continuous wave Doppler, the presence of a dense systolic spectral recording with triangular, early peaking velocity are suggestive of severe tricuspid regurgitation. The same severity includes an effective regurgitation orifice area (EROA) ≥0.4 cm2 and a large flow convergence (defined as PISA- proximal isovelocity surface—area radius > 0.9 cm) determined by the PISA method. Xin Zhang et al.2 have found PHT > 218 ms as the most effective parameter for detection of TV bioprosthesis stenosis; this value is greater than that specified by the current guidelines. However, PHT cannot be performed reliably in the presence of rounded spectral Doppler contours. Therefore, it is not recommended in these cases. In addition, heart rate and right-sided chamber compliance should be taking into consideration when we use PHT in the evaluation of TV prosthesis. The previous guidelines (published in 2019) recommended prosthetic gradients and PHT to evaluate prosthetic function. On the contrary, recently published guidelines underline that DVI (or VTI ratio) and EOA (except in patients with significant aortic regurgitation) are Doppler parameters recommended in the assessment of prosthetic function. In these patients, stroke volume (measured from the right ventricular outflow tract) must be included in a comprehensive Doppler assessment of TV replacement. The study of Xin Zhang et al.2 found that a DVI > 2.8 and EOA ≤ 1.1 cm2 are the most accurate parameters for TV prosthesis dysfunction. The DVI associated with normal bioprosthetic TV function varies significantly by valve type and size, with upper values ranging from 2.4 to 3.6.1 The DVI associated with normal mechanical TV function varies significantly by valve type and size, with upper limits ranging from 2.3 to 2.8.1 After 8 years, bioprosthetic TV stenosis increases significantly due to the pannus formation (host tissue overgrowth) and to the structural valve deterioration such as calcification.4 Therefore, this study by Xin Zhang et al.2 is important. In fact, the authors identified the most accurate Doppler parameters for tricuspid prosthesis dysfunction diagnosis: VTI ratio > 2.8 (OR = 9.00; p = 0.003) and TV mean gradient > 5.1 mmHg (OR = 6.50; p = 0.008).2 Integrative assessment of 2D/3D TTE/TEE data with Doppler parameters is strongly recommended. The likelihood of possible TV bioprosthesis dysfunction is higher if more parameters are abnormal. Early postoperative appropriate examination and periodic comparative echocardiographic follow-up studies may unmask possible TV prosthesis dysfunction. Bioprosthesis TV dysfunction implies, in some cases, valve-in-valve transcatheter intervention.5 Echocardiographic evaluation must be integrated with other imaging modalities for a successful procedure. Severe tricuspid bioprosthetic valve stenosis could be sometimes an unusual cause of pulmonary embolism.6 In these cases, the TV gradient increases during inspiration determining a louder diastolic rumble.7 It means a correspondence of the classic auscultatory findings of the Rivero-Carvallo sign. This makes the diagnosis of prosthetic TV dysfunction more challenging. After the integration of these echocardiographic Doppler parameters, the clinician could assess the need for additional testing using a multimodality-imaging algorithm (including TEE or computer tomography/cardiac magnetic resonance). The authors declare no potential conflict of interest.

title: Automatic geometric modeling of aortic valve and calcification using deep learning for biomechanical simulation
venue: Medicine in Novel Technology and Devices
abstract: Accurate geometric reconstruction of the aortic valve system is essential for patient-specific biomechanical simulation and transcatheter aortic valve replacement planning. However, thin valve leaflets, irregular calcifications, and complex leaflet–calcification interfaces remain difficult to model automatically from cardiac computed tomography angiography. This study proposes a unified deep learning framework for automatic reconstruction of the aorta, valve leaflets, left ventricle, and calcifications. A shared 3D U-Net encoder extracts multi-scale anatomical features, while two complementary decoders perform template-based deformation for anatomically stable structures and signed distance function-based implicit reconstruction for calcifications. Joint geometric, mesh, and contact consistency constraints are introduced to preserve structural continuity and improve simulation readiness. Experiments showed that the proposed method achieved better surface accuracy, leaflet thickness consistency, calcification reconstruction, and volumetric mesh quality than representative baseline methods. The reconstructed models exhibited anatomically plausible leaflet–calcification interfaces, stable topology, and no obvious mesh inversion. Finite-element simulations further demonstrated the technical feasibility of using the reconstructed geometries for downstream biomechanical analysis. These results indicate that the proposed framework can generate accurate, anatomically coherent, and simulation-ready aortic valve models, providing a practical basis for automated biomechanical analysis and preoperative assessment in structural heart disease.

title: From Raw Segmentations to Simulation-Ready Cardiac Meshes: An Automated Framework for Anatomical Reconstruction and Virtual Cohort Generation
abstract: Computational models of the human heart are widely used to study electromechanical and fluid-dynamical cardiac function and to support applications such as in silico clinical trials. However, most studies remain limited to single or patient-specific anatomies, restricting the inclusion of population-level variability required for uncertainty quantification. A key challenge is translating medical-image segmentations, which may contain artifacts, mesh defects or disjoint domains, into topologically coherent geometries suitable for multiphysics simulations. In this work, we present a semi-automatic pipeline that converts CT-based segmentations into simulation-ready cardiac meshes within a few minutes while preserving anatomical and topological consistency. Building on modern deep learning segmentation methods, the framework incorporates a template-based registration stage to regularize artifacts and enforce mesh-quality constraints. A Chamfer-distance morphing strategy deforms a high-quality template toward each segmented heart, matching individual chambers while preserving topology. The resulting meshes are watertight, isotopological, and endowed with consistent point-to-point correspondence. The pipeline is validated on 58 healthy cardiac CT scans, including all cardiac chambers and proximal vessel segments. The resulting meshes can be represented in a unified shape space, enabling the construction of a statistical shape model of the heart and major vessels. Principal Component Analysis shows that a low-dimensional latent space efficiently captures population variability, while Gaussian Mixture Modeling enables synthetic anatomy generation. Overall, the proposed framework (released open-source) provides a pathway from raw segmentations to simulation-ready cardiac geometries, enabling anatomically consistent virtual cohorts for large-scale in silico studies.

title: Multi-Task Learning for Motion Analysis and Segmentation in 3D Echocardiography
abstract: Characterizing left ventricular deformation and strain using 3D+time echocardiography provides useful insights into cardiac function and can be used to detect and localize myocardial injury. To achieve this, it is imperative to obtain accurate motion estimates of the left ventricle. In many strain analysis pipelines, this step is often accompanied by a separate segmentation step; however, recent works have shown both tasks to be highly related and can be complementary when optimized jointly. In this work, we present a multi-task learning network that can simultaneously segment the left ventricle and track its motion between multiple time frames. Two task-specific networks are trained using a composite loss function. Cross-stitch units combine the activations of these networks by learning shared representations between the tasks at different levels. We also propose a novel shape-consistency unit that encourages motion propagated segmentations to match directly predicted segmentations. Using a combined synthetic and in-vivo 3D echocardiography dataset, we demonstrate that our proposed model can achieve excellent estimates of left ventricular motion displacement and myocardial segmentation. Additionally, we observe strong correlation of our image-based strain measurements with crystal-based strain measurements as well as good correspondence with SPECT perfusion mappings. Finally, we demonstrate the clinical utility of the segmentation masks in estimating ejection fraction and sphericity indices that correspond well with benchmark measurements.

title: Explicit differentiable slicing and global deformation for cardiac mesh reconstruction
abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) mesh reconstruction of the cardiac anatomy from medical images is useful for shape and motion measurements and biophysics simulations. However, 3D medical images are often acquired as 2D slices that are sparsely sampled (e.g., large slice spacing) and noisy, and 3D mesh reconstruction on such data is a challenging task. Traditional voxel-based approaches utilize non-differentiable pre- and post-processing that compromises fidelity to images, while mesh-level deep learning approaches require large 3D mesh annotations that are difficult to obtain. Differentiable cross-domain supervision from 2D images to 3D meshes is therefore crucial for enabling end-to-end optimization in medical imaging. While there have been attempts to approximate the voxelization and slicing of meshes that are being optimized, there has not yet been a method for directly using 2D slices to supervise 3D mesh reconstruction in a differentiable manner. Here, we propose a novel explicit differentiable voxelization and slicing (DVS) algorithm allowing gradient backpropagation to a 3D mesh from its slices, which facilitates refined mesh optimization directly supervised by the losses defined on 2D images. Further, we propose an innovative framework for extracting patient-specific left ventricle (LV) meshes from medical images by coupling DVS with a graph harmonic deformation (GHD) mesh morphing descriptor of cardiac shape that naturally preserves mesh quality and smoothness during optimization. The proposed framework achieves state-of-the-art performance in cardiac mesh reconstruction tasks from densely sampled (CT) as well as sparsely sampled (MRI stack with few slices) images, outperforming alternatives, including Marching Cubes, statistical shape models, algorithms with vertex-based mesh morphing algorithms and alternative methods for image-supervision of mesh reconstruction. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves an overall Dice score of 90% during a sparse fitting on multi-datasets. The proposed method can further quantify clinically useful parameters such as ejection fraction and global myocardial strains, closely matching the ground truth and outperforming the traditional voxel-based approach in sparse images.

title: Bi-PT: Bidirectional Cross-Attention Point Transformers for Four-Chamber Heart Reconstruction from Sparse Cardiac MRI Data
abstract: We propose Bi-PT, a pipeline for reconstructing 3D four-chamber human heart meshes from clinical sparsely sampled cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) data. This work addresses the error-prone generation of 3D cardiac shape from a sparse point cloud (SPC) extracted from 2D long-axis and short-axis views used in routine clinical CMR protocols. Bi-PT enables accurate inference of the four-chamber heart mesh from the SPC by learning robust point features via bidirectional point cross-attention between an atlas and the SPC, together with per-point semantic labels that improve correspondence estimation. We formulate the deformation field as a Neural Ordinary Differential Equation (NODE) parameterized by a per-point affine transformation and translation to deform the atlas toward the target heart shape. By learning such a NODE, we can guarantee the deformation field to be a locally affine diffeomorphic deformation. We also integrate a semantic label loss into the Chamfer distance to encourage label-consistent correspondences and add a smoothness regularization to stabilize and improve the learning of the deformation field. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Bi-PT achieves accurate and robust performance compared to baselines.

title: Meet the team: new Associate Editors Maja Cikes and Gemma Vilahur
abstract: All correspondence relating to this paper should be sent to: [email protected] The European Heart Journal is delighted to introduce two newly appointed experts who will serve as Associate Editors. Maja Cikes, of the University Hospital Centre Zagreb takes up the role on the Clinical Trials team, and Gemma Vilahur of the Research Institute Sant Pau, Barcelona, joins the Cardiovascular Research Team (Figures 1A and B). (A) Prof. Maja Cikes, MD, PhD Head of the Unit for Heart Failure at the Department of Cardiovascular Diseases, Zagreb, Croatia and (B) Prof. Gemma Vilahur, DVM, PhD, Director of the Cardiovascular Disease Area and Head of the Molecular Pathology and Therapeutics of Atherothrombotic Ischaemic Diseases Group at the Research Institute Sant Pau, Hospital de la Santa Creu i Sant Pau, Barcelona, Spain Professor Maja Cikes, MD, PhD Maja Cikes joins the Clinical Trials team as Associate Editor under the Deputy Editorship of John Cleland. Prof. Cikes is based at the University Hospital Centre Zagreb, Croatia, where she is Head of the Unit for Heart Failure at the Department of Cardiovascular Diseases and full professor at the University of Zagreb School of Medicine. Prof. Cikes undertook parts of her PhD in the UK at St. George’s Hospital, London, and spent post-doctoral periods at KU Leuven, Belgium. She was part of the first cohort of the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) Heart Failure Association’s (HFA) Postgraduate Course in Heart Failure that takes place in Zürich, Switzerland. The selective programme was designed to develop highly specialized, internationally connected clinicians with advanced expertise in heart failure (HF) management, research, and leadership.
