Describing the intensive programme as ‘life changing’ she says, ‘It offered me exceptional opportunities for international collaboration and networking and helped me develop my clinical focus in advanced HF and extend my research career through multiple randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in chronic HF in parallel.’ With her main research interests focused on chronic and advanced HF—she took a multidisciplinary approach collaborating with biomedical engineers and amalgamating cardiac imaging and machine learning to better phenotype patient populations. Involvement in RCTs helped to refine her research interests, with the opportunity to translate this experience from executing trials at the site level to leading investigator-initiated trials. The first multicentre prospective trial of HF therapies in patients implanted with left ventricular assist devices To date, she identifies her most important and personally relevant publications as the primary publication of the ENVAD-HF trial, a first multicentre prospective trial of HF therapies in patients implanted with left ventricular assist devices (LVADs)—an investigator-initiated trial that she has led across six European sites. She says, ‘By demonstrating the safety and tolerability of sacubitril/valsartan in this particular patient population and showing meaningful patient-centred benefits, I believe that we have informed clinical practice and created a basis for research towards additional improvement of outcomes for patients with LVADs.’ Prof. Cikes is an active member of the ESC, a regular contributor to ESC Congress educational sessions and presentations, and has contributed to multiple clinical practice guidelines. She is an active fellow of the HFA, where she chairs the Committee on Cardiac Devices and is the director of the HFA Advanced Heart Failure Course. In her new role on the Clinical Trials team, Prof. Cikes looks forward to contributing and collaborating with her peers as an active trialist involved in patient-related activities, as well as in trial design, data analyses, and publications. She also highlights her intention to involve emerging researchers with demonstrated expertise in specific fields as reviewers, ‘Please expect our invitation and share your feedback—your contributions are greatly valued and have the potential to shape the future landscape of the Journal.’ Professor Gemma Vilahur, DVM, PhD Gemma Vilahur has joined the Cardiovascular Research team as Associate Editor. She is Director of the Cardiovascular Disease Area and Head of the Molecular Pathology and Therapeutics of Atherothrombotic Ischaemic Diseases Group at the Research Institute Sant Pau, Hospital de la Santa Creu i Sant Pau, Barcelona, Spain. She serves as a group leader and Steering Committee member of the Spanish Cardiovascular Biomedical Research Networking Center (CIBER-CV), and as President of the European Society for Clinical Investigation. She trained in veterinary medicine and biomedical science at the Autonomous University of Barcelona, where she also completed a PhD in Pharmacology. She then undertook postdoctoral training in the United States at the Cardiovascular Institute at Mount Sinai School of Medicine in New York, supported by the Spanish Ministry of Science and Innovation. On returning to Barcelona, she progressed through competitive national research programmes and established an independent translational research group, leading to her current role. Working at the interface of basic and clinical research. Her research focuses on ischaemic heart disease across the disease continuum, from atherothrombosis and acute myocardial infarction (AMI) to adverse cardiac remodelling, with particular attention on the role of metabolic risk factors. Working at the interface of basic and clinical research, her group combines translational animal models, advanced cardiac imaging, multi-omic and molecular approaches, and human bio banked samples to uncover disease mechanisms and identify new biomarkers and therapeutic targets. She is the author of several patents and co-founder of two spin-off companies developing translational applications. She has led translational studies in AMI demonstrating the benefits of early intravenous statin therapy vs conventional oral statins for post-AMI patients, supporting a promising strategy to improve outcomes in high-risk STEMI patients. Her work has also explored additional cardioprotective approaches and advanced understanding of key metabolic determinants of myocardial injury, including the roles of high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol and triglycerides in acute MI and in the presence of comorbidities. She has contributed to ESC consensus documents and impactful scientific statements. Thanks to these collaborative efforts and original research publications, she has helped advance emerging concepts linking immune responses, metabolic alterations, and cardio protection in ischaemic heart disease. She brings a translational perspective, focusing on turning preclinical discoveries into effective clinical practice. Her expertise in translational models enhances the evaluation of experimental—especially animal—studies to maximize their clinical relevance. She says, ‘I am especially interested in rigorous preclinical, translational, or clinical studies with clearly defined biological rationale and potential clinical relevance. I hope to support well-designed work fostering collaboration between basic and clinical investigators, while ensuring conclusions remain balanced and grounded in solid data. I also see this role as an opportunity to help maintain the journal’s scientific quality and engage constructively with authors, so the review process strengthens their work, even when a manuscript is not accepted.’ All authors declare no disclosure of interest for this contribution.

title: Deep learning approaches for cardiac motion estimation, segmentation, and 4d reconstruction in echocardiography and cardiac MRI
abstract: Cardiac motion and morphology are fundamental to assessing cardiac function and congenital abnormalities. Echocardiography and cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging provide rich spatio-temporal information; however, their analysis remains largely manual or semi-automatic, making it time-consuming, operator-dependent, and difficult to reproduce. These challenges are compounded by image noise, ambiguous boundaries, limited annotations, high-dimensional data, and complex non-rigid motion, particularly in foetal echocardiography. This thesis addresses these limitations by developing a unified deep learning framework for cardiac motion estimation, segmentation, and 4D (3D over time) reconstruction that explicitly incorporates anatomical, temporal, and geometric priors to produce robust and clinically meaningful representations across 2D, 3D, and 4D echocardiography and CMR. For cardiac motion estimation, the thesis introduces anatomy- and texture-aware constraints that preserve physiological structures and realistic image appearance during deformable registration, improving motion estimation and downstream functional assessment. It further presents a feedback-based self-supervised framework that iteratively refines registration by identifying residual alignment errors, enabling reliable unsupervised 4D foetal echocardiographic motion estimation. For cardiac segmentation, a lightweight \ac{TAM} models cross-temporal interactions without increasing model dimensionality. The module integrates seamlessly into convolutional, transformer-based, and foundation models, consistently improving segmentation accuracy under sparse supervision while preserving computational efficiency. The thesis also proposes a geometry-aware framework for 4D foetal cardiac reconstruction based on a novel 2.5D radial slicing strategy that simplifies annotation while preserving anatomical structure. This work introduces the first public benchmark dataset for 4D foetal echocardiography, FeEcho4D, together with SCOPENet for symmetry-consistent segmentation. Sparse radial segmentations are reconstructed into temporally coherent 3D meshes using graph-harmonic deformation, enabling accurate functional quantification without dense volumetric annotation. Overall, the proposed framework demonstrates that integrating anatomical, temporal, and geometric priors produces more robust, physiologically meaningful, and clinically reliable cardiac analysis than conventional data-driven approaches.

title: Neural Phase Correlation
abstract: Correspondence is fundamentally relational: it seeks the unknown transformation between two observations of a common scene, not the content of either. Yet the dominant learning-based methods do not represent the transformation as a first-class object in the architecture. They encode each image independently and let a learned similarity function or a deep decoder discover the mapping implicitly. Phase correlation is the canonical exception, measuring the inter-image relationship directly in the Fourier domain, but the rigidity of its fixed basis confines it to global translation. We introduce a learned generalization of phase correlation that lifts this restriction by learning the basis on which the transformation decomposes. The same algebraic primitive extends to dense non-rigid deformations and to unitary dynamics. On the ACDC cardiac-MRI benchmark the framework matches or exceeds prior published baselines on both registration directions. On CAMUS echocardiography it matches state-of-the-art without auxiliary scoring or adaptive-smoothness mechanisms. Applied to time-evolved wavefunction pairs of the 1-D quantum harmonic oscillator, the same framework recovers the Hermite-function eigenstates and the quantized energy levels of the unknown Hamiltonian from observation pairs alone.

title: Cohort-Scale Neural Atlases of Ultrasound Video
abstract: Ultrasound is the most widely used real-time imaging modality in clinical practice, yet per-frame video annotation remains a major bottleneck: expert labels are scarce and costly, and image appearance varies with speckle, shadowing, attenuation, and operator-dependent probe pose. This is especially limiting because clinically relevant information is often dynamic, from left-ventricular motion in echocardiography to muscle and bone kinematics in musculoskeletal imaging. Population atlases can amortize annotation cost by registering observations to a shared canonical coordinate system, but existing neural atlas methods mainly target single videos, small test-time image sets, or object-centric image collections. We introduce a cohort-scale neural atlas for ultrasound video: a single canonical chart with per-video Generative Latent Optimization embeddings, trained jointly over thousands of frames in DINOv3 feature space. Across five cardiac and musculoskeletal datasets with point landmarks and segmentation masks, our method learns coherent canonical templates and enables accurate atlas-space annotation transfer. On EchoNet-Dynamic and MSK-Bone, it supports single- and few-shot transfer with accuracy competitive with strong dense-correspondence baselines, while training in minutes on a single consumer GPU. The learned embeddings are interpretable: linear projections reveal structured cohort variation, image-decoder interpolation produces anatomically plausible intermediate frames, and test-time latent inversion reconstructs held-out frames through the atlas. These results suggest that cohort-scale neural atlases offer a practical, interpretable representation for reducing expert annotation burden in ultrasound video analysis.

title: Cardiac Mesh Flow: One-Step Generation of 3D+t Cardiac Four-Chamber Meshes via Flow Matching
abstract: Spatio-temporal (3D+t) generative modelling of cardiac shape and motion is crucial for understanding heart structure and function at population scale. Existing generative models for cardiac shape synthesis either adopt volumetric shape representations that lack anatomical correspondence across different time points and subjects, or rely on VAE-based frameworks that suffer from a trade-off between reconstruction fidelity and generative diversity. In this work, we propose Cardiac Mesh Flow, a novel generative flow model for 3D+t cardiac four-chamber mesh generation with anatomical correspondence, temporal coherence, and periodic consistency. Leveraging the flow matching technique, Cardiac Mesh Flow performs efficient one-step generation of multi-scale free-form deformation fields, which warp a template mesh to generate cardiac four-chamber meshes across a cardiac cycle. Furthermore, Cardiac Mesh Flow enables controllable generation conditioned on cardiac chamber volumes, allowing precise control of the synthetic heart. Experimental results demonstrate that Cardiac Mesh Flow achieves high fidelity and diversity on both unconditional and conditional generation, compared to state-of-the-art 3D+t cardiac mesh generation methods.

title: Enhancing Cardiac MRI Without Contrast Agents: AI-Based OS-CMR Pattern Recognition and Synthetic T1/T2 Map Generation Using R-GAN
abstract: Background: Cardiovascular disease remains a major global health issue. Myocardial injury can result from ischemic and non-ischemic causes, inflammatory conditions, or other factors like arterial hypertension. Early, accurate detection is crucial for prevention and treatment. Myocardial injury results from acute or chronic stress caused by a lack of oxygenation, inflammation, toxicity, or infiltration. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) is the gold standard for visualizing myocardial abnormalities. T2-weighted imaging or T2-mapping can illustrate edema but faces challenges like low signal-to-noise ratio, motion artifacts, lengthy scan times, and variability between protocols. T1-mapping identifies diffuse fibrosis and is useful in conditions such as cardiac amyloidosis. Late Gadolinium Enhancement (LGE) remains the standard for identifying ischemic scars and infiltrations, although contrast agents carry potential risks and raise costs and extend scan times. Oxygenation-Sensitive CMR (OS-CMR) monitors changes in myocardial oxygenation dynamically and is increasingly used to evaluate microvascular dysfunction. However, its relationship to edema and fibrosis is still under investigation. Since OS-CMR provides multiphasic sequences, it may also measure wall thickness, motion, and strain measures, opening opportunities for both tissue characterization and functional assessment simultaneously. Methods: We developed DeepOxyMap, a classifier and feature-map visualizer based on VGG19, trained on OS-CMR images from 190 subjects to classify myocardium into four pathology groups (ICMP, NICMP, edema and Healthy). Training involved stratified 5-fold cross-validation with Monte Carlo Dropout and residual learning. Heatmaps identified regions influencing classification, converted into binary maps, and quantitatively compared to expert-guided LGE, T1, and T2-maps using similarity metrics. After confirming pathology-relevant features on OS-CMR, we developed a Residual GAN (R-GAN) to generate T1 and T2 parametric-maps from OS-CMR data. The dataset included 3,670 matched OS-CMR/T1 or OS-CMR/T2 pairs from two prospective registries. Preprocessing involved normalization, registration, and data augmentation. Model was compared against Pix2Pix (with and without augmentation) using PSNR, SSIM, and PCC metrics. Clinical validation included ROI-based signal intensity analysis, Extended Phase Graph (EPG) simulations, and T1/T2-curve assessments in edema, scar, and healthy myocardium and T1/T2-colour-map.Results: The DeepOxyMap achieved an average AUC of 0.94. Feature map analysis demonstrated strong spatial correspondence with expert-defined regions: Dice scores of 0.8520 (transmural ischemic scar), 0.8989 (subendocardial ischemic scar), 0.8333 (ICMP with HCM), 0.9299 (NICMP due to DCM phenotype), 0.8182 (localized edema, Recall 0.999), and 0.9340 (persistent global myocardial edema. Our novel R-GANT2 synthesis metrics: SSIM 0.672–0.739, PSNR 21.56–24.95 dB, PCC 0.862–0.923; synthetic T2 curves closely matched original data, with Pearson and Spearman correlations >0.99 and minimal errors (e.g., RMSE ≤ 0.0286 in edema regions). RGAN-T1 synthesis metrics: SSIM 0.810, PSNR 16.01 dB, PCC 0.748; T1 recovery curves from both sets displayed strong agreement in shape and amplitude: Amyloid: MAE 0.031, MSE 0.007, RMSE 0.088, R² 0.91, Pearson 0.96, Spearman 0.85, with EPG-simulated curves reaching R² up to 0.99 and MSE as low as 0.001. The T1 colour maps were also verified using CVI software. Conclusion: This study shows that OS-CMR images, when combined with DeepOxyMap and new R-GAN models, offer a contrast-free method for detecting myocardial issues, serving as a practical alternative to traditional native and contrast-enhanced CMR imaging. This AI-based method could greatly enhance the efficiency and safety of CMR by lowering scan durations and removing the requirement for contrast agents

title: Towards 3D heart mesh generation using contactless radar imaging and physics-informed neural network
abstract: Cardiac function evaluation necessitates continuous, non-invasive monitoring, a capability limited in MRI. Millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar and its Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) mode offer a privacy-preserving and portable point-of-care clinical applications. However, reconstructing high-fidelity 3D cardiac geometry from SAR remains an open challenge. Traditional radar methods generate sparse point clouds that lack continuous surface topology. Meanwhile, direct application of optical reconstruction networks performs poorly due to the severe speckle noise and ambiguous boundaries inherent in SAR images. To bridge this gap, we propose SAR2Mesh, a novel framework that reformulates the task as a coarse-to-fine mesh deformation process. By initializing with a topological template, our approach explicitly preserves anatomical connectivity through progressive mesh deformation.We introduce a geometry-aware feature projection module to extract multi-view features via 3D-to-2D sampling, and a physics-informed radar loss to enforce consistency between the predicted geometry and raw radar echoes. Furthermore, we present Cardiac Mesh-SAR, the first large-scale paired SAR-mesh dataset. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SAR2Mesh significantly outperforms existing image-based baselines, achieving accurate and physically consistent cardiac reconstructions.

title: Personalised normative cardiac phenotyping reveals clinically relevant heterogeneity in cardiac shape and outcome risk
abstract: Abstract Standard cardiac biomarkers such as ejection fraction, ventricular volumes, and strain compress complex three-dimensional heart dynamics into a small set of predefined measurements, leaving clinically important heterogeneity unrecognised. Here we propose a personalised normative cardiac frame-work in which each individual is compared to a digital twin representing expected healthy cardiac function given their age, sex, and body habitus. We show that structured patterns of deviation from these normative twins, discovered through systematic exploration of a generative cardiac dynamics space, constitute novel dynamic phenotypes that are not captured by conventional biomarkers. Applied independently to two UK Biobank cardiac cohorts with distinct shape representation, a 128-dimensional four-chamber statistical shape descriptor (HeartSSM, n = 52,365) and a 64-dimensional deep generative latent space from a conditional variational mesh autoencoder (MeshHeart cVAE, n = up to 39,376), we identify reproducible, continuous deviation-from-normative-twin scores (three discrete deviation phenotypes in the HeartSSM cohort) that improve cardiovascular risk stratification beyond ejection fraction, ventricular volumes, myocardial mass, and strain. The strongest effect was seen for incident atrial fibrillation among individuals with preserved ejection fraction (≥50%): incremental C-index Δ C = +0.068 (5-fold cross-validated Δ C = +0.063; likelihood-ratio P = 3.3 × 10 −8 ), with a separate, smaller effect for incident stroke in the same preserved-EF subgroup in the independent MeshHeart cVAE representation (which showed no signal for atrial fibrillation) (Δ C = +0.024, P = 2.6 × 10 −4 ). Both effects were checked against placebo controls in which the deviation scores were replaced by Gaussian noise. To test whether the normative twin generalises beyond UK Biobank’s specific scanning and processing pipeline, we applied the MeshHeart cVAE normative twin, unmodified, to an independent external cohort of healthy volunteers imaged at a different hospital (Gen-Scan/Hammersmith, n = 315): deviation scores in this cohort were of comparable magnitude to the UK Biobank healthy reference (ratio of means = 1.09; Mann–Whitney P = 1.4 × 10 −5 ), indicating that the normative twin captures cross-site-transferable structure rather than a scanner- or pipeline-specific artefact. Our findings suggest that cardiac phenotyping can move beyond predefined measurements toward data-driven dynamic phenotypes that better capture the heterogeneity underlying cardiovascular disease risk, even among individuals whose ejection fraction appears normal.

title: biv-me: Open-source software for generating time-varying biventricular meshes from cine cardiovascular magnetic resonance imaging with multi-cohort validation
abstract: The generation of geometric representations of the heart is essential for personalised approaches to cardiac assessment. Structured biventricular meshes customised to imaging data have demonstrated utility in a number of model-based applications that can provide more sensitive insights into patient health than routine cardiac indices alone. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging is a common starting point for the creation of digital twin geometries, with numerous published methods for mesh reconstruction. However, the majority of these methods are not open-source, are typically developed and validated using data from a single-centre, and lack deployability across heterogeneous scanning protocols and patient groups. We present an open-source, end-to-end pipeline (biv-me), to automatically generate time-varying biventricular meshes from cine CMR DICOM images, and perform external validation against a clinical reference software tool on 1313 CMR imaging studies across five publicly available datasets. We report excellent agreement in left and right ventricular indices and high scan-rescan reproducibility. Mesh generation was rapid, with a mean processing time of 2.5 min, and highly feasible, with 99% of meshes successfully generated to a high standard with median error of <1.5 mm. The biv-me pipeline - including code, models, and documentation - is available at https://github.com/UOA-Heart-Mechanics-Research/biv-me.

title: Transformer-Guided Graph Attention for Direct Cardiac Mesh Reconstruction: A Structural Digital Twin Framework
abstract: Building patient-specific cardiac models sits at the heart of precision cardiology, yet getting those models into clinical use keeps running into the same wall: mesh generation is slow, messy, and frustrating. The standard workflow -- segmenting the image, running Marching Cubes, and then manually cleaning up the result -- is time-consuming, inconsistent across operators, and demands specialist knowledge most clinical teams do not have. We take a fundamentally different approach. Instead of treating segmentation and mesh generation as two separate problems, we train a single end-to-end network that goes directly from a raw 3D medical image to a smooth, simulation-ready cardiac surface mesh. The core is a 3D Swin Transformer encoder-decoder that extracts volumetric features from CT or MRI volumes, paired with a Graph Attention Network (GAT) head that iteratively deforms a template mesh to fit the patient's cardiac boundary. We tested on the MM-WHS 2017 benchmark using both CT and MRI. Segmentation scores were competitive (Dice of 0.84 on CT, 0.83 on MRI), but the primary focus is mesh quality: mean Chamfer distance of 1.8 mm, with 95th-percentile surface distance below 5 mm. Every mesh is produced in a single forward pass -- no Marching Cubes, no smoothing filters, no manual cleanup. We argue that for cardiac digital twin pipelines, geometric fidelity and topological correctness matter more than pixel-level Dice scores. By removing the post-processing bottleneck, this approach makes patient-specific cardiac simulation substantially more accessible for clinical use.

title: Personalized 3D Myocardial Infarct Geometry Reconstruction from Cine MRI for Cardiac Digital Twins
abstract: Accurate 3D geometric characterization of myocardial infarction (MI) is essential for building cardiac digital twins (CDTs) to precisely simulate infarct-related electrophysiology. Late gadolinium enhancement magnetic resonance imaging (LGE MRI) is the clinical reference for locating MI, yet its reliance on contrast agents restricts use in renally impaired patients and limits longitudinal follow-ups. As an alternative, contrast-free cine MRI visualizes abnormal ventricular wall motion, which is highly indicative of the infarcted area. In this study, we propose a novel explicit geometry-motion embedded model to fully automatically reconstruct personalized, simulation-ready 3D MI geometries directly from multi-view cine MRIs. Specifically, we construct a 4D (3D + t) biventricular mesh to explicitly extract and decouple geometry-aware and motion-aware features. We further design a dual-branch module for adaptive geometry-motion fusion to capture spatiotemporal dependencies for mapping infarcted region. Furthermore, we introduce multi-scale supervision utilizing an AHA-17 segment-guided cross-attention mechanism to steer the prediction, ensuring biophysically consistent reconstruction. Experimental results on 225 cine MRIs demonstrated that the proposed 3D MI reconstruction achieved high performance with an average Dice score of 0.678 $\pm$ 0.011. In the downstream in-silico electrophysiological simulation evaluations, the results were highly consistent with the LGE-derived ground truth, highlighting the great potential of the proposed model for contrast-free scar characterization and seamless integration into CDT modeling. The code will be released publicly upon acceptance of the manuscript for publication.

title: UK Biobank: the world’s largest imaging project reaches 100 000 scans
abstract: UK Biobank is a world-leading biomedical resource supporting global research, with more than 24 000 academic and industry researchers from over 60 countries using its data for health-related research. Established two decades ago, baseline assessments were conducted between 2006 and 2010, during which 500 000 volunteers from across the UK attended one of 22 assessment centres for extensive phenotyping, biological sample collection, and consent for linkage to their electronic health records.1 In 2014, UK Biobank launched an ambitious initiative to re-assess at least 100 000 participants from the original cohort through a comprehensive multi-organ imaging study, including cardiac, abdominal, and brain magnetic resonance imaging and repeat measures of baseline assessments.2 The Imaging Project met its recruitment target in July 2025 and is now the largest study of its kind. To date, more than 105 000 UK Biobank participants have taken part, with a mean interval of 12.1 years from baseline and 24.8% acceptance rate. The unprecedented scale of the UK Biobank Imaging Project makes it possible for researchers to study patterns of disease that could not be seen otherwise. While the sheer volume of data posed unique image processing challenges, it propelled major methodological advances in computational image analysis, particularly for the cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) community. Initial labour-intensive manual segmentation of 5065 UK Biobank CMR scans by expert imaging core laboratories in London and Oxford has been used as a reference to create multiple AI-based automated cardiac segmentation pipelines.3 This significantly reduces the time to generate results and can provide more consistent and objective measurements of heart size and function.4 Importantly, AI-based pipelines trained using UK Biobank data are now used clinically in over 90 countries, streamlining clinical reporting. AI-based pipelines have also facilitated image-derived phenotypes (IDPs) being provided alongside the raw imaging data to UK Biobank researchers. The growing scope and granularity of multi-organ IDPs, made available at regular intervals, have democratized access to advanced imaging data, enabling collaborative research that connects subclinical risk factors and disease to population-level cardiovascular outcomes. Beyond conventional CMR-derived measures of cardiac structure and function (e.g. ejection fraction, mass, and volumes), computational mesh models have been developed to characterize the three-dimensional geometry of the left and right ventricles throughout the cardiac cycle.5 These models are available to the research community as IDPs. Anatomical model generation combined with 12-lead ECG data from UK Biobank has advanced the field of cardiac digital twins, which are personalized physics- and physiology-constrained in silico representations that can provide multi-scale insights to biological mechanisms and be useful for screening, prognosis, and treatment planning for cardiovascular diseases.6 The release of genotyping and whole-exome and whole-genome sequencing data for all half a million UK Biobank participants has enabled researchers to conduct numerous genome-wide association studies and to develop strong polygenic risk scores. This research provides insights into genetic components of disease risk, rare diseases, and drug targets when combined with the depth of data collected on UK Biobank participants over two decades.7,8 Further extended assays on the 12 million stored biological samples from UK Biobank participants to complement these genomic data remain a key scientific priority to enhance risk factor characterization, with metabolomic data generated using the NMR-based Nightingale Health panel recently being released for the full cohort. Proteomic data were first made available in 2023 for 54 000 randomly selected participants; subsequent large-scale profiling using the Olink Explore HT platform is now being conducted across the full UK Biobank cohort, together with 100 000 repeat samples obtained up to 15 years after baseline. Burns et al. demonstrated that integrating large-scale omics data with CMR-derived cardiac shape modelling in UK Biobank uncovers previously unknown genetic determinants of cardiac structure linked to cardiometabolic disease risk.5 Researchers have also combined multi-organ MRI data with genetic, metabolomic, and proteomic data to develop seven organ-specific MRI-based ageing clocks, uncovering links to novel drug targets as well as cardiometabolic diseases and all-cause mortality.9 The phenome is inherently dynamic, underscoring the importance of assessing change over time. Launched in 2022, the Repeat Imaging Project aims to re-invite at least 60 000 participants who previously took part in the Imaging Project to be re-scanned by the end of 2028. This will facilitate large-scale longitudinal evaluation of changes in a broad spectrum of IDPs over a 2 to 9-year period, spanning middle to older age. Twenty thousand participants have already attended for repeat imaging, with a mean interval of 6.1 years between imaging visits and 62.2% acceptance rate. This design will permit a better understanding of the genetic and lifestyle determinants underlying trajectories of imaging measures, as well as the identification of early imaging markers associated with subsequent disease risk. A third imaging timepoint is currently being piloted in approximately 3000 participants to assess its potential value for broader implementation. For certain conditions, such as dementia and Parkinson’s disease, health records alone are insufficient to capture heterogeneity and characterize disease subtypes. Brain-scanning processes developed from the UK Biobank Imaging Project have already become part of routine care for patients at memory clinics around the UK and demonstrated their value in improving dementia diagnoses.10 The Brain Health Study has been developed to collect new data, including brain magnetic resonance imaging, from UK Biobank participants who have a neurodegenerative disease diagnosis or related symptoms to improve disease characterization and subtype identification. This will increase power in UK Biobank to detect associations between risk factors and neurodegenerative diseases, and how different risk factors associate with disease subtypes. The Brain Health Study aims to recruit 10 000 participants in the first four years of main phase launch in mid-2026, with 5000 participants per year thereafter. UK Biobank is an unparalleled biomedical resource, integrating large-scale imaging, omics, and health record data, facilitating novel insights into disease aetiology and progression. Its ongoing longitudinal and multi-modal initiatives provide a growing foundation for advancing population health research and informing strategies for disease prediction and intervention. AJL is Deputy Chief Scientist for UK Biobank, RC is Chief Executive and Principal Investigator for UK Biobank, and HT is a Senior Epidemiologist for UK Biobank. UK Biobank receives funding from Wellcome Trust, UK Medical Research Council, British Heart Foundation, and Cancer Research UK.

title: Joint shape/texture representation learning for cardiovascular disease diagnosis from magnetic resonance imaging
venue: European Heart Journal - Imaging Methods and Practice
abstract: Aims: Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) are the leading cause of mortality worldwide. Cardiac image and mesh are two primary modalities to present the shape and structure of the heart and have been demonstrated to be efficient in CVD prediction and diagnosis. However, previous research has been generally focussed on a single modality (image or mesh), and few of them have tried to jointly consider the image and mesh representations of heart. To obtain efficient and explainable biomarkers for CVD prediction and diagnosis, it is needed to jointly consider both representations. Methods and results: We design a novel multi-channel variational auto-encoder, mesh-image variational auto-encoder, to learn joint representation of paired mesh and image. After training, the shape-aware image representation (SAIR) can be learned directly from the raw images and applied for further CVD prediction and diagnosis. We demonstrate our method on data from UK Biobank study and two other datasets via extensive experiments. In acute myocardial infarction prediction, SAIR achieves 81.43% accuracy, significantly higher than traditional biomarkers like metadata and clinical indices (left ventricle and right ventricle clinical indices of cardiac function like chamber volume, mass, and ejection fraction). Conclusion: Our mesh-image variational auto-encoder provides a novel approach for 3D cardiac mesh reconstruction from images. The extraction of SAIR is fast and without need of segmentation masks, and its focussing can be visualized in the corresponding cardiac meshes. SAIR archives better performance than traditional biomarkers and can be applied as an efficient supplement to them, which is of significant potential in CVD analysis.

title: RVDeformer: Sparse Point Cloud-Guided Right Ventricle 3-D Reconstruction in Echocardiograms
abstract: 3D reconstruction of the Right Ventricle (RV) from echocardiograms is crucial for accurate clinical evaluation of cardiac function. However, existing methods are hindered by the complex RV anatomy and the incomplete spatial information inherent in 2D multi-view echocardiograms. Therefore, we propose RVDeformer, a sparse point cloud-guided framework for RV 3D reconstruction. RVDeformer reformulates the reconstruction task as a mesh deformation problem, learning to deform a predefined template mesh to match the target structure under the guidance of the sparse anatomical point cloud. Specifically, this framework employs the end-to-end neural network RVDeformNet to extract the features of the point cloud and template mesh for predicting the displacement of each mesh vertex. We design a point cloud-mesh fusion module that can effectively align and fuse features from the two modalities to enhance the representation ability of the model. We conduct extensive validation on a clinical dataset of 1,278 cases and demonstrate that RVDeformer outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving a Chamfer Distance (CD) of $2.24\pm 0.55$ mm, an F1-score of $0.74\pm 0.10$ at the 3 mm threshold, and a Volumetric Similarity (VS) of $91.53\pm 2.28$ %, with significant potential for clinical applications. The code is available at https://github.com/onezh95/RVDeformer.

title: cMeta-INR: cohort-informed meta-learning-based implicit neural representation for deformable registration-driven real-time volumetric MRI estimation
abstract: Abstract Objective. Rapid and accurate reconstruction of high-quality three-dimensional magnetic resonance (MR) images from undersampled k -space data with variable sampling patterns remains a challenge due to limited available information and the need to preserve rich anatomical details. Deformable image registration provides a promising solution by warping a fully-sampled reference image to align with undersampled data acquired on-board (from an image-guided treatment delivery platform like MR-LINACs). In this study, we proposed a novel registration framework—cohort-informed meta-learning (cMeta)—to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of implicit neural representations (INR) for limited k -space data-driven patient-specific deformable image registration. Approach. cMeta-INR incorporated token-aware modulation and population-level deformation priors to guide an INR template-based meta-learning process. By encoding contextual information and leveraging cohort-informed priors, the resulting meta-learning framework enabled the INR to rapidly adapt to new registration cases with undersampled k -space data. Specifically, for the meta learning, a modulation module with token-awareness was introduced to modulate the INR template, and a pre-trained population-based registration network (KS-RegNet) was employed to generate coarse, reference deformation vector fields and latent embeddings for computing the deformation discrepancy loss and embedding similarity loss. During test-time adaptation, the INR, initialized from the meta-learned template, was efficiently fine-tuned to new k -space data with minimal iterations. Main results. Experiments were conducted on 14 abdominal and 11 cardiac 4D magnetic resonance imagings (MRIs) with 5–13 spokes. cMeta-INR outperformed state-of-the-art methods, achieving the best average (± s.d.) Dice similarity coefficients (0.778 ± 0.056 for abdominal and 0.894 ± 0.076 for cardiac data), and center-of-mass errors (3.04 ± 1.48 mm and 1.32 ± 1.02 mm, respectively), while enabling rapid test-time adaptation of only ∼35 s on an NVIDIA H100 GPU. Significance. The proposed cohort-informed meta-learning framework effectively enhanced the adaptation capabilities of INRs to individual patients under highly undersampled k -space scenarios, demonstrating strong potential for fast and accurate patient-specific deformable registration.

title: End-to-End 4D Heart Mesh Recovery Across Full-Stack and Sparse Cardiac MRI
abstract: Reconstructing cardiac motion from CMR sequences is critical for diagnosis, prognosis, and intervention. Existing methods rely on complete CMR stacks to infer full heart motion, limiting their applicability during intervention when only sparse observations are available. We present TetHeart, the first end-to-end framework for unified 4D heart mesh recovery from both offline full-stack and intra-procedural sparse-slice observations. Our method leverages deformable tetrahedra to capture shape and motion in a coherent space shared across cardiac structures. Before a procedure, it initializes detailed, patient-specific heart meshes from high-quality full stacks, which can then be updated using whatever slices can be obtained in real-time, down to a single one during the procedure. TetHeart incorporates several key innovations: (i) an attentive slice-adaptive 2D-3D feature assembly mechanism that integrates information from arbitrary numbers of slices at any position; (ii) a distillation strategy to ensure accurate reconstruction under extreme sparsity; and (iii) a weakly supervised motion learning scheme requiring annotations only at keyframes, such as the end-diastolic and end-systolic phases. Trained and validated on three large public datasets and evaluated zero-shot on additional private interventional and public datasets without retraining, TetHeart achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and strong generalization in both pre- and intra-procedural settings. Code and dataset is available at https://github.com/Scalsol/TetHeart.

title: Personalized 4D Whole-Heart Mesh Reconstruction from Cine MRI via Multi-Scale Temporal Modeling and Differentiable Contour Rendering
abstract: Accurate 4D whole-heart mesh reconstruction from sparse cine MRI is critical for creating cardiac digital twins, but remains challenging due to limited 2D slice coverage and the complex coupling between cardiac shape and motion. Existing methods often rely on intermediate contour fitting and typically reconstruct static, single-phase, or partial cardiac geometries, limiting their ability to capture full-chamber dynamics. We propose a novel end-to-end framework for reconstructing temporally resolved whole-heart meshes from multi-view 2D cine MRI sequences by learning an image-to-mesh mapping. The framework incorporates a differentiable contour renderer inspired by the Beer-Lambert attenuation principle, enabling anatomy-aware supervision of 3D+t mesh deformation through contour-based projection losses. To improve temporal consistency across the cardiac cycle, we further introduce a multi-scale temporal modeling module that integrates global cycle-level dynamics with local inter-frame coherence to generate smooth and physiologically plausible mesh trajectories. The proposed method achieved a whole-heart mean absolute error of 1.68 $\pm$ 0.31 mm and a motion jitter of 0.77 $\pm$ 0.17 $\mathrm{mm}/\mathrm{frame}^{3}$, outperforming existing methods with lower reconstruction error and substantially improved motion smoothness. It also improved 2D contour alignment across multiple cine MRI views and supported downstream proof-of-concept electrophysiological simulation. The code will be released publicly upon acceptance of the manuscript for publication.

title: The ESC President’s Award 2025: Béla Merkely
abstract: All correspondence relating to this paper should be sent to: [email protected] Béla Merkely is a Hungarian cardiologist with an international reputation. He has been associated with Semmelweis University in Budapest since his days as an undergraduate and has served as Rector since 2018. He was the first Hungarian specialist to receive advanced certification in clinical cardiac electrophysiology from the European Heart Rhythm Association (EHRA). He received the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) President’s Award in 2025, honouring his significant contributions to leadership and to advancing global heart health. Prof. Merkely’s career was shaped by a succession of pioneering physicians and health experts whose example and guidance inspired his lifelong commitment to cardiovascular medicine and academic leadership. He says, ‘My great-great-uncle, József Fodor—the founder of public health in Hungary and former Rector of the University of Science in Budapest, Semmelweis University’s predecessor—was a family role model and early inspiration for me. Equally influential was my grandfather, Dr Keresztély Merkel, an internist who taught me a principle that still guides me: to give patients not only our full attention, but also our time and presence. Another key influence on my medical career and passion for hands-on practice was my father-in-law, Dr Géza Tasnádi, a renowned paediatric vascular surgeon, whom I met in secondary school’. Prof. Merkely identifies three mentors who introduced him to distinct and complementary branches of medicine, playing a decisive role in shaping his career. During his university years, Prof. József Tenczer guided him towards cardiology, instilling in him a classical internal medicine-cardiology perspective and clinical rigour. Together with Dr László Littmann, Tenczer also published in Circulation. Dr Sándor Juhász-Nagy, head of experimental cardiology, shaped his scientific mindset and approach to structured research. A further formative influence was Dr Zoltán Szabó, the pioneering heart surgeon who performed Hungary’s first heart transplant, from whom Prof. Merkely learned clinical innovation, organization, and leadership, grounded in the belief that progress depends on continuous development. These mentors shaped an integrated approach in which patient-centric care, research, and institution-building are mutually reinforcing. Prof. Merkely is known for his innovative role in transforming cardiac care in Hungary. In 1993, after returning from a 2-year fellowship in Heidelberg, Germany, he introduced implantable cardioverter defibrillator therapy for the prevention of sudden cardiac death and cardiac resynchronization therapy for heart failure. He also helped establish 24/7 acute myocardial infarction care—first in the Budapest area and later nationwide—contributing to a marked reduction in both early and late mortality. In 2011, he assumed leadership of the country’s heart transplant programme, building it into the second largest within the Eurotransplant network. Under his leadership, the centre also strengthened translational research through an established animal model laboratory that now provides comprehensive non-invasive and invasive diagnostics for adult cardiovascular interventional and surgical care. He has been Director of the Semmelweis University Department of Cardiology since 2007. Since 2012, he has served as Director of the Városmajor Heart and Vascular Centre, following the merger of separate units into a single comprehensive centre that includes cardiology and cardiovascular surgery (Figure 1). Prof. Béla Merkely MD, PhD, DSc, Director of the Semmelweis University Department of Cardiology and Director of the Városmajor Heart and Vascular Centre. (L-R) ESC President Thomas F. Lüscher presents Prof. Béla Merkely with the President's Award at ESC Congress 2025 Innovation comes with challenges and introduction of state-of-the-art interventional procedures, device-based arrhythmia therapies, and later transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) into a traditionally conservative system—which required organizational and cultural change grounded in teamwork. July 2012 saw the foundation of Semmelweis University’s Városmajor Heart and Vascular Centre, uniting cardiology, cardiac and vascular surgery with cardiovascular imaging to create Hungary’s largest tertiary cardiovascular centre. Prof. Merkely says: ‘The success of this lay in multidisciplinary collaboration, international experience—particularly my years in Heidelberg—and the deliberate integration of clinical care, research, and education through continuous development’. He is proud of Semmelweis University’s sustained high ranking amongst the world’s Top 50 cardiovascular medical institutions—currently listed 35th by U.S. News & World Report. With the opening of a new seven-storey wing, the centre is positioned to function as a true European supercentre and the continent’s largest heart transplant facility, delivering care on a par with leading European and North American centres. Inspired by his background in sports, Prof. Merkely explains how he balances leadership with clinical and scientific work: ‘From my early years in swimming and water polo, I learned that achieving great results demands clear goals, perseverance, and strength. Medicine requires a 24/7 commitment. As a doctor, clinic director, and Rector of Semmelweis University, I view management not as separate from clinical work but as its extension. I have always stayed close to patient care, believing that leadership must be grounded in experience. Patient care energizes me and fuels my drive. I focus on one task at a time and maintain balance through delegation, teamwork, and careful time management’. He considers himself and his generation fortunate to have witnessed transformative technological advances in cardiology early in their careers. Comparing his medical training to current practice, he likens the shift to moving from a stone axe to a mechanized tower crane. He says: ‘My generation evolved alongside rapid technological advances, especially the explosive growth of interventional cardiology, particularly catheter and device-based treatments for arrhythmias and structural heart disease. Minimally invasive procedures have become vital for many elderly patients, and their use at our clinic has grown dramatically over the past decade. I’ve always striven to bring cutting-edge technology to Hungary at an international standard. Adopting new technology goes hand-in-hand with education, research, and training the next generation because I believe true innovation is only sustainable when rooted in knowledge’. He has the following advice for the next generation of cardiologists seeking to combine clinical excellence with research to fuel impact: ‘Don’t choose between clinical work, research, and education—learn to do all three simultaneously. Clinical excellence builds credibility, research drives progress, and education creates meaningful social impact. Finding good mentors—those who, as Goethe said, give you roots and wings—is essential for continuous growth. International experience and collaboration are vital; great results often come from cross-border cooperation. Above all, medicine is about human relationships. Despite advancing technology, the core remains the same: people entrust us with their greatest asset, their health, and we must serve with faith, humility, and responsibility, always putting patients first.’ As my grandfather taught me, ‘When seeing a patient, be fully prepared and give them your complete attention’. All authors declare no disclosure of interest for this contribution.

title: Leaders in Cardiology: Rebecca Hahn
abstract: All correspondence relating to this paper should be sent to: [email protected] Rebecca T. Hahn is an imaging specialist based in New York, USA. Her clinical and research work focuses on echocardiography and structural heart disease imaging, especially interventional imaging. She is the Director of Interventional Echocardiography at the New York Presbyterian/Columbia Campus Structural and Valve Center and serves as Chief Scientific Officer of the Echo Core Lab at the Cardiovascular Research Foundation in New York (Figure 1). Rebecca T. Hahn, MD, Professor of Medicine at Columbia University College of Physicians and Surgeons Prof. Hahn studied at Washington University School of Medicine in St Louis, MO, followed by a residency in internal medicine, a cardiology fellowship, and a research fellowship at New York-Presbyterian Hospital/Weill Cornell Medical Center in New York. She set out to become a biologist intending to pursue a career in basic science but was drawn to internal medicine by a strong desire to work directly with patients and to have a tangible impact on their lives. Cardiology emerged as a natural focus, combining clinical purpose with the intellectual appeal of cardiovascular physiology, particularly the mechanics of cardiac circulation. Her subsequent specialization in echocardiography was shaped both by this physiological interest and by a long-standing engagement with the visual arts, especially the challenge of translating complex 3D structures into clear 2D representations. As echocardiographic technology advanced, it increasingly intersected with the rapidly evolving field of structural heart disease interventions. Prof. Hahn says, ‘In 2007, when the first commercially available 3D transoesophageal probe became available, transcatheter therapies such as mitral transcatheter edge-to-edge repair and transcatheter aortic valve replacement were just taking off. This truly marked the beginning of a new imaging subspecialty, which my mentor Martin Leon appropriately named interventional echocardiography.’ Interventional echocardiography now plays a crucial role in guiding minimally invasive, catheter-based heart valve procedures. Prof. Hahn’s expertise spans the entire procedural timeline—from pre-procedural planning to real-time imaging support during interventions and post-procedural assessment. Her work focuses primarily on imaging techniques that support transcatheter structural heart interventions such as transcatheter aortic valve replacement, as well as mitral and tricuspid valve repair and replacement, among other device-based therapies. These procedures have transformed the landscape for patients with complex structural heart disease, providing less invasive alternatives to traditional open-heart surgery and ensuring the safety and success of interventions through precise, real-time imaging guidance. Beyond her clinical contributions, Prof. Hahn helps shape the future of the field by leading training programmes and defining competency standards for interventional echocardiographers. She is also at the forefront of advancing 3D and multimodality imaging techniques, which are essential for navigating the complexities of structural heart disease. As an authority in her field, she delivered the René Laennec Lecture in Clinical Cardiology at the European Society of Cardiology Congress 2025. Her lecture, ‘Transcatheter treatment of structural heart disease and the emergence of interventional imaging’, underscores the vital role of imaging in the evolution of catheter-based heart valve therapies and highlights her contributions to a rapidly advancing subspecialty that continues to redefine cardiology. In 2023, she received the Physician Lifetime Achievement Award from the American Society of Echocardiography (ASE) for her contributions in defining interventional echocardiography. She has served on the Board of Directors for the ASE and is currently a member of the American College of Cardiology Competency Management Committee and Scientific Sessions Planning Committee. She has published over 500 articles and 10 book chapters on Echocardiography and Valvular Heart Disease and has been on the writing committees for four ASE recommendations/guidelines and four Academic Research Consortium documents. She was the National PI for the SCOUT Trial (Trialign Annuloplasty Device) and is the National Co-PI for the Triscend Pivotal Trial (EVOQUE Transcatheter Tricuspid Valve Replacement device). She played a leading role in helping refine the value-based measurement of work for interventional echocardiographers, specifically in the early days of transcatheter valve therapies when there was no established reimbursement system that fairly accounted for the time and importance of the imaging specialist’s role in these complex procedures. She says ‘The main initial challenge in interventional echocardiography was creating an appropriate value-based measure of work. In the early days of transcatheter valve therapies, there was no reimbursement algorithm which could capture the time and value of the imager within a procedure for which they played an integral role. This is gradually changing as the imager’s role on the heart team and within the procedure has been solidified and supported by professional societies.’ There is more to come from such a rapidly evolving area; she suggests, ‘Echocardiography is far from a mature modality and continues to advance. During my career to date, the most important development has been 3D imaging which revolutionized the way we are able to visualize cardiac structures. But we have recently been involved in an advanced, artificial intelligence-based procedural imaging tool that could facilitate communication between the interventionalist and imager, contribute to procedural efficiency and improve device efficacy. This new programme has just received the “CE” mark of regulatory compliance in Europe and will likely change the way we perform our structural interventions and expand accessibility to sites with less experience or expertise.’ Her advice to early career hopefuls is to find a specialty or sub-specialty that continuously inspires and engages them, and then with persistence and adequate guidance, they will be able to develop the skills and aptitude to advance. Having a mentor who can motivate you and promote individual growth is essential. She says, ‘I frankly was in the right place at the right time, with the right set of technical skills and experience. I had the right mentor in Marty Leon and the right heart team at Columbia University.’ Achievement however does not come without spending a lot of time and effort in one’s chosen role, and Prof. Hahn suggests that work–life balance can be challenging to achieve or to offer advice about. She says, ‘What I did have early in my career, was an extremely supportive spouse and family. Without their encouragement and tolerance, I would not have been able to have the career I have now.’ Nothing to declare.

title: Expert guidance: Marco Metra named as inaugural editor in chief of the Journal of Valvular and Structural Heart Disease ( EHJ-VSHD )
abstract: All correspondence relating to this paper should be sent to: [email protected] As the new editor in chief (EiC) of the European Heart Journal—Valvular and Structural Heart Disease (EHJ-VSHD), Marco Metra is uniquely placed to advance the journal’s mission. Prof. Metra brings decades of clinical research and experience to the task of disseminating cutting-edge knowledge and science. He is currently the director of the Institute of Cardiology at the Civil Hospital and University of Brescia, Italy, and takes up a senior clinical academic role at the Vita-Salute University, San Raffaele Hospital in Milan, Italy, as of October 2025 (Figure 1). Prof. Marco Metra, MD, new editor in chief of the Journal of Valvular and Structural Heart Disease (EHJ-VSHD) The new journal—launched to address a growing trend in cardiology—was officially unveiled in Madrid, Spain, at the 2025 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) Congress. The impetus for the new publication, Prof. Metra says, came from his previous experience as EiC of the European Journal of Heart Failure (EJHF) between 2015 and 2023. ‘During those years, I noticed a rise in submissions related to valvular and structural heart disease. The focus of many of these articles was not necessarily directly related to heart failure, but to its cause, diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment. I became convinced that these were major areas of interest and it was time to give them their own journal.’ Prof. Metra’s main scientific focus has always been on heart failure which he first encountered when investigating cardiopulmonary exercise testing, followed by beta-blocker therapy and then acute heart failure. He has participated in and coordinated single- and multicentre trials of beta-blocker therapies, as well as the treatment of acute heart failure. More recently, he realized that a major change in the epidemiology of heart failure had taken place. ‘While heart failure was once primarily caused by coronary artery disease and heart attacks, now with improved acute coronary care and an ageing population, we have a situation that has made valvular heart disease a major contributor to heart failure,’ he says. He also notes that transcatheter treatment of valvular heart disease and progress in diagnosis and medical therapy of cardiomyopathies have opened up new indications for patients previously left with no treatment options. The changing epidemiology of heart failure also reflects improved diagnostics that now identify more cardiomyopathy patients, particularly those with cardiac amyloidosis. As major diagnostic and therapeutic advances are now available for both amyloidosis and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, he says that the field needs to evolve with a focus on cardiovascular therapy moving towards personalised medicine. Prof. Metra describes his time as EiC of the EJHF as among the most satisfying and rewarding periods of his academic career. During this time, the journal became ranked among the top publications for cardiovascular disease. His tenure coincided with the COVID-19 pandemic—a testing time for scientific journals that had to respond with accuracy and clarity to an unprecedented global challenge. This critical event, he says, required leadership and scientific excellence such as that demonstrated by the EJHF, which published early authoritative papers on heart failure and hospitalisations that occurred during the pandemic. He believes this was a major achievement and reflects the duty of an EiC to identify major areas of interest, publish articles that become the reference for others, and anticipate changes ahead of everyone else. The time is now right for a new journal to tackle valvular and structural heart disease, Prof. Metra feels. ‘Our journal will remain focused on these diseases, including their epidemiology, pathophysiology, diagnosis and therapy, rather than on technical aspects and/or their late manifestations, such as arrhythmias or heart failure. Maybe in the near future we will be able to prevent the development of valvular heart disease with specific medications and our journal may be among the first to publish these data. We aim not only to look beyond, but also prior to, the indications and effects of interventional therapies, a hugely progressing field in cardiology. When you have a therapy and something to propose to the patient, there is always an increase in interest about the condition.’ The new journal will focus on three main areas: valvular heart disease, including aortic, mitral, and tricuspid valves; adult congenital heart disease; and remaining structural heart diseases, including amyloid cardiomyopathy, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and conditions such as patent foramen ovale, or left atrial auricular thrombosis. Some of these conditions, such as grown-up congenital heart disease, have become major epidemiological problems, but are nevertheless underrepresented in the current literature. He believes that the rise of new diagnostic tools and new treatment options—either medical therapy or transcatheter treatment—has prompted an impressive rise in translational and clinical research with lots of data deserving publication. As the author of over 1200 papers, Prof. Metra is well qualified to identify a good manuscript. ‘In general, journals are still ranked by citations of their articles,’ he says. ‘This is measured as their Impact Factor (IF) or similar, and I agree that the IF value of a scientific article can be related to the number of times it is cited.’ As EiC, he enjoys being able to predict the citation potential of an article, but observes there are exceptions to IF metrics. ‘For instance, an article may be so far ahead of its time that it may be more widely cited 5–10 years later.’ Other ways of assessing impact such as the Altmetric Attention Score—alternative metrics that measure the impact of papers on social media, news outlets, and policy are also vital and possibly more important than the scientific impact alone, he says. ‘Additionally, we have introduced so-called “how to” papers to help clinicians handle challenging medical problems. With these articles, the number of downloads may be a more accurate measurement of their impact.’ Prof. Metra believes that topic interest and the relative novelty of the article—coupled with robust methodology and results that support the conclusions—is what matters when ranking the value of a submitted article and taking a decision on its publication. The role of EiC, he says, provides unique opportunities to shape future directions for research and to decide what is important—and what is not—from submitted articles. ‘It gives you the opportunity to build an editorial board, gather a high-ranking scientific community able to discuss the newest advances in research and take the best decisions. Scientific journals are the essence of scientific research, and the editorial board becomes the place where friendship, mutual trust, and authority allow the journal to grow and the possibility to offer our patients better options for their health and well-being.’ All authors declare no disclosure of interest for this contribution.

title: Leaders in cardiology: Renate Schnabel
abstract: All correspondence relating to this paper should be sent to: [email protected] Renate B. Schnabel, MD, MSc, is an accomplished interventional cardiologist and Professor of Cardiology at the University Heart and Vascular Center in Hamburg, Germany. Her dedication to advancing science and patient care has made her a leader in the field and a sought-after expert speaker. She delivered the Geoffrey Rose Lecture in Population Sciences at the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) 2023 Congress (Figure 1). Renate B. Schnabel, MD, MSc Prof. Schnabel graduated from the medical school of Johannes Gutenberg University, Mainz, in Germany, and later undertook a research fellowship at the Framingham Heart Study at Boston University in the USA, where she received her master’s degree. Her expertise encompasses both epidemiological and clinical trials, and her research interests are in coronary artery disease/acute coronary syndrome, atrial fibrillation, risk assessment, and prevention. She is funded by the German Research Foundation, the Federal Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF), and the European Research Council (ERC). Prof. Schnabel’s motivation to study medicine grew from a desire to help sick people. Her interest in the cardiovascular system goes back to her early years as a medical student. She says, ‘I was fascinated by the mechanics and fine-tuned action of the cardiovascular system very early on, so, cardiology was the sub speciality of choice. Interventional cardiology appeared to be a rapidly evolving discipline with dramatic therapeutic results that offered a chance to make a huge difference to patient outcomes’. This early interest and curiosity took her to the USA, where she investigated epidemiology and prevention at the Framingham Heart Study in Boston. It was a pivotal experience: ‘I learned that the majority of cardiovascular diseases in the population could be prevented by small changes in lifestyle and that the first contact with clinicians should not necessarily be in the cath lab’. Armed with this understanding, after 2 years in Boston, she returned to Germany, where she established her own research group. This marked the achievement of a personal goal—serving science and treating patients. Prof. Schnabel enjoys the role of the physician–scientist with its ‘three pillars’ comprised of patient care, research, and teaching. ‘This is such a multi-faceted job that it never gets boring. You encounter new situations every day in the clinic and with students and fellows who ask questions about areas you have never thought about. This fires your curiosity and drives your motivation’. She emphasizes the pivotal role mentors and sponsors played in shaping her career trajectory and highlights Emelia J. Benjamin of Boston University and her current head of department, Stefan Blankenberg, for their guidance and encouragement. She is also grateful for her supportive family, who understand the demands of a busy clinical academic career. Although Prof. Schnabel characterizes her professional progress as ‘smooth’, she acknowledges the challenges she faced, particularly as a woman in the male-dominated field of interventional cardiology in Germany. Despite encountering disparities, she believes the landscape has changed since then, especially in research circles. She values the ESC environment, where innovative ideas are objectively discussed on a level playing field, and individuals are valued irrespective of gender or ethnicity. Cardiology, she says, offers an unparalleled sense of fulfilment from the impact on patient outcomes to the exhilaration of advancing scientific frontiers. Aspiring cardiologists should cultivate a deep-rooted interest, seek diverse experiences, and, above all, find mentors who will champion their growth. ‘If you want to succeed, you need to be fascinated by what you are doing, and you need to like it. And beyond that, sound training and background knowledge is the basis for a career. It also helps to have a pioneering spirit and the ability to think out-of-the-box’. Her advice to anyone seeking a career in interventional cardiology is to simply make a start. She says, ‘If you’re truly interested in cardiology, the future is bright. I don’t think you can take a wrong step because it’s very broad-based and is such a fast-advancing field that you’ll find your place. Try to get experience in diverse areas of modern cardiology, from prevention to imaging, to coronary structural procedures, and then later on, it will be easier to find a sub-speciality’. As a cardiologist whose career now spans several decades, she notes how the field is ever-evolving. ‘Cardiology has been able to reinvent cardiovascular medicine again and again through blockbuster interventions, new drugs, devices, and new treatment strategies and now digitalization will significantly advance prevention and treatment making maximum use of big data resources’. Machine learning or artificial intelligence (AI) will advance remote monitoring and treatment, with patients taking more personal responsibility for their health in response to growing demands on the health care system. All of which future cardiologists will need to weigh up and implement into clinical practice. Her own work reflects her long-standing experience in coronary and structural interventions, and she has pushed to advance the field of risk prediction, prevention, and screening. In epidemiology, she has demonstrated and raised stakeholder awareness of the huge burden of arrhythmias and atrial fibrillation at the population level. In genetics, multi-omics, and multi-scale imaging approaches, her team endeavour to understand mechanisms of disease for primary and secondary prevention. Prof. Schnabel’s overarching goal remains to leverage technology and expertise for the betterment of patient care. The AFFECT-EU project for atrial fibrillation, which focuses on digitalization and screening, is an example of this. She says, ‘We are trying to understand what the best screening strategy is, how to use digital devices best, and which type of devices to use. We are looking at what type and intensity of monitoring we should use in order to identify AF that needs treatment in terms of anticoagulation to prevent strokes and also in terms of heart failure or dementia’. This international project involves 26 partners, many beyond Europe, and will deliver an understanding of disease mechanisms, risk stratification, and earlier disease detection in order to reduce the burden of cardiovascular diseases. Keeping yourself updated on developments in the field is time consuming but essential, and she advises emerging professionals to form their own networks and attend organized cardiology meetings such as those of the ESC, as well as those of the main subspecialities. National cardiac societies are a useful source of information; emerging knowledge, good journals, and dedicated resources play a part; and the opportunity to attend in-person events and engage directly with the researcher and other colleagues is an invaluable way to stay up to date. For those thinking about entering the field, she has the following advice: ‘The future of cardiology is bright, and for those truly interested, the opportunities are endless’. All authors declare no disclosure of interest for this contribution.

title: Personalized Heart Digital Twins Detect Substrate Abnormalities in Scar-Dependent Ventricular Tachycardia
abstract: BACKGROUND: Current outcomes from catheter ablation for scar-dependent ventricular tachycardia (VT) are limited by high recurrence rates and long procedure durations. Personalized heart digital twin technology presents a noninvasive method of predicting critical substrate in VT, and its integration into clinical VT ablation offers a promising solution. The accuracy of the predictions of digital twins to detect invasive substrate abnormalities is unknown. We present the first prospective analysis of digital twin technology in predicting critical substrate abnormalities in VT. METHODS: Heart digital twin models were created from 18 patients with scar-dependent VT undergoing catheter ablation. Contrast-enhanced cardiac magnetic resonance images were used to reconstruct finite-element meshes, onto which regional electrophysiological properties were applied. Rapid-pacing protocols were used to induce VTs and to define the VT circuits. Predicted optimum ablation sites to terminate all VTs in the models were identified. Invasive substrate mapping was performed, and the digital twins were merged with the electroanatomical map. Electrogram abnormalities and regions of conduction slowing were compared between digital twin-predicted sites and nonpredicted areas. RESULTS: <0.001). Digital twins correctly identified 21 of 26 (80.8%) deceleration zones seen on isochronal late activation mapping. CONCLUSIONS: Digital twin-predicted sites display a higher prevalence of abnormal and prolonged electrograms compared with nonpredicted sites and accurately identify regions of conduction slowing. Digital twin technology may help improve substrate-based VT ablation. REGISTRATION: URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov; Unique identifier: NCT04632394.

title: GHOST-CAT: An Efficient and Practical Network for Mesh Generation from 3D Echocardiography
abstract: Recent advances in deep learning have significantly accelerated cardiac imaging workflows, from segmentation to the generation of meshes for computational modelling. Nevertheless, analysis of 3D echocardiograms presents unique challenges due to their low contrast-to-noise ratio, conical field of view, and susceptibility to acoustic shadowing. Here, we present an efficient and practical network tailored for 3D echocardiograms. Our method consists of a two-stage network that combines convolutional neural networks, graph convolutional networks, and transformers, to create accurate time-varying 3D meshes of the left ventricle that are topologically consistent and temporally coherent throughout the cardiac cycle. Our model achieved superior mesh reconstruction accuracy compared to current state-of-the-art methods on a held-out test dataset of 100 3D echo images, with a Dice coefficient of 0.87 +/- 0.05 (cavity) and 0.75 +/- 0.07 (myocardium), and mean +/- SD surface distances of 3.3 +/- 0.6 mm (endocardium) and 3.5 +/- 0.5 mm (epicardium), against reference segmentations derived from cardiac magnetic resonance imaging. The reconstructed mesh enables automated calculation of routine clinical indices, such as volume, mass, and strain, and enables advanced applications with biophysical digital twins. Source code is openly shared at https://github.com/EdwardFerdian/ghost-cat.

title: The Mathematics of the Heart: Taming Chaos in Atrial Fibrillation
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Discover the Hidden Math Behind a Beating Heart Hey there, if you've ever wondered why hearts go haywire in atrial fibrillation (AF), this book breaks it down like a friendly chat over coffee. It starts with the basics: the heart as a biological oscillator gone chaotic. We dive into the monodomain equation that models electrical waves in cardiac tissue. Anisotropy in fiber directions stabilizes those tricky scroll waves. Ionic currents like sodium and potassium drive the nonlinear reactions. Patient-specific meshes from MRI scans bring virtual atria to life. Fractional diffusion handles fibrotic delays better than standard models. Inverse problems map conductivity to spot slow zones. Ablation tweaks boundaries to shrink reentry areas. Restitution curves explain why fast rates lead to wavebreaks. Slopes over 1 trigger alternans and rotors. Dynamic pacing builds slope maps in the lab. Drugs flatten curves to prevent chaos. Phase singularities define rotor cores with topological charge. Hilbert transforms extract phases from signals. Filaments in 3D twist through walls. Eikonal equations approximate wavefront speeds with curvature effects. Fast marching methods simulate activations quickly. Entropy quantifies signal disorder in complex electrograms. High entropy flags rotor pivots. Frequency hierarchies reveal dominant drivers via Fourier analysis. Gradients show mother rotors overdriving tissue. Drift equations predict rotor movement toward scars. Percolation theory explains fibrosis thresholds for zig-zag conduction. Fractal dimensions measure scar roughness for anchoring risks. Graph theory finds minimum cuts to break circuits. Hopf bifurcations model triggers like early afterdepolarizations. Bioheat equations govern ablation heating. Bayesian inference guides decisions under uncertainty. Optimization minimizes ablation costs. Digital twins integrate multi-physics for personalized sims. What sets this book apart is its laser focus on math as the cure, not just a tool—other books skim the surface with biology or procedures, but here we connect equations directly to clinical wins, like using topology to pinpoint rotors or percolation to homogenize scars. No fluff; it's a roadmap from chaos theory to bedside, filling gaps in fragmented texts by weaving non-linear dynamics, simulations, and real-world apps into one cohesive story. You'll get why empirical ablations fail and how computational engineering triumphs, with fresh insights from recent models that outdated books miss. This book is independently produced under nominative fair use. The author Azhar ul Haque Sario has no affiliation with any board or entity mentioned.

title: Abstract 4367687: Development of Personalized Myocardial Surface Mesh Models with LGE Scar Integration: a Pipeline for Machine Learning and Digital Twins
abstract: Introduction: Advances in cardiac imaging offer new insights into the electrophysiologic correlates of myocardial fibrosis and scarring. Applications taking advantage of cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging are gaining traction, such as ventricular arrhythmia ablation guided by a substrate-based approach. However, a robust methodology to directly apply substrate level information from CMR imaging in conjunction with the planning and execution of electrophysiology studies is needed. This work addresses the development of 3D surface mesh models representing myocardial surfaces that integrate late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) scar from CMR to facilitate downstream risk stratification, pre-procedural planning, and intra-procedural navigation.
