title: Encoding Culture, Embodying Identity: A Study of Somatic Proverbs
abstract: This article presents a cross-cultural investigation into somatic paroemias (proverbs and idioms structured by bodily imagery) positioning them as fundamental linguistic expressions that encapsulate a culture’s embodied memory and actively shape conceptions of national identity. By integrating an analytical methodology that couples corpus linguistics with conceptual metaphor theory, the study delineates the implicit, body-based cognitive schemas structuring proverbial language across Russian, English, and Japanese. The methodology synthesizes quantitative pattern identification from corpus data with qualitative conceptual analysis, further enriched by insights from gesture ethnography and phenomenological theory to establish the lived, experiential grounding of these linguistic forms. Through this triangulated approach, the research identifies three distinct cultural templates: the Russian logic of vertical ascent and descent frequently linked to the SOUL; the Anglo-American model of internal containment, centred on the HEART and GUT; and the Japanese principle of abdominal centrality HARA and fluid integration. The findings demonstrate how these proverbial patterns function not merely as figurative speech but as cognitive repositories of sedimented, “frozen” lived experience, preserving historical bodily dispositions in transmissible form. Consequently, the study argues that this proverbial layer constitutes a crucial mechanism for the tacit, communal transmission of corporeal identity, serving as a vital bridge between universal human physicality and culturally specific meaning systems. Engaging analytically with this embodied dimension of language thus offers a profound pathway for deepening our understanding of how collective identity is intuitively formed, mnemonically sustained, and phenomenologically differentiated across cultures.

title: Handbook of Communication in Anaesthesia, Pain Management, and Intensive Care
abstract: Abstract Learning more about communication is an effective strategy for improving patient safety, making teams work, and resolving complaints. Perhaps most importantly, good communication skills allow the development of expertise and professionalism in all interactions whether with patients, colleagues, trainees, or even administrators! Communication at its heart, is the means of expressing both to ourselves and others, how we perceive and influence the world around us. It is a tool for exchanging information and meaning, but also a way to connect with others. The many human dimensions of communication—the practical, the subliminal, its ability to soothe and to injure, to inform, to entertain, to terrify—are what makes this topic so challenging. Communication skills are integral to every aspect of anaesthetic care, including procedural skills. An important concept running throughout the book is that most communication is being processed subconsciously. Such implicit processes affect how language brings about changes in perception, mood, and behaviour. These intuitive skills can be taught in an explicit, structured, and evidence-based fashion resulting in therapeutic effects that elicit trust, rapport, patient engagement, and even anaesthesia. In contrast, awareness of nocebo effects of words that result in anxiety, pain, PONV, and distress can be alleviated by modifying communication. The ‘LAURS’ and ‘GREAT’ templates provide learnable structures to enhance communication when the usual anaesthetic strategies aren’t working (e.g. patients with needle phobia and chronic pain). Such concepts can also be applied to facilitate communicating with surgeons, theatre nurses, and other colleagues, with important benefits to patients.

title: Erskine-Hill, Howard. Alexander Pope: A Literary Biography
abstract: Everyone who knew Howard Erskine-Hill and who benefited from his lifelong study of Pope will be glad to have his last word on the subject, albeit a full decade after he died. We owe Alexander Lindsay, who revised the last completed draft for publication, and Greg Clingham, who redirected the book toward publication by Clemson University Press, grateful thanks.All biographies of Pope are to some extent “literary” ones, since (whatever nonchalant pose he might occasionally have struck) his significance was as a writer—or “Poet,” as he tended to refer to himself in the poetry itself. One of the great pleasures of reading this book, designed to be accessible to anyone with an interest in the subject, is to follow a habit of attention to shape, rhythm, rhyme, and nuance—what used to be called “close reading”—as Erskine-Hill dips (with judicious selectivity) into Pope’s major writings, to present sensitive, humane accounts of transitions of thought and image. The emphasis on naturalistic imagery in the Pastorals is (for example) well handled; the emotionalism of set scenes in the Iliad translation impressively subtle; the latent confessionalism of “Eloisa to Abelard” convincingly sketched within an account of Pope’s sexual feelings. The Imitations of Horace, or Pope’s “I-poems,” as Erskine-Hill calls them, are enjoyably displayed as the invention of poetic autobiography. Much of this is noncontroversial: Erskine-Hill fights no battles with the critiques of Pope that followed the rise of feminist studies in the academy, for example, beyond acknowledging that the opening of the Epistle to a Lady has “certainly angered contemporary feminists”; nor does the book engage combatively with anyone in any direct way.Alexander Pope is, however, a book which knows its own mind. Erskine-Hill’s own contributions to Pope studies have used his “social milieu” to energize analysis of the writing; latterly his attention especially focused on political nuances during the succession crises of Pope’s lifetime. If Maynard Mack’s lovingly monumental Alexander Pope: A Life (1985) is the rock on which all modern biography of Pope is founded, at something like a third the length of Mack’s, this biography has to choose its emphases, which fall upon the germinal and sustained nature of Pope’s Catholic upbringing, connections, and allegiances, within a history of political tension, unresolved (it seems) then or now. A great deal of contextual information, and quite a lot of speculation, lies here. Pope’s religious identity always constituted an easy line of attack for Dunces seeking to cheapen or tarnish Pope’s commercial and cultural success, their ignorance and malice rendering such attention itself suspect. But as a keen investigator of Jacobite culture in Pope’s period, Erskine-Hill brings some fresh shading to a picture he regards as often ignored by “Whig historians” (those who take for granted the legitimacy of the events of 1688 and 1714). Citing a section of Swift’s Verses of the Death of Dr. Swift that Pope and William King cut from the poem before it was published because of its denunciation of the post-Anne settlement, Erskine-Hill declares: “All those Whig historians, of whom there are still many, might take a second look at the verdict of the greatest political writer of that era: the testimony of a Protestant, on what happened at the succession of the House of Hanover.” This has something of an eighteenth-century bitterness about it: Swift was hardly writing from an impersonal or neutral perspective, and the suggestion that we are somehow “still” overrun by “Whig historians” hardly reflects the burgeoning of Jacobite studies in recent decades. His confessedly “over-simple” summary of the situation after 1688 propounds an even split: the Tory “half of the nation” was sympathetic to a king over the water characterized in soupily benevolist terms here. Walpole, a stage villain on the national scale (there is a sour joke about how tedious it must have been to have to keep bribing the corruptible electorate), apparently calculated that the Sacheverell trial showed that “probably about half the nation disagreed with the Whig view of 1688.” No references substantiate any part of this claim. When narrating what we know of Pope’s actual relations with Walpole, mediated socially through William Fortescue, the story is conspicuously more balanced and interesting: the stories are humanely told and brightly lit.Erskine-Hill’s earlier academic studies, such as his remarkable lecture on “Pope and Slavery,” are here remodeled for a nonacademic context, and duly referenced—although the comforting assertion that Britain “never became a big player in this dreadful game” (the slave trade) might raise an eyebrow or two, while it is a stretch to envisage Lord Mansfield’s landmark decision in the Somerset case as influenced by a line of Pope’s. A few fragments of new documentary evidence are also offered. One is a 1722 letter from Thomas Southcott (or Southcote), the Catholic priest who once taught Pope, to “James III.” in which Southcott intriguingly states “Mr Popes late crown of Bayes has let him mightily into the secret of his own strength.” This breezy aside appears to be the only mention of Pope in a “rambling” correspondence, but Southcott clearly expects James to know what he is talking about, and Erskine-Hill speculates about what the “Bayes” might refer to and why contemporary writers might fear Pope’s satiric acts of revenge. There follows an ingenious house-of-cards argument that the satiric element indicates knowledge of Pope’s “Atticus” sketch, and the “crown of Bayes” an offer of laureateship in a restored Stuart monarchy. Erskine-Hill concedes, however, that Pope probably had no idea that any such conversation was taking place.Another item is a letter of 1730 apparently from Pope himself to the exiled Jacobite leader Francis Atterbury. This, having been smuggled across the water (and somehow recollected to the archive of the Mulgrave family), discusses many matters of interest (the death of Atterbury’s daughter, relations with the fractious Duchess of Buckingham) before pleading with Atterbury: “why will you defer the Vindication of my Friend?,” meaning, it is argued, Bolingbroke, whose dismissal by the Stuart claimant after the failed rising of 1715 had led to his denunciation of the Jacobite cause and return to England at the very moment Atterbury was heading into exile (an “exchange” in Atterbury’s terms). If so, it seems a naïve appeal, and as often in the book, one is tempted to feel that Pope, for all the “stratagem” he showed in his literary career, would have made a poor conspirator in practice.Actually, Erskine-Hill is too scrupulous to represent Pope as a thoroughgoing Jacobite, instead resorting to regretful concessive clauses such as “If he was too circumspect to be a committed Jacobite himself. . . .” Rather, he draws into a brightly illuminated foreground the Catholic or Jacobite allegiances of his associates, reminding readers that many who looked like reliable figures of the Whig establishment (such as William Murray, the future Earl of Mansfield and addressee of two verse epistles by Pope) had had, or might have had, their Jacobite moments during the uncertain years of Anne or George I. We are reminded several times that the Earl of Burlington showed himself sympathetic to Pope and his friends, perhaps signaling some deeper allegiance. The tabulation of the (probable) political identities of the addressees of Pope’s epistles comes out, with a little finessing, more or less even, and it is an interesting exercise, but one does not have to be a “Whig historian” to feel that the thumb is sometimes on the scale. There is a good deal of airily assertive phrasing: “Pope would have been impressed . . . St. John . . . must have thought. . . . He may have assumed, probably wrongly. . . .” Biographers have to join the dots because written evidence is so scanty, particularly when the subject is from a suspect minority, but this type of thing too often comes into play where the political subject (here, the unreliable Bolingbroke) is difficult to assess.Erskine-Hill is attentive to the self-revealing aspects of Pope’s textual revision, but neglectful of his actual engagement with the book trade, high and low: there is surely good biographical—even political—narrative in the subscription campaign for the Iliad, in arrangements to publish the Correspondence both clandestinely and officially in the 1730s, in relations with Curll, and in the preparations for a final edition of Works. Though personal—nobody handled this shift in author-publisher relations as Pope did—these matters are predominantly secular, and are eclipsed by other concerns, such as the falling-out with Ralph Allen over Martha Blount. Allen comes out of this badly, as a local politician unable to accommodate the ancient allegiances of Martha—ones which Pope himself (an “unorthodox Catholic”) played down, always presenting a common-ground version of faith to the world.In a perhaps tongue-in-cheek gesture, Erskine-Hill claims to have given the best account of Pope’s death. There is some suggestive (if, again, speculative) discussion of what Pope’s alarming visions (such as the arm coming through the wall) might have been prompted by, but the evidence of the deathbed itself is as usual confined to the observations of Joseph Spence, Pope’s friend and biographical note taker. Among these stands the suggestion by Nathaniel Hooke, a Catholic friend, that Pope could receive the last rites, upon which Pope said, according to Spence (who wrestled with the wording), “I do not suppose that is essential, but it will be right, and I thank you heartily for putting me in mind of it.” Erskine-Hill preemptively calls this an “apparently (but not necessarily) last-minute decision” but cites no evidence to show it was in his mind until Hooke’s intervention. The priest who attended claimed that Pope regretted “everything he had said or wrote, that was against the Catholic Faith,” a remark Erskine-Hill emphasizes more than the offenses themselves (such as the praise of Erasmus and critique of monkish ignorance in the Essay on Criticism, which upset John Caryll’s friends). Erskine-Hill explains Pope’s variety of deathbed remarks as necessary, with his house full of non-Catholic friends, but that it was full of non-Catholic friends is also telling. When Pope told Spence (an Anglican clergyman), that he had not changed doctors “any more than I have renounced the errors of our Church and taken up with those of yours,” Erskine-Hill counts it one of Pope’s “serious and suitable” remarks as he approached death, which seems unusually deaf to some deft ironies about religious dogma.The book ends with a chapter called “Posthumous Responses,” in reality something of a misnomer. This is no trawl of the “Critical Heritage” of the later eighteenth century but consists rather in large measure of the marginal jottings of Hesther Lynch Piozzi, in a copy of William Bowles’s 1806 edition of Pope, from a previously unexplored copy in the Beinecke. These are entertainingly vibrant notes, albeit of very mixed character, but it is an oddly specialized ending to the book. It mirrors a reinvestigation of Pope’s annotations to Montaigne (like Erasmus, the kind of Catholic maverick Pope could do literary business with). Piozzi’s hostility to “Romanists” perhaps provides a thread of continuity—she maintains this prejudice at a time when it did not seem to matter to others. But the comments add only a slight adjustment to our understanding of how the Romantic era appreciated a poet still more widely read in 1806 than Wordsworth was.There are a few slips: there is no Spectator paper of 27 April 1713 in which Philips’s pastorals are praised because that date belongs to Guardian 40, Pope’s spoof response. While some repetitions have been edited out, a few more could profitably have gone, such as the explanation that when Johnson calls Pope’s Imitations of Horace “relaxations of his genius” he could have had other senses of “relax” in mind—a good point, which only needed making once. There is no bibliography, and, apart from the cover image of Pope (studio of Kneller, ca. 1721), and a pleasing commemorative image of Professor Erskine-Hill himself (in what is, in effect, a kind of memorial-testimony), there are no illustrations; this seems a shame for the literary biography of a writer so much depicted and so interested—as the biography itself richly demonstrates—in what things looked like, or could be made to look like.

title: PyMeshTool — A framework for building efficient automated image-based cardiac anatomical twinning workflows in Python
venue: Computer Methods and Programs in Biomedicine
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Digital twin models representing human cardiac electrophysiology have evolved from being primarily research-oriented tools to becoming integral components in clinical decision-making and patient-specific simulations. The development of such models fundamentally begins with the construction of an accurate anatomical twin, which is typically derived from high-resolution clinical imaging data. This anatomical modeling phase, while essential, is often computationally intensive and time-consuming, necessitating efficient tools to streamline the workflow. To address this need, PyMeshTool, a Python interface for MeshTool, was developed with the primary objective of simplifying and accelerating the anatomical twinning process. METHODS: The C/C++ codebase of MeshTool was restructured to avoid unnecessary source code duplication and to ease the development of the Python interface PyMeshTool. Particular emphasis was placed on the design of PyMeshTool as a streamlined interface that exposes core functionalities of MeshTool in a consistent and user-friendly manner. To evaluate the effectiveness of this design, two Python scripts were implemented running the same anatomical twinning pipeline, one utilizing PyMeshTool and the other calling MeshTool as an external tool. For this purpose, a basic bi-ventricular model generation pipeline was implemented that comprises the generation of simplified universal ventricular coordinates and the assignment of rule-based fibers & sheets. Runtimes and data output of the two workflows were compared for a series of numbers of parallel OpenMP threads. RESULTS: In addition to the primary advantage of PyMeshTool- easy interaction with other Python modules via the Python interface and the compatibility with NumPy- the computational benefits of PyMeshTool have been demonstrated in several comparisons: (i) the PyMeshTool workflow produced less output, 4 files with 89.5MB instead of 418 files with 774.9MB (∼88% less storage usage), (ii) the Python source code was ∼63% shorter in terms of code lines, and (iii) an up to four times faster runtime. CONCLUSION: With the release of the freely available PyMeshTool module, our work aims to streamline image and mesh processing in Python to ease the development of complex pipelines.

title: Development of a User-Friendly Pipeline for Constructing Atrial Models at Scale: Importance of the End-User for Clinical Uptake
abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a common cardiac arrhythmia with high recurrence rate post-treatment.Personalised computational models can be used to investigate patientspecific mechanisms underlying AF, explore personalised treatment approaches, and for large-scale in silico trials.To ensure accuracy, reproducibility, and realistic uptake in clinical practice, investigations require consistent construction of models from patient-specific data.Clear and user-friendly model pipelines are therefore critical and should be developed with the end-user in mind.The atrial modelling toolkit (atrialmtk: https://gi thub.com/pcmlab/atrialmtk)allows users to produce atrial meshes for electrophysiological simulation, incorporating atrial regions, fibres, and transmural variations across the atrial wall.Multiple workflows allow the use of several input data types that may be available to the user, while mesh type and fibre distribution options allow users to investigate the effect of various factors on fibrillatory dynamics.The pipeline has been tested by multiple users across operating systems to ensure compatibility and usability, and its success at scale demonstrated in a previous study of 1000 atrial geometries.By expanding testing to a wider audience, we aim to increase clinical engagement and the uptake of modelling and digital twins in clinical practice.

title: Figures and frozen data for Detectability of Regional Ventricular Conduction Slowing from ECGs under Baseline Activation Variability
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This dataset accompanies the CinC 2026 study "Detectability of Regional Ventricular Conduction Slowing from ECGs under Baseline Activation Variability" by Julia Camps and Oscar Camara. It provides the authored Figure 1 and Figure 2 assets, frozen derived result tables, selected synthetic geometry/LAT/root fields, supporting baseline-selection data, and analysis/verification scripts. It supports numerical analyses and diagnostic figure views from frozen results, not reproduction of the entire simulation pipeline. It does not contain the manuscript or rerun forward simulations, raw ECG processing, lag optimisation or all-810 alternative-window QC. The saved 104-row targeted-QC extract contains repeated evaluations for two highlighted baselines, not 104 independent cases. Manually composed publication figures are distinguished from regenerated diagnostic views. The solver used to generate the simulations is available at https://github.com/juliacamps/Cardiac-Digital-Twin . This link identifies the solver, not a complete archive of the study-specific scripts, configurations and simulation inputs. The synthetic ventricular meshes were obtained from Doste et al.'s anatomy dataset: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.15372896 . Code and associated software documentation are MIT-licensed. Scientific data, figures and metadata are licensed under CC BY 4.0, with retained third-party attribution. See README.md, DATA_GUIDE.md, THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md and the per-file licence/provenance manifests for the exact scope and reuse terms.

title: Transformer-Guided Graph Attention for Direct Cardiac Mesh Reconstruction: A Structural Digital Twin Framework
venue: ACM International Conference on Bioinformatics, Computational Biology, and Health Informatics (ACM-BCB)
abstract: Building patient-specific cardiac models sits at the heart of precision cardiology, yet getting those models into actual clinical use keeps running into the same wall: mesh generation is slow, messy, and frustrating. The standard workflow—segmenting the image, running Marching Cubes, and then spending hours manually cleaning up the result—is time-consuming, inconsistent across operators, and demands a level of specialist knowledge that most clinical teams simply do not have available.

abstract: October 22-25, 2025, Toronto, Canada Abstract #: SESS-133 Topic: Basic/Others Title: Mechanisms Of Histopathological Vascular Damage Caused By Pancreatic Juice Leakage Authors:Yusuke Seki, The University of Tokyo; Takeaki Ishizawa, Department of Hepatobiliary-Pancreatic Surgery, Graduate School of Medicine, Osaka Metropolitan University, 1-4-3 Asahi-machi, Abeno-ku, Osaka 545-8585, Japan; Genki Watanabe, Department of Hepatobiliary-Pancreatic Surgery, Graduate School of Medicine, Osaka Metropolitan University, 1-4-3 Asahi-machi, Abeno-ku, Osaka 545-8585, Japan; Yujiro Nishioka, Hepato-Biliary-Pancreatic Surgery Division, Department of Surgery, Graduate School of Medicine, The University of Tokyo, 7-3-1 Hongo, Bunkyo-ku, Tokyo, 113-0033, Japan; Akihiko Ichida, Hepato-Biliary-Pancreatic Surgery Division, Department of Surgery, Graduate School of Medicine, The University of Tokyo, 7-3-1 Hongo, Bunkyo-ku, Tokyo, 113-0033, Japan; Takeshi Takamoto, Hepato-Biliary-Pancreatic Surgery Division, Department of Surgery, Graduate School of Medicine, The University of Tokyo, 7-3-1 Hongo, Bunkyo-ku, Tokyo, 113-0033, Japan; Yoshikuni kawaguchi, Hepato-Biliary-Pancreatic Surgery Division, Department of Surgery, Graduate School of Medicine, The University of Tokyo, 7-3-1 Hongo, Bunkyo-ku, Tokyo, 113-0033, Japan; Nobuhisa Akamatsu, Hepato-Biliary-Pancreatic Surgery Division, Department of Surgery, Graduate School of Medicine, The University of Tokyo, 7-3-1 Hongo, Bunkyo-ku, Tokyo, 113-0033, Japan; Kiyoshi Hasegawa, Hepato-Biliary-Pancreatic Surgery Division, Department of Surgery, Graduate School of Medicine, The University of Tokyo, 7-3-1 Hongo, Bunkyo-ku, Tokyo, 113-0033, Japan Introduction: To investigate the enzymatic interactions that cause histological changes in the vascular wall to help prevent bleeding complications after pancreatic surgery. During pancreatic surgery, severe hemorrhage can result from the accumulation of pancreatic juice and digestive fluids around vascular stumps. However, the specific digestive enzymes and their interactions that cause histological damage to vascular walls remain unclear. Methods: Histopathological changes in porcine arterial and venous walls were examined 48 h after exposure to enzymatic solutions and human pancreatic juice, with or without a mixture of other digestive fluids obtained from four patients undergoing pancreatoduodenectomy. Moreover, the protective effect of a protease inhibitor added to active pancreatic juice against histopathological damage was evaluated. Results: Thinning of the arterial walls, with degeneration of smooth muscle nuclei and muscle/collagen fibers in the media, was significant after exposure to trypsin or chymotrypsin, and, among human digestive fluids, only after exposure to pancreatic juice mixed with intestinal fluid. Venous walls were more vulnerable to proteases and digestive fluids. Histopathological changes in the arterial wall were prevented when 10 units of nafamostat mesylate (protease inhibitor) were added to the pancreatic juice mixed with intestinal fluid. Conclusion: The activation of pancreatic proteases through mixing with intestinal fluids is a major factor causing histological damage to the arterial media, leading to aneurysm formation and rupture of the vascular wall. Developing methods for the localized and continuous administration of protease inhibitors around vascular stumps could reduce life-threatening bleeding complications after pancreatic surgery. Abstract #: SESS-18 Topic: Basic/Others Title: Value-Based Surgical Outcome Score for Comprehensive Healthcare Assessment: Novel Metric for Prioritizing Patient-Centered Care Authors:Dimitri Raptis, King Faisal Specialist Hospital and Research Center, Riyadh,; Dimitri A. Raptis, Organ Transplant Center of Excellence, King Faisal Specialist Hospital and Research Centre, Riyadh; Milo A. Puhan, Epidemiology, Biostatistics and Prevention Institute, University of Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland; Elizabeth A, Pomfret, Division of Transplant Surgery, Department of Surgery, University of Colorado Health, Denver, Colorado; Pierre-Alain Clavien, Wyss Translational Center, University of Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland; Dieter C. Broering, Organ Transplant Center of Excellence, King Faisal Specialist Hospital and Research Centre, Riyadh Introduction: Rising healthcare costs demand a strategic reallocation of resources and the development of metrics that evaluate financial, patient-reported, and clinical outcomes comprehensively. Traditional surgical metrics often overlook cost and patient experiences. The novel Value-Based Surgical Outcome Score (VBS) integrates these aspects to enhance resource allocation and patient care across surgical disciplines. Methods: The VBS Score combines patient satisfaction, quality of life (QoL), cost, and traditional surgical outcomes into a unified metric. It categorizes surgical disciplines and procedures into high, middle, and low priorities to guide resource distribution. This study utilizes simulation data of 5200 cases generated through Python, and surgical expertise to replicate real-world clinical scenarios. Data analysis was conducted using R. Results: The VBS Score using simulation data ranked for example Cardiac, HPB Surgery, and Organ Transplantation as top priorities, with scores of 70, 69, and 69 respectively, indicating high patient satisfaction and QoL impacts. Lower-priority disciplines like Maxillofacial and Plastic/Reconstructive Surgery scored 53 and 51, respectively, showing lesser patient satisfaction and QoL. Statistical analysis revealed patient satisfaction and QoL as the most influential factors in the VBS Score (r=0.81&r=0.80). Conclusion: The VBS Score effectively demonstrates the importance of integrating patient satisfaction, QoL, and cost into surgical prioritization. This framework aids in optimizing resource allocation and enhancing patient outcomes. By focusing on patient-centered care, healthcare institutions can improve clinical outcomes and potentially receive more funding and support. The VBS Score offers a comprehensive tool for assessing and prioritizing surgical care, promoting a value-driven approach in healthcare. Abstract #: SESS-264 Topic: Basic/Others Title: Effect of Hepatic Steatosis on Immune Profile of Perfused Livers Authors:Joshua Badshah, Stanford University; Greta Cywinska, Stanford University, Surgery; Shuling Han, Stanford University, Surgery; Tetsuya Tajima, Stanford University, Surgery; Olivia Martinez, Stanford University, Surgery; Sheri Krams, Stanford University, Surgery; Marc Melcher, Stanford University, Surgery; Varvara Kirchner, Stanford University, Surgery Introduction: The shortage of high quality donor organs in liver transplantation has prompted the need to use marginal grafts like steatotic livers, despite higher risks. Normothermic machine perfusion (NMP) has emerged as a promising strategy to improve outcomes of marginal grafts by enabling functional assessment before transplantation and facilitating therapeutic interventions. However, its effects on the hepatic immune landscape remain unclear. This study uses whole-genome RNA sequencing to profile immune responses in viable and nonviable lean and steatotic human livers during NMP. Methods: Lean (n = 6) and steatotic (n = 5) human livers underwent 12 hours (h) of NMP. Viability was assessed based on lactate levels, pH, flow rates, glucose metabolism, bile production, and perfusion homogeneity. Bulk RNA sequencing was performed on liver biopsies collected at 0 and 3 h. Immune deconvolution was conducted using CIBERSORT, and molecular pathways were analyzed via Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA). Results: Viability assessment classified 3 lean and 2 steatotic livers as viable, and 3 lean and 3 steatotic as nonviable. Immune deconvolution of 22 cell types revealed baseline (0 h) enrichment of CD8+ T cells in steatotic nonviable livers and plasma cells in lean nonviable livers. After 3 hours of NMP, steatotic nonviable livers showed increased CD8+ T cells, activated NK cells, and M2 macrophages, with reduced Tregs—changes absent in lean grafts. Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) at 3 hours revealed that steatotic nonviable livers had significant upregulation of immune-related pathways. In contrast, lean nonviable livers lacked immune pathway enrichment and instead showed downregulation of IL-17 and NF-κB signaling—key mediators of inflammatory cytokine production and immune cell recruitment. Conclusion: Our findings demonstrate that NMP affects the hepatic immune cell repertoire differently in steatotic and lean livers. Therefore, tailoring immune modulation strategies to graft type may optimize the preservation and recovery of grafts. Love and the Working Class: The Inner Worlds of Nineteenth Century Americans
venue: Labor Studies in Working-Class History of the Americas
abstract: Historian Karen Lystra explores a fascinating and almost wholly overlooked subject in her new book: the inner lives of everyday Americans. Love and the Working Class: The Inner Worlds of Nineteenth Century Americans is in some ways a sequel, albeit a meaty one. Thirty-five years ago, she published Searching the Heart: Men, Women, and Romantic Love in Nineteenth Century America (1989), an account that challenged ideas of “Victorian” prudery with robust evidence that bourgeois Americans expressed passion and enjoyed marital sex. Her newest book, much like the former, depends almost entirely on letters that everyday people sent each other. The marvel of Love and the Working Class is that Lystra succeeded in locating letters among a far less literate subset of Americans, who did not have the educational advantages of the middle class. From the thousands of letters she read, Lystra identifies key differences in working-class expressions of love, marriage, and family connection. The result is a densely researched account of how working-class Americans in the nineteenth century approached marriage, expressed affection, and valued community.In Love and the Working Class, Lystra challenges the standard narrative about the ascent of romantic love in nineteenth-century American marital expectations. Among the working class she instead finds a persistent pragmatism that produced what she calls “nonromantic” courtship and marriage; an emphasis on “tribal intimacy,” with working-class people expressing affection for their (usually homogeneous) hometown peer group and family members, rather than for a special someone; and a reliance on popular poetry in lieu of original expressions of sentiment or desire. Lystra provides evidence of young men who ask a sibling or friend to “give my love to all the girls,” rather than to any girl in particular. Finding a mate, according to Lystra, was a process of elimination from the candidates available in the local community, not a love quest. Working-class people, Lystra argues, recognized marriage as a pathway to family-making and economic survival. Marriages faltered not when love died but when husbands failed to provide or wives neglected their household responsibilities.These arguments challenge long-standing historical truisms about the ascent of romantic ideals in the young nation, and they also recast the inner lives of nineteenth-century Americans. Lystra compiles data from the vast trove of letters she collected over decades of research to argue that “working-class Americans in nonromantic relationships did not invest sex with the meanings of selfhood or individual authenticity,” a direct challenge to historians (myself included) who have previously identified this century as a moment when sexuality became a key aspect of American ideas of the self. That may have been true among middle-class people, Lystra explains, but working-class people almost never wrote about sex as “spiritual communion” or waxed poetic about its pleasures. She cites examples of sexual teasing among working-class partners but suggests that a general lack of privacy—and fear of embarrassment—dampened working-class people’s expression of passion in their correspondence. Nonliterate people hired scribes to write their letters for them, and families tended to pass around any communications that came into their homes, making privacy scarce. Here Lystra suggests that a practical concern about public exposure was also a reflection of working-class people’s sense of self: Working-class people omitted romantic details from their letters not only because they feared teasing or shaming but also because they did not view sexuality as key to their inner lives or associate romance with courtship or love.Lystra spent decades researching this book, traveling to archives throughout the United States and making excellent use of the growing body of digitized source material. She provides a primer in how to decipher nonstandard spelling and grammar, highlighting the interplay of oral and written language in working-class people’s letters. This expertise enabled her to locate subtleties in colloquial expressions, the commonality of certain simple poetic phrases (of the “roses are red / violets are blue” variety), and patterns in working-class people’s understanding of their place in the world.Lystra defines the scope of “love” with an implicit focus on heterosexual couples. She covers nonromantic courtship and love, affection among family members, and the importance of hometown communities. But what of same-sex or queer desires? Given the wealth of information we have learned over the last thirty years about the visibility, expressiveness, and importance of queer desires for nineteenth-century Americans, the omission deserved an explanation. Otherwise, the oversight becomes another unfortunate example of simply ignoring the reality that many people felt their deepest passions not for a different-sex spouse but for a same-sex friend or lover. I wondered in particular about how Lystra might interpret the evidence from Jonathan Ned Katz’s Love Stories: Sex Between Men Before Homosexuality (2001), which featured many mixed-class couples with older, middle-class men and their younger, working-class lovers, or the letters exchanged between two Black women in the mid-nineteenth century, beautifully annotated in Farah Jasmine Griffin’s Beloved Sisters and Loving Friends: Letters from Rebecca Primus of Royal Oak, Maryland and Addie Brown of Hartford, Connecticut, 1854–1868 (1999). Primus came from a middle-class family and became an educator, but Brown was working class and likely a self-taught writer. I look forward to other studies that might bring these research discoveries into conversation with one another, providing an even richer history of working-class love and intimacy in the nineteenth century.This book makes a tremendous contribution to what we know about how nineteenth-century working-class Americans thought about sex, marriage, family, and community. Lystra conducted a truly monumental amount of research to produce this clearly written, often touching book about the inner lives of working-class Americans, and her contribution is original and important.

Dust beyond the torus: revealing the mid-infrared heart of local Seyfert ESO 428-G14 with JWST /MIRI
venue: Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
abstract: ABSTRACT Polar dust has been discovered in a number of local active galactic nuclei (AGN), with radiation-driven torus models predicting a wind to be its main driver. However, little is known about its characteristics, spatial extent, or connection to the larger scale outflows. We present the first JWST/MIRI study aimed at imaging polar dust by zooming on to the centre of ESO 428-G14, part of the Galaxy Activity, Torus, and Outflow Survey (GATOS) survey of local AGN. We detect extended mid-infrared (MIR) emission within 200 pc from the nucleus. This polar structure is co-linear with a radio jet and lies perpendicular to a molecular gas lane that feeds and obscures the nucleus. Its morphology bears a striking resemblance to that of gas ionized by the AGN in the narrow-line region. We demonstrate that part of this spatial correspondence is due to contamination within the JWST filter bands from strong emission lines. Correcting for the contamination, we find the morphology of the dust continuum to be more compact, though still clearly extended out to $r\approx 100 \, \rm pc$. We estimate the emitting dust has a temperature of $\sim 120\, \rm K$. Using simple models, we find that the heating of small dust grains by the radiation from the central AGN and/or radiative jet-induced shocks is responsible for the extended MIR emission. Radiation-driven dusty winds from the torus is unlikely to be important. This has important implications for scales to which AGN winds can carry dust and dense gas out into their host galaxies.

title: Contextual Variability in Nurses' Discourses on Environmental Sustainability Across Intensive Care Settings: An Exploratory Lexical Analysis
abstract: BACKGROUND: Intensive care units (ICUs) are among the most resource-intensive hospital settings, generating substantial greenhouse gas emissions and waste. While ICU nurses play a central role in advancing sustainability, how clinical context shapes their understanding and enactment of sustainable practices remains unclear. AIM: To explore how nurses frame and integrate environmental sustainability across different intensive care settings. STUDY DESIGN: A qualitative exploratory design was adopted using semi-structured interviews with ICU nurses from Trauma, General, Cardiac and General Surgery ICUs in Italy. Textual data were analysed through Automatic Analysis of Textual Data within the framework of Exploratory Multidimensional Data Analysis. Correspondence analysis identified lexical associations and latent semantic dimensions differentiating sustainability discourses across settings. FINDINGS: A total of 29 ICU nurses participated in the study. Discourses varied markedly by clinical context. Trauma ICUs emphasised cultural awareness and collective responsibility. General ICUs reflected institutional coordination and procedural integration. Cardiac ICUs described systemic barriers and operational strain, while Surgical ICUs highlighted pragmatic alignment with infection prevention. Two latent dimensions, cultural promotion versus institutional coordination and integration versus operational strain, captured how sustainability transitions from value-driven awareness to structured policy practice. CONCLUSIONS: Environmental sustainability in intensive care is not a universal construct, but a negotiated, context-dependent practice shaped by cultural, organisational and material factors. RELEVANCE TO CLINICAL PRACTICE: Promoting sustainability in critical care requires setting-specific strategies that align ecological principles with clinical priorities. Nursing education and leadership should foster both bottom-up engagement and top-down institutional support to embed sustainability into the culture and operations of intensive care.

title: Learning to Unify Deformable Shape and Texture Representations for Cardiac Video Classification
Leaders in Cardiology: Agnieszka Tycińska
abstract: All correspondence relating to this paper should be sent to: [email protected] Agnieszka Tycińska is a prominent Polish cardiologist specializing in intensive cardiac care based at the University Hospital in Białystok, northern Poland. She combines clinical practice with medical education and her expert contributions to consensus statements have helped shape cardiovascular care standards in Poland. Additionally, she serves as the President of the Association of Intensive Cardiac Care (AICC) and holds positions in the Association for Acute CardioVascular Care (ACVC) and Polish Cardiac Society (Figure 1). She is President Elect of the Polish Cardiac Society. My career developed at the intersection of clinical practice, research, and education, based entirely at the Medical University of Białystok, where I combine intensive cardiac care with academic and scientific activities. title: PHRASEOLOGICAL INTERTEXTS IN TRANSLATION: APPROACHES TO PROVERBS AND TO SOMATIC UNITS BUILT ON “HEART”
abstract: Phraseological units such as proverbs and somatic idioms built on “heart” function as intertexts that encode cultural wisdom and embodied metaphor, yet their translation across languages risks loss of connotative depth and pragmatic force. This study investigates translation strategies and intertextual retention in English-to-Russian, Uzbek, Spanish, and Arabic transfers, aiming to model equivalence patterns in culturally dense expressions. A mixed-methods approach combined parallel corpus compilation (50 proverbs, 120 heart units), multi-tier annotation in ELAN, cognitive metaphor mapping via correspondence analysis, and a novel Intertextual Density Index (IDI). Results revealed proverbs favor equivalence (42%) to preserve canonical allusions, while heart idioms rely on paraphrase (61%) due to metaphorical divergence (e.g., EMOTION vs. CHARACTER in Arabic/Uzbek). Native-speaker ratings confirmed functional success of adaptive strategies. The findings propose a predictive hierarchy of translation methods and validate IDI as a replicable metric. This work advances cognitive and contrastive phraseology, offering translators and educators a unified framework for managing intertextual complexity in cross-cultural mediation.

title: Dust beyond the torus: Revealing the mid-infrared heart of local Seyfert ESO 428-G14 with JWST/MIRI
abstract: © 2024 The Author(s). Published by Oxford University Press on behalf of Royal Astronomical Society. Polar dust has been discovered in a number of local active galactic nuclei (AGN), with radiation-driven torus models predicting a wind to be its main driver. However, little is known about its characteristics, spatial extent, or connection to the larger scale outflows. We present the first JWST/MIRI study aimed at imaging polar dust by zooming on to the centre of ESO 428-G14, part of the Galaxy Activity, Torus, and Outflow Survey (GATOS) survey of local AGN. We detect extended mid-infrared (MIR) emission within 200 pc from the nucleus. This polar structure is co-linear with a radio jet and lies perpendicular to a molecular gas lane that feeds and obscures the nucleus. Its morphology bears a striking resemblance to that of gas ionized by the AGN in the narrow-line region. We demonstrate that part of this spatial correspondence is due to contamination within the JWST filter bands from strong emission lines. Correcting for the contamination, we find the morphology of the dust continuum to be more compact, though still clearly extended out to. We estimate the emitting dust has a temperature of. Using simple models, we find that the heating of small dust grains by the radiation from the central AGN and/or radiative jet-induced shocks is responsible for the extended MIR emission. Radiation-driven dusty winds from the torus is unlikely to be important. This has important implications for scales to which AGN winds can carry dust and dense gas out into their host galaxies.
