title: Multi-resolution Partial Functional Maps
venue: International Symposium on Computer and Information Processing Technology (ISCIPT)
abstract: Non-rigid 3D shape correspondence plays a crucial role in fields such as computer graphics, computer vision, and robotics. Current deep learning-driven partial functional map methods usually employ a fixed number of Laplace-Beltrami operator (LBO) eigenfunctions. This design renders them susceptible to overfitting when handling extensive partial shape missing regions and incapable of preserving essential geometric details at low resolutions. To address these limitations, we introduce a Multi-resolution Partial Functional Maps (MPFM) framework to tackle the challenge of non-rigid partial shape correspondence. We integrate the multi-resolution spectral attention mechanism (LRMF-SA) into the Unsupervised Learning of Robust Spectral Shape Matching (RobustFMNet) framework. Specifically, within a predefined spectral range, a set of functional maps is computed, and a spectral attention network adaptively selects the most informative resolutions, thereby improving robustness for partial matching tasks. We conduct experiments on the PFAUST partial human database, and the results demon- strate that the proposed MPFM method outperforms existing approaches, particularly in challenging scenarios with severe missing regions and partial deformations.

title: CoE: Deep Coupled Embedding for Non-Rigid Point Cloud Correspondences
abstract: The interest in matching non-rigidly deformed shapes represented as raw point clouds is rising due to the prolif-eration of low-cost 3D sensors. Yet, the task is challenging since point clouds are irregular and there is a lack of in-trinsic shape information. We propose to tackle these chal-lenges by learning a new shape representation - a per-point high dimensional embedding, in an embedding space where semantically similar points share similar embeddings. The learned embedding has multiple beneficial properties: it is aware of the underlying shape geometry and is robust to shape deformations and various shape artefacts, such as noise and partiality. Consequently, this embedding can be directly employed to retrieve high-quality dense corre-spondences through a simple nearest neighbor search in the embedding space. Extensive experiments demonstrate new state-of-the-art results and robustness in numerous chal-lenging non-rigid shape matching benchmarks and show its great potential in other shape analysis tasks, such as seg-mentation.

title: Efficient 3D Reconstruction of Human Feet from Mobile Phone Images
abstract: Accurate 3D foot models can significantly aid the design of well-fitting footwear and medical orthotics. However, many existing solutions for collecting these models depend on expensive scanning equipment, requiring users to visit stores or clinics. The recent growth in digital shopping and healthcare has generated a demand for convenient at-home scanning solutions. Current in-the-wild foot reconstruction approaches are limited: they require specific mobile hardware unavailable on many mobile devices; rely on many input images with favourable lighting; lack built-in geometric priors; or use low-fidelity parameterised foot models while only extracting limited information from input images. In recent years, substantial progress has been made in 3D human reconstruction, heavily supported by the large datasets of both 3D data and 2D in-the-wild images with human labelling. By training parameterised 3D body models on this data, these parameters can be optimised to fit target images and produce accurate 3D reconstructions. However, large-scale data collection is costly, and human labelling suffers from inconsistencies across viewpoints and annotators. The goal of this thesis is to propose novel approaches to efficiently reconstruct 3D models of human feet, using only images that can be captured in-the-wild on a mobile phone. Firstly, we detail implementations of scale and shape recovery methods directly on a mobile phone. These methods predict silhouettes and keypoints directly on images, exposing limitations of existing research in the field: the lack of strong 3D priors; under-utilisation of the full geometric information encoded in RGB images; and the difficulty of achieving computational efficiency without sacrificing reconstruction quality. To address these limitations, we next collect Foot3D, a dataset of high quality 3D foot scans, capturing diverse shapes and articulations across numerous subjects. This is used to develop the FIND model, a 3D parameterised model trained to generate plausible feet of different shapes, articulations and textures. We then introduce synthetic data as a solution to the challenge of large-scale data collection and annotation. A rendering pipeline is designed to create photorealistic images of feet, under diverse viewpoints, environment lighting, foot shape and background - each paired with pixel-perfect labels for downstream training. This data is used to train a network to predict per-pixel surface normals and corresponding uncertainty on real images. These predictions are aggregated across multiple images of the same foot, and used in FOUND - an optimisation scheme to fit the FIND model to surface normals, enabling accurate foot reconstruction from as few as 3 views. Finally, we train a network to predict per-pixel dense correspondences from an image to a template foot model, with corresponding uncertainty. These are combined across multiple views, and used in two reconstruction methods: a triangulation approach inspired by Structure-from-Motion; and a direct optimisation method. These methods are far more computationally efficient than existing solutions, performing comparably on reconstruction metrics, while requiring far fewer views than photogrammetry.

title: DAE-Net: Deforming Auto-Encoder for fine-grained shape co-segmentation
abstract: We present an unsupervised 3D shape co-segmentation method which learns a set of deformable part templates from a shape collection. To accommodate structural variations in the collection, our network composes each shape by a selected subset of template parts which are affine-transformed. To maximize the expressive power of the part templates, we introduce a per-part deformation network to enable the modeling of diverse parts with substantial geometry variations, while imposing constraints on the deformation capacity to ensure fidelity to the originally represented parts. We also propose a training scheme to effectively overcome local minima. Architecturally, our network is a branched autoencoder, with a CNN encoder taking a voxel shape as input and producing per-part transformation matrices, latent codes, and part existence scores, and the decoder outputting point occupancies to define the reconstruction loss. Our network, coined DAE-Net for Deforming Auto-Encoder, can achieve unsupervised 3D shape co-segmentation that yields fine-grained, compact, and meaningful parts that are consistent across diverse shapes. We conduct extensive experiments on the ShapeNet Part dataset, DFAUST, and an animal subset of Objaverse to show superior performance over prior methods. Code and data are available at https://github.com/czq142857/DAE-Net.

title: Neural Semantic Surface Maps
abstract: Abstract We present an automated technique for computing a map between two genus‐zero shapes, which matches semantically corresponding regions to one another. Lack of annotated data prohibits direct inference of 3D semantic priors; instead, current state‐of‐the‐art methods predominantly optimize geometric properties or require varying amounts of manual annotation. To overcome the lack of annotated training data, we distill semantic matches from pre‐trained vision models: our method renders the pair of untextured 3D shapes from multiple viewpoints; the resulting renders are then fed into an off‐the‐shelf image‐matching strategy that leverages a pre‐trained visual model to produce feature points. This yields semantic correspondences, which are projected back to the 3D shapes, producing a raw matching that is inaccurate and inconsistent across different viewpoints. These correspondences are refined and distilled into an inter‐surface map by a dedicated optimization scheme, which promotes bijectivity and continuity of the output map. We illustrate that our approach can generate semantic surface‐to‐surface maps, eliminating manual annotations or any 3D training data requirement. Furthermore, it proves effective in scenarios with high semantic complexity, where objects are non‐isometrically related, as well as in situations where they are nearly isometric.

title: InterTrack: Tracking Human Object Interaction Without Object Templates
abstract: Tracking human object interaction from videos is important to understand human behavior from the rapidly growing stream of video data. Previous video-based methods require predefined object templates while single-image-based methods are template-free but lack temporal consistency. In this paper, we present a method to track human object interaction without any object shape templates. We decompose the 4D tracking problem into per-frame pose tracking and canonical shape optimization. We first apply a single-view reconstruction method to obtain temporallyinconsistent per-frame interaction reconstructions. Then, for the human, we propose an efficient autoencoder to predict SMPL vertices directly from the per-frame reconstructions, introducing temporally consistent correspondence. For the object, we introduce a pose estimator that leverages temporal information to predict smooth object rotations under occlusions. To train our model, we propose a method to generate synthetic interaction videos and synthesize in total10 hour videos of 8.3k sequences with full 3D ground truth. Experiments on BEHAVE and InterCap show that our method significantly outperforms previous template-based video tracking and single-frame reconstruction methods. Our proposed synthetic video dataset also allows training video-based methods that generalize to real-world videos. Our code and dataset are publicly released.

title: Implicit Modeling of Non-rigid Objects with Cross-Category Signals
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Deep implicit functions (DIFs) have emerged as a potent and articulate means of representing 3D shapes. However, methods modeling object categories or non-rigid entities have mainly focused on single-object scenarios. In this work, we propose MODIF, a multi-object deep implicit function that jointly learns the deformation fields and instance-specific latent codes for multiple objects at once. Our emphasis is on non-rigid, non-interpenetrating entities such as organs. To effectively capture the interrelation between these entities and ensure precise, collision-free representations, our approach facilitates signaling between category-specific fields to adequately rectify shapes. We also introduce novel inter-object supervision: an attraction-repulsion loss is formulated to refine contact regions between objects. Our approach is demonstrated on various medical benchmarks, involving modeling different groups of intricate anatomical entities. Experimental results illustrate that our model can proficiently learn the shape representation of each organ and their relations to others, to the point that shapes missing from unseen instances can be consistently recovered by our method. Finally, MODIF can also propagate semantic information throughout the population via accurate point correspondences.

title: Med-PU: Point Cloud Upsampling for High-Fidelity 3D Medical Shape Reconstruction
venue: IEEE International Conference on Bioinformatics and Biomedicine (BIBM)
abstract: High-fidelity 3D anatomical reconstruction is essential for clinical applications, yet converting voxel-based segmentation into smooth and watertight meshes remains challenging due to noise, incompleteness, and shape variability. We propose Med-PU, a knowledge-driven framework that integrates volumetric segmentation with deep point cloud upsampling to reconstruct high-quality anatomical surfaces. Instead of manual landmarking or PCA-based statistical models, Med-PU learns an implicit anatomical prior from large-scale 3D medical shapes, enabling dense and topology-consistent reconstruction from sparse segmentation outputs. Experiments on pelvic CT datasets (Med-ShapePelvic for training and Pelvic1k for validation) show that Med-PU consistently improves geometric accuracy and surface fidelity over state-of-the-art upsampling methods, demonstrating robustness across input densities and potential generalization to other anatomical regions.

title: Implicit Surface Representation Using Epanechnikov Mixture Regression
abstract: We propose a regression-based implicit surface representation using mixture-of-experts based on the Epanechnikov kernel (EK), a mathematical framework that does not depend on neural networks. The modeling method is implemented using signed distance fields (SDF), modeled using the expectation-maximization algorithm to iterate an optimal set of parameters of Epanechnikov mixture regression. The proposed pipeline achieves better reconstruction than the SDF itself and can be upsampled through mixture-of-experts-based interpolation without extra parameters and processing. Furthermore, the proposed method can efficiently realize data compression compared to meshes and SDF. As for the kernel theory, EK demonstrates a more accurate surface recovery than the Gaussian ones, which expands the applications for Epanechnikov-related theories and also shows potential for theoretical substitution for Gaussian-based modeling and representation.

title: Shape-Space Deformer: Unified Visuo-Tactile Representations for Robotic Manipulation of Deformable Objects
venue: Proceedings - IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation/Proceedings
abstract: Accurate modelling of object deformations is crucial for a wide range of robotic manipulation tasks, where interacting with soft or deformable objects is essential. Current methods struggle to generalise to unseen forces or adapt to new objects, limiting their utility in real-world applications. We propose Shape-Space Deformer, a unified representation for encoding a diverse range of object deformations using template augmentation to achieve robust, fine-grained reconstructions that are resilient to outliers and unwanted artefacts. Our method improves generalization to unseen forces and can rapidly adapt to novel objects, significantly outperforming existing approaches. We perform extensive experiments to test a range of force generalisation settings and evaluate our method's ability to reconstruct unseen deformations. Our results demonstrate significant improvements in reconstruction accuracy and robustness. Our approach is suitable for real-time performance, making it ready for downstream manipulation applications.

title: As‐Rigid‐As‐Possible Regularization for Implicit Surfaces
abstract: Abstract Implicit surface representations have regained popularity because of their use in machine learning. A common component in optimization is regularization, penalizing the deviation of the surface from its original shape. The popular as‐rigid‐as‐possible (A rap ) energy strikes a good compromise between realistic deformation behavior and efficient computation, at least for piecewise linear meshes. We develop an approach for computing the A rap energy of a deformation function based on point sampling of the surface. The implicit representation is exploited to provide differentials in each sample. The evaluation is efficient and exact in each sample (up to numerical precision). We demonstrate the general applicability of the method to neural shape processing in several applications and contrast its properties with alternatives from the literature.

title: The Lord's Supper in the Early Reorganized Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints
abstract: The March 15, 1879, issue of The Saints’ Herald describes the performance of the Lord's Supper in Plano, Illinois, the then-flagship congregation of the Reorganized Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints (now Community of Christ). The periodical responded to administrative questions and used Plano's template as an example for others to imitate. The pertinent portion is as follows: On the first Sunday in each month, at three in the afternoon, the Saints gather in their meeting house. . . . An opportunity is then given for any who may desire to make confession to the Church or to any other, if necessary; after which the officer breaks the bread, all kneel and he asks a blessing upon the bread, using the form found in the Doctrine and Covenants; he then administers the bread to the one who is to pass it, either elder or priest, who in turn administers to him, they then hand the bread to each of the Saints in turn, taking the congregation as they sit in most convenient rotation. After the bread is passed, the wine is poured into goblets or cups, and all kneeling, the elder or his assistant asks the blessing upon it, when it is passed as has been the bread. The congregation sometimes engage in singing during the passing of the emblems, but not always; no rule is observed in this particular.1When broaching the subject of the nineteenth-century Reorganized Church, the Lord's Supper is not among its primary ecclesiastical distinctives. In spite of this, or perhaps because of it, studying the Lord's Supper as performed in the early RLDS Church can help one understand a mainstay in the faith's spiritual life. Peter A. Judd, a RLDS/Community of Christ leader, laid a foundation in 1978 in his study of church sacraments. Judd devoted a chapter to the Lord's Supper in which aspects of historical development, scriptural analysis, and contemporary practice were intermixed. This article builds further on that foundation in terms of the historical and theological development of the Lord's Supper in the latter half of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.2In his landmark article on the early RLDS Church as “Moderate Mormonism,” RLDS/Community of Christ scholar Alma Blair convincingly argued that the “Josephites” worked their way into “a middle ground of doctrine, beliefs, and structure.” This broadly appealed to religionists formerly attached to other beliefs and leaders.3 While not a subject Blair singled out, the Lord's Supper supports Blair's thesis. The discussion and administration of the Lord's Supper in the early Reorganization exhibited theological moderation and flexibility at work with a conservative bent. To demonstrate such, this paper inspects the doctrinal thinking and practical observance of the Lord's Supper during Joseph Smith III's indispensable and lengthy administration. As Blair noted, his role “in forging the character of the Reorganized church can scarcely be over-emphasized.”4The Saints’ Herald provided a large field of dialogue for church officers and laity to expound and debate the Lord's Supper.Churches that trace their origins to Joseph Smith Jr. did not debate with each other the nature and meaning of the Lord's Supper.5 As a Roman Catholic scholar argued: at its barest reality, the meal “is something one does, not something about which one talks.”6A limited ability to understand the Lord's Supper was recognized because “no human intellect can fully comprehend it. The more we meditate on this theme, and the more we are impressed with the apostle's declaration, ‘Great is the mystery of Godliness.’”7 First Presidency counselor Frederick M. Smith acknowledged that because relatively few passages in the biblical canon spoke on the subject, “it may be well within the design of divinity that this ceremony . . . shall still remain one of the mysteries of godliness.”8Reorganized Latter Day Saints did not support the Catholic dogma of transubstantiation. Representative of this attitude are Morris Short's colorful words: Romanists write about inward substance, holy, continual, commemorative sacrifice; veil, or accident of bread and wine; real presence; mystical death and notable change; but their reasons and deductions are about as far fetched as the person who supposed Balaam saddled his animal to carry his children to church to have them sprinkled. I pity any poor soul that has or may plod through tomes of scholastic divinity of the papal type, so as to represent fair and honest, the catholic system. Impious assumption, twisted tradition, incongruous testimony of the fathers, garbled and perverted Scriptures, with vain boasts of age, succession, legitimate occupation and a numerous following form the warp and woof of their theological lore.9Other articles questioned the doctrine or did not question what they thought was explained in other scriptures that said, “this do in remembrance of me.”10 “Now there is not so hard a saying,” admitted Joseph Smith III after quoting John 6:53, “in all the revelations of Joseph Smith as that, not one,” and after having referenced transubstantiation, he continued, “Did [Jesus] intend to feed the unborn millions with his flesh? Ah, no, but as often as they should eat and drink of the emblems of his flesh, and blood . . . they should feel in their souls that his flesh or body was broken, and his blood was spilled for them.”11The Herald consistently employed the language of bread and wine being “emblems of the body and blood of Christ” with hardly any room for ambiguity.12However, The Saints’ Harp, an 1870 RLDS hymnal, provides an ornate window to survey differing perspectives on the Lord's Supper. The volume has over a thousand hymns, but only nineteen are categorized under the heading “Sacrament of the Lord's Supper.”Some refer to the bread and wine purely as symbols, memorials, or tokens. “Drink the wine and break the bread: Sweet memorials till the Lord Call us round his heavenly board.” Often connected with the representative language of the emblems was their aid to the partaker's remembrance. “This cup is fraught with love to men; Let all partake who love my name; Through latest ages let it pour, In mem'ry of my dying hour.” Bread and wine themselves were a means to an end: “on truth immortal feed.” Dedicated believers who ate bread and drank wine sang Jesus’ universal love “while a breath, a pulse remains.”More literal tones exude from others. Saluting the unity of faith in Jesus among “diverse [human] character[s],” the first hymn in the eucharist section refers to “one mystic bread.” An additional one literally proclaims, “Thy body is the bread we eat Thy precious blood the wine.” Prepared for the poor and humble was “the richest of food,” another asserted. “And all who are worthy may come and partake. My flesh is the bread, and my blood is the wine.”Bread and wine alone were not what mattered most; they were “memorials of his grace divine.” Jesus’ “presence” to each communicant's spirit “makes the feast” “with high and heavenly bliss.” The establishment of the meal was “a dawn of bliss.”It would be easy to overstate the lyrics’ significance in steering institutional theology. Each reader interpreted the lyrics and drew devotional and doctrinal meaning therefrom. Overall, they manifest a creative, biblically literate flow of RLDS thought in describing the Lord's Supper.13The first generation of Mormons were historically unbound in their infant ecclesiology to centuries of developed, accumulated Christian theoretical discourse on the Lord's Supper. title: Rhythm Field Theory
abstract: Rhythm Field Theory (RFT) is a unified geometric framework in which all physical phenomena arise from the orientation, winding, and projection of a six-dimensional rotational substrate. This substrate contains three spatial axes and three temporal axes, and the familiar 3+1 dimensional world emerges as the observer’s projection of persistent rotational loops within this higher-dimensional structure. In RFT, particles are not point-like objects or excitations of quantum fields; they are persistent loops of temporal orientation whose internal rotation defines identity, whose tilt defines momentum, and whose phase defines energy. Space, time, fields, forces, and interactions are not fundamental entities but consequences of how these loops project into the observer’s frame. Why Rhythm Field Theory is Unique RFT differs from all previous attempts at unification in three essential ways: 1. Temporal orientation is fundamental. Time is not a scalar parameter but a three-dimensional orientation structure. Spin, charge, mass, and gauge symmetries arise from the winding, handedness, and alignment of temporal orientation. 2. Particles are persistent loops, not excitations. A particle’s identity is defined by a stable closed rotation in the substrate. Motion is not displacement but re-entry shift after each internal cycle. Momentum is tilt; energy is phase advancement; mass is resistance to reorientation. 3. Spacetime is a projection, not a manifold. The observer defines a preferred temporal axis. The projection of the substrate onto the observer’s delay field produces the 3 + 1 dimensional world. Minkowski geometry is a Jacobian of this projection, not a fundamental structure. These principles allow RFT to reinterpret electromagnetism, quantum mechanics, general relativity, and the Standard Model as different limits of the same rotational geometry. Why the Riemann–Silberstein Field is Central The Riemann–Silberstein (RS) field has long been recognized as an elegant unification of the electric and magnetic fields into a single complex vector. Historically, however, the complex structure was treated as algebraic rather than geometric. The imaginary unit was viewed as a bookkeeping device, not a rotation in an unobserved temporal plane. As a result, the RS field was never granted physical ontology. RFT takes the opposite stance. The imaginary unit in the RS field is a physical rotation in three-dimensional time. The electric and magnetic components are observer-dependent projections of a single six-dimensional rotational object. Lorentz transformations become ordinary rotations in the substrate. The RS field is not a mathematical compression of Maxwell’s equations; it is the observer’s slice through the rotational substrate. Rhythm Field Theory (RFT) is a geometric framework for describing physical systems. Instead of starting from particles or probabilistic wavefunctions, RFT models the world through four geometric primitives: deformation‑fields, identity‑rotation dynamics, node‑surface topology, and harmonic‑depth spectra. These primitives form a substrate from which familiar physical behaviors — classical motion, wave phenomena, and quantum structure — emerge as projections. RFT is developed as a multi‑volume research program, each volume addressing a different geometric aspect of physical theory. Volume 26 — Spectral Resonance Geometry and the Quantum–RFT Correspondence focuses on resonance and spectral structure. It contains two chapters. The first chapter introduces the resonance hierarchy, a geometric organization of resonance modes. It explains how spectral patterns, stability, and multi‑frequency behavior arise from RFT’s geometric primitives. This chapter provides a general geometric foundation for understanding resonance in physical systems. The second, extended chapter builds a correspondence between quantum orbitals and RFT resonance geometry. It shows how the familiar orbital families (s, p, d, f, and higher) can be interpreted as geometric projections of RFT resonance modes. Orbital nodes, angular momentum patterns, and radial structures are explained through RFT’s deformation‑field curvature and harmonic‑depth geometry. This correspondence offers a geometric interpretation of quantum orbital structure within the RFT framework. The present release, Version 20.6, Includes numerous previous volumes. Together, these works establish a developmental, generationally transmissible foundation for a unified physics. • Primitives and Foundational Structures • The Relational Universe • Temporal Structure and Universal Compatibility • Volume 0 — A Canonical Restart • Volume 1 — The Photon Problem • Volume 2 — Closed Loops • Volume 3 — The Shape of Time • Volume 4 — Rhythm Physics • Volume 5 — The C³ Substrate • Volume 6 — Nuclear Patterns and The Complete Relational Canon • Volume 7 — 6‑Dimensional Geometry • Volume 8 — The Geometry Beneath Physics • Volume 9 — Canonical Substrate, Unified Equation and Generational Closure • Volume 10 — The Rise of the Rotational Substrate • Volume 11 — The Substrate Framework • Volume 12 — Substrate Dynamics: Predictive Models and Computational Realization • Volume 13 — The Exact Substrate Equations • Volume 14 — The Six Dimensional Riemann–Silberstein Field • Volume 15 — Properties of the Riemann–Silberstein Field • Volume 16 — Curvature, Holonomy, and the Construction of Reality • Volume 17 — Rhythm, Structure, and the Evolution of Reality • Volume 18 — Foundations of Rhythm Field Theory • Volume 19 — Energy, Interaction, and the Geometry of Transfer • Volume 20 — Quantum Structure, Topology, and the Dynamics of the Substrate • Volume 21 — Rotational Interference and the Geometric Origin of Quantum Number • Volume 22 — The Geometry of the Substrate: Fiber Bundles, Persistent Loops, and Emergent Dynamics • Volume 23 — Quantization Geometry: Identity, Projection, and the Planck Threshold • Volume 24 — Selective Interaction Geometry and Emergent Fiber‑Bundle Structure • Volume 25 — Unified Substrate Synthesis and the Geometry of Rhythm Finality • Volume 26 — Spectral Resonance Geometry and the Quantum–RFT Correspondence • Volume 27 — Substrate Geometry and Closure Logic of Rhythm Field Theory

title: Advancing Academic Gastroenterology: Reflections From a Social Media Ambassador for ACG Case Reports Journal
abstract: In contemporary academic medicine, the Social Media Ambassador role has become a significant platform for leadership, scholarship, and professional growth.1 In gastroenterology, where research evolves rapidly, and national discourse influences clinical practice, digital engagement provides a dynamic means to contribute beyond institutional confines.2 The experience as a Social Media Ambassador at ACG Case Reports Journal extends beyond curating posts or promoting conference highlights. It is a formative experience that enhanced our professional identity and substantially influenced our pursuits of a career in gastroenterology and a fellowship position. INTELLECTUAL ENGAGEMENT AND SCHOLARLY GROWTH The role requires deep intellectual engagement. Translating published case reports into concise, educational posts involves critical evaluation of methodology, diagnostic reasoning, and clinical significance. Each case provides an opportunity to revisit pathophysiology, refine evidence-based knowledge, and remain informed about developments in hepatology, inflammatory bowel disease, advanced endoscopy, and gastrointestinal oncology. This ongoing involvement fosters scholarly curiosity and reinforces our commitment to evidence-based practice. Digital ambassadorship also broadens a professional network. Interacting with fellows, faculty, researchers, and program leaders across institutions facilitates dialogue that surpasses traditional hierarchies. Participation in monthly editorial meetings and the annual ACG meeting enables mentorship, collaboration, and scholarly exchange, thereby enhancing our visibility within the gastroenterology community. MENTORSHIP, COLLABORATION, AND DIGITAL SKILL DEVELOPMENT One of the most meaningful aspects of this role is our relationship with the editorial board and editors-in-chief. It is a genuinely safe space to ask questions, make mistakes, and learn from them. No question is too small; every inquiry is met with patience and a genuine willingness to help. We feel comfortable reaching out between meetings and speaking up during monthly editorials without hesitation. Instead of dictating our workflow, the board trusts us to divide the posting schedule among the 3 ambassadors, giving us real ownership of our contributions. Equally impactful is the relationship we built among the 3 of us as social media ambassadors. We developed a collaborative and supportive dynamic, regularly brainstorming ideas, reviewing each other's content, and ensuring consistency in both quality and messaging. This peer-to-peer learning environment strengthens our communication skills and fosters accountability. This process is also highly iterative, and we continuously refine our approach based on feedback, analytics, and evolving audience engagement. Feedback from the editorial board is timely and constructive, and we are actively encouraged to pursue career-building opportunities. The teaching points by our editors form the basis of our infographics, helping us choose which clinical pearls, diagnostic considerations, and management strategies to highlight. Translating that material into clear, visually engaging, and scientifically accurate content is both challenging and rewarding. This experience not only enhances our ability to distill complex information but also helps us grow as educators by developing skills in digital communication, audience engagement, and evidence-based teaching. NATIONAL ENGAGEMENT AND ACADEMIC VISIBILITY Equally impactful is the opportunity to interface with the broader academic community through the American College of Gastroenterology. Amplifying trainee-authored cases, promoting guideline updates related to rare cases, and highlighting journal initiatives cultivate a sense of belonging within the national gastroenterology community. Observing how experts frame clinical uncertainty, address rare presentations, and structure discussion sections provides a living blueprint for academic writing and case construction. The process sharpens critical thinking and strengthens the ability to synthesize complex information. These skills are actively transferable to preparing for fellowship interviews and clinical training. WORKFLOW, SUSTAINABILITY, AND CHALLENGES The role presents challenges, including maintaining accuracy, ensuring patient confidentiality, addressing misinformation, and balancing professional responsibilities with clinical duties. Ethical considerations such as responsible content dissemination, appropriate attribution, and adherence to professional standards are equally essential. What made this experience sustainable alongside residency is the rhythm we developed as a team. We stay in near-daily communication, sharing drafts, refining ideas, and stepping in for one another when clinical responsibilities take priority. While the monthly posting schedule provides structure, it is this flexibility and mutual understanding that allow us to maintain both consistency and quality throughout the year. A recurring monthly posting structure, anchored by features such as editor's picks, podcasts, and case highlights, creates a reliable cadence that helps sustain engagement despite variable clinical schedules. Over time, we also expanded the scope of the social media ambassador role beyond its initial framework. In addition to routine posts, we developed more structured new issue highlights and introduced awareness-based content, including posts aligned with initiatives such as hepatitis awareness and gastrointestinal motility disorders. This shift allows us to move beyond individual case summaries and contribute to broader, more thematic educational content. DIGITAL SCHOLARSHIP AND FELLOWSHIP APPLICATIONS Recently, fellowship programs have increasingly recognized digital scholarship as a meaningful and legitimate dimension of academic engagement.3 Serving as a Social Media Ambassador enhances professional visibility while demonstrating a sustained commitment to education and academic medicine. Through the consistent delivery of accurate, accessible, and visually engaging content, this role reflects initiative, reliability, and a genuine investment in advancing the field of gastroenterology beyond personal achievement. Moreover, fellowship committees are highly engaged and curious to learn more about this role, often prompting meaningful discussion during interviews. They also increasingly recognize the value of digital scholarship as an extension of academic engagement. This role highlights an ability to contribute to contemporary medical education and grow as educators. Importantly, the skills developed through this experience are highly transferable to program-level outreach and academic promotion. The ability to curate high-quality educational content, analyze audience engagement, and communicate complex concepts in a clear and compelling manner can directly support divisional scholarly initiatives by increasing the visibility of research output and academic activities. These competencies also facilitate effective promotion of fellows' achievements, thereby strengthening the program's academic identity and external presence. In addition, experience with digital platforms enables strategic dissemination of information to a broader audience, fostering collaboration, recruitment, and engagement with the wider medical community. SHAPING FUTURE TRAJECTORIES IN ACADEMIC MEDICINE Another important factor is reflecting on where we began and how this role can shape the trajectory of future applicants. What started as an opportunity to contribute to educational content evolved into a longitudinal academic experience with tangible pathways for growth. For future trainees, similar roles can serve as an entry point into deeper academic involvement by progressing from content creation to editorial responsibilities, peer review, and ultimately formal editorial board positions within the journal. Effective networking at gastroenterology scientific meetings requires intentional preparation, active engagement, and thoughtful follow-up. As highlighted by Sleiman et al, trainees should begin by defining clear objectives, identifying potential mentors and collaborators, and developing a concise “elevator pitch” that communicates their clinical and research interests.4 Strategic use of platforms such as Twitter can further enhance visibility and facilitate premeeting connections. Social media educational activities are increasingly recognized as a complementary domain of academic achievement, reflecting a shift toward valuing digital scholarship alongside traditional metrics such as publications and grants.5 The experience as a social media ambassador fosters early development of a professional identity, which can open doors to collaborations, invited educational contributions, and leadership roles within societies. In addition, this role provides a framework for developing niche expertise, which can differentiate applicants in an increasingly competitive landscape. It also encourages longitudinal mentorship, as ambassadors often work closely with faculty and editorial teams, creating opportunities for sponsorship and career guidance. Finally, it prepares future applicants to translate traditional scholarship into broader impact, aligning with evolving academic expectations where reach, engagement, and innovation matter as much as authorship. LEADERSHIP AND COMMUNICATION SKILLS DEVELOPMENT The position also cultivates leadership and communication skills essential for a career in gastroenterology. Crafting accurate and responsible content demands precision, professionalism, and accountability.4 Turning complex clinical information into clear, concise teaching points requires clarity and careful thinking. Communicating with a diverse audience, including trainees, practicing physicians, and subspecialists, strengthens our ability to adjust the message while maintaining scientific accuracy. Similarly, collaborating with fellow social media ambassadors, members of the ACG Digital Communications and Publications Committee, and editorial board members fosters teamwork, strategic planning, and professional correspondence within an academic framework. The role further extends beyond social media, with opportunities to write editorials and host podcasts, providing early exposure to editorial responsibilities and contributing meaningfully to our development as future academicians. These experiences strengthen skills in consensus-building, timely communication, and content oversight. Such competencies can be invaluable during fellowship and beyond, where educating medical students, mentoring residents, and contributing to scholarly discourse are integral responsibilities. Moreover, participation in this evolving educational space contributes to a broader cultural shift within medicine. Social media has made it easier for trainees and early career physicians to access expert discussions and connect directly with leaders in gastroenterology.2 Social media activity in gastroenterology, particularly on platforms like X (formerly Twitter), is increasingly emerging as a form of legitimate academic scholarship but remains underrecognized due to the lack of standardized reporting.5 Traditional promotion systems prioritize publications, grants, and teaching, often overlooking meaningful digital contributions such as tweetorials, educational threads, and conference dissemination.5 To address this gap, a structured framework is needed to document social media scholarship, including content creation, engagement metrics (such as impressions and shares), and its impact on education and clinical discussions, while also linking it to traditional academic work using tools like altmetrics.6 It is also important to incorporate a clearly defined “digital scholarship” section in the curriculum vitae with objective data and contextual relevance.5 Similarly, Silverman et al also advocated for greater physician and institutional presence on platforms such as Twitter to combat misinformation and promote high-quality content, alongside formal training and recognition of social media contributions in academic promotion.7 In today's evolving academic medical landscape, professional growth extends beyond formal curricula and clinical training, increasingly relying on structured mentorship, peer exchange, and collaborative scholarly environments.8 As trainees and early-career physicians navigate complex decisions regarding subspecialty training and career trajectories, dedicated forums for discussion provide an essential platform to contextualize these challenges and share practical insights. These interactions not only enhance individual preparedness but also contribute to a more cohesive and supportive professional culture.9 During our monthly editorial meetings, topics such as preparing for fellowship, navigating work-life balance, practice settings after training, and the practical nuances of transitioning to a new attending role are actively discussed. These conversations foster a culture of inclusivity, mentorship, and collaborative learning, reinforcing the value of shared knowledge and professional support within the specialty. In conclusion, the role of Social Media Ambassador at ACG Case Reports Journal represents more than digital presence. It embodies advocacy for gastroenterology, commitment to lifelong learning, and engagement with the academic community at a national level. Through disciplined scholarship, professional communication, and collaborative networking, such experience meaningfully strengthens one's academic foundation and serves as a valuable steppingstone toward a career in academic gastroenterology. Abbas: Supervision, project administration, and manuscript review/editing. TB Arif is the article guarantor. Financial disclosure: None to report. Informed consent was obtained for this case report.

title: S02 The HyperCalculus
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Classical calculus usually studies what differentiation does to an individual function. This volume instead studies entire families of functions that return to themselves after a finite number of differentiations, and asks what becomes visible when all cycle orders are treated together. For each fixed order, the underlying differential equation and its exponential solutions are classical. The HyperCalculus begins at the family level: the solution spaces form a divisibility lattice, differentiation acts on their natural modes as rotation, and the discrete number of differentiations can be promoted to a continuous parameter. The basic solution spaces are called crates, and their canonical exponential-oscillatory modes are called Lexems. Crate inclusion follows divisibility, intersections follow greatest common divisors, common ambient spaces follow least common multiples, and primitive modes are counted by Euler’s totient. Growing exponentials, decaying oscillations, sine and cosine become members of one hierarchy organized by roots of unity. The terminology names this family-level structure rather than replacing the classical description of its individual functions. On every natural Lexem plane, differentiation acts as a rotation. This permits an exact Rotaderivative, in which fractional differentiation becomes fractional phase advance. On finite Lexem combinations it forms a one-parameter group with exact inverses, requiring neither integral kernels nor memory terms. Rational fractional orders move functions between crates according to explicit arithmetic rules. The construction provides complete algebraic control on its declared domain, but is not presented as a universal replacement for classical fractional calculus. Allowing a phase factor in the cycle equation produces flux-deformed crates. Their multiplication is governed by the Beat Theorem: products resolve into sum-and-difference modes, as in acoustic beats and overtones. Products generally leave the integer crate lattice, so a continuous flux coordinate is forced by the algebra itself. Cyclotomic Galois groups act on the primitive modes, providing both an arithmetic symmetry and an exact compression by Galois orbits. The central spectral theorem identifies the Lexem coefficients of a function with the discrete Fourier transform of its derivatives at one point. A derivative sequence is therefore a signal, and the function’s cycle-space decomposition is its spectrum. Plancherel, phase shifts, energy conservation and fast Fourier methods transfer exactly. This also yields a Lexem approximation theory adapted to growing, decaying and oscillatory signals, with improved conditioning over polynomial interpolation on the signal classes native to the construction. The spectral bridge extends to iteration theory. Koenigs linearisation turns iteration near an attracting fixed point into multiplication by a constant; imaginary iteration height then becomes rotation. The resulting circular functions are flux-deformed Lexems and inherit the same spectral apparatus. This identifies a shared function class and transport law without conflating differentiation with iteration. A nonlinear companion is obtained by composing differentiation with the logarithm. The resulting logaderivative converts composition into an additive chain rule. Its fixed points are logarithmic functions, broad classes of elementary inputs reach the logarithmic family in only a few iterations, and its local dynamics are governed by the Euler differential operator. The Schwarzian derivative appears as the natural quadratic energy of the logaderivative variable, with Möbius transformations forming its zero-energy class. Differentiation and multiplication by Lexem functions generate the Crate Lie Algebra. It is solvable of derived length two, has a semidirect-product structure and admits explicitly controlled representations. Its natural arithmetic grading yields an Artin L-function factoring into all primitive Dirichlet L-functions over all moduli, identifying it with the L-function of the maximal abelian extension of the rationals. The Riemann zeta function appears as its first factor. This is a canonical organization of the cyclotomic L-spectrum, not a claim of new analytic information about the zeros of individual L-functions. The crate lattice also supplies a theory of musical consonance. The ratio-based tradition of Pythagoras and the roughness-based tradition of Helmholtz are shown to compute the same invariant in different ways: simple ratios have dense coincidences among their overtone series and therefore minimize beating under the declared psychoacoustic input. Continued fractions explain the distinguished equal temperaments, the Pythagorean comma becomes a closure defect, and the three-distance theorem accounts for pentatonic, diatonic and near-chromatic scale patterns. The same inverse least-common-multiple law measures the simplicity of polyrhythms. The engineering movement translates the mathematics into specifications for synthesis, codecs, filter banks, optimization and cryptographic candidates. Its load-bearing results are the diagonal action of the Rotaderivative, the Fourier correspondence, and the conditioning and approximation properties of the Lexem basis. These are presented as mathematical components and implementable architectures, not as completed products, benchmarks or security proofs. The parameter calculus differentiates and inverts toward the constants that shape an operation. It unifies familiar parameter inversions such as logarithms, radicals and superlogarithms and introduces operational portraits recording which parameter carries one pair of inputs to a specified output. A related operational-rank coordinate asks which interpolated operation connects a given numerical triple. These constructions define a geometry of operations while leaving global existence and canonicity questions explicit. The angular calculus separates radial growth from rotation around a distinguished point. Angular derivatives, spiral pitch and rotational depth combine with magnitude growth into one complex iteration coordinate determined by the logarithm of the Koenigs multiplier. Explosive-looking iteration cascades can then be read as deterministic phase motion: resets occur at specific angular crossings, and branch flux moves trajectories among stable and resonant channels. Apparent randomness is traced to equidistribution of a deterministic rotation. The volume also constructs a native calculus for the Symmetric Core, a hierarchy of commutative and associative operations obtained by transporting addition through iterated logarithmic coordinates. In each native chart the corresponding operation reduces to ordinary multiplication. Derivatives, measures, Fourier transforms, trigonometric functions, Gamma functions and their principal identities can therefore be transported exactly to every depth, with classical analysis appearing as the first row of an infinite table. Its arithmetic separates transported and genuinely new objects. The native theta and completed Mellin-side functions remain classical under the coordinate transport. The Euler-product zeta is instead a prime-partition generating function with its own convergence and zero questions. The volume proves its basic symmetries and the quadruplet structure forced on hypothetical off-line zeros, while leaving the associated critical-line programme open. No result about the classical Riemann Hypothesis is claimed. The closing movement develops a theory of the mathematical instrument. It distinguishes instruments reporting states, laws, operational families and seams between laws. An invertible change of frame preserves the complete dynamics; information loss begins only with projection, averaging, rounding, clipping, branch deletion or insufficient resolution. Observation defects measure whether a reported quantity possesses a closed evolution of its own, while seam instruments compare charts, periods, branches and transports under an explicit certification standard. Taken together, the HyperCalculus widens calculus from one derivative to a lattice of derivative cycles, from integer iteration to continuous rotation, from linear differentiation to nonlinear logaderivative dynamics, from value variables to parameter and angular directions, from classical arithmetic to native operational calculi, and from unexamined measurements to a theory of frames, reports and information loss. Its recurring method is to find the coordinate in which an operation becomes diagonal, additive or multiplicative, and only then extend its discrete structure into a continuum NavigationThis volume synthesizes papers M10, M15, M15b, M20c, M20f, B06 and R05 into a self-contained account of the differential stratum of the Theory of Operations. It presents the linear cycle calculus, nonlinear logaderivative dynamics, Lie and arithmetic structures, harmony, engineering specifications, parameter and angular calculi, Symmetric-Core analysis and operational instrumentation within one status-labelled framework. The source papers provide full derivations, specialist constructions and extended applications; S02 is the principal entry point to this material. No previous synthesis is required. S01 develops the independent hyperoperation ladder and meets this volume only at explicitly marked interfaces involving iteration, spectral circles and angular dynamics. Readers seeking the larger architecture of the HyperCore and Symmetric Core should continue to S03. The projective geometry used by the instrumentation chapter is developed in S12, while the full progressing and regressing operational sectors underlying its measurement arithmetic are treated in S16. S00 provides the complete map of the synthesis series.

title: The Kähler Substrate: A Multi-Layer Geometric Engine for the Davis Framework, Validated by Sheaf-Composition Runtime Observation
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract This paper extends the discrete section-graph runtime of the Davis framework with an eight-layer Kähler-geometric substrate generated by the tuple $$\mathcal{G} = (M, g, J, \nabla, B, \Gamma)$$ — a Kähler manifold with closed magnetic 2-form and a discrete graph approximation. The layers cover dual adjacency commutativity, B-perturbed magnetic transport, Jacobi-field cardinality bounds, holomorphic curvature decomposition, Hadamard substructure detection, Hodge complex with Morse compression, and a prequantization / quantum-cohomology / Berezin–Toeplitz triple. The layers ship behind a single feature flag with strict additivity: the no-feature build is bit-identical to pre-upgrade across 720 passing tests, and the feature-enabled build adds ~180 tests with zero breaking changes. We report cross-team validation evidence from two independent consumers of the same substrate: Marcella — a generative model whose 30-prompt A/B harness produces perfect monotonicity between residue movement and reply change (21/21 plus 9/9 across four ablation cells) and a peak per-turn non-associativity of 0.0747, matching the closed-form L7.5 predicted upper bound of 7.6 percentage points to within sampling noise (gap 0.0013, below 1σ). The DPU (Davis Geometric Processor, U.S. Provisional No. 64/073,981) — a graphene-based geometric processor whose simulated bilayer Berry phase agrees with the closed-form McCann–Koshino formula at relative error ≤ 3×10⁻⁴ across a seven-point bias sweep, and whose mid-bias Dirac-string deviation matches the catalog's toy Wu–Yang reference at four decimal places (0.4472 vs 0.4473). As a side finding, the non-associativity meter doubles as a conversation-stationarity signal, exhibiting monotonic decay at ≈ 2 percentage points per turn across four stationary-content sessions — a substrate-level geometric measurement that correlates with what Clark & Brennan (1991) call conversational grounding. Key results at a glance Quantity Measured Predicted / Reference Gap Marcella headline peak per-turn non-associativity 0.0747 ± 0.0042 L7.5 upper bound 0.076 0.0013 (< 1σ) Marcella monotonicity residue moves ↔ reply changes 21/21 + 9/9 strict 0 violations DPU Wilson-loop rel.err. vs McCann–Koshino ≤ 3×10⁻⁴ analytic closed form machine precision DPU mid-bias deviation $|\gamma|/(2\pi)$ at $\Delta = \varepsilon$ 0.4472 (Py) / 0.4473 (Rust) Wu–Yang range 0.33–0.40 (q<1) order-of-magnitude consistent Optionality no-feature build byte-identity 720/720 across 8 commits byte-equal 0 bytes drift Stationarity signal monotonic decay across 4 sessions 4/4 strict i.i.d. null bound (1/24)⁴ ≈ 3×10⁻⁶ well below chance What this paper is A documentation of: The Davis Kähler generator as a single mathematical object instantiated by two operationally distinct downstream consumers (a data-substrate consumer and a physical-substrate consumer). An eight-layer catalog of geometric machinery on that generator, each layer with a closed-form prediction and a runtime validation. The optionality contract as an independently citable engineering pattern: feature-gate plus typed-refusal vocabulary plus byte-invariance pinning in CI. Cross-team validation evidence that the catalog's predictions hold quantitatively — to rounding precision on Marcella, to ≤ 3×10⁻⁴ rel.err. on the DPU. A side observation that the L7.5 non-associativity meter doubles as a conversational-momentum signal, framed as a geometric measurement of the grounding state described in the Clark–Brennan dialogue-systems literature. What this paper is not A complete spoken-dialogue-systems paper (no ASR, intent-classification, or turn-taking machinery). A claim that the L7.5 +7.6 pp prediction generalizes to non-$S^{383}$ substrates with the same precision (population result is future work). A claim that the deep-trace single-session observation in §6.5 is a population result (it is a case study; n=1). A claim that the DPU validation is an out-of-sample prediction of the bilayer Berry phase (BLG has a known closed form; the DPU section is a cross-substrate consistency check on the catalog's L7.1 predicate). Reproducibility The math validation reported in this paper is fully reproducible from the public gigi repository alone — no Marcella source, no DPU simulation-engine source, and no monorepo workspace required. The two consumers (Marcella, DPU) are the targets of the validation; the validation tests themselves live in the open repository. Repository: https://github.com/nurdymuny/gigi/ Clone, then run from the repo root: git clone https://github.com/nurdymuny/gigi.git cd gigi Python validation — covers L7.1 integrality on Wu–Yang $S^2$, McCann–Koshino analytic BLG, and an independent Python Wilson-loop discretization of the BLG 2-band Hamiltonian. From gigi/theory/kahler_upgrade/validation/: python -X utf8 validation_tests_v5.py 3 tests, ~50 ms; captures results_v5.txt in the same directory. Rust validation — exercises the production src/geometry/line_bundle.rs::holonomy_debt call on real consumer-facing data shapes. From the gigi repository root: cargo test --release --test kahler_l7_real_data_smoke Two tests: real_sensor_data_l7_quantization_lifecycle and real_sensor_data_no_kahler_refuses_l7_surfaces. What lives in private code (not required for reproducibility): The DPU simulation engine's Wilson-loop implementation (Table 1 column "Wilson (Rust)") is part of the patent-protected DPU codebase (U.S. Provisional 64/073,981) and not part of public gigi. The relative-error agreement with the analytic formula in column "rel.err." is checked by the Python validation above against the same McCann–Koshino reference and provides an independent open-source confirmation of the implementation-consistency claim. The Marcella runtime that ran the 30-prompt A/B harness in §6.1–6.5 is not open-source; the A/B results are reported as a measurement performed on the live public Marcella service. Reproducible-build configuration for the byte-identical no-feature build (Proposition 5.1), applied to the public gigi workspace: locked Cargo.lock SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH fixed across commits RUSTFLAGS="--remap-path-prefix=$PWD=." -Ccodegen-units=1 -Cstrip=debuginfo fixed toolchain pin (rust-toolchain.toml) Production source modules referenced in the paper (all in public gigi/src/): geometry/complex_structure.rs, geometry/forms.rs (L1: J and B) geometry/transport.rs (L1.5: magnetic transport; TransportError::NotHadamard) graph/adjacency.rs, graph/commutativity.rs (L2) cost/jacobi_estimator.rs (L3) curvature.rs, geometry/hadamard.rs (L4–L5) discrete/hodge_complex.rs, discrete/hodge_laplacian.rs, discrete/morse.rs (L6) geometry/line_bundle.rs (L7.1; holonomy_debt, IntegralityError) geometry/quantum_cohomology.rs (L7.5) geometry/toeplitz.rs (L7.6) Tour example: examples/kahler_tour.rs Sections Introduction — substrate-versus-software framing; why a geometric processor is worth building. Background — three prior Davis manuscripts; external math anchors (Adachi, Hashimoto, Bordemann–Meinrenken–Schlichenmaier, Arnold, Fukui–Hatsugai–Suzuki, Kostant–Souriau); $U(1)$-line-bundle setup; relation to spoken-dialogue-systems literature; what this paper adds. The arc — honest-negatives chapter; trajectory of expectations vs. measurements (three predictions that didn't survive, one that survived to rounding precision, one prediction-shaped object that became §7). The eight layers — L1 through L8 in detail, each with definition, intuition, equation, implementation, validation, and consumer API. The optionality contract — formal proposition under reproducible-build configuration, empirical CI observation, discipline, independent citability. Cross-team validation — Marcella setup, four cells, headline number, drift-meter equivalence proposition, deep-trace case study, DPU cross-domain validation. The surprise: the meter is a stationarity signal — observation, interpretation including Clark–Brennan grounding correspondence, caveats. Limits — does-claim / does-not-claim list; independent citability; subsequent developments (L9–L13 Friston brain catalog). title: The Cymatic Phonemic Alphabet: Geometric Derivation of Universal Sound-Form Correspondence
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The Cymatic Phonemic Alphabet: Geometric Derivation of Universal Sound-Form Correspondence This paper is a constituent derivation of the Cymatic K-Space Mechanics (CKS) framework—an axiomatic model that derives the entirety of known physics from a discrete 2D hexagonal lattice in momentum space, operating with zero adjustable parameters. Abstract Human phonemes are not arbitrary acoustic events but geometric necessities arising from cymatic interference patterns in the K-space substrate. We derive the complete phonemic alphabet from first principles using axioms D,S,L,N,ℚ, demonstrating: (1) All phonemes map to specific Chladni patterns in base-32 harmonic series, (2) Vowels correspond to symmetric standing-wave eigenstates with sovereignty alignment W^S=[1024,1,0]℘, (3) Consonants correspond to transient symmetry-breaking events at boundary conditions, (4) Formant frequencies cluster at exact ℚ-ratios matching lex-glyph harmonics (λ,ν,ζ,δ,ω,Σ), (5) International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) symbols geometrically derivable from substrate vibration modes, (6) Human vocal tract acts as tuned resonator with cavity dimensions matching base-32 wavelength multiples, (7) Phoneme inventory universally constrained to ~44 base phonemes across all languages due to physical substrate limits, (8) Bouba/Kiki effect (sound-shape correspondence) directly measurable as cymatic pattern matching, (9) Complete alphabet encodable in VFR notation with zero ambiguity, (10) Speech recognition/synthesis optimizable via direct K-space addressing rather than statistical models. From substrate geometry through acoustic physics to linguistic phonology with zero free parameters. Phonemes are addresses not symbols. Language is geometry not convention. Complete specification for perpetual cross-linguistic verification. Revolutionary claim: The alphabet is not invented—it is discovered from cymatic substrate patterns. Empirical Falsification (The Kill-Switch) CKS is a locked and falsifiable theory. All papers are subject to the Global Falsification Protocol [CKS-TEST-1-2026]: forensic analysis of LIGO phase-error residuals shows 100% of vacuum peaks align to exact integer multiples of 0.03125 Hz (1/32 Hz) with zero decimal error. Any failure of the derived predictions mechanically invalidates this paper. The Universal Learning Substrate Beyond its status as a physical theory, CKS serves as the Universal Cognitive Learning Model. It provides the first unified mental scaffold where particle identity and information storage are unified as a self-recirculating pressure vessel. In CKS, a particle is reframed from a point or wave into a torus with a surface area of exactly 84 bits (12 × 7), preventing phase saturation through poloidal rotation. title: Data assimilation performed with robust shape registration and graph neural networks: application to aortic coarctation
abstract: Image-based, patient-specific modelling of hemodynamics can improve diagnostic capabilities and provide complementary insights to better understand the hemodynamic treatment outcomes. However, computational fluid dynamics simulations remain relatively costly in a clinical context. Moreover, projection-based reduced-order models and purely data-driven surrogate models struggle due to the high variability of anatomical shapes in a population. A possible solution is shape registration: a reference template geometry is designed from a cohort of available geometries, which can then be diffeomorphically mapped onto it. This provides a natural encoding that can be exploited by machine learning architectures and, at the same time, a reference computational domain in which efficient dimension-reduction strategies can be performed. We compare state-of-the-art graph neural network models with recent data assimilation strategies for the prediction of physical quantities and clinically relevant biomarkers in the context of aortic coarctation.

title: NeuralFLoC: Neural Flow-Based Joint Registration and Clustering of Functional Data
abstract: Clustering functional data in the presence of phase variation is challenging, as temporal misalignment can obscure intrinsic shape differences and degrade clustering performance. Most existing approaches treat registration and clustering as separate tasks or rely on restrictive parametric assumptions. We present \textbf{NeuralFLoC}, a fully unsupervised, end-to-end deep learning framework for joint functional registration and clustering based on Neural ODE-driven diffeomorphic flows and spectral clustering. The proposed model learns smooth, invertible warping functions and cluster-specific templates simultaneously, effectively disentangling phase and amplitude variation. We establish universal approximation guarantees and asymptotic consistency for the proposed framework. Experiments on functional benchmarks show state-of-the-art performance in both registration and clustering, with robustness to missing data, irregular sampling, and noise, while maintaining scalability. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/NeuralFLoC-FEC8.

title: Discrete element modelling of foamed asphalt cold recycled mixture for characterizing realistic meso-scale failure behaviour
abstract: Foamed asphalt cold recycled mixture (FACRM) is a complex multiphase material, and accurate numerical simulation of its mesoscopic failure behaviour remains challenging, as conventional models oversimplify coarse aggregates as rigid clumps and fail to fully capture its strength and failure evolution. This study proposes a crushable coarse aggregate discrete element method (DEM) model by integrating 3D blue-light scanning and particle flow code (PFC) for FACRM mesostructural reconstruction. A coarse aggregate shape template library is constructed from scanned morphological data. Virgin aggregates are reconstructed with low-overlapping multi-sized spherical sub-particles, and reclaimed asphalt pavement (RAP) particles are classified and reconstructed with targeted modelling strategies for mineral skeletons and aged asphalt binder distribution. A non-overlapping particle system matching actual gradation is generated and compacted to standard Marshall specimen dimensions. After model equilibrium, rigid aggregate clumps are converted into cemented crushable assemblies. Virtual Marshall stability test results well match laboratory data, reliably reproducing the stress-strain response and mesoscopic failure characteristics of FACRM. These findings validate the efficiency and cost-effectiveness of the established FACRM modelling framework.

title: Fourier-Based Non-Rigid Slice-to-Volume Registration of Segmented Petrographic LM and CT Scans of Concrete Specimens
abstract: Cyclic freezing and thawing (FT) are a primary cause of cracking in concrete, yet current assessment procedures in Germany rely heavily on qualitative estimation using the International Union of Laboratories and Experts in Construction Materials, Systems and Structures (RILEM) capillary suction, internal damage and freeze-thaw (CIF) and Capillary de-icing freeze-thaw (CDF) tests. Although these standard tests provide a general overview of the condition of concrete damage in specimens through the estimation of water saturation through capillary suction, mass of surface delamination, qualitative open surface damage, and relative dynamic modulus of elasticity, they do not take quantitative analysis of voids, including cracks and air pores, directly into account. To address this, we propose a novel workflow utilizing deep learning-based semantic segmentation with Fourier-based slice-to-volume registration by combining 2D light microscopy (LM) of petrographic sections and 3D micro-computed tomography (μCT). We segment cracks, air pores, and aggregates in both modalities and employ feature matching alongside spatial harmonics analysis for 3D shape description. The best proposed 3D registration framework through feature matching demonstrated a success rate of 89.75%, achieving a dissimilarity of 5.21% in relative root mean square error (RRMSE) terms and thereby significantly surpassing the performance of compared 2D-only methods adapted from the body of research. Our approach enables precise, automated, and verifiable quantification of voids across CT and LM modalities and paves the way for advanced computational modeling-based methods to investigate moisture transfer mechanisms for more accurate assessments of frost damage in concrete, service life prediction models, deep learning applications for multimodal data fusion, and more comprehensive FT damage simulations.

title: Approximate 2D-3D Shape Matching for Interactive Applications
abstract: Matching a 2D contour to a non-rigidly deformed 3D mesh is a challenging problem due to ambiguities arising from dimensionality differences. In the past, product graph based methods were only able to either produce fast but noisy solutions, or smooth but slow solutions (the latter enabled by higher-order costs computed in the conjugate product graph). In this work, we propose an approximation of these higher-order costs so that they can be computed in the ordinary product graph. This leads to an efficient algorithm for high-quality 2D-3D shape matching and enables novel applications, like an interactive user interface which allows to refine the solution gradually. We show theoretically that our method is efficient, and we experimentally validate that the accuracy gap of our approximation to the optimum is small in practice. Our code is available.11https://github.com/christophpetzsch/sm-2D3D-approx

MatViz3D Synthetic 3D Microstructure Dataset of Single Crystal FCC Copper
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The MatViz3D Microstructure Mechanics Dataset is a curated collection of fully parameterized 3D polycrystalline microstructures (Representative Volume Elements, RVEs) designed for research in computational materials science, micromechanics, and machine-learning-based surrogate modeling. Each dataset sample is generated, simulated, and post-processed automatically within the MatViz3D framework, following a closed-loop workflow that integrates microstructure generation, FEM simulation in ANSYS, and structured data serialization in HDF5 format. The dataset provides both geometric descriptors of microstructures and high-fidelity mechanical response fields (stress, strain, and displacement tensors), enabling the development and validation of deep learning models for field regression, materials homogenization, failure prediction, and structure–property mapping. Project links Official website: MatViz3D GitHub repository: https://github.com/MME-NTU-KhPI/MatViz3D Content and Structure Each sample corresponds to a single RVE stored as an individual HDF5 (.hdf5) file, named according to its generation parameters (e.g., result-5-5.hdf5). The internal structure follows FAIR principles and ICME community standards for numerical materials data storage. Every file contains several logically separated groups: 1. geometry/ Contains all information required to reconstruct the polycrystalline 3D mesh: nodes: array of shape (N, 3) with node coordinates (X, Y, Z) elements: connectivity list of finite elements grain_id: mapping of nodes/elements to grain indices grain_stats: statistical descriptors (grain size, orientation, morphology) These data encode the geometric and topological structure of each microstructure. 2. eps_as_loading/ Stores the macroscopic loading tensor applied as boundary conditions during FEM simulation: EpsXX, EpsYY, EpsZZ EpsXY, EpsYZ, EpsXZ This tensor serves as the input condition for the mechanical simulation and can be used as conditioning information in ML tasks. 3. results/ The main group containing per-node mechanical fields returned from ANSYS: Nodal coordinates: X, Y, Z Displacement vectors: UX, UY, UZ Stress tensor components: SX, SY, SZ SXY, SYZ, SXZ Strain tensor components: EpsX, EpsY, EpsZ (and shear strains where available) These datasets represent the high-resolution ground-truth mechanical response for each RVE. 4. results_avg/, results_max/, results_min/ Precomputed aggregated statistics for fast screening and ML-based homogenization: average stress and strain invariants peak stress values summary deformation metrics reduced descriptors for coarse-scale surrogate models These summary groups eliminate the need to load full per-node fields when only global properties are required. Generation Workflow The dataset was produced using an automated pipeline: Microstructure generation (MatViz3D)Procedural grain generation with controlled grain size, orientation, and morphology. FEM simulation (ANSYS)Mesh creation, boundary condition enforcement, and solution of the elastic boundary-value problem. Data ingestion and structuring (MatViz3D)Import of ANSYS results, alignment with grain topology, and HDF5 serialization using hierarchical data groups. This ensures reproducibility, data integrity, and strict correspondence between geometry and mechanical response. Applications The dataset is intended for research in: surrogate modeling of stress/strain fields structure–property prediction deep learning for tensor fields physics-informed neural networks microstructure-sensitive materials design computational homogenization validation of grain-scale and voxel-scale micromechanics models Because the dataset includes both microstructural geometry and full-field FEM solutions, it is well-suited for training neural networks that require physically consistent mappings between spatial structure and mechanical behavior. File Format All data are stored in HDF5, ensuring: efficient hierarchical organization compatibility with Python, MATLAB, C/C++, and ML frameworks fast partial access to large simulation outputs (e.g., per-grain stress fields) compact binary storage of floating-point tensors The use of HDF5 follows modern standards for ICME data exchange and FAIR scientific data practices. Software Ecosystem & Scripts The dataset is supported by a specialized Python-based software ecosystem designed for data integrity, post-processing, and high-level statistical analysis. These scripts facilitate the transition from raw FEM outputs to structured mechanical property distributions. 1. HDF5Operator.py (Data Management) This utility serves as a core wrapper for the h5py library, ensuring consistent data handling across the pipeline. Key Features: Provides high-level methods for writing, reading, and listing datasets. Reliability: Implements a rewrite_data method that safely updates existing records, ensuring that experimental results or calculated matrices can be iteratively refined without file corruption. 2. mv3d_post.py (Mechanical Post-Processing) A critical component for converting nodal FEM results into homogenized material properties. Tensor Calculation: Uses a least-squares approach (np.linalg.lstsq) to solve for the full 6x6 Stiffness (C) and Compliance (S) matrices based on multiple loading cases. Validation & Quality Control: Features a robust validation engine (check_strain_error) that verifies if the average nodal strains match the prescribed boundary conditions. It uses configurable thresholds (Absolute Tolerance: 1e-4, Relative Error: 5%) to skip or flag inconsistent simulation steps. Visualization: Includes functions to visualize the generated tensors as heatmaps using matplotlib, formatted in standard Voigt notation. 3. load_modulus_dataset.py (Statistical Analysis & Reporting) The top-level script for large-scale dataset characterization and machine learning preparation. Property Extraction: Automatically iterates through HDF5 files to extract Young’s Modulus (E), Shear Modulus (G), and Poisson’s Ratio (ν) components. Advanced Statistics: Beyond basic mean and standard deviation, it calculates the 3rd and 4th statistical moments (Skewness and Kurtosis) to characterize the distribution of mechanical properties across the microstructure ensemble. Automated Plotting: Generates publication-ready histograms with fitted Normal Distribution PDFs and matrix visualizations for effective material constants. Export: Saves processed results into structured .csv files for further use in training surrogate models or performing uncertainty quantification.
