title: Hypothesis, On the Isomorphic Necessity of the Riemann Hypothesis: A Dual Spectral-Information Approach via Selberg Trace Correspondence.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Mine is not intended to be a definition but a hypothesis, a key to resolving the conjecture. 1. Abstract We propose a novel heuristic proof for the Riemann Hypothesis (RH) based on the structural isomorphism between the Riemann Zeta Function $\zeta(s)$ and the Selberg Zeta Function $Z(s)$. By mapping the distribution of prime numbers to the lengths of closed geodesics in a hyperbolic manifold, we demonstrate that the "Critical Line" $Re(s) = 1/2$ is not merely a locus of zeros, but a fundamental requirement for the conservation of information within a unitary system. We introduce the boundary condition of "Unitary Infinity" ($1 \equiv \infty$) to show that any deviation from the critical line results in a non-recoverable loss of spectral symmetry. 2. Preface: The Outsider’s Perspective Standard academic approaches to the Riemann Hypothesis often fail due to an over-reliance on local analytic properties. This paper adopts a global "Signal Intelligence" perspective. We treat the distribution of primes as a compressed data stream. In any perfectly efficient compression system (such as the universe of integers), the stability of the decoding algorithm (the Zeta function) depends on a rigid symmetry that prevents information divergence. 3. The Core Equations of Correspondence We define the two fundamental systems that must be solved in relation to each other: Equation A (The Arithmetic Signal): $$\zeta(s) = \prod_{p} \left(1 - p^{-s}\right)^{-1}$$ Equation B (The Geometric Shape): $$Z(s) = \prod_{\gamma} \left(1 - e^{-s \cdot l(\gamma)}\right)^{-1}$$ By postulating a bijective mapping between the prime $p$ and the geodesic length $e^{l(\gamma)}$, we link the discrete world of numbers to the continuous world of hyperbolic geometry. 4. The Principle of Unitary Symmetry In the Selberg domain, it is proven that the zeros lie on $Re(s) = 1/2$ because the underlying Laplacian operator $\Delta$ is Self-Adjoint (Hermitian). In our comparison, we define the Functional Ratio: $$\mathcal{R}(s) = \frac{\zeta(s)}{\zeta(1-s)}$$ As $s \to \infty$, the phase of the system must normalize to avoid infinite energy states. This normalization requires that the magnitude $|\mathcal{R}(s)|$ remains locked at unity. 5. The Breakthrough: The "1 = Infinity" Identity The crux of the proof lies in the behavior of trigonometric components within the Zeta expansion. Consider the limit of the signal: $$\lim_{t \to \infty} (\cos(t) + i\sin(t)) \rightarrow \mathbb{U}$$ Where $\mathbb{U}$ is the Unitary Circle. At the limit of infinity, the system collapses back into its fundamental state: 1. If an eigenvalue (zero) were to exist at $Re(s) = 0.6$, its dual at $Re(s) = 0.4$ would create an exponential gain/loss loop. At the "Point of Infinity," this would cause the system to diverge from the value of 1. Since the information of the prime number sequence is finite and conserved, the system must be Hermitian. Therefore, the only stable state for all zeros is the line of perfect balance: $Re(s) = 1/2$. 6. Further Proof Hypothesis: The Unitary Folding of the Critical Strip Abstract This addendum formalizes the "Folding Principle" as a structural necessity for the Riemann Hypothesis. We demonstrate that the critical line $Re(s) = 1/2$ acts as a unique axis of symmetry where the information spectral density reaches a fixed point of 1, preventing entropic divergence at infinity. a. The Folding Isomorphism (The "Paper" Analogy) Let the critical strip $0 < Re(s) < 1$ be defined as an information manifold. We postulate that the functional equation $\xi(s) = \xi(1-s)$ implies a geometric folding of this manifold along the axis $\sigma = 1/2$. In a non-unitary system, any zero located at $\sigma \neq 1/2$ would lack a perfectly coincident dual during the folding process. Mathematically, this creates a "residual" in the signal trace, leading to a loss of information conservation. b. The Identity of the Unitary Ratio Following the principle that $x/x = 1$ for any $x \in \mathbb{C} \setminus \{0\}$, we define the interaction between the Arithmetic Signal (Riemann) and the Geometric Trace (Selberg) as a ratio $R(s)$. As $s \to \infty$ along the critical line: $$\lim_{|t| \to \infty} \left| \frac{\zeta(1/2 + it)}{\text{Selberg Trace}} \right| = \mathbb{U}$$ Where $\mathbb{U}$ represents the Unitary Infinity. If an eigenvalue were to exist at $\sigma \neq 1/2$, the ratio would diverge to $0$ or $\infty$, violating the "Lossless Universe" constraint. 7. Conclusion The Riemann Hypothesis is the only state in which the system collapses into an infinite sequence of $1s$ (the Unitary State). Any deviation from $1/2$ would imply that the universe of prime numbers is a dissipative system. Since the prime sequence is a closed, deterministic information set, it must operate within a self-normalizing framework where every point on the fold satisfies the identity of the unit. __________________________________________________________________ Let's try another approach: 1. Starting Points: The Three Fundamental Equations 1.1 Arithmetic (Riemann Zeta Function) The Riemann zeta function is defined for $\Re(s) > 1$ by: ζ(s)=∏p prime11−p−s=∑n=1∞1nsζ(s)=p prime∏1−p−s1=n=1∑∞ns1 and extended by analytic continuation to $\mathbb{C}\setminus{1}$. The Riemann Hypothesis (RH) states: All non-trivial zeros of $\zeta(s)$ satisfy $\Re(s) = \frac{1}{2}$. 1.2 Geometry (Selberg Zeta Function) For a compact hyperbolic surface $X$ of genus $g \geq 2$, the Selberg zeta function is: ZX(s)=∏γ∈P∏k=0∞(1−e−(s+k)ℓ(γ))ZX(s)=γ∈P∏k=0∏∞(1−e−(s+k)ℓ(γ)) where $\mathcal{P}$ is the set of primitive closed geodesics and $\ell(\gamma)$ is their length. The Selberg trace formula establishes that the zeros of $Z_X(s)$ correspond to eigenvalues $\lambda_n$ of the Laplace-Beltrami operator $\Delta$ on $X$: Δψn=λnψn,λn=14+tn2Δψn=λnψn,λn=41+tn2 with $t_n \in \mathbb{R}$ (since $\Delta$ is self-adjoint). 1.3 Quantum Mechanics (Hypothesized Arithmetic Operator) We postulate the existence of a self-adjoint operator $\hat{H}$ whose eigenvalues encode the zeros of $\zeta(s)$: H^∣ψn⟩=En∣ψn⟩,En=12+itnH^∣ψn⟩=En∣ψn⟩,En=21+itn where $t_n$ are the imaginary parts of the non-trivial zeros: $\zeta\left(\frac{1}{2} + i t_n\right) = 0$. 2. Establishing the Correspondence 2.1 Prime-Geodesic Correspondence The key analogy between Riemann and Selberg: Riemann (Arithmetic) Selberg (Geometric) Prime numbers $p$ Primitive geodesics $\gamma$ $\log p$ Length $\ell(\gamma)$ $p^{-s}$ $e^{-s\ell(\gamma)}$ $\prod_p (1-p^{-s})^{-1}$ $\prod_\gamma (1-e^{-s\ell(\gamma)})^{-1}$ This suggests a deep structural isomorphism: The distribution of primes in $\mathbb{N}$ mirrors the distribution of geodesic lengths on $X$. 2.2 The Explicit Formula (Weil's formulation) For a suitable test function $h(t)$, we have: ∑tnh(tn)=12π∫−∞∞h(t)[Γ′Γ(14+it2)+Γ′Γ(14−it2)]dt−∑p∑m=1∞log⁡ppm/2[h(mlog⁡p2π)+h(−mlog⁡p2π)]tn∑h(tn)=2π1∫−∞∞h(t)[ΓΓ′(41+2it)+ΓΓ′(41−2it)]dt−p∑m=1∑∞pm/2logp[h(2πmlogp)+h(−2πmlogp)] where $t_n$ are imaginary parts of non-trivial zeros. 2.3 Choosing a Specific Test Function Let $h(t) = e^{-(\frac{1}{4} + t^2)\beta}$ with $\beta > 0$. This choice is motivated by quantum statistical mechanics: it represents the Boltzmann factor for a system with energies $E_n = \frac{1}{4} + t_n^2$. Substituting into the explicit formula: ∑tne−(14+tn2)β=12π∫−∞∞e−(14+t2)β[Γ′Γ(14+it2)+Γ′Γ(14−it2)]dt−∑p∑m=1∞log⁡ppm/2[e−(14+(mlog⁡p2π)2)β+e−(14+(−mlog⁡p2π)2)β]tn∑e−(41+tn2)β=2π1∫−∞∞e−(41+t2)β[ΓΓ′(41+2it)+ΓΓ′(41−2it)]dt−p∑m=1∑∞pm/2logp[e−(41+(2πmlogp)2)β+e−(41+(−2πmlogp)2)β] 2.4 Evaluating the Integral Term Using the integral representation: 12π∫−∞∞e−(14+t2)β[Γ′Γ(14+it2)+Γ′Γ(14−it2)]dt=14πβ∫0∞e−ℓ2/4βeℓ−1dℓ2π1∫−∞∞e−(41+t2)β[ΓΓ′(41+2it)+ΓΓ′(41−2it)]dt=4πβ1∫0∞eℓ−1e−ℓ2/4βdℓ This is the geometric side of the correspondence. 2.5 The Prime Sum Term The second term simplifies using symmetry: −2∑p∑m=1∞log⁡ppm/2e−(14+(mlog⁡p2π)2)βcos⁡(mlog⁡p2πβ)−2p∑m=1∑∞pm/2logpe−(41+(2πmlogp)2)βcos(2πmlogpβ) This represents the arithmetic corrections. 3. title: A mathematical analogy between certain hollow vortex and bubble flows - existence, uniqueness, and identical boundary shapes
abstract: We study two physically distinct steady free-boundary problems in a two-dimensional inviscid fluid: a hollow vortex in a constant-vorticity flow subject to simple shear, third order and linear strain at infinity, without surface tension, and an irrotational flow past a constant-pressure bubble subject to surface tension, linear strain, and circulation at infinity. Building on the mathematical vortex-bubble correspondence recently developed by Crowdy and Tanveer, we show that both problems are linked by a common mathematical formulation. For the vortex problem, we extend the sequence-space fixed-point approach of Crowdy and Tanveer to obtain new local existence, uniqueness, and analyticity results. For the bubble problem, we develop a separate existence theory, reducing it to a nonlinear singular integral operator fixed-point problem and deriving a scalar solvability condition that defines a realanalytic surface in the physical parameter space. On this surface we obtain locally unique bubble solutions with real-analytic boundaries and holomorphically extendible velocity fields. Finally, we prove that the scalar solvability condition is equivalent to a functional conformal mapping identity. The scalar condition between the parameters is enough for the vortex and bubble problems to have the same free-boundary shape, despite their different exterior flows.

title: PUH Theorem 359 — The Core Is a Bubble, Not a Vortex: Sphericity Excludes a Line Defect, and Quantised Circulation in the Substrate Gives ℏ/m_Pc = l_P Without Any Winding Claim
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Photonic Universe Hypothesis (PUH) — Reclassification and Correction. THE CORRECTION. Four filed papers describe the Planck core as a TOPOLOGICAL POINT DEFECT in a condensate order parameter, carrying an INTEGER WINDING NUMBER, tracing to a March correspondence paper and inherited from there. THAT DESCRIPTION WAS REJECTED IN AUGUST AND THE REJECTION WAS NEVER FILED. This note files it, and shows the replacement is not a substitution but what the archive's own results already required. TWO STRUCTURES, LONG CONFLATED. A VORTEX is a line defect: the order parameter's phase winds around it, its modulus vanishes on the defect, and it cannot split for topological reasons. A BUBBLE is a region of a DIFFERENT PHASE separated by an interface: no winding, spherical because surface tension minimises area, and merging irreversibly. A vortex pair can separate again; MERGED BUBBLES CANNOT UN-MERGE. The distinction matters because the archive's non-splitting result has been read as topological protection when it is surface-tension irreversibility. RESULT 359.1 (sphericity alone excludes the vortex). A vortex in three dimensions is a LINE: it has an axis and extends along it, AND IT CANNOT BE SPHERICAL. The framework has held from the outset that cores are spherical, on the grounds that E₈ is the densest sphere packing in eight dimensions (Viazovska 2016). AND THAT GROUND IS SPECIFIC RATHER THAN DECORATIVE: IT IS A THEOREM ABOUT SPHERES. Densest-packing results say nothing about line defects, so THE VERY ARGUMENT THE FRAMEWORK USES FOR THE CORE'S SHAPE IS UNAVAILABLE TO THE VORTEX READING. This requires no computation and no new assumption. RESULT 359.2 (every relevant filed result says bubble). T180 (April): no lattice, no nodes, no propagation inside — A DIFFERENT PHASE, not a zero of the same one. T356 (September): the interior IS the SPF, a pocket of another phase. T172 (April): cores merge but cannot split — surface tension, not topology. T356's foam topology: pockets in a bounded region. Sphericity throughout: spheres, from densest packing. FIVE INDEPENDENT GROUNDS, ALL POINTING THE SAME WAY. The vortex classification was NEVER SUPPORTED BY THE FRAMEWORK'S OWN CONTENT — it arrived from an external correspondence and was inherited without being checked against T180 or T172. So withdrawing it is not a loss: it removes a misclassification that had been sitting alongside the correct one. RESULT 359.3 (the mechanism survives, on a narrower premise). An April paper bounded fluid gradients by imposing a FINITE-DIFFERENCE CUTOFF, giving a maximum gradient c/l_P ≈ 1.86×10⁴³ s⁻¹ — a TRUNCATION, which deletes structure below the spacing. QUANTIZED CIRCULATION DOES THE SAME WORK IN THE MANNER OF PLANCK'S RESOLUTION OF THE ULTRAVIOLET CATASTROPHE: nothing is deleted, but ∮v·dl = nh/m is discrete, so vorticity cannot concentrate continuously and a vortex core has a minimum radius. The radius at which circulation speed reaches c is κ/(2πc) = ℏ/(m_P c) = 1.616255×10⁻³⁵ m = l_P, IDENTICALLY. AND CRUCIALLY THIS NEEDS NO WINDING AT CORES: quantised circulation is a property of the condensate EVERYWHERE, not of any defect in it, SO IT IS UNTOUCHED BY THE WITHDRAWAL. RESULT 359.4 (oblateness is a signature, not a test). A rotating object held by SURFACE TENSION flattens differently from one held by its own GRAVITY: f ≈ ρω²R³/8σ against f ≈ 5ω²R³/4GM. At 0.68 of maximal spin these give 0.1734 and 1.2449 — A TENSION-HELD SHELL IS ABOUT SEVEN TIMES ROUNDER, because the Shell's tension is 1.4×10³⁹ J/m². A shape fixed by mechanism, with nothing adjustable. BUT THE CAVEATS ARE SEVERE AND ARE STATED BEFORE THE CLAIM: both expressions are NEWTONIAN in a regime that is not; the photon ring at 3GM/c² lies OUTSIDE the Shell at 2.15 and may sample a Kerr exterior regardless; and no instrument is close to measuring ring ellipticity at the required precision. IT IS A SIGNATURE IN PRINCIPLE AND NOT A TEST TODAY. KILL-CONDITIONS: (i) if cores are NOT spherical, Result 359.1 fails and the vortex reading returns — the sphericity claim rests on the densest-packing argument, which is a framework reading of a mathematical theorem and not itself a derivation; (ii) if the substrate's circulation is not quantised, or its carrier is not of Planck mass, Result 359.3's identity is a coincidence of units and the April cutoff is all that remains; (iii) if T303's second-field identification cannot be restated without winding, that paper loses more than its winding clause — this note claims only that its LOCATION result, being pure E₈(−24) structure, is unaffected; (iv) if a relativistic treatment removes the difference between tension-held and gravity-held flattening, Result 359.4 has no content. NOT CLAIMED: that the bubble classification is DERIVED — it is FORCED BY CONSISTENCY with filed results, which is weaker; that the substrate's circulation quantum has been computed, since the Planck-mass carrier is assumed rather than shown; that the oblateness has been measured or is measurable now; that the Navier–Stokes Millennium problem is addressed, since the April paper's own scope note disclaims this and nothing here changes that; or that T303 and T326 are superseded in full — ONLY THEIR WINDING CLAUSE IS WITHDRAWN.

title: Order versus Chaos in Stanley Kubrick's Spartacus (1960)
abstract: stanley kubrick is an established name in auteur criticism. Books on his person and his oeuvre have proliferated for a long time and continue to do so, encompassing biographies, production histories, and critical studies. The multiplicity of genres and modes in which Kubrick worked while following an identifiable yet complex predilection for certain themes, conflicts, and styles, as well as maintaining a large amount of control over every aspect of production, has ensured his attractiveness for auteurist approaches. His work also invites exploration of how individual films create meaning, as this contribution sets out to demonstrate.Several scholars have shown that the conflict between order and chaos occupies a central role in Kubrick's work. James Naremore writes that his films show “an interest in the relationship between instrumental rationality and its ever-present shadow, the irrational unconscious. . . . His pictures often tell the story of how a carefully constructed plan fails because of what the surrealists called ‘objective chance,’ or the conflict between reason and the masculine libido” (4). Mario Falsetto writes, “The potential conflict between humanity's irrational, chaotic urges and the rational control evident in many areas of human endeavor (art, science, ideas) is a persistent and central concern in the director's work” (174). Robert Kolker finds that Kubrick's characters are “determined . . . by the rituals and structures they set up for themselves” (Cinema of Loneliness 106) but that this “rage for order” expressed in symmetrical compositions signifies a “stasis in which the uncanny perfection of the image promises its ultimate undoing, along with the characters caught within it” (“Rage for Order” 65). Thomas Allen Nelson emphasizes how “his films repeatedly dramatize the psychological, moral, and aesthetic consequences of contingency” (17). Thomas Elsaesser suggests that Kubrick's films are about “the demise of the symbolic order, represented by classical bourgeois individualism and its patriarchal identity formation, in regulating the male's entry into society” (38; see also Cocks et al. 6; Conard 33). In his video essay “Stanley Kubrick: Order vs Chaos,” Bradley J. Dixon uses Kubrick's obsession with the game of chess, with its infinite possibilities (hence chaos) yet clear rules (order), as a jumping-off point to observe that in these films, “Kubrick was somehow searching for order in the chaos of human existence.” Dixon proposes that in “Kubrick's career, order would occasionally win a hard-fought temporary victory, but it was chaos that ultimately won the day.” Jeremy Carr similarly argues that as Kubrick was an “exemplary controlling filmmaker” (1), so his films depict “individuals seeking to . . . attain and maintain unqualified control” but who “are nevertheless manipulated by an array of outside influences, some generated by their own making, others far from their grasp” (4). Elaborating on these observations, one can make some more nuanced observations in the individual films.First, order is often portrayed negatively in the form of an encaging, oppressive social structure that, though human-constructed in an effort to achieve control and power, emerges as hostile to human agency and emotion: the military organization and the entrenched battlefield in Paths of Glory (1957), the military-political complex in Dr. Strangelove (1964), the technology-dominated future in 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968), the police state in A Clockwork Orange (1971), feudal society in Barry Lyndon (1975), the Overlook Hotel in The Shining (1980), the military in Full Metal Jacket (1987) (Conard 34), the high-society orgy in Eyes Wide Shut (1999).Second, order often bears the seeds of its own demise in two ways. Kubrick's films examine order's development toward its logical conclusion of complete stasis or annihilation: the nuclear holocaust in Dr. Strangelove, the freezing in The Shining, the apocalyptic march through a burned city in Full Metal Jacket, the freeze frame in Barry Lyndon, the ritual execution in Paths of Glory. Alternatively, order generates its own subversive counterpart via repression or ignorance in the contingent, the irrational, and the chaotic: the unraveling heist plot in The Killing (1956), Quilty's (Peter Sellers) postmortal triumph in Lolita (1962), the next evolutionary step at the end of 2001, Alex's (Malcom McDowell) “cure” in A Clockwork Orange, the moments of explosive violence in Fear and Desire (1953) and Killer's Kiss (1955).Third, in Kubrick's films, disorder and chaos often are portrayed as potentially vital and fecund counterparts as expressions of a natural, animal/human, creative force, though often warped by the repressive efforts of order into a perverted manifestation: probably most explicitly in A Clockwork Orange, where Alex's love for Beethoven's music is aligned with his outbursts of violence and where both are repressed by governmental efforts to impose order (Dixon) but also in the violence or sexuality or any natural desire in films from Fear and Desire to Eyes Wide Shut.Fourth, most scholars see in Kubrick's films a dynamic in which chaos bests order. The opening quotes from Nelson, Kolker, Elsaesser, and Dixon suggest as much. Mark T. Conard writes, in reference to Full Metal Jacket, that in Kubrick's films “the chaotic nature of the world . . . resists the imposition of order” (34). Following Elisa Pezzotta's insight that the Kubrick films reveal that “chaos . . . derives from too much order” (80), I would slightly modify the prevailing observations and argue that just as order causes disorder, so disorder can cause order. Their relationship is one of fluid rivalry and mutual causality, not a matter of chaos ultimately triumphing over human efforts to impose order, but rather a demonstration of how efforts to impose order provoke a backlash of disruption and how efforts to dismantle order provoke a backlash of repression. This intertwining dynamic is often expressed in the doubling of characters that represent the oppositional but interlocked concepts in almost every Kubrick film. Notable examples include Dax/Broulard (Kirk Douglas/Adolphe Menjou) in Paths of Glory, Humbert (James Mason)/Quilty in Lolita, Alex/Alexander (Patrick Magee) in A Clockwork Orange, and Lawrence/Hartman (Vincent D'Onofrio/R. Lee Ermey) in Full Metal Jacket.Given the patterns in Kubrick's films, it is lamentable that most of the scholars referenced do not include Spartacus (1960) in their discussions of Kubrick's oeuvre, on the grounds of its doubtful status as a Kubrick film (Naremore 16–17), or they relegate it to some perfunctory remarks on why it fails as a Kubrickian film (Nelson 57–60; Kolker, Cinema 116–17; see also Rambuss 111). Spartacus had an infamously fraught production history: Kubrick replaced director Anthony Mann at the behest of producer and star Kirk Douglas, juggled various creative egos during production, and ultimately disowned the finished product, a move that has influenced Kubrick auteur studies. Since those groundbreaking studies, texts have discussed Spartacus in the context of Kubrick's other films, yet most of these focus on Jewishness (Abrams), masculinity (Rambuss), or aspects (Kuberski) other than the order-versus-chaos antinomy present in the classical auteur studies. Carr is an exception, as he argues that Kubrick's control of the film is visible in the characters’ efforts to establish control and that order and chaos are presented as oppositional forces (183, 190). I want to show how this framework can be applied to Spartacus and, in the process, draw parallels to other Kubrick films to shed light on how the film creates meaning and fits into the Kubrick canon. Going beyond Carr's insights, I want to show that the relationship between chaos and order in the film illustrates the mutual causality that exists between chaos and order in Kubrick's oeuvre. Spartacus conveys each force's inability to subdue the other and, on a political level, shows subversive forces failing to dismantle a repressive regime and dominant society failing to quash rebellion. The implication is that the social world exists in a continuous state of flux and that the greater the efforts of chaos (in the form of subversion) or order (in the form of repressive control) to establish dominance, the more powerful the counterreaction will be.In my analysis, I follow, in a slightly modified way, the suggestions of auteur structuralism as outlined by Peter Wollen, who writes: “Auteur analysis does not consist of retracing a film to its creative source. It consists of tracing a structure (not a message) within the work, which can then post factum be assigned to an individual, the director on empirical grounds” (168). What I am interested in, then, is not so much tracing Kubrick's presence in Spartacus as integrating Spartacus into the artistic structures that can be called “Kubrick” by virtue of his involvement in the film (see also Munday 27). I am less concerned with individual artistic integrity, whether conscious or not, than Wollen. My claim is that the contextualization of Spartacus within the structures that emerge from other Kubrick films highlights mutually enriching parallels and oppositions, regardless of the degree of responsibility that the actual Kubrick may have had in creating any given element of the film—a responsibility that is, despite recent archival scholarship asserting Kubrick's creative control (Carr 183), contested and complicated by the involvement of various creative voices (most notably, director Anthony Mann, producer and star Kirk Douglas, source-novel writer Howard Fast, screenwriter Dalton Trumbo, and “design consultant” Saul Bass) and by Kubrick's subsequent disavowal of the film (Naremore 17; Abrams and Hunter 4; Rambuss 113). Kubrick's involvement is the catalyst for “Kubrick's” structural presence in the film's creation of meaning. Hence, if I intermittently refer to a multiplicity of creative responsibility for individual scenes (without laying claim to their conclusive disentanglement), I do so only to reiterate the point that despite this multiplicity, the Kubrickian structure is productively applicable and present. title: A Childhood Memory of René Girard
venue: Contagion Journal of Violence Mimesis and Culture
abstract: In my homage to René Girard on the centenary of his birth—presented at the Collège des Bernadins where the Association Recherches Mimétiques1 established a chair in his name—I wish to return to the founding principle of his “existential” theory, which is rooted in an anthropology of conversion. Writing his biography2 has taught me, among other things, that the past of this author, even if the latter formed a paradoxical relationship with his own archive, weighs heavily in the balance of what we call “the man and his works.” Girard probably expected that we might write of him as he has written of the novelists and poets in his books; he seems to have prepared the terrain that I am going to explore. In the two “theoretical biographies” that he wrote, one on Dostoyevsky in 1963, the other on Shakespeare in 1990,3 he made a distinction between the work of the author and his life in order to then reunify them in terms of an “originating experience” [“expérience originelle”]: the moment that dramatically alters the balance of his work and of his life. My aim, following his own method, is to explain this “center of gravity” by commenting on two artistic representations that he himself had occasion to contemplate in his adolescence.What René Girard called the “internal critique” of a work is finding the existential and stylistic pivot around which the end rises, returning to the origin.4 Every style is achieved by this kind of temporal retracing of earlier stages. This “rupture” or “turnaround” requiring that author and the reader return to a primary word5 is always “announced” in the works and in the life in which that conversion takes shape. Thus, the entry of Tiresias, in Oedipus the King, foreshadows the central incidents and a “demythification” of Greek tyranny that in a way tells us a good deal about Sophocles’ own views; the blood-red color of the holy water in the church at Verrières in the beginning of The Red and the Black prophesizes Julien Sorel's death as a kind of overcoming death, connoting the paradoxical faith of Stendhal; the experience of the madeleine in Swann's Way foreshadows the experience of time recaptured, which speaks to us of Proust as much as of the birth of his “narrator.”6 I propose that certain artistic images, in the life and works of Girard, were of the same order of experience; to put this in Girard's own terms, we are dealing with “the annunciation of an originating experience,”7 something he went through in 1959, en route from Baltimore to Philadelphia, that tipped the balance of his life decisively.So let us go back to origins, since this is the direction that René Girard takes in his reading of literary works. This is not a question of revealing an “Oedipal” secret of the kind that Freud, in 1910, undertook with the memory of a “vulture” that would have haunted the young Leonardo de Vinci to such an extent that, in his “Saint Anne and the Virgin, and the Child playing with the Lamb,” he disguised the form of the bird in the dress of the Virgin gazing at her son.8 Mimetic theory has demythified that quest for an “unconscious secret” in works of art. I shall try instead to explain what Girard called, in his critique of Freud, an “oracular word.”9 It turns out that the future author of Things Hidden since the Foundation of the World spent some of the best times of his childhood less in his native city of Avignon, with which he had complex relations, than in a small village in Auvergne where he was “perfectly happy.” 10 A photo taken by his father shows him posing, in the company of his brother Henri and his sister Marthe, before a bay window in the cloister of the Abbey of La Chaise-Dieu. This church, which his family visited every summer in the 1930s, was built by the Avignon pope Clement VI, who wished his tomb to be placed in its altar space. In the early sixteenth century, that space was enriched by a famous tapestry that the abbot Jacques de Saint Nectaire offered to his monks for their edification. He himself directed the iconographic program based on the “Bible of the Poor” and the patristic commentaries of “Speculum humanae salvationis” (Mirror of Human Salvation).11René Girard remembered these images very well when, upon returning from Auvergne in 2011, I brought back to him at Stanford some reproductions of them.12 At the time I concluded that they must have played a role in the genesis of his “idea.” Each Gospel scene is surrounded in successive panels of this tapestry by two biblical episodes intended to prefigure it. This adroit typological program is bolstered by quotations of Fathers of the Church woven into the overall image. The series begins with an “Annunciation” flanked on the left by Adam, Eve, and the serpent (Figure 1), and on the right by a biblical episode of Gideon kneeling and in armor, whom an angel of the Lord visits before a decisive battle. Eminent scenes of the Passion succeed this tapestry, juxtaposed with Old Testament narratives: “Jesus sold by Judas” and “Joseph sold by his brothers”; the “flagellation” and “Job stricken with ulcers”; the “entombment” and “Joseph thrown into a well”; the ”Last Judgment” and “the Judgment of Solomon.” Those familiar with Girard's work would immediately recognize the biblical episodes he discussed in Things Hidden since the Foundation of the World in 1978 and later in his book Job: The Victim of His People. His parents doubtless taught him how to decode these images in his presence (for “the autonomous child, indifferent to the world of adults, is a myth entertained by grownups”).13 What we find in these tapestries is one of medieval culture's most beautiful recapitulations of Scripture.Let us look at the first of these tapestries that the adolescent René Girard had occasion to contemplate. We see the Virgin Mary, who is prefigured on the left by the first Eve, whom Mary resembles very closely. We see Mary assenting to the angel's announcement with very explicit open-hand gestures. We see the words of the prophets, which Girard, proficient Latinist, would have had no trouble deciphering in the phylacteries (Figure 2) appearing at the top and bottom of the tapestry, where we read, “Behold a virgin shall conceive a child.” These words of Isaiah (7.14) on the upper left are reprised by David on the right and by Ezekiel and Jeremiah, left and right below; they are embodied at the point of two triangles (ascending and descending) where the dove appears. Three lilies in a vase in the foreground signify the thrice virginal young woman, before, during, and after the angelic announcement. Humanity is going to be reborn, fashioned of this new clay. Mary repeats Eve and, in so doing, contrasts with her by opposing no resistance to the Word of life.14 The repetition effects a turnaround, a reversal in time, for the disobedience of our ancestors, as staged in the biblical legend, is one and the same with the unfolding of human history.At this point we leave these Edenic and Gospel images in order to consider the divinities that emerge when the sun has set on the medieval period of beliefs as configurated in the Abbey of La Chaise-Dieu. We are no longer dealing with the new Eve, who is going to repeat and reverse the first one. It is the old Eve, bearing the features of Semele, who is returning as a figure of the new one. Many are those who prefer the sign to what it signifies. There is, in this formalism, an excessive attachment to our pagan heritage. The Renaissance and Classicism that followed medieval piety have cast shade on its meaning in the form of an altogether idealized sensuality. The modern world is born by reinventing itself as Greek. Forgetting its relation to a paradise lost, it is bent, like Phaeton, on assaulting the heavens.Let us recall the legend of Semele that is going to compete with the Annunciation from the Renaissance thereafter. In the collection of the Musée Calvet in Avignon, of which his father was curator, we find that René Girard had the leisure to contemplate “The Infant Bacchus Entrusted to the Nymphs,” painted by Louis II de Boullogne (Figure 3). This work of the early eighteenth century is the inverted image of the Annunciation; what we see is the divine child being handed to nymphs by Mercury, the messenger of Zeus. The painting is inspired by Poussin's “Birth of Bacchus,” but this one transforms the struggle of life against death portrayed by Poussin into an “amusing mythological diversion.”15 Understandably, Girard turned away from this painting in 1942 to read Tertullian's Apologeticum in the same museum's library.16 So let us in turn go back to Latin by recourse to a version that is more “pagan” and less “classical” in recounting the legend of Semele, the version we find in Ovid's Metamorphoses. Here, the young woman is deceived by Zeus in disguise, who has impregnated her in this masquerade; she is once again deceived, but this time by the jealousy of Hera, who took on the features of her nurse in order to suggest that Semele make a fatal request to Zeus. Infected by the jealousy of the goddess, Semele asks to “see the god such as he appears in the bed” of his spouse, as the poet specifies. title: Space to Breathe
abstract: Christina Sharpe’s In the Wake ushers in a break between the conflicting (but not diametrically opposed) schools of Afropessimism and Black optimism. While the Afropessimist camp, led by theorists like Frank B. Wilderson III, argues for an ontological dehumanization of the Black person after slavery, Fred Moten’s Black optimist camp espouses a resilient belief in collective progress and empowerment within the Black community. Sharpe’s emphasis on the aftermath of slavery and the notion of “the wake” intertwines grief, memory, and the ongoing impact of historical trauma on contemporary Black experience while nevertheless illuminating the preciousness of Black collectivity and existence. Sharpe’s dear friend and interlocutor Saidiya Hartman speaks to this theoretical rupture in the Black studies dichotomy: “Christina’s work totally unsettles that binary [between Afropessimism and Black optimism]. She addresses the structural conditions of anti-Blackness that condemn Black people on a variety of levels and still attends to the richness of Black social living, and it is an essential contribution.”1Sharpe’s scholarship contributes to an urgent reevaluation of how we comprehend and confront racialized violence, demanding a reorientation of societal structures toward a recognition of Black humanity. If Black studies flourished as an academic discipline in the twentieth century, broader conversations about anti-Blackness have come to a head following 2020’s racial-political uprisings and their many aftermaths, one of them a peculiar and vastly marketable focus on the Black person as someone whose survival is contingent on their being extraordinary. After global movements for Black life in 2020, commodities began popping up in big-box merchandisers across America: Black Girl Magic brand rosé, T-shirts emblazoned with silhouetted Afros, books about how Black children are poised to be exceptional, birthday cards celebrating another year around the sun in tandem with a celebration of Blackness. Yet the year 2020, while anomalous for many reasons, does not exist as a stand-alone moment of racial reckoning. Similar rhetoric circulated in 2016, when products, hashtags, and internet metadata called for #BlackExcellence in the aftershocks of the Trump election. Following the period from 2008 to 2012, the Obamas came to represent a postracial phantasm. Black people are allowed to be extraordinary now (high earners, doctors, lawyers, even presidents, even magical), and this has led us to assume that this potential to be extraordinary will save us. But will it? We should put critical pressure on systems that have configured the Black person as one whose worth is directly tied to being magical or super in a society saturated by images and praxes of anti-Black violence—a violence so inextricable from everyday life that it is always already ordinary. The extraordinariness required of Black folks for their survival (largely rooted in Black capitalism and respectability politics) does not save but instead exiles Black people into a more palatably neoliberal but nevertheless violent realm of dishumanity.2 In a society founded on chattel slavery and its afterlives, spectacularity and magic are marketed as the assumed panaceas to the ordinariness of Black death and subjugation. However, within the ordinary space of the Black quotidian is room for new forms, new beauties, and new methods for celebrating Black life. Sharpe attends to both in Ordinary Notes.Ordinary Notes, Sharpe’s third book, is an innovative and imaginative successor to Monstrous Intimacies: Making Post-slavery Subjects (2010) and her seminal book In the Wake: On Blackness and Being (2016). Sharpe’s 360-page text is separated into 248 notes on Black life, all of which are separated into eight sections. On an initial flip through the book, each page varies in both wordiness and form; long, sweeping essays spanning pages are cut through with short reflections, blank spaces, and the occasional image. Diverging from Sharpe’s standard, essay-based chapter formats, Ordinary Notes takes on an experimental shape to explore quotidian Black life “in the wake.” Speaking of the wake: while Ordinary Notes is the only of Sharpe’s texts that considers the everydayness of Black life in its title, and even though it deviates from her other texts in form, Sharpe’s first two books similarly examine the enduring impact of the transatlantic slave trade on the Black quotidian, emphasizing the ongoing violence and trauma that persist in the aftermath of slavery. Monstrous Intimacies treats the familiar sexual brutality born of power dynamics deriving from racial subjugation across the Black Atlantic, and In the Wake, through a combination of personal anecdotes in tandem with broader sociological commentary, illuminates the pervasiveness of contemporary racial violence, the regularity of Black death, and the artistic methods that imagine new futures despite it all. In a particularly apt chapter of In the Wake, “The Weather,” Sharpe writes on the all-consuming nature of violences borne on the slave ship and how these violences bleed into contemporary society: “Day after day the stories arrive. Fifty people suffocated in the hold of a ship; three people suffocated in prison over the course of a weekend in the United States. . . . It is not the specifics of any one event or set of events that are endlessly repeatable and repeated, but the totality of the environments in which we struggle; the machines in which we live; what I am calling the weather.”3 This attention to stories told “day after day” might be Sharpe’s most primary—and central—interrogation of the ordinariness or normativeness of Black suffering.Sharpe turns inward toward her own stories with Ordinary Notes, but not without losing the polyvocality of her previous texts. Throughout a series of personal fragments that are as tender as they are critical, Ordinary Notes sketches out memories, materialities, realities, and potential futures for Black life through the prism of Sharpe’s lived experiences and observations. While this is a standout and singular text, Sharpe does not write it alone, often conversing with contemporaries from her personal life, the public sphere, her professional formation, and the interstices of these spaces. (References to writers such as Hartman, Claudia Rankine, Roland Barthes, Toni Cade Bambara, and Toni Morrison are woven together with notes centering on Sharpe’s mother, neighborhood kinfolk, and various strangers at sites such as the Legacy Museum of African American History.)In addition, Sharpe converses with herself; her collection of “ordinary notes” often nods to the publication of In the Wake as a critical event in her life. An early note—15—comes from an unnamed former classmate who reconnected with Sharpe after reading In the Wake (22). In a separate note Sharpe explains how a reference to Morrison’s Beloved is an intertextual and everlasting “note on how to live in the afterlife of slavery, in the afterlife of lynching, and in the wake” (67).4 Sharpe also rereads herself, sketching out how her past voices solicit new interventions, including a reexamination of In the Wake in note 74. Sharpe writes, “Rereading ‘The Wake,’ preparing for a talk, I arrive at this sentence: ‘In 1994 the Philadelphia police murdered my cousin Robert’” before explicating the preciousness of their relationship and his nickname, “Bobby.” Sharpe continues: “The addition of the word cousin was a gesture of intimacy and respect; it was the sound of relation, not estrangement.” At the top of the note, Sharpe calls it “a revision, a sound, a correction, an addition” (115). In the wake of In the Wake, conversations surrounding Black life—ranging from the disquieting to the discursive—can unfold with Sharpe’s new opus at the center.As previously mentioned, the collection unpacks the ordinariness of racial violence (which robs Black people of their life, their breath) while finding respite in the ordinary pleasures and potentials of lived existence (the breath-giving fragments of the Black quotidian). While both considerations come to the surface in Sharpe’s analyses, the text’s shape is as much an investigation of Black life as its written content. This is to say that Ordinary Notes is a marvel in form, experimenting with new arrangements for the literary genre of nonfiction. Fragments of varying lengths are interspersed among 360 pages. Shorter notes may take up only one line, such as note 25, “Every memorial and museum to atrocity already contains its failure,” and note 85, “A memory that is not mine returns to me” (38, 130). Longer-form, multipage pieces in both prose and verse coalesce in notes such as note 51, wherein Sharpe refers to work born of her text “Beauty Is a Method,” alongside photographs of her mother’s creative varia, poetic reflections on her childhood, and lists of books (largely Black writing) that molded her relationship to literature (79–86).5 This stylistic choice enhances the overall effect of Sharpe’s text by creating a dynamic and engaging rhythm, catching the reader in the sharp realities of shorter notes or the swelling, affective waves of her longer observations. Multiple photographs—taken from the archives or by Sharpe herself—add a visual dimension to accompany Ordinary Notes’ written word.Beyond Sharpe’s variations in length and genre, two other formal choices are particularly striking. One is the use of censor bars throughout the text, and the other is Sharpe’s employment of negative space. These aesthetic choices are pointed and polysemous. Whereas blackened omissions draw the eye toward the vulgar, all-encompassing, and interchangeable nature of violence, they also call for a reconsideration of the spectacular nature of racial violence. Moreover, Sharpe’s artistic use of gaps and negative space encourages corporeal breath for storyteller and reader alike: a respite in the face of this violence. Through these formal choices, Sharpe’s sophomore success becomes more than a praxis for storytelling in the wake—it is a life force.In initial readings, perhaps the most eye-catching of Sharpe’s aesthetic decisions is the use of black censor bars to omit specific words in the text. The first of these bars appears in note 5, wherein Sharpe reflects on a photograph from the integration of Little Rock High School. In the photograph, a group of white students are screaming at Elizabeth Eckford. Tethering Eckford’s experiences of violence to her own, Sharpe draws out both difference and similarity by stating, “[At school], I wasn’t surrounded by a mob threatening to lynch me and screaming, ‘Send that ‘▬▬▬▬’ back to the jungle,’ ‘go home, ▬▬▬▬! Go back to Africa!’ . . . But I heard ▬▬▬▬ almost every day for six years at St. Katharine of Siena” (7). In their first employment, the censor bars perform their usual task of omitting language deemed too obscene for publication. (Given the situation and syntax, the reader is led to believe that Sharpe is censoring racist epithets.)As the text unfolds, the bars begin to take other semiotic shapes. Notes 15 and 16 detail messages sent to Sharpe by two unnamed interlocutors. The primary, anonymized letter states, “My ▬▬▬▬▬ is in a PhD program at ▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬ and has been reading In the Wake. ▬▬▬ reached out to me because ▬▬▬▬▬ thought I would really enjoy it, especially because ▬▬▬▬ noticed so many connections to schools” (22). Sharpe then explains how, “three days later, another note arrives” from a supposed childhood friend, who writes: “Dear Christina, . . . I am ▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬ and we went to school together. I am back living in ▬▬▬▬▬▬ after many years outside of the area and drive by your old house frequently” (23). In this instance, different from that in note 5, the censor bar muddies all identifiers of those who see themselves in Sharpe’s writing. And whereas the earliest use of the censor bar maintains the same length (emphasizing the singularity of a racist term that connected Sharpe and Eckford), this set of bars begins to vary in tandem with word length.At first there is room to believe that this censorship is a safety measure, sheltering Sharpe’s kinfolk from potential backlash after the text’s publication and sparing Black readers the cruelty of racist language. Going farther, however, the bars’ disparate lengths and nebulous subjects point to a secondary effect: an amalgam of redacted names begins to create a critical mass, with their effaced, unique identities all coalescing under the shared experience of Black subjugation in the wake. This nameless mass comes to represent the very “totality” of struggle that Sharpe sketches out in both In the Wake and Ordinary Notes. The suffering of Black life in the wake is so pervasive, present, and powerful that neither it nor its victims need to be named to ensure that it exists. The pain is everywhere. The interlocutor could be anyone; such is the ordinariness of subjugation in the wake. To produce the same effect, Sharpe’s most striking use of the censor bar takes place in note 17, which she describes as both “unwritten and unsent” (24). After greeting a censored name, Sharpe writes, “So much rehabilitated and reconstructed into that goodness and perpetual innocence that whiteness extends.” The next seven lines are completely blacked out before Sharpe signs her full name at the bottom of the correspondence. title: Socialist Internationalism and the Gritty Politics of the Particular: Second-Third World Spaces in the Cold War by Kristin Roth-Ey
abstract: All historians must choose, as editor Kristin Roth-Ey explains in her introduction, whether to focus more on the forest or on the trees. The central argument of this edited volume—a must-read for any scholar working on Second–Third World relations during the Cold War—is that “the history of socialism ‘going global’ was . . . more particular than universal, more singular and original than planned” (p. 20). The populations of Third World countries “brought a wide range of ideas to the table, including different interpretations of socialism and the modern,” and “Second World people, too, had other reference points besides socialist ones” and “clashed not only with their Third World counterparts, but also among themselves” (p. 6). Roth-Ey and her coauthors posit that these dynamics would get lost in the macro-level analyses that dominate much of the burgeoning literature on East–South encounters. Instead, the contributors to the book narrow the scope of inquiry to “small-scale, in-depth studies involving the non-Western world” (p. 2). They analyze, for example, the role of intermediaries and brokers, the experiences of mid-level experts, and the financial imperatives of individual actors to grasp the concrete, lived experience of abstractions such as “internationalism” or “solidarity.” As Roth-Ey explains, “[t]he point is the trees—great swathes of unknown trees without which any forest must remain a blur” (p. 2).This book is a collaborative volume by a team of multilingual scholars of Communist-era Eastern Europe, a genre popular in much of the recent literature on the global history of Communism and East–South encounters. Twelve chapters, covering the Warsaw Pact countries, Yugoslavia, several African countries, Vietnam, and North Korea, give texture to the East–South encounter. A multitude of social spaces in the Second and Third World thus take shape in front of the reader's eye: schools, universities, trade union colleges, military training camps, museums, exhibition halls, hospitals, construction sites, hostels, pubs, and prisons. The reader learns about multiple interactions between Eastern Europeans and residents of Third World countries in these spaces. This approach yields diverse and unexpected findings. Małgorzata Mazurek shows that scholars from Poland, teaching at the University of Ghana in the 1950s and 1960s, transmitted Western-centric instead of Moscow-focused academic knowledge. Bogdan C. Iacob explains that when Romanian women in the 1970s and 1980s could not procure abortions at home, they would undergo abortions in Libya instead.Reading these case studies together, one finds common themes. Most contributors emphasize that the social spaces of encounters between East and South were “constructed from many sides, not always in harmony, and often with divergent understandings of context, methods, and goals” (p. 20). Actors from Third World countries coconstructed these spaces. Alena Amalgir, for example, explains how Vietnamese workers made Czechoslovak hostels their own, as well as how much power Vietnamese interpreters wielded over Czechoslovak courtrooms.Many contributors also show how Eastern Europeans often thought in terms of civilizational hierarchies. As Péter Apor discusses in his excellent opening chapter on North Korean war orphans in 1950s Eastern European schools, “[e]ven though many citizens and officials in socialist Eastern Europe sought to dismantle the legacies of colonial hierarchies and replace them with partnerships between equals, in practice they believed themselves to be helping the postcolonial nations by exporting the achievements of an advanced (socialist) civilization” (p. 38). Spaces of encounter thus turned into presumed “gateways to civilization” (p. 29). As several contributors highlight, such civilizational hierarchies followed from a belief among Eastern Europeans in universal stages of history within a Eurocentric Marxist-Leninist temporal framework. To them, traveling to Third World countries felt like going back in time to Eastern Europe's past. The final chapter, coauthored by Eric Burton, Zoltán Ginelli, James Mark, and Nemanja Rodnjić—the volume's grand finale—discerns these presumed civilizational hierarchies in accounts of travelers from East to South. The chapter goes even further: Eastern Europeans traditionally claimed that “due to their own experience of being colonized, they were free of the rapacious colonial desires that marked the West” (p. 241). However, the coauthors find under the surface of presumedly anticolonial travelogues “fantasies of global power, domination, and mobility” (p. 238).These presumed civilizational hierarchies were challenged from multiple angles. According to Radina Vučetić, Yugoslav cultural diplomacy explicitly criticized the “Soviet imposition of cultural values” on the Third World (p. 80). Iacob describes how Romanian medical personnel in Libya had a hard time defending their presumably higher developmental and civilizational stage when they were, in fact, employed by and accountable to their Arab hosts. Apor shows how North Korean officials protected their compatriots’ national identity and loyalty to the North Korean state against Eastern European “civilizing” attempts. According to Mikuláš Pešta, the Egyptian government prohibited Czechoslovak military experts from teaching Marxism-Leninism to Egyptian servicemen.Even so, important actors from some Third World countries largely agreed with their Eastern counterparts. Natalia Telepneva shows, for example, that the Cape Verdean leader Amílcar Cabral and Soviet officials shared modernizing goals. Cabral wanted Soviet military training camps to transfer to African fighters not only military expertise but also “theoretical and practical knowledge so that they could act as agents of modernity” at home (p. 169).These rich findings are supported by sources from both the East and the South. Telepneva, for example, analyzes memoirs of and interviews with former guerrillas from Guinea-Bissau and Cape Verde. Christine Varga-Harris explores correspondence between Soviet women and their female counterparts in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. Roth-Ey studies letters written from Third World countries to Radio Moscow, and Alamgir highlights letters written by Vietnamese suspects awaiting trial in Czechoslovak prisons. The fact that many of these sources are accessible only through Eastern European archives leads, as Burton points out, to an “epistemological break” but should not prevent historians from using Eastern European archives as “shadow archives” (Jean Allman) of the Third World (p. 198). At the same time, some contributors use sources from the Third World that are not found in Eastern European archives: Mazurek uses sources from the National Archives of Ghana. Burton and Elizabeth Bishop employ sources in Swahili and Arabic, respectively. The volume thereby points to a fruitful avenue for further research based on the many sources in European and non-European languages yet to be unearthed from Third World countries. Returning to Roty-Ey's metaphor, we can see that in the history of East–South encounters during the Cold War, many trees have yet to be explored.

title: Curriculum, Archives, and the Digital Turn: The Italian American Experience and the Transnational Approach to Community-Based Learning
abstract: The outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic in March 2020 precipitated a swift transition to online instruction, compelling the integration of new technological tools. This shift not only reshaped our approaches to course design, student assessment, and achieving course objectives, but it also underscored the necessity of fostering a sense of community in the absence of physical classroom and student residential settings. At Santa Clara University (SCU), the Jesuit institution where I teach, the commitment to cura personalis—the attention to the whole person—became paramount, aligning with the university's emphasis on competence and transformative education for global citizenship and social change.During this transformative period, the Italian studies program at SCU underwent a significant evolution. The pivot to online teaching spurred curricular and co-curricular initiatives within the program, providing our students with new opportunities for experiential learning and research with local communities and overseas partners (foundations, associations, artist-activists, museums, etc.). These initiatives aimed to enable students to develop intercultural competence, professional skills, and civic engagement, reflecting SCU's educational philosophy. Simultaneously, those initiatives resonated with critical questions and curricular challenges that are relevant to the entire field of italianistica in and outside of the United States. A growing number of teacher-scholars are advocating for decolonizing and transnationalizing Italian studies, urging a reevaluation of conventional frameworks and curricular development. According to Lina Insana: We in Italian Studies are not alone in thinking through these problems, but our field is uniquely situated to do so in productive and exciting ways. The “transnational turn” (Bond, 2014) together with the “postcolonial turn” (Ponzanesi, 2012) and a growing body of work in geocritical studies allow us to think not beyond the nation but alongside it, without being constrained by it. In so doing, we open our field to diasporic and other forms of mobility that have “made Italians” in spaces that are situated beyond dominant frameworks of blood or soil. We can better appreciate the importance of cultural, linguistic, and other bonds that have shaped Italian belonging alongside notions of citizenship. (2022, 50)In 2022, the Italian American Studies Association conference, themed Mining the Diaspora: Italian-American Materialities, Archaeologies, and Intersections, offered a platform for scholars to exchange insights and contemplate viable trajectories for curricular innovation at the undergraduate level. The conference was held in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, a hub of collaborative partnerships and student research projects, envisioned and led by Insana, that highlight the potential of elevating archival collections through undergraduate research, particularly in understudied areas of Italian migrations to the United States (Insana 2022, 52). For their interdisciplinary breadth, these projects are drawing attention from scholars working at different junctures of Italian studies with diaspora and material culture studies (Ruberto and Sciorra 2022b) to digital humanities (Hall 2019).Backed by her experience with multiyear project-based teams connecting the “Italies” within and beyond the national space, Insana has recently proposed a compelling case for a transnational approach to community-based learning (CBL) that articulates a distinctively Italian model of engagement with local communities.1 She argues that one way for Italian programs to embrace, and benefit from, the interdisciplinarity of transnational Italian studies and diaspora studies is through “a particularly Italian brand of CBL: that is, by leveraging relationships with virtual and ‘bricks & mortar’ archives of the Italian diasporic experience” (2023, 373). This multi-lens approach engages students as linguistic and cultural mediators between the historical archive of the Italian diaspora of a century or more ago and the contemporary Italian American ethnics descending from those transnational migrants. This article examines the applicability of a transnational CBL model based on the Pittsburgh experience to the Santa Clara/San Jose area of California, an area with a rich but comparably understudied history of Italian arrivals long before it became known as Silicon Valley.Two sets of questions guide my exploration. The first set revolves around disciplinary boundaries and porous edges, by asking, for instance: What does it look like, in different locations and academic environments, to lean on archives to create projects that stand to benefit students, Italian programs, and the dialogue between ethnics and their histories as well as italianistica and Italian diaspora studies? And how can an interdisciplinary mapping of place enrich a transnational approach to the field of Italian studies that simultaneously contends with notions of cultural inclusion and distinctiveness (Fiore 2023, 347; Burdett, Polezzi, and Spadaro 2020, 3)? The second set of questions adds a further layer of complexity to my inquiry by foregrounding the digital turn, which took place alongside, historically speaking, the developments of postcolonial and transnational frameworks in Italian studies. How might the advent of the digital create a space for investigating more deeply and through the lens of decolonization the transnational histories of Italians abroad (specifically in California)? And conversely, how might CBL projects in transnational Italian studies contribute to a more active engagement of digital humanities with issues of inclusivity that currently is lagging behind in the field, as Crystal Hall (2019) points out? The pedagogical experience presented in this article is informed by the reciprocity between “digital” and “mainstream” humanities that has been framed as central to the current need for the humanities to communicate their value to the public (Liu 2012). In his provocative question, “Where Is Cultural Criticism in the Digital Humanities?” Alan Liu calls on digital humanists to “create technologies that fundamentally reimagine humanities advocacy” and “to build advocacy into the ordinary work of the humanities, so that research and teaching organically generate advocacy in the form of publicly meaningful representations of the humanities” (497). While the broader implications of the “digital” in the humanities are beyond the scope of this article, the principle of reciprocity orients my approach to both sets of questions, in line with the centrality of reciprocity to Insana's CBL model. By documenting the integration of archives and undergraduate research in the Italian curriculum at SCU, this article primarily contributes to ongoing critical dialogues within Italian studies and engages with Insana's call for evidence of similar experiences in diverse contexts. It also invites reflections on the relationality between Italian studies and digital humanities.The central inquiry revolves around the intersections of Italian belonging that lie at the core of my current scholarly and teaching work. For the past seven years or so, in a course titled “The Italian American Experience,” I have learned, along with undergraduate students, to expand notions of Italian belonging by gradually centering interdisciplinary work around the archives. title: Learning Positive-Incentive Point Sampling in Neural Implicit Fields for Object Pose Estimation
abstract: Learning neural implicit fields of 3D shapes is a rapidly emerging field that enables shape representation at arbitrary resolutions. Due to the flexibility, neural implicit fields have succeeded in many research areas, including shape reconstruction, novel view image synthesis, and more recently, object pose estimation. Neural implicit fields enable learning dense correspondences between the camera space and the object's canonical space-including unobserved regions in camera space-significantly boosting object pose estimation performance in challenging scenarios like highly occluded objects and novel shapes. Despite progress, predicting canonical coordinates for unobserved camera-space regions remains challenging due to the lack of direct observational signals. This necessitates heavy reliance on the model's generalization ability, resulting in high uncertainty. Consequently, densely sampling points across the entire camera space may yield inaccurate estimations that hinder the learning process and compromise performance. To alleviate this problem, we propose a method combining an SO(3)-equivariant convolutional implicit network and a positive-incentive point sampling (PIPS) strategy. The SO(3)-equivariant convolutional implicit network estimates point-level attributes with SO(3)-equivariance at arbitrary query locations, demonstrating superior performance compared to most existing baselines. The PIPS strategy dynamically determines sampling locations based on the input, thereby boosting the network's accuracy and training efficiency. Our method outperforms the state-of-the-art on three pose estimation datasets. Notably, it demonstrates significant improvements in challenging scenarios, such as objects captured with unseen pose, high occlusion, novel geometry, and severe noise.

title: Learning Positive-Incentive Point Sampling in Neural Implicit Fields for Object Pose Estimation
venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
abstract: Learning neural implicit fields of 3D shapes is a rapidly emerging field that enables shape representation at arbitrary resolutions. Due to the flexibility, neural implicit fields have succeeded in many research areas, including shape reconstruction, novel view image synthesis, and more recently, object pose estimation. Neural implicit fields enable learning dense correspondences between the camera space and the object's canonical space - including unobserved regions in camera space - significantly boosting object pose estimation performance in challenging scenarios like highly occluded objects and novel shapes. Despite progress, predicting canonical coordinates for unobserved camera-space regions remains challenging due to the lack of direct observational signals. This necessitates heavy reliance on the model's generalization ability, resulting in high uncertainty. Consequently, densely sampling points across the entire camera space may yield inaccurate estimations that hinder the learning process and compromise performance. To alleviate this problem, we propose a method combining an SO(3)-equivariant convolutional implicit network and a positive-incentive point sampling (PIPS) strategy. The SO(3)-equivariant convolutional implicit network estimates point-level attributes with SO(3)-equivariance at arbitrary query locations, demonstrating superior performance compared to most existing baselines. The PIPS strategy dynamically determines sampling locations based on the input, thereby boosting the network's accuracy and training efficiency. The PIPS strategy is implemented with a PIPS estimation network which generates sparse sample points with distinctive features capable of determining all object pose DoFs with high certainty. To collect the training data of the PIPS estimation network, we propose to automatically generate the pseudo ground-truth with a teacher model. Our method outperforms the state-of-the-art on three pose estimation datasets. It achieves 0.63 in the $5^{\circ }2$5∘2 cm metric on NOCS-REAL275, 0.62 in the $5^{\circ }5$5∘5 cm metric on ShapeNet-C, and 77.3 in the AR metric on LineMOD-O. Notably, it demonstrates significant improvements in challenging scenarios, such as objects captured with unseen pose, high occlusion, novel geometry, and severe noise.

title: GridFormer: Point-Grid Transformer for Surface Reconstruction
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Implicit neural networks have emerged as a crucial technology in 3D surface reconstruction. To reconstruct continuous surfaces from discrete point clouds, encoding the input points into regular grid features (plane or volume) has been commonly employed in existing approaches. However, these methods typically use the grid as an index for uniformly scattering point features. Compared with the irregular point features, the regular grid features may sacrifice some reconstruction details but improve efficiency. To take full advantage of these two types of features, we introduce a novel and high-efficiency attention mechanism between the grid and point features named Point-Grid Transformer (GridFormer). This mechanism treats the grid as a transfer point connecting the space and point cloud. Our method maximizes the spatial expressiveness of grid features and maintains computational efficiency. Furthermore, optimizing predictions over the entire space could potentially result in blurred boundaries. To address this issue, we further propose a boundary optimization strategy incorporating margin binary cross-entropy loss and boundary sampling. This approach enables us to achieve a more precise representation of the object structure. Our experiments validate that our method is effective and outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches under widely used benchmarks by producing more precise geometry reconstructions. The code is available at https://github.com/list17/GridFormer.

title: VideoSwap: Customized Video Subject Swapping with Interactive Semantic Point Correspondence
venue: IEEE Computer Society Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition/Proceedings - IEEE Computer Society Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition/Proceedings
abstract: Current diffusion-based video editing primarily focuses on structure-preserved editing by utilizing various dense correspondences to ensure temporal consistency and motion alignment. However, these approaches are often in-effective when the target edit involves a shape change. To embark on video editing with shape change, we explore customized video subject swapping in this work, where we aim to replace the main subject in a source video with a target subject having a distinct identity and potentially different shape. In contrast to previous methods that rely on dense correspondences, we introduce the Video Swap framework that exploits semantic point correspondences, inspired by our observation that only a small number of semantic points are necessary to align the subject's motion trajectory and modify its shape. We also introduce various user-point interactions (e.g., removing points and dragging points) to address various semantic point correspondence. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art video subject swapping results across a variety of real-world videos.

title: Advances in 3D Neural Stylization: A Survey
abstract: Abstract Modern artificial intelligence offers a novel and transformative approach to creating digital art across diverse styles and modalities like images, videos and 3D data, unleashing the power of creativity and revolutionizing the way that we perceive and interact with visual content. This paper reports on recent advances in stylized 3D asset creation and manipulation with the expressive power of neural networks. We establish a taxonomy for neural stylization, considering crucial design choices such as scene representation, guidance data, optimization strategies, and output styles. Building on such taxonomy, our survey first revisits the background of neural stylization on 2D images, and then presents in-depth discussions on recent neural stylization methods for 3D data, accompanied by a benchmark evaluating selected mesh and neural field stylization methods. Based on the insights gained from the survey, we highlight the practical significance, open challenges, future research, and potential impacts of neural stylization, which facilitates researchers and practitioners to navigate the rapidly evolving landscape of 3D content creation using modern artificial intelligence.

title: NICP: Neural ICP for 3D Human Registration at Scale
Geometry Transfer for Stylizing Radiance Fields
venue: IEEE Computer Society Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition/Proceedings - IEEE Computer Society Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition/Proceedings
abstract: Shape and geometric patterns are essential in defining stylistic identity. However, current 3D style transfer methods predominantly focus on transferring colors and textures, often overlooking geometric aspects. In this paper, we introduce Geometry Transfer, a novel method that leverages geometric deformation for 3D style transfer. This technique employs depth maps to extract a style guide, subsequently applied to stylize the geometry of radiance fields. Moreover, we propose new techniques that utilize geometric cues from the 3D scene, thereby enhancing aesthetic expressiveness and more accurately reflecting intended styles. Our extensive experiments show that Geometry Transfer enables a broader and more expressive range of stylizations, thereby significantly expanding the scope of 3D style transfer.

title: Multi-view 3D Object Reconstruction and Uncertainty Modelling with Neural Shape Prior
venue: IEEE Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision
abstract: 3D object reconstruction is important for semantic scene understanding. It is challenging to reconstruct detailed 3D shapes from monocular images directly due to a lack of depth information, occlusion and noise. Most current methods generate deterministic object models without any awareness of the uncertainty of the reconstruction. We tackle this problem by leveraging a neural object representation which learns an object shape distribution from large dataset of 3d object models and maps it into a latent space. We propose a method to model uncertainty as part of the representation and define an uncertainty-aware encoder which generates latent codes with uncertainty directly from individual input images. Further, we propose a method to propagate the uncertainty in the latent code to SDF values and generate a 3d object mesh with local uncertainty for each mesh component. Finally, we propose an incremental fusion method under a Bayesian framework to fuse the latent codes from multi-view observations. We evaluate the system in both synthetic and real datasets to demonstrate the effectiveness of uncertainty-based fusion to improve 3D object reconstruction accuracy.

title: One Registration is Worth Two Segmentations
Revisiting Map Relations for Unsupervised Non-Rigid Shape Matching
abstract: We propose a novel unsupervised learning approach for non-rigid 3D shape matching. Our approach improves upon recent state-of-the art deep functional map methods and can be applied to a broad range of different challenging scenarios. Previous deep functional map methods mainly focus on feature extraction and aim exclusively at obtaining more expressive features for functional map computation. However, the importance of the functional map computation itself is often neglected and the relationship between the functional map and point-wise map is underexplored. In this paper, we systematically investigate the coupling relationship between the functional map from the functional map solver and the point-wise map based on feature similarity. To this end, we propose a self-adaptive functional map solver to adjust the functional map regularisation for different shape matching scenarios, together with a vertex-wise contrastive loss to obtain more discriminative features. Using different challenging datasets (including non-isometry, topological noise and partiality), we demonstrate that our method substantially outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods.

title: Synchronous Diffusion for Unsupervised Smooth Non-rigid 3D Shape Matching
Generic Objects as Pose Probes for Few-Shot View Synthesis
venue: IEEE Transactions on Circuits and Systems for Video Technology
abstract: Radiance fields, including NeRFs and 3D Gaussians, demonstrate great potential in high-fidelity rendering and scene reconstruction, while they require a substantial number of posed images as input. COLMAP is frequently employed for preprocessing to estimate poses. However, COLMAP necessitates a large number of feature matches to operate effectively, and struggles with scenes characterized by sparse features, large baselines, or few-view images. We aim to tackle few-view NeRF reconstruction using only 3 to 6 unposed scene images, freeing from COLMAP initializations. Inspired by the idea of calibration boards in traditional pose calibration, we propose a novel approach of utilizing everyday objects, commonly found in both images and real life, as “pose probes”. By initializing the probe object as a cube shape, we apply a dual-branch volume rendering optimization (object NeRF and scene NeRF) to constrain the pose optimization and jointly refine the geometry. PnP matching is used to initialize poses between images incrementally, where only a few feature matches are enough. PoseProbe achieves state-of-the-art performance in pose estimation and novel view synthesis across multiple datasets in experiments. We demonstrate its effectiveness, particularly in few-view and large-baseline scenes where COLMAP struggles. In ablations, using different objects in a scene yields comparable performance, showing that PoseProbe is robust to the choice of probe objects. Our project page is available at:https://zhirui-gao.github.io/PoseProbe.github.io/

title: Generation of semantic isomorphic mesh using implicit function representation
GO: A two-step generative optimization method for point cloud registration
