title: From the Editors
abstract: Regularly, the Journal of Appalachian Studies welcomes proposals for special issues that allow the entire issue to focus on one topic within our broad and expansive field of study. This issue, which focuses on emerging and intersectional women's and gender studies grew organically from the community of Appalachian studies scholars. As you will read below, the issue is a collaborative and interdisciplinary project highlighting the best of the field. Huge thanks to Anna Rachel Terman and Krystal Brooke Carter, to our late colleague and friend Tammy “Tambone” Clemons, and to all of the contributors to the issue.Thanks, as always, for support from the Appalachian Studies Association office. Mary Thomas and Ann E. Bryant work together tirelessly to keep the organization running and to help shepherd these issues into your hands. Thanks, also, to Associate Editor Michael Martin for his consistent energy and attention in service of the Journal of Appalachian Studies. Meredith McCarroll, EditorThis themed issue of the Journal of Appalachian Studies has its origins in a series of roundtables organized by a consistent but evolving group of participants at the Appalachian Studies Association (ASA) annual conferences. As a graduate student at the University of Kentucky in 2015, Kathryn Engle proposed the first roundtable as a response to the recently published Women of the Mountain South: Identity, Work, and Activism (Rice and Tedesco 2015). That first conference session took place in 2016 and inspired the organization of a roundtable the following year, focused on “Examining Feminism in Appalachia Through Contemporary Issues: A Discussion of Intersections and Place.” For about a decade, this roundtable became an annual tradition, with some new participants joining in and others cycling out. Well over one hundred people attended and engaged in discussions with panelists and each other. It was those series of roundtables that brought us together as co-editors.Likewise, the process of publishing this themed issue spanned quite a chunk of time. As we approach this final part of the process, we reflect on the beginning, which in some ways seems like a distant era where the topics and themes were less weighed down by the current political context, in addition to the grief we feel about losing one of our roundtable mainstays and co-editors, Dr. Tammy Clemons. In 2022, when our “Feminism in Appalachian Studies” roundtable group started making plans for the themed issue, Tammy was an enthusiastic leader. She did a lot of work in the beginning phases when we were discussing the focus, drafting and revising language for the call, making lists of potential contributors and reviewers, and even considering submitting her own article to the issue. In her correspondence on the themed issue, she was always enthusiastic about the progress being made, celebrating the small wins, always signing off emails on a positive note, followed by “Tambone.” In August 2024, Tammy had to take a step back to focus on her health, and we very much hoped for her return so that she would be able to participate in the outcome of not just this journal project, but a culmination of the many years of feminist thinking and collaboration at ASA annual conferences.1 Tammy passed away on January 4, 2025, and while we are so sad she is not able to be here with us to celebrate the completion of this project, her influence and contributions remain an integral part of this issue. Tammy was a force to be reckoned with and a fierce advocate for the next generation of Appalachian writers and scholars. We feel the loss of a life and career cut short but carry her spirit through this issue focused on emerging and intersectional scholarship. This themed issue is for her!In keeping with Tammy's passionate spirit, we find ourselves increasingly energized and appreciative of the scholarship in this issue. The continued ASA sessions have served as our annual in-person brainstorming opportunity, a time to bring forth new issues in the field and learn from others. These shared moments at the conference provided us with re-energization and focus as well as a place to challenge and be challenged in our thinking. At the 45th annual ASA conference in 2022, our roundtable titled “Forming an Intersectional Women's and Gender Studies Interest Group at ASA” yielded conversation about the need for ongoing work surrounding gender and feminism in Appalachia and how to continue that work. In the months that followed, we began conversations to propose this themed issue of the Journal of Appalachian Studies, in hopes of formalizing and publishing current work in the field. That summer, in the wake of the overturn of Roe vs. Wade, roundtable participants worked together with ASA staff to organize an ASA online meetup for reproductive rights in Appalachia, continuing the focus on scholarship and praxis central to intersectional approaches to feminism. The following 2023 roundtable session, titled “Intersectional Women's and Gender Studies Interest Group,” led to conversations on the state of and threats to higher education and specifically pushback for teaching and engaging with gender and identity studies issues on our campuses. One participant found our session by recommendation from a colleague after experiencing discipline and punishment for organizing a community event through their institution that featured gender and sexuality issues and identities. Sharing this story opened the conversation for many others to voice the fear and pushback surrounding teaching and engaging with issues of women, gender, sexuality, race, and other intersections of identity on our campuses and communities. Since that time, we have witnessed the intensification of efforts to dismantle places and spaces for discussing and addressing issues of gender and identity-based inequalities.Indeed, this themed issue is being published during a time of pronounced backlash to decades of progress for women's and gender studies.2 Changes at all levels of government have impacted women's and gender rights and the lived experience of gender in our region and well beyond. Of course, in Appalachia, gender has never been a settled issue, and in Appalachian studies, we have a wealth of scholarship interrogating gender from multiple disciplines and perspectives. The work included in this issue is part of a growing body of scholarship on women, gender, and feminism in Appalachia.It would be impossible in this brief format to name all of the scholars, activists, and people who have contributed to the historiography of women, gender, and feminist thought in Appalachian studies. It is an honor to be in conversation with their scholarship and legacies. Perhaps most notably, many of us would not be here without Helen Lewis's founding work in Appalachian studies, where she was compelled by the intersection of place, gender, and race early on when working on her master's thesis completed in 1949 (Jennings 2012). While it is common to point to Lewis as the “Grandmother of Appalachian studies” for her foundational work, Appalachian studies also includes the biographies and stories of influential figures and work from earlier eras, such as Mother Jones, Memphis Tennessee Garrison, and the Frontier Nursing Service, to name just a few. Likewise, feminist and social justice work has been prominent in Appalachia and social movements in Appalachia for decades. For example, Jessie Wilkerson's and Shannon Bell's works highlight women's historic and ongoing contributions to fighting for social, political, economic, and environmental justice (Wilkerson 2016; Bell 2013). Jillean McCommons's recent work shows us that Black Appalachian women were trailblazers of intersectional racial justice and feminist thought and action during the early 1970s (McCommons 2025). History is always close, as our current realities are impacted by the past. For example, the work of Staysha Quentrill, featured in The New York Times (Morgan 2025) and highlighted in Black By God, The West Virginian (Black By God2025), reveals the ongoing legacy of Black midwives and the structural inequalities they faced in doing their work in the past and still face today.As the field of Appalachian studies has developed, scholarship on women's contributions to Appalachian life, such as sustaining family, working in paid labor, engaging in activism, resisting extractive industries, and leading the fight for education in the region, represents a long-term commitment in Appalachian studies to issues of gender and feminism.3 Yet many questions remain. How have our understandings of gender become more expansive in the region? How do we understand and practice feminism in Appalachia? Furthermore, how do intersectional identities and experiences confront, imagine, and impact understandings of, within, and outside the region? Thinking about these questions among others, participatory discussions during the ASA roundtable sessions addressed intersections of power and privilege for women and feminist ideas in Appalachia; the importance of social media and feminism in the region; ecofeminist activism and livelihoods; material, performative, and symbolic aspects of Appalachian feminism(s); and meanings of intersectionality as understood by diverse regional feminist scholars, activists, and artists. This themed issue of the Journal of Appalachian Studies provides a venue for continuing and formalizing these conversations by examining the intersections of gender and place through feminist scholarship and diverse marginalized positionalities.Despite the longtime presence of intersectional feminist thought in the Appalachian region, the intersection of gender and place is an exciting and emerging area of scholarship in Appalachian studies.4 The relationship between feminism and Appalachia; the tensions between feminism and Appalachian identity; the intersecting and/or intersectional work that women in Appalachia do; the way that place shapes gender; and the way that gender is expressed, lived, cultivated, and constrained by place are all topics deserving of more understanding from academic, activist, artistic, and community perspectives. This issue brings attention to these ongoing and developing ideas in order to push forward and crystallize current perspectives on women, gender, and feminism in Appalachia. We also recognize this issue is again just one part of a broader and unfinished project on gender, women, and feminism in Appalachia. The current political and cultural backlash raises many new questions, while ongoing obscured voices and buried histories are still awaiting attention.Included here are three research articles, a teaching note, and two research notes. First, Leia K. Cain's article, “Guided by Starlight: Story Constellations of Queer Women's Resistance in Southern Appalachia,” centers on queer women who choose to remain in Appalachia for their university education rather than migrate to areas with more affirming cultural climates, further developing bell hooks's concept of belonging in Appalachia. Second, Emily C. Cobb's article “A ‘slice of heaven’: The Cosplaying of Rural Life with #Homestead Tradwives in Appalachia” examines the intersection of the #Tradwife/#Homestead movements on social media within an Appalachian context. Third, Hannah Krull's article “Butched Embodiment: Working Bodies and the Appalachian Landscape” poses the idea that many rural and Appalachian women engage in a queer gender embodiment informed by manual labor and working-class experience—working the land in particular—which she calls “butched embodiment.”Next, LeAnna T. Luney and E. Gale Greenlee's teaching note “Holla!: Black Girlhood Pedagogies in an Abolitionist Appalachian Classroom” argues that embracing Black girlhood studies pedagogy bolsters students’ critical consciousness and resists the very sociopolitical contexts that wrongly dismiss Black girls as having little to contribute to feminist theories and praxes. Finally, two research notes round out the issue. First, Tess Ann Simpson and Mary Jo Hedrick's research note “‘What Makes an Appalachian?’: An Intersectional Psychological Investigation of Appalachian Identity and Protective Factors” explores, through an intersectional and strengths-based perspective, who endorses an Appalachian identity. Second, Jacqueline Yahn's research note “Gladys and Margaret Dysart, a Silhouette: ‘Well, then just leave it alone’” uses portraiture methodology to reveal the legacy of women's social and environmental activism in rural Appalachia.Taken together, these articles, teaching note, and research notes represent various Emerging and Intersectional Women's and Gender Studies themes in Appalachia. Interrogating gender as it intersects with other social identities, age, materiality, space, place, and power helps expand our understanding of what Appalachia is and who Appalachians are. Furthermore, the scholarship here points us to better understanding how gender and intersecting identities matter for Appalachian experiences and outcomes, whether that is in the classroom, the workplace, the home, the woods, on social media, or the endless possibilities of places and spaces where gender matters in Appalachia. We hope you find insights and inspiration in these pages. Thank you to the authors for their time, patience, and scholarly contributions to this issue, Appalachian studies, and the interdisciplinary fields to which their scholarship belongs.Five important, recent nonfiction books in Appalachian studies are reviewed in the final section. Four of the books are monographs, while one, The Foxfire Book of Appalachian Women: Stories of Landscape and Community in the Mountain South (2023), is an edited collection. Cassie Dawn Ball reviews that collection, while Lucy M. Long reviews Erica Abrams Locklear's Appalachia on the Table: Representing Mountain Food and People (2023), a new work that studies Appalachian foodways. Another foodways-centered book, Ashli Quesinberry Stokes and Wendy Atkins-Sayre's Hungry Roots: How Food Communicates Appalachia's Search for Resilience (2024), is reviewed by Jed DeBruin. Meanwhile, an early Appalachian studies intervention, Amanda E. Hayes’ The Madison Women: Gender, Higher Education, and Literacy in Nineteenth-Century Appalachia (2024), is reviewed by Elizabeth “Betsy” DiSalvo Osborne. Finally, West Virginia and Kentucky labor history is the topic of John Hennen's A Union for Appalachian Healthcare Workers: The Radical Roots and Hard Fights of Local 1199 (2021), reviewed by Luke Manget.In addition, we again thank Tammy Clemons; her legacy continues through this journal. Thanks to Kathryn Engle, a longtime supporter of this work and participant on panels and the development of this issue. Thanks to Meredith McCarroll and Ann E. Bryant for supporting this issue through JAS. Thank you to everyone who took the time to submit abstracts, manuscripts, and reviews, and to provide feedback for this issue. Thanks to recent roundtable participants who influenced this issue including Hallie Chillag, Kathryn Engle, Crystal Good, Zada Komara, Jordan Laney, Cassie Patterson, Jess Scott, Brandi Slider, and Lucy Thompson. Finally, thank you to the attendees of those ASA sessions, whose questions and contributions kept the conversations evolving and relevant, guiding the theme of this issue. title: سيميائية الحواس في ديوان علقمة ذي جدن الحميري [ت10هـ]
abstract: الملخص تعدّ حياة الإنسان سلسلة متراكبة من المشاعر التي تتحول بمرور الزمن إلى علامات دالة تكشف ما خَفِي منها. وإذا كانت التجارب الإنسانية تسهم في تشكيل رؤية الشاعر وتصوره للواقع المعيش فإن المدركات الحسية عند عَلْقَمَة ذِي جَدَن الحِمْيَرِيّ [ت10هـ]، المتمثلة في المدركات البصرية والسمعية والذوقية واللمسية والشمية، قد أنتجت فاعليتها على مستوى الخطاب الرثائي والدلالة؛ إذ تحولت هذه المدركات من واقعها المادي/الحسي إلى مدلولات ثقافية واجتماعية وحضارية ذات طاقات إيحائية ومحمولات إشارية انبثقت بطبيعة الحال من خلال العلاقة بين الدوال ومدلولاتها في ظل معطيات الإدراك اللغوي. ويهدف هذا البحث إلى دراسة سيميائية الحواس في ديوان عَلْقَمَة ذِي جَدَن الحِمْيَرِيّ[ت10هـ]؛ وذلك بغية إبراز جماليات الصور الحسية عند ذلك الشاعر الضرير الذي فاق بعض المبصرين في توظيف الحواس الخمسة في تشكيل مضامينه الشعرية والتعبير عن رؤيته الفكرية، وذلك بوصف النص الشعري بنية علاماتية لا تقتصر على تجاور الكلمات والمفردات؛ إنما هو بنية معقدة ومتداخلة ومركبة من الرموز والعلامات التي تتلاحم لإنتاج المعنى والدلالة وفق نسق إشاري. وقد توصل البحث إلى مجموعة من النتائج؛ أهمها: أن عَلْقَمَة ذِي جَدَن الحِمْيَرِيّ اتخذ من سيميائية الحواس مدخلا لتجسيد المجد الحِمْيَريّ والهوية القَحْطانية كنظام دلالي متكامل يشير إلى البنية الرمزية للعروبة والمجد التليد. فضلا عن ابتكار عَلْقَمَة ذِي جَدَن الحِمْيَرِيّ ما يمكن تسميته بتراسل الأصوات؛ وأقصد به إحلال الشاعر صوت حيوان مكان آخر لدلالة ما، إذ راسل بين أصوات الحيوانات؛ فأنزل ضُباح الثعالب منزلة عواء الذئاب؛ علامة سيميائية على الغدر والخيانة والتلصص. وقد يكون هذا التراسل الصوتي دالا على أشخاص بعينهم حمّلهم الشاعر مسئولية الخراب والدمار الذي حلّ بالمجد الحِميَرِيّ. وقد اعتمد هذا البحث على المنهج السيميائي الذي يعدّ النص الشعري مجموعة من العلامات الدالة الحاملة لأسرار كثيرة تتكشف في ضوء العلاقة الجدلية القائمة بين الدال والمدلول، وبين الحضور والغياب. وهو أحد المناهج الجديدة التي تسعى إلى بناء نمط ثقافي لقراءة النص الحامل لأسرار كثيرة ودلالات متعددة، والوقوف عند علاماته، وفكّ رموزه وشفراته التي تتخذ من السمات الشكلية مؤشرا رئيسا للنفاذ إلى عمق النص وتأويله. الكلمات المفتاحية: السيميائية، الحواس، علقمة ذي جَدَن الحِميريّ، الشعراء المخضرمون. Abstract Human life is a layered sequence of emotions that, over time, transform into semiotic signs revealing what lies hidden within them. Since human experiences contribute to shaping the poet’s vision and perception of lived reality, the sensory perceptions of ʿAlqamah Dhū Jadan al-Ḥimyarī (d. 10 AH)—including sight, hearing, taste, touch, and smell—proved effective at the level of elegiac discourse and meaning. These perceptions shifted from their material/sensory reality to cultural, social, and civilizational signifiers charged with evocative powers and semiotic connotations, emerging naturally through the relationship between signifiers and their signifieds within the framework of linguistic perception. This study aims to explore the semiotics of the senses in the dīwān of ʿAlqamah Dhū Jadan al-Ḥimyarī (d. 10 AH), in order to highlight the aesthetics of sensory imagery in the work of this blind poet who surpassed some sighted ones in employing the five senses to shape his poetic content and articulate his intellectual vision. The poetic text is approached here not as a mere sequence of words and vocabulary, but rather as a complex, intertwined structure of symbols and signs that converge to generate meaning and significance according to a semiotic system. The research reached several conclusions, the most important of which is that ʿAlqamah Dhū Jadan al-Ḥimyarī employed the semiotics of the senses as a means to embody Ḥimyarite glory and Qaḥṭānite identity as an integrated semiotic system pointing to the symbolic structure of Arabism and its noble heritage. Furthermore, he innovated what may be called a “correspondence of sounds,” by which the poet substitutes the sound of one animal for another to convey a certain meaning. He thus correlated animal sounds—placing the yelping of foxes in the position of wolves’ howls—as a semiotic sign of betrayal, treachery, and stealth. This sound correspondence may well allude to specific individuals whom the poet held responsible for the ruin and devastation that befell Ḥimyarite glory. The study is based on the semiotic method, which regards the poetic text as a network of signs bearing many hidden secrets that unfold in light of the dialectical relationship between signifier and signified, between presence and absence. It is one of the new approaches that seeks to build a cultural model for reading texts laden with multiple meanings and secrets, by identifying their signs and deciphering their codes, which take formal features as key indicators for penetrating into the depth of the text and interpreting it. Keywords: Semiotics, senses, ʿAlqamah Dhū Jadan al-Ḥimyarī, Mukhaḍram poets.

title: Jan Shipps
abstract: This memorial essay blends professional and personal recollections, in part because its subject was adept at doing so herself. Reflecting on this dear friend, I have cobbled together a reminiscence that brings me comfort, even as I miss Jan's laugh, her addiction to checking all word choices in her thesaurus, her strong morning coffee, and her love of telling stories. What follows does not live up to her standards but is written in the sure knowledge that she would have loved the outpouring of affection and gratitude that accompanies this and other remembrances of her long and interesting life.Born Jo Ann Barnett in 1929, the remarkable woman who was known as Jan married Tony Shipps when she was nineteen. Jan grew up in the deep South—as anyone who ever heard her pronounce the word “evidence” will testify. She grew up in a family struggling to hold onto its commitment to education, music, and reading. Her father, as Jan used to say, ran a “one-horse coal mine” in Alabama. Her mother, Thalia, about whom she talked frequently, clearly was a force to be reckoned with. Thanks to Thalia, Jan studied piano and spent one year at college before the family's finances cratered so drastically that she had to come back home to work. Jan's talent as a musician frequently put food on the table, even after she married Tony. She often told stories of her work as a piano player in bars, clearly a role that she relished, in spite of (or likely more accurately, because of) the raucous tendencies of her audience.Jan and Tony moved to Michigan, where he trained as a librarian. They ran a home for “wayward girls,” with whom Jan soon realized strict discipline could protect everyone from catastrophe. Tony's talents lay more in collecting books, identifying the often-obscure sources of famous sayings, and publishing his erudite correspondence in the (London) Times Literary Supplement. He was a born librarian and his skills soon brought him to the attention of universities. His first really important job was at Utah State—a job shortened considerably by the fact that Tony did not like Logan, the university, or, it seems, the larger Mormon culture. Jan, on the other hand, found herself enthralled. She loved the beautiful mountains, the people she met, especially but not only the women, and the religion that permeated all aspects of life. “The Saints,” as she often said, appealed to her in deep and lasting ways. She began to understand that learning about these fascinating people and their faith was important to her—she finished her undergraduate degree at Utah State in 1961.Well before Jan was ready to leave Logan, Tony was offered a post more suited to his own preferences in Colorado. In Boulder, Jan began to train as a historian, completing a master's degree in 1962 and a PhD in 1965. Her thesis was a detailed study of Mormons and Mormonism as seen by others, especially as depicted in newspapers, magazines, and other print sources. She and Tony soon moved again, this time to Bloomington, Indiana. There, with her baby Stephen and with Tony coming home every day for lunch, Jan turned from that more limited study to a broad and sweeping study of the Saints, which became her field-defining work, Mormonism: A New Religious Tradition, first published in 1980. The book is bold, theoretically rich, and stunningly well-written. Jan Shipps arrived with a bang.1Well before the book was released, she was already known and admired in organizations such as the Mormon History Association (MHA), the John Whitmer Historical Association (JWHA), and more. As she often said, there are many “Mormonisms,” and Jan was interested in all of them. Her essay in the first issue of the Journal of Mormon History (1974), which the journal is republishing in this issue, testifies to Jan's influence and leadership. The questions raised in “The Prophet Puzzle: Suggestions Leading Toward a More Comprehensive Interpretation of Joseph Smith” continue to shape scholarly and popular efforts to understand and make sense of Mormonism's founding figure. Her writing style was firmly in place in this article, which opened by noting that in upstate New York in the 1820s and ‘30s, “pathways to paradise ran in all directions.” But the many and varied “preachers and prophets” who offered such choices to spiritual pilgrims produced only one “important American religion: the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.” She argued that the Book of Mormon “plainly reflects the religious experiences and concerns that had been a part of [Joseph Smith's] life until [1830]” and urged scholars to recognize that visions and revelations are distinct and different: “God initiates the vision and man responds; man asks for revelations and God responds.” One is an eruption of the sacred, the second a pragmatic prophetic tactic.2 MHA president Benjamin Park notes that this article was also “revolutionary in that it pointed toward the eventual Mormon Studies movement, as part of the interdisciplinary field of religious studies, in which Jan's work was always considered pathbreaking and important.”By the mid-1980s, she was the editor of a book series at the University of Illinois Press, and had formed close friendships with other scholars and editors, including those she told me about later—Dean May, Doug Alder, Val Avery, Leonard Arrington, Liz Dulany, Juanita Brooks, Tom Alexander, Philip Barlow, Armand Mauss, Klaus Hansen, Greg Prince, Kathleen Flake, Polly Aird, her own student and dear friend Kathy Daynes, and many more, as well as several members of the Church Education System, whose work she found riveting, but who I found eye-glazingly immersed in minutia.3I met Jan in 1992, when I attended my very first MHA. I was a fledgling historian of Mormonism, a topic I came to because of my own experience in graduate school. In my second year as a PhD student at Princeton, I put together a bespoke reading course in American religious history with John Wilson, a member of the Religion Department and a specialist in history, titled Church and State in America, something that, as a lawyer, I also study with great interest. Three other graduate students signed on, and we had a genuine seminar. I put together the readings by weeks, generally two or three books and accompanying articles per week (Princeton is infamous for its gargantuan reading loads). I dedicated a full week to the Latter-day Saints, with two recent books and one older: Jan's Mormonism, Richard Bushman's first volume on Joseph Smith, and Leonard Arrington's older and wonderful Great Basin Kingdom (a doorstopper) from the late 1950s.At our meeting, I was stunned to learn that at least two of my fellow students felt that I had wasted their time. The third wasn't so contemptuous, but no fan of the reading either. They did not take the subject seriously, arguing that I had included charlatans and a fake prophet with other more suitable and worthy topics. The evening after our meeting, I simply could not shake my sense of distress—even outrage. I phoned the good Dr. Wilson at home, and he kindly took my call, telling me that he was not surprised to hear from me. He summarized brilliantly the central problem: I had been given a dose of anti-Mormonism, something that Professor Wilson by no means sanctioned, but that he saw more as a challenge to me. “What are you going to do about it?” he asked. And I began to understand that he treated this as a teaching moment. I wasn't quite sure exactly what I would do about it, I said, but I would get back to him.My own dissertation began to take shape then and there. Two years later, I came to Utah as a bona fide ABD student. I was greeted by the “white shirts” when I arrived at the old Church History Library and was told that there was nothing left to say about polygamy. I explained that I was most interested in the topic from outside the faith and had absolutely no interest in anyone's dirty laundry. David Whittaker took me under his wing, a great and generous effort that still strikes me as above and beyond the call of duty. I began to correspond with Davis Bitton, heard from the librarians about MHA, and began to appreciate how much I had to learn.I have to admit that my Princeton colleagues, even those who had not been in the seminar, thought my topic was ill-advised. The Mormons will check your footnotes, they predicted. They don't take anyone outside the faith seriously, others added. I could feel then, and do so now, John Wilson's clear-eyed injunction to push back against derision and to prove that “real” historians could find important insight in the Church History Library.Finally, I proposed a paper for MHA and met Jan there. Immediately, I felt her interest and her benevolence. I must have shown how green I was because almost immediately Jan took me aside. She gave me great pointers on how to describe the Latter-day Saints to those outside the faith, especially to scholars and the press. Her vocabulary lesson has stayed with me always. While I will never be anywhere near her league, I became then and still am aware that as people outside the faith, Jan—and now I and others in the field—owe a duty to be honest but respectful and to search for the words and phrases that would be recognizable to those who are part of (or orthogonal to) the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.When I met Jan, she was at the top of her game. Not only was her book a smash hit and already a classic, she was trusted as a commentator by smart journalists—Peggy Fletcher Stack springs to mind—and able to explain outside attitudes and actions to those inside the church in terms they could work with.4 I will never forget one trip that had Jan and me both at BYU. We were driving back up to the airport, and Jan's flight left several hours after mine. She called (then-Apostle, now a member of the First Presidency) Dallin Oaks, who picked up right away when he heard it was Jan calling. I left her at the Church Office Building, and he took her to lunch. For years, Jan laughed when she told this story—she said my jaw dropped! Also important, especially from the perspective of the church leadership, she could explain the Latter-day Saints sympathetically and honestly to those outside the faith. She always chose her words carefully, conveying her meaning with meticulous care for her subject and the audience. One dear friend described her talent as trilingual fluency: Jan spoke academese, mediaspeak, and Mormonish.5Jan could be a powerful and dogged critic, and she frequently called for the evidence behind a claim. She also was fierce in defense of new scholarship, especially work that pushed the boundaries and took chances, provided that such work met her standards (not an easy ask, for sure). By the mid-1990s, she had become a doyenne to the field, with deep influence among religious studies folk as well as Mormons. And here is where she began to see that the field could be expanded—deepened, broadened, situated more securely in academic circles: Mormon studies began to acquire a following. Of course, no individual is responsible for the creation of a new field, but Jan was as influential as anyone and more than almost everyone. Her development of the vision, her work to raise funds, and her support of candidates for inaugural jobs in the field were notable. Among her coterie that became holders of the first Mormon studies chairs are long-time friends Philip Barlow and Kathleen Flake. Jan took such joy in their success. She said that she was the grandmother (Leonard Arrington called her “den mother,” another term Jan used often) of Mormon history in general, and Mormon studies in particular.6We remained close as my own career unfolded on the East Coast, and I visited her many times in Bloomington at what she and Tony called Balmy Gilead Farm.7 When Tony moved to assisted living, Jan missed him terribly. I proposed that we consider working together on an article, and she leapt at the suggestion. We debated several topics, and Jan wanted badly to work both on Methodists (her own church) and the Saints—naturally, we read Chris Jones's fine work, and we began to explore the 1857 Mountain Meadows Massacre from the outside, thinking more generally about the violence and dispossession of Native peoples that were central to mid-nineteenth century westward migration, as well as the ways that religion played deeper roles than many of us have internalized. Jan and I decided that the Methodists had done their fair share of slaughtering and that one could imagine either Methodists or Latter-day Saints as victims of that massacre, an insight that became one of our central arguments.8We had a great time working together. We fought over more than we agreed on and enjoyed every battle because we both felt the work got better as a result. We developed a distinct voice as we debated which words were most apt, whether our introduction was too detailed or too general, how to work with informal family histories and make sure bloodthirsty men didn't hog all our attention, and more. Generally, there was a bottle of wine involved and plenty of Jan's very good cooking, especially her cheesy grits, my favorite.And speaking of libations, Jan was noted for her late-night soirées (often in her hotel room and lasting well past midnight) following the Presidential Banquet at MHA conferences. These celebratory gatherings generated energy, ideas, bonds, partnerships, and much candor and intuitive and social learning that complemented the formal sessions of each conference. I think perhaps they became part of the informal tensile strength of the Association. For at least three decades, Jan, as hostess, helped cement the intellectual and social values behind the growth of the field and the MHA. As a sage observer noted, we can learn from Jan's attention to the myriad ways of exchanging ideas; her soirées were “a testament to the worth and potency and distinctiveness of what the MHA hath wrought, and what current attendees might be well served to not to forget.”I close this brief essay with a few additional facts about Jan that may not be widely known outside her inner circle. First, Jan was always a terrible driver and she only got worse with age. It was literally terrifying to drive with her. She would stop cold in the middle of busy intersections, for example, because she forgot whether the light she had just passed was green or red. This is relevant because she had a challenging commute. She taught in the history and religious studies departments at Indiana University/Purdue University Indianapolis (IUPUI, or “oowie-poowie,” as Jan put it). Her dear friend David Bodenhammer agreed to commute together with Jan to their jobs at IUPUI. She offered to drive first and he accepted. Decades later, David announced to a large audience that he shook with fear the whole trip and told Jan he would never agree to drive with her at the wheel again.9 Jan and I got to the point where she handed me the keys to her beloved Rav4 the moment I arrived (I tried to ignore the bent fenders and dents in the doors and such). Our mutual friend Philip Barlow commented that those alarming trips often included some brilliant analysis by Jan. One might say that she had an unerring grip on ideas and history, which was more reliable than her grip on the steering wheel. I can almost hear her laughing at that one.Second, Jan really hit her stride at about midnight. She would take us painstakingly over every topic sentence and every quotation in our draft article many times, as I yawned and occasionally even nodded off. She would poke me hard and laugh. She often sent out 3 am emails, particularly to her church study group that met on Sundays after the main church service —the participants had to read fast to get in their homework plus attend the discussion. Whenever I was in town, I would attend and was given the pleasure of seeing Jan in another of her elements—a sacred space, fellow parishioners, her dear friends Ed and Linda Stevenson, and the life of the mind in Bloomington.Finally, Jan was also a passionate liberal, something that may not have been obvious in the Great Basin but was central to her identity and her deep Methodist faith. She always pointed with pride to Utah's support for FDR during the Great Depression, when the voters defied the church and carried the state for the Democrats. title: Chema, Alexis, and Betty A. Schellenberg, eds. The Manuscript Book in the Long Eighteenth Century
abstract: This special issue volume of Eighteenth-Century Life addresses the viability and agency of manuscript in an age of expanded, elevated print culture. The case in point here is the long eighteenth century. The eleven essays and an afterword are authored by a wide variety of primarily female scholars, most well-established, some less so, all drawn from the US, the UK, and Canada. The manuscripts are all anglophone writings, many of them created and/or received in the context of the anglophone Atlantic world. The essays attend to what the volume editors label “manuscript books,” which, in the final analysis, may not be the best label for the manuscripts studied here. We find a more convincing descriptor in Margaret J. M. Ezell’s afterword, in her term “invisible books.” This more accurately conveys the marginality of many manuscript texts and their creators, both generally and specifically demonstrated by those showcased here. Ezell’s presence looms large throughout here, which is more than fitting the scholar who issued one of the earliest calls for a wider and deeper understanding of the manuscript in the face of a substantial scholarship obsessed with print.At a fundamental level, this volume presents eleven microhistories of particular manuscript texts or groups of texts that are fascinating in and of themselves. A massive text such as Robert Forbes’s The Lyon in Mourning, consisting of 2,140 pages in ten volumes, arguably necessary to provide the complete history of a wide network of people and events he set out to create, is difficult to conceptualize as invisible or marginal. The substantial 700-page “personal history” of John Martin falls into the same category. Other works here are more easily classifiable as ephemeral, and, indeed, some nonexistent. See the edition of poems and letters written by Phillis Wheatley Peters, intended to be published but never achieving print in the long eighteenth century; this apocryphal manuscript copy can be found in any archive.Manuscripts studied here span a wide variety of genres—among them poetry, correspondence, sermon notes, music, penmanship, and commonplace books—covering a variety of topics, including autobiography, methods of courtship, how-to books, creating and maintaining kinship networks, and the textual output of marginalized religious communities and groups. However, given the very personal origins and reception of manuscript works, the topic/genre of the journal might be expected to be explored here, but interestingly is only addressed as part of large compilations. The authors and creators of these manuscripts span the margins of early modern Anglo-Saxon society, where they existed, as might be expected of a marginal media illuminating different genders, different races, different socioeconomic and legal statuses, political rebels, religious dissenters, emigres, exiles, craftsmen, and amateurs.What figures most importantly in this volume is the more than remarkable contributions it makes to a significant number of over-arching ideas generally applied to print and its evolution over time, as well as to the somewhat disparate existing scholarship on manuscripts. This work confirms the findings of pioneering research in both mediums. Foremost is the complementarity of manuscript and print in a relationship that is symbiotic rather than adversarial and at the same time circuitous rather than linear. These studies show definitively that the fluidity of manuscripts is more versatile than yet imparts just as much authority as print. Lack of fixity is no impediment. As a matter of fact, many of these invisible books successfully adopt and deploy the conventions of print—title pages, indexes, illustrations, legibility, typefaces, for example. Additionally, these manuscripts show the emergence of new conventions, such as tables and grids, and digital databases that make many manuscript works just as or even more navigable than those in print. It should be noted that a number of these manuscripts are not only copied from printed books but in fact physically incorporate actual printed books and other printed elements in their compilation. These amalgams are yet something else that merit a new, unique label that better serves to describe them than the term concordance applied to the books created through the “new form of printing,” integrating print and manuscript elements as practiced by the Little Gidding religious community in seventeenth-century Essex.The relationship between materiality and meaning and reception is clearly visible here as well. Format determines use, creation, and content. An illuminating example is the oblong book and books with blank leaves, originally created by individuals for not only their personal use but also to accommodate particular information that demanded a more flexible format than the standardized codex sizes such as quarto, octavo, etc. Notably, music required a wider page than that provided by standard sizes. But rotate an oblong book and it presents a vertical format attuned to other uses and information someone desired to record such as keeping accounts, taking notes of sermons at church services, and copying original documents. Further, some of these manuscripts employ an attribute most closely associated with the works of seventeenth-century poet George Herbert where words and lines of text are arranged in the shape of objects that graphically illustrate and thus reinforce meaning and interpretation. Forbes in his monumental work took materiality to yet a higher level with his inclusion of every medium available to the creators of manuscript texts including wood from the boat that spirited Bonnie Prince Charlie away after Culloden and cloth from the prince’s garter.The current ECL volume also shows that discontinuous reading, first facilitated by the transition from scrolls to the codex treated by Peter Stallybrass, among others, advanced practices of reading in manuscript as well as printed books. This function is true of common-placing generally, as an example, and as demonstrated by several essays in this volume, Lockean common-placing specifically. Arguably it is also in operation in another example, namely, private manuscript prayerbooks as it is in printed prayerbooks and bibles. Discontinuous reading of manuscripts also features in consideration of the effects of printing on the intended meaning of manuscript texts, linking manuscript solidly to the debate over who creates meaning in printed texts—author, compositor, publisher, reader, illustrator, all of the above. Finally, it is disruptive reading at play in reconstruction of invisible books such as the scattered collection of Peter’s poems as well as the reconstruction of communication networks and geographically diverse communities in digitized archives and databases such as the Ballitore Collection of Quaker correspondence and the sources that enabled the amazing detective work on display in a number of these essays.The modelling of anonymity in manuscript texts and collections provided by this volume asserts that manuscript imparts a sense of self and constructs identity as much as does signing or attributing poems, signing the pages of a book, creating prayerbooks to be used exclusively within a religious community.Perhaps the weightiest contribution here is the call for a redefinition of modern notions of authorship and the author, as well as readers and writers.The editors here quite correctly point out that although recent studies of manuscripts have shed light on a variety of recently popular topics, the study of manuscripts has taken a back seat to that of printed books for far too long. Certainly, due to its vital place in the history of reading and reception, history of the book, and the history of print culture generally, the volume’s topic deserves scholarly attention. Moreover, perhaps all of these labels should be revised or replaced in light of this volume of work.

title: Networks and Transnational Communities of Letters: How Can Literary Studies Reclaim the ‘Network Turn’?
abstract: In recent years, scholars in Literary Studies have increasingly been encouraged to move beyond disciplinary boundaries and engage with what has been termed the ‘Network Turn’ in the humanities. This approach, while it encourages scholars to benefit from – and contribute to – the ‘visual and quantitative analysis of networks to shed light on the study of culture’, also acknowledges the value of ‘critical skills native to humanistic inquiry’ in the ‘theorisation and critique of our networked world’.1 Such advocacy is found in key scholarly volumes, such as The Network Turn: Changing Perspectives in the Humanities (2021),2 which has argued for the value of adopting network-based methodologies and frameworks – typical of fields like computer science – to expand and enhance the scope and reach of humanities research, beyond disciplinary boundaries. Within the ever-evolving domain of the Digital Humanities, network analysis has indeed often been used to uncover and visualize hidden connections, sometimes revealing unpredictable patterns, and to tease out and highlight important socio-cultural nodes emerging from complex webs of intersecting links. In particular, in the past twenty years, the use of Digital Humanities tools has been increasingly applied to Literary Studies to map out cultural networks. For instance, historical-bibliometric datasets have been used to trace the dissemination of ideologies across space and time,3 while Social Network Analysis (SNA) has been used to map relationships between authors or between authors and cultural agents, extrapolating data from biographical works, epistolary correspondence and paratexts.4 More recently, scholars in the field of the Digital Humanities have highlighted how visualizing networks via computational methods can yield immediate insights from larger corpora, thereby enhancing the effectiveness of research across disciplines and increasing its accessibility to a much larger public.5 As this growing body of scholarship demonstrates, this network approach is undeniably providing literary specialists with new tools to explore, systematize and disseminate hidden complexities, often in a transdisciplinary fashion, across texts, genres and literary and historical contexts. Some such tools have had the ambition to ‘[open] the inquiry to a wider diversity of actors and to redefine our understanding of creativity’.6 Within such discussions, the ‘Network Turn’ is often viewed as a more contemporary, democratizing, and ostensibly impartial, horizontal approach – one that stands in sharp contrast to more traditional notions of socio-cultural hierarchy and literary value. Such notions have long shaped the formation of the literary canon and have frequently been bound to specific nation-states, linguistic contexts, disciplinary domains and established traditions. In fact, visualization and mapping projects rooted in the Digital Humanities, such as the ‘Encyclopedia of Romantic Nationalism in Europe’ (ERNiE), to mention but one, have shown, not without irony, how the very boundaries of nationalism have transcended the frontiers of a given nation-state.7 In June 2024, the Literary Worlds Research Network at the University of New England in Australia held a two-day international workshop to encourage a broader discussion around the ongoing productivity of the idea of ‘network’ within Literary Studies. This original gathering aimed to foster a cross-disciplinary, diachronic, multilingual and innovative discussion of network as a framework for the inclusion of silenced, neglected or unjustly underrepresented voices in our literary worlds. Some of the papers then presented are now reworked in this ‘Talking Point’, which, beyond its original scope, also sets out to consider, and demonstrate in practice whether this relatively recent ‘Network Turn’ in Literary Studies might be a passing methodological trend, or whether it may indeed offer a meaningful path towards a more democratic, pluralistic, decentred and interdisciplinary Literary Studies. It might therefore come as a surprise that, broadly speaking, most of the contributions in this issue set aside – at least for the purposes of this discussion – Digital Humanities methodologies based on large datasets and visualization tools in order to return to a more foundational exploration of the concept of the network itself as a critical tool. The idea of network as a theoretical framework owes much to the French sociologist Bruno Latour’s Actor-Network theory, which postulated that our natural and social world is construed as a constantly shifting network of relationships. As Rita Felski has warned us, however, ‘the alliance of actor-network theory and Literary Studies, like all alliances, requires translation, tinkering, and diplomacy’.8 In particular, we would argue, embracing such an alliance should not be a leap of faith. For instance, during our original discussion, the Digital Humanities scholar John Ladd invited us to consider how network analysis is far from a completely objective and unbiased tool. Networks are just as neutral and fair as data permit and cannot account for archival gaps, silenced voices and the powerful forces that determined which historical and literary sources would or would not survive and be deemed worthy data points in the first place. In other words, ‘Humanities’ – and the human element – within ‘Digital Humanities’, remains an essential element, as the contributions in this issue demonstrate, whether by engaging directly with the concept of ‘network’ or by illustrating its potential through specific case studies. In this context, Pierre Bourdieu’s writings on the cultural field – with its inevitable corollary of power struggles – remain highly relevant. Within a network approach, we cannot forget that the champ [field] remains a structured social space, ‘un réseau de relations objectives (de domination ou de subordination, de complémentarité ou d’antagonisme, etc.) entre des positions’ [a network of objective relations (of domination or subordination, of complementarity or antagonism, etc.) between positions].9 Within the champ, cultural agents compete using their cultural capital and ultimately contribute to the development of cultural trends. Bourdieu’s cultural capital is relevant to literary production and consumption, as these processes are always mediated not only by the authors themselves, but also by a wide range of cultural agents, including patrons, translators, editors and publishers. Recent scholarship has demonstrated that Bourdieu’s theories of the cultural field can be strengthened when complemented by network analysis, since ‘the interaction within the field is consequential to its structure and to the classifications and qualifications used within the field’.10 In light of all this, the first two contributions in this collection use epistolary networks as a productive framework to explore women’s cultural agency in the early modern period. Studies on epistolary exchanges between elite women, particularly in England, have demonstrated the sociability of letter writing and its role in forging ‘female alliances’.11 Yet, these women’s cultural networks remain largely unexplored and, within Italian Studies for instance, the emphasis placed on Isabella d’Este has resulted in a discounting of the complex and diverse networks within which she operated. Cultural agents do not operate in isolation.12 Thus considering networks as social and textual relationality enables us fully to understand the contribution of cultural agents towards the development and dissemination of cultural objects. Bourdieu’s theory of cultural capital underpins Giulia Torello-Hill’s ‘Epistolary Networks: Elite Women as Cultural Agents in Early Sixteenth-Century Italy’, which examines the cultural agency of elite women in early sixteenth-century Italy, focusing on their role in the dissemination of Spanish chivalric romances Tirant lo Blanc (1490) and Amadís de Gaula (1508). This study highlights how elite women like Isabella d’Este and Antonia del Balzo leveraged epistolary networks to acquire, translate and circulate these texts, reinforcing their social prestige and shaping the literary canon. By adopting a networked approach to literature, Torello-Hill demonstrates how transnational and multilingual interactions enriched the chivalric genre, offering a nuanced understanding of literary production as a dynamic and transnational cultural process. Diana G. Barnes’s ‘Madame de Sévigne’s Letters and the Formation of Elite Community’ analyses Madame de Sévigné’s epistolary exchange with her daughter Françoise-Marguerite de Grignan as a model of elite, familial and transnational networking, emphasizing their role in shaping sociability, cultural transmission and epistolary traditions. Published posthumously after a heavy-handed editorial intervention, their letters were welcomed in England as a model of tasteful sociability and translated into English not long after. Their influence on the development of the epistolary genre both in the private and public sphere, invites a reflection on the very definition of the literary canon. The essay collection Early Modern Women and Transnational Communities of Letters has offered tangible examples of the interconnections between early modern women writers, their cultural geographies and their crossing of linguistic, cultural and literary borders.13 These encounters often determine a cross-fertilization of genres. As Kate Chedgzoy contends, an exploration of cultural geographies would help enlighten the complexities of these networks of authors, as well as cultural agents, ‘simultaneously demanding a reconsideration of the canon and proposing new methodologies for reading it’.14 Building on Steve Pile’s definition of location as ‘places defined and places taken up through experience, identity and power’, Chedgzoy urges scholarship to remap what ‘delineated the boundaries of communities and nations, and thus inflected the meanings of location, in the early modern period’.15 This, in turn, challenges the principle of the nation as a network, inviting us to think about literary outputs as the product of transnational networks. Lateral networks of this kind can tell us a lot about the (un)making of the very idea of the nation and national identity. By embracing Caroline Levine’s reorientation of Literary Studies around the network rather than the nation, the ambition of this Talking Point is thus to highlight ‘patterns of circulation rather than rootedness, zigzagging movements rather than stable foundations’.16 Delving into the expanding field of the Digital Humanities and data visualization, Valentina Gosetti, Paul Gibbard and Alistair Rolls’s ‘Translation Nation: Literary Translation as Cultural Mediation in Australia’ introduces a larger project that aims to construct the first chronological map of French literary texts circulating in translation in Australia from the colonial period, when translations were largely imported from Britain and disseminated, adapted and edited to suit local conditions, through to the present day, when a local industry is flourishing and exporting to the world translations featuring distinctively Australian characteristics. The overall idea is to use the mapping of this unexplored network as a springboard to propose an alternative cultural history of Australia via its consumption and production of translations and adaptations of French literary texts. In doing so, the project critically engages with the ‘network turn’ by focusing on the human element. By means of close textual analysis of historical documents and interviews with contemporary Australian translators, the project brings otherwise unheard voices to the fore. In this light, the theoretical approach that underpins this Talking Point invites us to ‘look sideways to lateral networks that are not readily apparent’, thus decentring the traditional canon.17 Networks invite us to view literature as the result of transnational and translingual encounters that often bypass the ‘centre’. Clara Sitbon’s ‘Decentring through Islands: Archipelagic Approaches to Multilingual Crime Fiction’ explores islands as a metaphor to reflect upon networks in their articulation of distance/difference and encounters/multiplicity that dynamically shape crime narratives. Combining literary analysis, cultural geography and transnational studies, her essay calls for scholarly collaboration to expand the thematic and geographic scope of island-based crime fiction. To investigate the multiplicity of dynamic encounters that shape autobiographical texts authored by twentieth-century Italian-Australian women, Alice Loda’s ‘Entanglements: Emplaced, Transnational and Transcultural Trajectories in Life-Writing by Italian-Australian Women’ draws upon the concepts of ‘locational feminism’ and ‘transduction’.18 This theoretical framework captures the transcultural nature of women’s writings, which are grounded in the local and at the same time adapt and transform. This Talking Point also explores networks as theorized scholarly practices, drawing on diverse approaches – including First Nation epistemologies – which encourage us to recognize our ‘true status as a single node in a cooperative network’ and to understand that non-linearity should not be seen as an anomaly, but indeed as the norm, accepting that ‘the winding path is just how a path is’.19 This process enhances critical differences and encourages us to engage with the text in non-linear ways, creating new meanings. Alistair Rolls and Brooke Collins-Gearing’s ‘Imperfect Seclusion: Critiquing Networks and Networking Critique’ explores the challenges of reading a topical text of crime fiction such as ‘The Murders in the Rue Morgue’ uncritically, resisting genre seclusion and the model of linearity that comes with it – the reader is guided by the detective who in the end unravels the truth – and reorienting our reading of the text. A ‘networked critique’ can enable scholars to appreciate critical differences reaching beyond the confines of disciplinarity. Networks also enlighten the dynamics of intertextuality, calling into question the role of the reader and the layering of a text that borrows, adapts and reinvents materials, style and imagery from other authors, traditions and genres. Jennifer Rushworth’s ‘Reading Dante with George Eliot and Co.’ takes the first chapter of George Eliot’s Daniel Deronda (1876) as a case study to approach intertextuality as a ‘transtemporal, multilingual network’, exploring the complexity and fragmentariness of the mediated experience of both author and reader. ‘Reading with’ an author allows one to understand intertextuality not as a linear process, but as a complex network of mediated readings, including translations, adaptations (sometimes through other mediums) and paratexts. A networked approach to literary texts has the potential of unveiling the layered and relational nature of cultural transmission. The transnational and translingual dimensions of texts, which are disseminated, adapted and translated across space and time, underscore the porousness of national boundaries. This is likely to encourage a more inclusive and nuanced picture of cultural transmission that recognizes collaboration and cross-cultural adaptation as the driving forces that have shaped and continue to shape literary texts. At the same time, by collectively embracing and exploring a broadly conceived network-based approach to Literary Studies, this Talking Point also aims to foster constructive critique, invite thoughtful feedback and encourage an ongoing collective critical reflection on its inevitable limitations, oversights and opportunities for growth and improvement, with a view to providing an ever-expanding critical network of scholarly voices on the very idea of network.

title: ‘This is like Guadalajara’: politics, identity and the management of natural resources in late colonial Spanish Sahara
abstract: This article examines the late colonial political economy of Spanish Sahara, with a particular focus on the management of marine resources and the competing interests within Francoist Spain’s authoritarian structure. The study draws upon archival materials, particularly political and industrial reports, as well as personal correspondence. The findings illustrate how the exploitation of natural resources became a focal point for ideological conflict among Francoist elites, as well as a means of asserting cultural and political dominance over the territory. This analysis demonstrates the economic and symbolic value ascribed to natural resources in maintaining colonial control and shaping the discourses surrounding decolonisation.

title: Robert Lowell in Context edited by Thomas Austenfeld and Grzegorz Kość
abstract: Following her 2014 National Book Award for Citizen: An American Lyric, Claudia Rankine cites Robert Lowell’s Life Studies (1959) as an influence, before noting, “It’s difficult to find critical work on the construction of whiteness in Lowell, but that is what I am reading in there—a struggle with that” (quoted in Javadizadeh 2019: 477–78). Rankine’s public and ambivalent engagement with Lowell’s work has encouraged readers to reconsider the poet’s oeuvre and his place in the twenty-first century. It is precisely such a reconsideration that Robert Lowell in Context, edited by Thomas Austenfeld and Grzegorz Kość, provides in its broad range of chapters on the literary, historical, and cultural contexts shaping Lowell’s poetry and writing. Like other volumes in Cambridge University Press’s Literature in Context series, Robert Lowell in Context supplies readers a series of short, accessible chapters—twenty-six in total, along with an introduction—across six parts: “Places,” “American Politics, American Wars,” “Some Literary Models,” “Contemporaries: Modernists and Beyond,” “Life, Illness, and the Arts,” and “Reputation and New Contexts.” Many of the chapters offer brief and often insightful moments of close reading, but as the editors’ introduction states, the focus remains on “a traditional approach” (2) to literary history. The editors and contributors provide context for Lowell’s work “on two historical planes, that of the object of study and that of the literary historian’s present moment.” The collection’s series of interventions thus aims at once to synthesize Lowell’s critical reception, accounting for recent research and biographies, and to open new avenues of interpretation, providing scholars and teachers—both of Lowell and of twentieth- and twenty-first-century American poetry more broadly—useful frameworks for an important literary figure.For readers unfamiliar with the arc of Lowell’s career and life, the collection’s first part, “Places,” provides a concise biographical sketch organized chronologically of some of the most important places Lowell lived. The contextualizing work of this first part helpfully sets up the chapters that follow by providing readers an overview of Lowell’s life and writing. In the first chapter, “Boston,” Grzegorz Kość maps class onto the urban landscape, showing how the various changes of address by the Lowell family and by Lowell himself reflected their changing class status. In his discussion of the Boston Common and the notion of public space, Kość also suggests that class anxieties appear imbricated with anxieties about race, a topic that returns in later chapters, such as Jeffrey Gray’s “New York,” which shows Lowell’s often ambivalent relation to the Civil Rights era protests: his critique of police brutality, on the one hand, and his “fear of violence and of racial conflict” (37), on the other.Following this more linear, biographical opening series of chapters, the second part, “American Politics, American Wars,” pursues Lowell’s political activism, as well as his poetic celebrity. In “War,” Walt Hunter argues that a focus “on war helps to bring Lowell’s prosodic changes into relief” (56). This comment—repeated in different ways in different chapters—gestures to one of the collection’s strengths: in its provision of context for Lowell, it also provides different lenses—not always perfectly compatible—through which to read and reread his work. One of the pivotal moments in his career that gets referenced throughout the chapters is emphasized in this part of the collection. As Gray notes earlier, because of his anti–Vietnam War position, Lowell rejected President Johnson’s invitation to the White House in 1965 and published a letter of protest in the New York Times. Other poets, writers, and intellectuals signed on to the letter, the public nature of which made Lowell “a celebrity among activists” (33). The chapters on “War” and “US Presidency” thus offer necessary interventions for such a public and political poet, even one whose commitments often revealed a profound ambivalence.Other early chapters offer less intuitive, but welcome, contributions to the contextualization of Lowell and his work. “American Politics, American Wars” ends, for example, with a chapter entitled “Eco-consciousness.” Here Adam Beardsworth begins by acknowledging Lowell as an unlikely subject of a discussion of “ecological concerns,” yet, he convincingly argues, “even if Lowell’s poetry does not fit within the wilderness tradition, its preoccupation with the anxiety in the Cold War era maps concerns about nuclear—and by extension environmental—catastrophe” (74). Reading the “affective politics” (79) of Lowell’s poetry offers readers yet another way into his body of work, including his confessional poetry, whose focus on the personal becomes broadened by Beardsworth to a staging of the effects of environmental destruction on individual subjects. In other words, Lowell’s poetry proves to be an exemplary mode of expressing the affective politics of ecological destruction and nuclear war and states of being that readers would now recognize as “climate anxiety” (78). Beardsworth thus exemplifies a reading of Lowell on “two historical planes” mentioned in the introduction, and his self-conscious treatment of Lowell’s eco-consciousness constructs useful insights into the poetry’s continued relevance.The following two parts address Lowell’s relationship to other literary figures, movements, and genres, including John Talbot’s discussion of Lowell’s preference for the literature of Imperial Rome “rather than Greece” (87), Stephen Matterson’s chapter on his longstanding engagement with Herman Melville, and Meg Tyler’s reflections on his relation to the “complaint,” as well as a series of chapters on Lowell’s engagement with contemporaries: T. S. Eliot, Ezra Pound, John Berryman, Robert Penn Warren, Randall Jarrell, and Elizabeth Bishop.1 Cumulatively, these two parts offer a rich literary field within which to situate Lowell’s work. In some cases, his proximity to other literary figures offers revealing insights, such as his generative relationship to Bishop, whose “mastery of indirection and understatement” “directly inspired” (163) Life Studies and its famous poem, “Skunk Hour”; but his relationships, often ambivalent, also help generate new appreciation of his poetics. For example, according to Philip Coleman, common groupings of Lowell and Berryman as confessional poets wrongly assume that they “share the same poetics, but this is not borne out by a close reading of their work” (144). Coleman’s chapter instantiates the way the collection carefully rehearses familiar readings of Lowell while also providing nuanced qualifications and correctives.The most polemical chapter in the collection appears in the fourth part on contemporaries. In “Warren and Jarrell,” Joan Romano Shifflett argues against the confessional label for its “inaccurate representations of Lowell’s career” (149). For Shifflett, “it is problematic to conceptualize the arc of Lowell’s work as merely a chronological shift between mutually exclusive binaries: closed to open, formal to free, rigorous to loose, objective to subjective, and ‘cooked’ to ‘raw,’ to employ Lowell’s words” (150); instead, she wants readers to recognize the nuanced overlaps across his oeuvre. Arguably—and commendably—none of the chapters in this collection succumb to the misrepresentations criticized by Shifflett. The chapter develops an alternative reading by showing that Warren, Jarrell, and Lowell influenced one another, but they were also all influenced by the work of Robert Frost. Shifflett therefore positions Frost rather than William Carlos Williams as a central influence on Lowell’s work in the 1950s. One of the most productive insights in this chapter is its demonstration that Lowell’s “artistry” “was merely taking on a new shape” (153) in Life Studies. In other words, Lowell—along with Warren and Jarrell—insisted on the imbrication of form and content while constantly searching for new configurations that could achieve their desired effects. There is, then, a continuous, if nonlinear, development both internal to Lowell’s career and with respect to midcentury American poetry.The collection’s critique of the “confessional” label often considered synonymous with Lowell’s poetics and exemplified by Life Studies represents one of its most insightful contributions across its chapters, and this critique occurs most pointedly in parts three and four. For example, in “Plaints,” Tyler suggests “complaint” rather than “confessional” as a generic label for Lowell’s poetry: “There is a ritualistic aspect, a dignity, and a formal investment to plaints that the word confession has not perhaps hinted at since the time of Augustine” (108). The complaint, according to Tyler, emphasizes the “formal, mannered” style that constructs a sense of authenticity. This point is especially crucial today in the era of the memoir and autofiction, genres that often produce an illusory sense of immediacy.2 In his contribution, Stephen Regan offers the most persuasive critique of the confessional mode when applied to Lowell, arguing that reading his work with and through T. S. Eliot enables “a deeper appreciation and understanding of a poetic process that is sometimes too neatly and too simply conveyed as an opposition between impersonality and confessionalism” (124). According to Regan, “Lowell himself did not see any contradiction in writing a poetry that was both ‘impersonal’ in the manner prescribed by Eliot and ‘confessional’ in drawing on the most troubling personal experience” (125).Such a conjunction—or perhaps a disjunctive synthesis—can be helpful for teachers of poetry associated with the confessional label. When reading a Lowell poem like “Waking in the Blue,” or a poem by confessional poets such as Sylvia Plath or Anne Sexton, the temptation is to be seduced by the first-person, lyric speaker such that the reader conflates the poetic voice with the authorial voice. For Lowell, this is especially the case in poems in which he offers a seemingly direct representation of his own struggles with mental illness, a topic most elaborately treated by Astrid Franke’s contribution, “Desensationalizing Madness.” When teaching such poems, however, part of the reward comes from showing students how the poetic form carefully shapes and mediates intimate and personal details. It is a mistake, as Coleman argues, to see confessional poetry as “not only personal or autobiographical but solipsistic and disengaged” (145). Recognizing Lowell’s poetic mediation of the personal can be emphasized by attending to details in the poems that have been invented for poetic effect or those that deviate from biographical facts, but, more significantly, the difference between author and lyric speaker can be shown through an attention to the form, style, and figurative economy of the poetic text. In other words, the “authentic” representation of the self is produced through carefully manipulated poetic artifice. As Regan puts it, Lowell himself admired poetry—like Eliot’s “Ash Wednesday”—“that gave compelling artistic form to complex states of thought and feeling” (125).After the two parts devoted to his influences, part five turns to themes particularly significant for interpreting the specific and general concerns of Lowell’s poetics. Thomas Austenfeld’s “Religion,” for example, explores the topic of Lowell’s religiosity to speak to two persistent claims made throughout Robert Lowell in Context. The first is the insistence that Life Studies did not mark a linear break in Lowell’s career, from the dense formalism of the early work to the looser confessionalism of the later work. Instead, as many of the contributors argue, Lowell’s career can be read as a continuous, if often surprising, series of developments; early preoccupations persist just as later confessional gestures can be read in his early interest in drawing on the personal for his poetry, as in “The Quaker Graveyard in Nantucket” (CP 14–18). Austenfeld similarly argues for a continuity across Lowell’s career by following his persistent attention to religion and its ethical implications, in various guises, from his early conversion to Catholicism to his later return to his New England Puritan and Protestant heritage. The second claim has to do with Lowell’s ever-shifting search for a poetic form that can give expression to the inexpressible. “The spiritual nature of the craft of poetry,” Austenfeld writes, “its attempt to express the ineffable in recognizable form, attracted the young Lowell and stayed with him beyond his active participation in the Catholic Church” (176).3 Religion therefore offers a useful heuristic through which readers can trace the ongoing concerns of Lowell’s work across their changing manifestations.The final part of the collection, “Reputation and New Contexts,” addresses Lowell’s relation—personal and poetic—to both gender and race. While both topics appear throughout the collection, they are most extensively addressed in Nikki Skillman’s “Whiteness” and Hannah Baker Saltmarsh’s “Appropriation.” While Lowell’s relationship to racial (mis)representation appears in a variety of chapters—as when Coleman acknowledges, “In some ways, Lowell and Berryman represent the worst excesses of white male institutional privilege in American poetic culture in the second half of the twentieth century” (146)—Skillman’s explicit treatment of this subject offers a necessary contribution. For Skillman, Lowell proves to be aware of race in ways his critics have not always recognized, even if this awareness appears limited and incomplete. His poetic representations of race include the use of a racist epithet in “Colloquy in Black Rock” (CP 11), as well as his (in)famous “blackface” poem, “A Mad Negro Soldier Confined at Munich” (118). As Skillman and others in the collection acknowledge, Rankine’s “ambivalent allusions to Lowell” (239) in Citizen and in her subsequent interviews have led to an increased attention to his work in relation to race.4 Part of Rankine’s ambivalent attitude has to do with a critical blindness in Lowell’s readers, rather than an inattention by Lowell himself, for failing to recognize “a striking pattern in Lowell’s literary configurations of whiteness in terms of suspended states of liminal awareness” (240). The most extensive textual example offered by Skillman is Lowell’s dramatic adaptation of Melville’s “Benito Cereno.” Matterson’s earlier chapter on Melville helpfully anticipates this reading, providing readers more context for this lesser-known text by Lowell. In a “self-incriminating” move, Lowell identifies most with “the murderous white supremacist Delano,” which reveals a “striking self-awareness about the fragility of his own racial identity and his conflicted views on civil rights” (243). Skillman then rereads Life Studies through the lens of Lowell’s Melville adaptation, which enables her to argue that “Lowell links white power and violence with psychic circumstances . . . that he perceives brewing in the halls of his childhood home and in the fenced-in Public Garden” (246) in Boston. Skillman thus shows that Lowell performs, despite his limited self-awareness, what his critics often fail to recognize, namely, an attention to “the chaotic phenomenological and emotional territory into which the psychic drama of white racialization extends” (247).In the following chapter, “Appropriation,” Saltmarsh continues this critical rereading of Lowell’s work in terms of gender. She considers Lowell’s practice of repurposing language from his private correspondence into the material of his poems, a practice discussed in different ways in many of the earlier chapters. Matterson, for example, claims, “No poet ever had less anxiety about influence than Lowell” (98). The negative implication of Lowell’s method appears to be his ethically fraught recycling of others’ words for his own poetry. The most controversial example of this form of appropriation is Lowell’s manipulation of the words of Elizabeth Hardwick, his second wife, in his late collection, The Dolphin, which addresses the breakdown of their marriage and the beginnings of Lowell’s life with his third wife, Caroline Blackwood, in England and Ireland. On this decision to manipulate Hardwick’s voice, Elizabeth Bishop famously wrote to Lowell, “Art just isn’t worth that much” (quoted in Austenfeld and Kość 251). While Bishop and Lowell remained close, the controversy of The Dolphin, which won the 1973 Pulitzer Prize in Poetry, ended the friendship Lowell had with Adrienne Rich, who published a scathing review of the collection and Lowell’s conflation of art and life. Saltmarsh rereads Lowell’s poetic methods of appropriation “in the wake of #MeToo, #BlackLivesMatter, and #ownstories” to respond to the following question: “How has male privilege and artistic agency perpetuated women’s historic dispossession of their own life stories?” (250–51). The chapter thus returns to a fundamental ethical question raised by Lowell’s poetry and his decisions concerning poetic voice. Although Saltmarsh acknowledges her desire “to vindicate Hardwick from the choke hold of the letter-poems,” she recognizes that “there is no end to this literary-historical entanglement” (258). Nevertheless, the chapter ends with an attempt to center Hardwick as “a subject unto herself.” While readers may desire more work on Lowell in relation to gender and race, these chapters, along with their suggestions for further reading, offer important starting points.The collection concludes with Kacper Bartczak’s “Language and Post-Language Poets,” which contrasts Lowell’s humanist, confessional mode with the posthumanist, Language poetry that challenges the subjectivity and ideas of authorship that organize Lowell’s aesthetic practices (286–88).
