title: Recent Articles
abstract: These two essays demonstrate that even after three centuries we can still gain significant textual insights from manuscripts. In neither case were the manuscripts in question unknown, but both scholars have identified new relevance and details, and each presents a clear, engaging narrative about why these insights matter. RES also deserves recognition for publishing such useful and readable criticism and for including admirably clear supporting images.Joseph Hone focuses primarily on Alexander Pope’s manuscripts of the early poetry through Windsor Forest (published 1713), demonstrating that the poet’s obsession with the appearance of his manuscripts intended for circulation went deeper than simply imitating printed letter forms: he would delicately scrape away a layer of paper to delete material or to make corrections or additions, sometimes cleverly incorporating existing shapes into new letters. While scholars are familiar with such surface erasures in vellum manuscripts, I am not aware of instances of the practice on paper. Flat-sheet LED lights assist scholars to look through paper and have greatly advanced work on watermarks, but the same technique also facilitates recognition of spots where the paper has been thinned by clever erasures. Perhaps the practice was more widespread than we have realized, though I suspect few writers had either the patience or manual dexterity to indulge in such amendments. As Hone explains, “For Pope to have worked like this, he must have known precisely what words were going into an erased blank before he put blade to paper, accounting for overlapping letters or strokes.” However, Pope also used the method to erase comments prior to passing a fair copy of his poems to another mentor or friend. “He wanted to revise his poems, but he did not want to spoil how they looked and nor did he want to copy them out again from beginning to end, which would entail a good deal of work.” Hone is a master of understatement here, but his scholarship reveals the true extent of the lengths to which Pope went to sustain the appearance of orderly print in his manuscripts.Paul Davis also works from a unique manuscript and presents an edition of the Latin poem Arcus Triumphalis (composed as part of the celebrations of the Peace of Ryswick on December 2, 1697) that he firmly attributes to Addison for the first time. He does not apply new scholarly techniques to read the manuscript but brings to that text his immense appreciation for Latin poetry of the late seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries. Davis cites parallels to Addison’s other Latin verse in order to date this poem more precisely, but his expertise really shines when he contextualizes the poem amid the gratulatory poetry of Restoration Britain: the Greek and Latin echoes that such poetry depended upon to achieve sonic effects, and, indirectly, to convey fulsome praise. The most intriguing aspect that Davis explores concerns the tension between celebration and uncertainty, marking this as a poem more of the Restoration than of the Augustan period. Davis, I think rightly, attributes this tension to Addison’s own uncertainty as an established Oxford scholar increasingly interacting with the political world of London: “we tend to forget what an unlikely transformation it was that made the notoriously reticent and reserved Addison, a classic product of ‘Libraries’ and ‘Colleges,’ into the archetypal eighteenth-century ‘public man.’”This important pair of essays helps to account for Pope’s attraction to the older poet as a possible mentor: Addison was not merely the leader of a literary circle in London but also someone who had experienced the competing attractions of the contemplative world of high literary culture and the ethical calling to public engagement. In his discussion of Pope’s first published translation from the Iliad (“The Episode of Sarpedon” in 1709), Hone highlights how Pope’s deletion and erasure highlights the youthful poet’s uncertainty about whether to remain anonymous. Both these essays merit (and require) close reading, with implications well beyond the textual details they so ably expound.Shef RogersUniversity of OtagoBefore Blake wrote off blank verse, its monotony “as much a bondage as rhyme itself,” but after Young lauded it as “verse unfallen, uncurst; verse reclaimed, reinthron’d,” there was Cowper. For Cowper, the versatility and variety of blank verse could spring verbal surprise in ways that rhyming couplets could not. Blank verse was attention-grabbing, energetic, and demanding, while the “clock-work tintinnabulum of rhime,” as Cowper called it in Table Talk (1782), encouraged readerly inertia. A distinctive feature of Cowper’s blank verse, fully displayed in The Task (1785), and the focus of Turner’s fine article, is the pause, a moment of metrical and temporal suspension with moral and spiritual implications for the reader. Turner discusses the significance of pauses and cadence for Cowper’s prosody, contending that the deferral and duration made manifest in caesuras, line-endings, and punctuation (the third of these, Cowper wrote to William Unwin, was “of the last importance”) speak to Cowper’s religious experience and practice. In moments of pausing between syllables, phrases, and lines, as Turner argues with great nuance, Cowper’s blank verse requires of the reader attention that is commensurate to that of the Christian faithful. The reader of The Task, made mindful of moral regulation through metrical regulation, is analogously positioned between redemption and damnation, grace and its absence. Reading and writing poetry, Cowper’s starts and stops imply, is of great religious import; pausing can be of use, a way of redeeming the past, present, and future with improvement and reflection, or no more than another way of killing time. That Cowper, with what Turner identifies as a “digressive and distractable mode of writing,” most appropriate for blank verse and the long poem, leaves pausing open-ended, neither industrious nor indolent, demonstrates that this life has its consolations. Living in fear of divine judgment is far from a comfortable position, but “it is a habitual property of the Christian’s relationship with God and a necessary precondition for his ultimate redemption.” The gist of Cowper’s pauses, ambiguous though they may be, is divine judgment, but divine judgment deferred.Turner’s argument is amply supported by careful readings of Cowper’s poems and prosody, and it broaches contemporaneous debates about blank verse. Less is said about Milton and what Cowper called “the music of the Paradise Lost” than one might expect, and the prosiness and “familiar stile” of Cowper’s favorite, Prior, are not discussed, but this saves the focus for Cowper himself, who was determined to set his poetry apart from that of his predecessors and contemporaries. In addition to pointing out the capaciousness of Cowper’s blank verse, Turner calls attention to the spiritual, ritual-like aspects of Cowper’s prosodic art, opening up the relationship of absence and silence to recuperation in Cowper’s poetry and religious practice. Why else would Cowper, dedicating The Task to God, whose grace he could not be certain of, end with a pause: “But all is in his hand whose praise I seek / . . . Whose frown can disappoint the proudest strain, / whose approbation—prosper even mine”?Philip TrotterUniversity of TorontoAlthough the foci of these two essays are different—the by on the the from to title: How to Shift Your Attention
abstract: Willis Jenkins's “Migrations of the Sacred” is about how to notice, understand, value, and grieve the diminishment of animals whose numbers are dwindling. Specifically, Jenkins attends to Red Knot and their kin. Red Knot are small birds that fly a great distance. They are about the size of a robin, and most of them travel 19,000 miles every year, from one end of the Earth to the other, from Tierra del Fuego in Argentina to the Hudson Bay in the Arctic. Red Knot are declining in huge numbers, “dwindling, diminishing” in Jenkins's haunting idiom, headed toward extinction.How, Jenkins asks, might true apprehension of Red Knot loss affect the framing and practice of climate equity initiatives in the world the Red Knot is leaving? This question arises directly from Jenkins's experience. Jenkins has been involved in two simultaneous research projects, both focused on effects of climate change, both on Virginia's Eastern Shore. Nonetheless, these two projects are life worlds apart from one another. The first focuses on the diminishment of the Red Knot. The second, a “Coastal Futures Hub,” responds to community-driven concerns in this low-lying area on the Atlantic Ocean, in a place where people are experiencing increasing salt-water incursion, failing septic fields, and road flooding, all of which often reproduce longstanding social inequalities. Where these inequities are affecting people's lives and livelihoods, Red Knot are not—generally—a key priority. The world of Red Knot biology and the world of climate equity, both on Virginia's Eastern Shore, are often not in conversation with one another.Sometimes Red Knot flourishing and human coastal futures may even seem to be in tension, as pressing survival concerns for human communities present obvious priorities for folks living on the coast, some of whom don't even know they share their home with Red Knot. In this way, Jenkins's involvement in these two projects presents him with a laboratory of what I consider among the most interesting concerns in contemporary environmental ethics: what do we make of values that we hold dear when they seem to be in tension with one another? With so many ongoing troubles, how do we direct our focus without leaving something vital out?While Jenkins appreciates a wide array of values in this scene, he is also clear about what he wants to get into the picture. He is struck by the absence of Red Knot from the vision of justice in the “Coastal Futures Hub,” and he wants to know: how would values need to transform for people living on Virginia's Eastern Shore to see these two worlds—the Red Knot flyway and human vulnerabilities to changing climate conditions—as belonging to one another? And then, what would that world look like and to whom?In responding to “Migrations of the Sacred,” I will focus on two things—the first an observation about Jenkins's questions, and the second a meditation on what Jenkins's proposal looks like from my classroom. First, I describe one of Jenkins's key questions, which is how humans come to see themselves as caught up in sacred networks of kinship with other creatures living in their communities. Second, I respond to Jenkins's proposal that environmentally focused research in religious studies might build practices of attention that contribute to small, pragmatic shifts in the appreciation of sacred value among our communities. Ultimately, I will suggest that building these kinds of experiences is complicated and difficult, but also deeply related to pedagogical questions about what education is for, whether it is possible, and how we might go about doing it. If teachers are going to build these kinds of experiences for our students, we probably need to learn to create them for ourselves as well.How do humans value Red Knot as part of our world? In popular discourse, human concerns with other species’ diminishment are often oriented by the threat of extinction, which is to say the end of the species and its ability to make its home on Earth. But Jenkins describes how the concept of extinction—with its focus on individuated species and individual organisms—fails to capture the disvalue in Red Knot diminishment and dwindling. “How to name the loss in that diminishing, the disvalue in a migration's dwindling?” Jenkins is wondering what metaphors of connectedness can represent the loss of a lifeway. As Red Knot numbers decrease, we lose not only the Red Knot themselves, but the entire network of relations that support that fabulous migration. This includes the other species with which the Red Knot have been enmeshed in kin networks longer than any human history (with horseshoe crabs, snails, mussels) and even the climactic conditions that enabled those networks to sustain themselves. “Part of the challenge for ethics is to repair conceptual language that obscures the relations involved in extinctions.” When we consider Red Knot apart from their kin, Jenkins seems to say, we fail to mourn what is lost. When we do not mourn the communities undone by the extinction of one species, because we are missing concepts for the relations at stake, this is an ethical failure for which the scientific method so far lacks a language.Because of course Red Knot are not the only creatures in Virginia who are impacted by a changing climate. They are caught up—as all of us are—in webs of relations, a whole world of give and take that has gone on for millennia. Through this, they have accrued world wisdom that many humans barely fathom. Sometimes these webs are called “ecosystems,” but Jenkins's essay reminds us that such an idiom may undervalue what Red Knots and the lifeways they share with their kin are communicating. Through their massive annual migration, they know where to return, year after year, to keep their “appointments with sand-dwelling mollusks” and other species. And they continue to keep these appointments, or they keep trying to, even as their numbers dwindle from hundreds of thousands to tens of thousands.1In this essay, Jenkins is taking up an effort to imagine, as he writes, “ways otherwise, what might happen.”2 He is searching for how humans might transform ourselves to value the Red Knot and their kin. As examples, he observes places where humans have become susceptible in new ways to dwindling migrations—to Monarch Butterfly, to Chum Salmon, to Bowhead Whale, to Black-necked Crane.3 In relation to these species, new traditions have developed around the migration as it diminishes. When this happens, those migrations are not, he argues, merely providing “cultural ecosystem services” by transforming the human cultures made newly susceptible to their presence. The phrase—“cultural ecosystem services”—undersells the phenomenon it aims to describe. Something significantly more profound is happening. There is a form of “religious valuing in which a being or relation has status due to its power to change the beholder's imperfect moral regard.”4 The claim is grander than we might at first notice. Jenkins suggests that rather than simply contributing to cultural values, these animals have moral significance. They aren't merely part of our lives in ways we usually fail to recognize—they can make us better people by teaching us to do justice.This idea, that there is moral value in the relations between beings, is often presented as a recent intervention in sustainability literature under the category of “relational values.”5 While Jenkins is allied with the importance of relational practice, he thinks there are a couple of important problems with the framing of relational values as new-found in the sustainability literature. Presenting relational values as a recent discovery “1) deprives itself of available genealogies of relational value in ethics and 2) obscures the kind of moral regard evident in the expectation of some communities that their values should be transformed by multispecies relation.” By presenting “relational values” as an innovation in an academic literature, this rhetoric ignores assets it could otherwise retrieve, and it misrepresents already underrepresented communities.Communities who take it that multispecies relations are a moral matter have always existed, Jenkins reminds us. In Indigenous cultures, yes, and in dissenting movements from a supposed European Enlightenment consensus, and among contemporary, everyday people on Virginia's Eastern Shore, people Jenkins meets through his work on these interdisciplinary projects. In communities like that, “people may recognize that their present norms are not fully those they want to reproduce and, especially when thinking about the future, may identify values by which they hope their communities will be reshaped.”6 The hope that we might be able to improve our moral lives is far more widespread than academics sometimes make it seem. Some people are looking out for how they might meet their obligations better. Humans are often people who want to be transformed.Jenkins's question is how sacred values come into being for us, how humans might come to appreciate the Red Knot and their lifeway as the sacred things they are. Jenkins suggests this would require transformation. And yet he describes how it's increasingly easy to find examples of people hoping to be transformed into deeper relationship with Red Knot and hoping to transform others. In one example that Jenkins cites, the author Phillip Hoose wrote a large format book illustrated with many photographs, focused on a famously long-lived Red Knot known as Moonbird. (The name refers to the incredible distances this individual has flown over the course of its life—migrations combining to equal the distance from the Earth to its Moon and part of the way back.) This book, entitled Moonbird: A Year on the Wind with the Great Survivor B95, traces the annual migration of Red Knot, focusing specifically on one individual (B95) who lived at least 20 years.7 The book is written by an author who clearly cherishes the birds, and it is written for people (specifically children) who want to learn to appreciate the Red Knot migration. In its descriptions of the places that Red Knot stop on their route, the book repeatedly appeals to the category of the sacred. In at least three instances, Hoose marks the places that Red Knot stop on their migration as sacred: “sacred stepping-stone places” (56), “a sacred slice of the Earth” (76), “the sacred places . . . had sustained this amazing aviator” (104–105). In each case, Hoose suggests that the migration's stopping places are sacred sites, without ever thematizing what such an attribution means exactly. While Jenkins does not spend much time analyzing this particular source, Hoose himself may be doing something like what Jenkins is interested in understanding.For Jenkins, drawing on the sociologist Hans Joas, conceptions of the sacred move, and they ought to—when conceptions of the sacred shift, we see a value transformation of the kind increasingly studied by sustainability researchers. Thus, religious studies is particularly situated to understand such value transformation, as the study of religion often focuses on the continuities, transformations, and possibilities of intellectual, spiritual, and moral traditions with deep histories. This means it has particular strengths for just the thing these sustainability researchers are interested in.Jenkins is not focused on the ways that the rhetoric of the sacred in children's books might contribute to value transformation.8 Instead, he offers a practical focus on specific practices of attention that people do every day. He focuses on shifting what we look at in the small ways we can and letting those relational engagements in a particular place transform us. title: Review: A New Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere and Deliberative Politics, by Jürgen Habermas
abstract: Jürgen Habermas’s early work causes real problems for today’s readers. This has less to do with what he says or how he says it than the mysterious state of academic publishing in the 1960s and ’70s. Habermas’s first three books were translated into English a few years after they first appeared in German, although some of their chapters were swapped around. This is, however, less problematic than the fate that befell his first major work, The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere (1962), which didn’t appear in English for another twenty-seven years.1 The unevenness with which those early books appeared has inevitably shaped the interpretation of Habermas’s work up to this point.2 It also shaped the reception of other works inspired—implicitly or explicitly—by Habermas’s early reflections, all of which appeared at least five years before The Structural Transformation was published in English.3The Structural Transformation started as Habermas’s Habilitationsschrift (the postdoctoral thesis required to get a professorship in Germany), written under the supervision of critical theory pioneers Max Horkheimer and Theodor W. Adorno at the Institute for Social Research in Frankfurt. Adorno and Horkheimer didn’t receive it well, though, reproaching the young Habermas for two apparent faults at the same time. On the one hand, they alleged that Habermas wasn’t critical enough about Enlightenment ideas about democracy and public life in a mass society, evading the apocalyptic critique of this material they pursued in their Dialectic of Enlightenment (1947). At the same time, however, Habermas stood accused of being too politically radical, optimistically looking for radical democratic potential in and beyond the liberal constitutions of states like West Germany, the United Kingdom, and the United States.Although Habermas did manage to successfully submit his thesis to Wolfgang Abendroth at Marburg, The Structural Transformation didn’t appear in English until 1989, although he admits that one of the reasons for the delayed translation of the text, which had gone out of print after eighteen editions, was that he had intended to rework it but never did.4 By this point, Habermas had already become a major figure, publishing at least eight significant works—all of which saw him refine his earlier concepts, aims, and theoretical paradigm—which had been translated into English. The year 1989 also saw two events that would lead Habermas to further emphasize the nuances of his 1970s and ’80s work: the huge upheaval that came with the collapse of communism, which led many thinkers to reassess what they understood by historical progress, revolution, and democracy, and a far less cataclysmic event: an academic conference about Habermas’s earlier achievements. Indeed, two months prior to the fall of the Berlin Wall, the conference “Habermas and the Public Sphere” at the University of Chapel Hill, North Carolina, celebrated his first book’s English translation, papers from which were published in an edited essay collection of the same name three years later.5It is clear, however, that The Structural Transformation anticipates many of Habermas’s later themes. And it does so using historically specific examples in a way found nowhere else in his work, such as the development of the parliamentary system in England since the seventeenth century, the publishing industry and free press both there and in post-Revolutionary France, and specific legislation and theories about the mass media of West Germany in the 1960s. Even though the latter example dated quickly, perhaps if the book had appeared in English sooner, it would, as Thomas McCarthy puts it in his introduction to the translation, “likely have facilitated the reception of [Habermas’s] thought among Anglo-American scholars by showing how the more abstract and theoretical concerns of his later work arose out of the concrete issues raised in this study.”6 Indeed, one reviewer of the English translation commented, convincingly even then, on the “simultaneous relevance and anachronism”7 of Habermas’s book. This situation is made even more frustrating by Habermas’s influence on other works that were originally in English. In the preface to The Function of Criticism (1984), for example, Terry Eagleton writes that Habermas’s understanding of the public sphere is the “guiding concept”8 for his history of English literary criticism since the eighteenth century, without the original inspiration being available to many readers of Eagleton’s book. Nancy Fraser, meanwhile, was a key contributor to the Chapel Hill conference and essay collection. However, her influential essays on the “gender subtext” in Habermas’s mature work, which could have been strengthened by a fuller critical discussion of Habermas’s understanding of the public sphere, appeared in journals two years earlier, and four years before the translation The Structural Transformation.9This admittedly very partial tracing of the original book’s reception history isn’t just a pedantic academic boast, the scholar-as-detective gleefully hunting for clues amid the endnotes. On the contrary, as Fraser points out, the concept of the public sphere was “subsequently resituated but never abandoned”10 in Habermas’s later work. This suggests that any critical assessment of Habermas’s latest contribution to these problems, A New Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere and Deliberative Politics, must be at least aware of that history. That includes rejoinders by key figures in the “third generation” of critical theory and their readers, some of whose contributions appear in Habermas and the Public Sphere (1992, edited by Craig Calhoun) and have no doubt shaped the direction of academic debates about these issues long prior to the new volume.11As its title suggests, Habermas’s latest offering builds on his analyses of the public sphere in The Structural Transformation while taking stock of how his work has developed since then. He writes, for instance, that political disputes in democratic societies have a “fundamentally agonal character” in which “the participants’ orientation to the truth is supposed to ignite an open-ended conflict of opinions that gives rise to competing public opinions” (17–18). Claims like this build on his reformulation of critical theory toward communicative action and deliberative democracy.The public sphere sustains, for the early Habermas, “ideology and simultaneously more than mere ideology”12 because it sustains bourgeois society’s false consciousness of itself and its own ideals while also transcending the current state of things by promising an end to political domination. Since the late-1970s and ’80s, however, Habermas has revised his understanding of ideology and replaced the dominant model of the “philosophy of consciousness” with communicative rationality. The essence of this shift is that the subject no longer treats the world and the people in it as something to be known and acted on for the sake of self-preservation, but is oriented toward intersubjective understanding achieved by communicating with others.13 This is the basis for democratic deliberation, in which citizens are able to disagree with each other, criticizing each other’s positions while regarding each other in “a spirit open to compromise as opponents and no longer as enemies” (23).A New Structural Transformation bears the marks not just of Habermas’s changed emphasis, but also his responses to the post-1989 political and economic climate, more recent developments, and his own critics. Indeed, prompted by new social movements like second-wave feminism and the criticisms of figures like Fraser, Habermas reviewed his theory of the public sphere. Following the revisions in Between Facts and Norms: Contributions to a Discourse Theory of Law and Democracy (1992), in A New Structural Transformation, Habermas considers how, rather than enjoying access to the public sphere in one singular form that is available in principle for everyone, modern democratic societies consist of multiple different overlapping spaces for communication. This stresses the “interpenetration of private and public autonomy”14 in which citizens’ capacity to articulate their opinions is shaped by their social status.Following this, Habermas’s dramatic first claim in A New Structural Transformation is that, since the rise of the internet and the intensive global spread of smartphone technology and use of social media platforms, we are faced with “a caesura in the historical development of the media comparable to the introduction of printing” (33). The substance of his second claim is no less intense, even if it is more subtly technical. Habermas suggests that, although social media may offer certain technical advantages over earlier forms of spoken and written communication, because the messages that are sent are ever more concise and arrive instantly, they “prompt a kind of exchange about implicit or explicit political views that, through the changed mode of use, could influence how the public sphere is perceived as such” (50), which may threaten the very existence of democracy. Assessing this as part of a transformative development relies, of course, on an understanding of Habermas’s argument in the original The Structural Transformation. This provides, he says, subsequent research and the new work with a “preliminary social-historical analysis” (3).The Structural Transformation offers, Habermas says, “not only a sociological clarification of the concept [of the public sphere] but a systematic comprehension of our own society from the perspective of one of its central categories.”15 Habermas can even be credited with coining the term “public sphere” (Öffentlichkeit).16 This means the space, in democratic societies, between two sources of social influence. On the one hand, the people, who vote for governments and whose lives are shaped by political and social institutions. On the other hand, the government they vote for, whose policies shape the direction and character of those institutions, and which is ultimately accountable to voters. The public sphere consists of a society of free, equal citizens who come together to discuss issues that concern all of them, institutionalized in the media with a professional class of journalists and editors who articulate, and seek to sway, public opinion to persuade voters to cast their ballot for one or another political party or cause. The public sphere is not only, however, the enabling condition that constitutes the people as a people who can and do debate matters of common interest, but a kind of discursive interaction in its own title: Six Characters in Search of a Prophet: Emerson's Representative Men
abstract: I title this essay “Six Characters in Search of a Prophet”; it might equally have been called “Six Aspects of a Problem in Search of a Solution.” Prefaced by the introductory “Uses of Great Men,” delivered as a course of lectures in the winter of 1845–46, and enlarged and revised only slightly for book publication in 1850, Representative Men belongs in its thematic concerns to the earlier half of the decade, a period of crisis and would-be transition for Emerson most openly on display the preceding year in “Experience” (1844) but visible as well in attitudes toward nature, history, and the capacities of the self in “The Method of Nature” (1841), “The Transcendentalist” (1841), “The Young American” (1844), and in contemporary volumes of the journals.1Among the most accessible of Emerson's books, if also among the least attended to critically, Representative Men occupies the position of a fulcrum, or potential fulcrum, within the course of his career. Faced with the disjunction between “the world I converse with in the city and in the farms” and “the world I think,” Emerson might attempt to synthesize the actual and the ideal within the terms of his newly emerging thought; he might try to reaffirm established ideas with whatever retrenchments or modifications seemed necessary; or he might intellectually mark time as he awaited life and thought to deliver him from an impasse that admitted of no visible solution.2Of the seven “Lords of Life” designated in the poetic headnote to “Experience” and again in the text, five (Illusion, Temperament, Succession, Surprise, Subjectivity) refer to an internal condition (the limitations imposed by temperament, heredity, and the inconstancy of moods), two (Surface and Reality) to an external condition (the ways of the world). The former were long-standing subjects of frustration in Emerson's journals, if only marginally in his public writings through Essays: First Series (1841). The latter grew increasingly prominent in the mid-1840s as rapid industrialization and the coming of the railroad to New England forced him to concede the present-day immovability of capitalism and the fact that its leading figures, nature's “darlings” as he called them in “Experience,” “are not children of our law, do not come out of the Sunday school, nor weigh their food, nor punctually keep the commandments.”3 On one side was the world envisioned by the active soul, on the other the world of material power operative upon and within the self. “Cannot Montaigne & Shakespeare consist with Plato & Jesus?” he had asked in a journal entry of 1839.4Representative Men substitutes Swedenborg for Jesus, but the issue remains the same: the incongruity between the mind's impulse toward unity and the unruly plenitude of the world.Originating in a lecture on Napoleon Emerson gave in the winter of 1844–45, Representative Men developed into a vehicle through which he might explore and attempt to resolve the perplexing doubleness of experience. Unlike Carlyle's On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History (1840), which had preached reverence for and submission to great men, Emerson's opening “Uses of Great Men” enlists its characters as instruments for the instruction of the self and the furtherance of universal design. title: A Survey on Deep Learning for Design and Generation of Virtual Architecture
abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) shape generation techniques leveraging deep learning have garnered significant interest from both computer vision and architectural design communities, promising to enrich the content in the virtual environment. However, research on virtual architectural design remains limited, particularly regarding designer-AI collaboration and deep learning-assisted design. In our survey, we reviewed 149 related articles (81.2% of articles published between 2019 and 2023) covering architectural design, 3D shape techniques, and virtual environments. Through scrutinizing the literature, we first identify the principles of virtual architecture and illuminate its current production challenges, including datasets, multimodality, design intuition, and generative frameworks. We then introduce the latest approaches to designing and generating virtual buildings leveraging 3D shape generation and summarize four characteristics of various approaches to virtual architecture. Based on our analysis, we expound on four research agendas, including agency, communication, user consideration, and integrating tools. Additionally, we highlight four important enablers of ubiquitous interaction with immersive systems in deep learning-assisted architectural generation. Our work contributes to fostering understanding between designers and deep learning techniques, broadening access to designer-AI collaboration. We advocate for interdisciplinary efforts to address this timely research topic, facilitating content designing and generation in the virtual environment.

title: LaPose: Laplacian Mixture Shape Modeling for RGB-Based Category-Level Object Pose Estimation
Localized Gaussian Splatting Editing with Contextual Awareness
venue: IEEE Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision
abstract: Recent advancements in text-guided 3D object generation using diffusion priors struggle with illumination inconsistencies when applied to scene editing tasks like object replacement or insertion. To address this, we propose an illumination-aware 3D scene editing pipeline for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). Our method leverages state-of-the-art 2D diffusion inpainting [56] to handle global illumination context effectively. Specifically, we identify representative anchor views that capture scene-wide illumination, inpaint them using 2D diffusion models, and integrate the results into a coarse-to-fine 3DGS optimization process. In the fine step, we introduce Depth-guided Inpainting Score Distillation Sampling (DI-SDS) to refine geometry and texture details, capitalizing on the diversity of 2D priors. Our approach achieves locally precise edits with globally consistent illumination, demonstrating robustness in real scenes with highlights and shadows. Comparisons show superior results over state-of-the-art text-to-3D editing methods. Project page: https://corneliushsiao.github.io/GSLE.html.

title: Spice·E: Structural Priors in 3D Diffusion using Cross-Entity Attention
abstract: We are witnessing rapid progress in automatically generating and manipulating 3D assets due to the availability of pretrained text-to-image diffusion models. However, time-consuming optimization procedures are required for synthesizing each sample, hindering their potential for democratizing 3D content creation. Conversely, 3D diffusion models now train on million-scale 3D datasets, yielding high-quality text-conditional 3D samples within seconds. In this work, we present Spice · E – a neural network that adds structural guidance to 3D diffusion models, extending their usage beyond text-conditional generation. At its core, our framework introduces a cross-entity attention mechanism that allows for multiple entities—in particular, paired input and guidance 3D shapes—to interact via their internal representations within the denoising network. We utilize this mechanism for learning task-specific structural priors in 3D diffusion models from auxiliary guidance shapes. We show that our approach supports a variety of applications, including 3D stylization, semantic shape editing and text-conditional abstraction-to-3D, which transforms primitive-based abstractions into highly-expressive shapes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Spice · E achieves SOTA performance over these tasks while often being considerably faster than alternative methods. Importantly, this is accomplished without tailoring our approach for any specific task. We will release our code and trained models.

title: Towards patient-specific hemodynamics of the aorta: A comprehensive CT-guided approach for moving boundary CFD simulations
Fast and Accurate Category-Level Object Pose Estimation Without Shape Priors for Robotic Grasp Detection
venue: IEEE Transactions on Automation Science and Engineering
abstract: Category-level object pose estimation is crucial for enabling robot grasping. Currently, many methods rely on 3D shape priors for pose estimation, but obtaining priors for specific categories often requires a significant amount of time to generate. Although some methods do not rely on priors, However, these methods struggle to achieve a balance between speed and accuracy. Achieving fast and accurate category-level object pose estimation remains a challenging issue. In this paper, we propose an algorithm called FAPose, which aims to simultaneously achieve speed and accuracy in category-level object pose estimation without any shape priors. Firstly, we design an RGB-point cloud feature aggregation method based on transformers to fuse RGB and point cloud features. Secondly, we develop a dual-constraint object pose estimation method to effectively leverage both feature space and geometric space information. This approach constructs pose constraints in both feature space and geometric space to achieve optimal pose prediction. Finally, we validate FAPose through benchmark datasets and real robot grasping experiments. The experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method surpasses most existing state-of-the-art pose estimation methods, achieving superior pose estimation performance. The code for FAPose will be available after the paper is accepted for publication.

title: Image Warping and Its Application for Data Augmentation when Training Deep Neural Networks
abstract: The paper focuses on the improvement of the quality of learning for deep neural networks for a small data set in a classification task. One of the possible approaches to improve the quality of learning is researched which is based on the use of data augmentation (artificial reproduction of the data set) by image warping. The presented mathematical model and fast algorithm for warping make it possible to transform the original image while preserving its structural basis. The proposed algorithm is used to augment image data sets containing a small number of training samples. The augmentation consists of two stages including horizontal mirroring and warping of each of the samples. The effectiveness of such augmentation is tested through the training of neural networks of various types: convolutional neural networks (CNN) of a standard architecture and deep residual networks (DRN). A specific feature of the implemented approach for the solution of the problem under consideration consists in the refusal to use pre-trained neural networks with a large number of layers as well as further transfer learning, since their application incurs costs in terms of the computational resources. The paper shows that the efficiency of image classification when implementing the proposed method of augmenting training data on small and medium-sized data sets increases to statistically significant values of the metric used.

title: Partial reconstruction of sparse and incomplete point clouds applied to the generation of corneal topographic maps of healthy and diseased patients
Authenticity as discursive gaze: a critical review of social media research on authenticity
abstract: Authenticity has long been a central concept in academic discussions of media, particularly in the context of digitization and the Internet. Early scholars working in this area have demonstrated how the internet’s participatory affordances, alongside the rise of surveillance-style reality television programming, led to an increase in discourses that praised authenticity for its “unfiltered” representation of the self and its supposed democratization of media entertainment (Andrejevic, 2002). Despite the initially celebratory tone that surrounded these early participatory media forms, scholars have criticized their democratic promises for ultimately reinforcing established power dynamics (Turner, 2010). Others have demonstrated how the purported authenticity of the “ordinary people” participating in these participatory media forms is often a theatrical performance that aims to appear genuine through the use of media skills and technologies (Senft, 2008). These core themes of authenticity as performance, the interplay between democratization and commodification, and the power dynamics embedded in participatory media have continued to shape critical discussions in the digital age. Scholars have increasingly interrogated how authenticity is constructed, negotiated, and commodified across diverse media landscapes, from social media platforms (e.g., Maddox, 2023; Marwick & boyd, 2011; Papacharissi, 2010; Van Dijck, 2009) to influencer cultures (e.g., Abidin, 2017; Arriagada & Bishop, 2021; Duffy & Hund, 2019). The books discussed in this critical review essay affirm the continued relevance of authenticity as academic concept and as sociocultural discourse. Together, they encompass three areas related to authenticity and social media: Authenticity and social media identity performance (Taylor, 2022; Gill, 2023; Piazzesi, 2023), authenticity in the cultural and influencer industries (Hund, 2023; Serazio, 2023), and authenticity and social media cities (Banks 2023; Hurley 2023). Allan S. Taylor’s Authenticity as Performativity on Social Media (2022) explores how authenticity is enacted as a performative process on social media, discussing its mimetic, affective, and ephemeral nature. Rosalind Gill’s Perfect: Feeling Judged on Social Media (2023) discusses the pressures and vulnerabilities that are experienced by women social media users as a result of pervasive norms of perfection, constant surveillance, and the demands of an authentic self-performance. Chiara Piazzesi’s book, The Beauty Paradox: Femininity in the Age of Selfies (2023), explores the complex and paradoxical relationships between beauty, femininity, and self-representation in the context of selfie culture, examining how women navigate the contradictory demands made of them in the name of “authentic” beauty. Together, these works illustrate the multifaceted nature of authenticity and self-representation on social media, demonstrating how individuals, especially women, engage with and negotiate the pressure of self-performance, beauty standards, and cultural expectations as mediated by social platforms. Emily Hund’s The Influencer Industry: The Quest for Authenticity on Social Media (2023) examines the centrality of authenticity to the influencer economy and its supporting industries, exploring how social media platforms and industry structure commodify personal identity and foster an economy of curated self-performance. Michael Serazio’s book, The Authenticity Industries: Keeping It “Real” in Media, Culture, and Politics (2023), equally discusses the commodification of authenticity, analyzing how it is strategically manufactured across a range of industries and arenas, from pop music to reality TV to contemporary politics. Moving from industry to urban development, David A. Banks in The City Authentic: How the Attention Economy Builds Urban America (2023) reveals how authenticity is equally coveted and commodified in urban contexts, highlighting tensions between local identity, place branding, and the economic forces shaping contemporary city scapes. Similarly, Zoe Hurley’s Social Media Influencing in the City of Likes: Dubai and the Postdigital Condition (2023) examines the interplay between social media influencer, urban branding, and digital culture, focusing on the aspirational images constructed by and about Dubai. These books illustrate how discourses on authenticity have moved beyond legacy and social media to inform industries, urban development, and politics. This essay contends that recent academic work on authenticity reveals a distinctive discursive gaze: a socio-technical mechanism that trains individuals and institutions to evaluate the self and others according to shifting, yet structured, norms of authenticity. Unlike earlier forms of social evaluation, this gaze is institutionalized through platform infrastructures, data metrics, and aesthetic conventions that systematically shape self-presentation for visibility and judgment. The term discursive emphasizes how this gaze functions through structured systems of communication and representation embedded within these digital and algorithmic frameworks. This gaze is directed both inward, prompting individuals to assess their own performances, and outward, urging them to read and evaluate the people, places, and things they encounter as objects for the construction and validation of authenticity. Authenticity is therefore a situated and relational construct—a performance of the self that is legible as coherent with both prior self-performances and social scripts, and that is validated by others. Authenticity is experienced as affectively “true” within these interactions, yet it remains an ephemeral and dynamic negotiation of identity. Beginning with an analysis of how these books each frame authenticity, this essay will demonstrate how together these discussions reveal authenticity’s discursive gaze and its relational, situated, and shifting contours. It will then discuss how this gaze operates and structures specific contexts, from the cultural industries to urban planning and promotion to individual practice and self-representation. This essay will therefore demonstrate how authenticity is shaped by historical, economic, and technological contexts. It will also show that authenticity functions as a dynamic gaze, shifting across cultural industries, urban spaces, and social media to reveal how subjects and institutions engage in cycles of validation and critique. The books reviewed for this essay each discuss authenticity to different degrees. While authenticity is central to the arguments of Hund (2023), Banks (2023), Serazio (2023), and Taylor (2022), it is a secondary concern for Gill (2023), Piazzesi (2023), and Hurley (2023), for whom authenticity is just one of many constructs shaping their respective case studies. However, for all books authenticity is something necessary, yet often difficult, to define. For example, Emily Hund (2023) discusses the many different connotations that authenticity carries within influencer industries, noting its associations with unfiltered “realness,” relatability, truth, and naturalness. However, Hund also notes that authenticity is increasingly constructed, quantified, and commodified for commercial gain. Similarly, Serazio (2023, p. 66) discusses the ideas of “rough cut” authenticity that have governed celebrity and status in music and reality television, demonstrating how an “aesthetic bias” for raw and informal self-presentation is largely catered to through an emphasis on local roots and emotional self-disclosure. Both Hund (2023) and Serazio (2023) demonstrate that authenticity is a shifting goal post around which the cultural and influencer industries pivot; if “realness” relies on presenting something in its original, unmediated form, then the act of mediation inherently compromizes its authenticity. For this reason, the influencer and cultural industries are always looking for new authentic persons and places to capitalize on. Hurley (2023), Serazio (2023), and Banks (2023) each demonstrate that authenticity is highly contextual, with its meaning contingent on the setting in which it is mobilized and the power dynamics between individuals, institutions, and the cultural frameworks through which it is performed. This constantly shifting nature explains why Piazzesi (2023) argues that inauthenticity is easier to define than authenticity; her respondents noted that, while authenticity remains an elusive and paradoxical concept, failures to achieve it are readily identifiable and easy to critique. Taylor (2022) would argue that this difficulty in capturing authenticity lies with its relational and ephemeral nature, suggesting that authenticity is “a trace of something known tacitly but unavailable to access in a permanent way” (p. 13). He asserts that authenticity is performativity, an affective and resonant thing that emerges in the moment when people use familiar words, images, or gestures to make something feel real. For this reason, authenticity is also relational, as it is dependent on both performer and audience being able to recognize and understand this performance as familiar. title: DF‐3DNet: A Lightweight Approach Based on Deep Learning for 3D Telecommunication Tower Asset Classification
abstract: ABSTRACT The transition from 4G to 5G communication systems and the phase‐out of 3G equipment have increased the demand for efficient telecommunication tower inspection and maintenance. Traditional manual methods are time‐consuming and risky, prompting the adoption of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) equipped with LiDAR sensors. This research introduces a framework for telecommunication tower asset inspection, utilising a lightweight, deep learning‐based 3D classifier called DF‐3DNet. The process involves raw 3D point cloud data collection using DJI's Zenmuse L1 LiDAR, optimal flight planning, data pre‐processing, augmentation, and classification. The study focuses on two key asset classes—radio frequency (RF) panels and microwave (MW) dishes—which are prevalent in telecommunication towers. DF‐3DNet, an enhanced version of PointNet, incorporates advanced data augmentation methods and class balance compensation to optimise performance, particularly when working with limited datasets. The model achieved classification accuracies of 0.6613 on ScanObjectNN, 0.8171 on ModelNet40, and 0.869 on the telecommunication tower dataset, demonstrating its effectiveness in handling noisy, small‐scale data. By streamlining inspection workflows and leveraging AI‐driven classification, this framework significantly reduces costs, time, and risks associated with traditional methods, paving the way for scalable, real‐time telecommunication tower asset management.

title: Learning Hierarchical Adaptive Code Clouds for Neural 3D Shape Representation
LegoACE: Autoregressive Construction Engine for Expressive LEGO® Assemblies
abstract: Automated LEGO® design is challenging due to the extensive variety of LEGO® brick types and the necessity of constructing semantically meaningful models from individually meaningless components. Current automatic LEGO® generation methods face two key challenges: i) They typically rely on explicit modeling of brick connectivity to ensure structural validity. However, this requires extensive manual annotation, which is labor-intensive as the variety of LEGO® primitives increases. This limits training data diversity, restricting the variety of LEGO® bricks that can be effectively utilized. ii) To facilitate learning within neural networks, current methods often employ either volume or text-based descriptions to represent LEGO® models. However, volumetric representations are computationally expensive and hamper large-scale generative training, while text-based approaches rely on large language models and dedicated text-to-brick mapping rules, introducing a semantic gap between language tokens and 3D brick structures.

title: Time-archival camera virtualization for sports and visual performances
Infrared and Visible Image Fusion with Dual Decomposition Features
venue: International Joint Conference on Neural Networks (IJCNN)
abstract: Infrared and visible image fusion aims to extract richer image information and enhance the visual quality of images by fusing images from both modalities. Through the improvement of the CDDFuse model, this paper effectively mitigates the instability of the convolutional network in the training process and improves the ability of the infrared and visible image fusion network to extract feature information. To address the above issues, residual connections are first introduced into the encoder to stabilize the network architecture, reduce the possibility of situations such as gradient vanishing, and speed up the training process. Second, a multi scale feature enhancement module is added to Restormer to further improve the model’s ability to extract feature information. Finally, the subjective and objective contrast between the improved algorithm and the mainstream demonstrates that the methods discussed in this paper are able to retain detail while also better extracting target information.

title: 3D Congealing: 3D-Aware Image Alignment in the Wild
3D Synthesis for Architectural Design
venue: IEEE Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision
abstract: We introduce a 3D synthesis method for architectural design to allow for the efficient generation of diverse and realistic building designs. In spite of advances in 3D synthesis, current off-the-shelf 3D synthesis techniques are inappropriate for architectural design: they are trained primarily on isolated objects, have limited diversity, blend building facades with background and produce overly complex geometry that is difficult to edit or manipulate, a major issue in an iterative design process. We propose an alternative pipeline that integrates auto-generated coarse models with segment-wise texture inpainting and semantics-based editing, resulting in diverse, style-consistent, and shape-precise designs. We show through qualitative and quantitative experiments that our pipeline generates more diverse, visually appealing architectures with clean geometries without the need for any extensive training. title: A polyhedral reconstruction of a 3D object from a chain code and a low-density point cloud
abstract: Abstract The manipulation of 3D objects is becoming crucial for many applications, such as health, industry, or entertainment, to mention some. However, these 3D objects require substantial energy and different types of resources. With the goal of obtaining a simplified representation of a 3D object that can be easily managed, for example, for transmission, in some recent works, the authors associate low-density point clouds with a 3D object that simplifies the original 3D object. More precisely, given a 3D object in a polyhedral format, some authors associate a chain code and then use grammar-free context to obtain key points that give rise to several point clouds with different densities. In this work, we complete the cycle by developing a polyhedral reconstruction from an associated low-density point cloud and the chain code. The polyhedral reconstruction is crucial for handling 3D objects because it allows us to visualize them after they are efficiently compressed and transmitted. We apply our algorithms to well-known 3D objects in the literature. We use the Hausdorff and Chamfer distances to compare our results with the state-of-the-art proposals. We show how our proposed polyhedral reconstruction based on a helical chain code reconstructs a medical image represented or transmitted by slices into a 3D object in a polyhedral format, helping thus to mitigate and alleviate the management of 3D medical objects. The polyhedron that we propose provides better compression when compared with the original set of slices of a 3D medical object.

“He Who Loves His Brother Shall Walk in the Light”: The Fight for a Fair Housing Law in Illinois by the United Citizens’ Committee for Freedom of Residence, 1959–1963
venue: Journal of the Illinois State Historical Society (1998-)
abstract: The lawyer from Illinois, Abraham Lincoln, saw the United States as a nation “conceived in liberty and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal.”1 During his presidency (1861–1865), Lincoln knew that a nation where all citizens might achieve “a just and lasting peace” was an ambition that would be harder won than any battle in the Civil War. Through the succeeding years, initiatives to understand the “architecture of segregation” in the United States and then take meaningful action have long been brought forth—some with a degree of success, some ending with failure. But, as I argue in this article, any worthy attempt, even if ultimately unsuccessful, should not be considered a complete defeat, for it is said that “once your consciousness has registered inequity, it is always there, forcing the question, ‘Do I ignore, justify, or do I act, and if so, to what degree?’”2The civil rights era of the late 1950s through the 1960s gave rise to marches, protests, and grassroots movements that brought to the public eye the scourge of housing discrimination. This study of the Evanston-based United Citizens’ Committee for Freedom of Residence in Illinois (UCCFORI; sometimes shortened to Freedom of Residence [FOR]) reveals early and meticulous fair housing work that served coevally to influence hundreds of other “open housing” programs in cities and states across the nation.3 Through mostly original work, the FOR developed prototypes for community organizing, education programs, literature, fact-based arguments, step-by-step guiding flyers, judicial prototypes, and replication of their business model methodology that were easy to use, re-create, and expand upon.4 While the UCCFORI never fully achieved their own stated goals, they set up the fundamental scaffolding for other state fair housing activists to try to realize a measure of success. Look close enough in the archives of any open housing group in the Midwest and you will most assuredly find an FOR flyer, booklet, or guide that was used as a model for their own action.The groundwork for the FOR unofficially started to be laid in early 1959, when members of the Illinois State Bar Association Subcommittee on Zoning, Housing, and Building Ordinances published a study titled “High Challenges Offered Lawyers in Citizens’ Efforts for Urban Renewal.”5 The chairman of this group was a Yale-educated lawyer named Donald S. Frey, who—in addition to his work with the Illinois State Bar Association, in a private practice, and as a ranking member of many other civic organizations—was the president of the Evanston Human Relations Council (EHRC). Frey devotedly studied how organized networks were passing fair housing legislation in New York, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Colorado.6 This piqued his curiosity to ask such questions as: How could you embolden the better part of Illinois’ ten million souls to write their state representatives and ask them to vote for a fair housing act that would put “teeth” behind the federal Civil Rights Act of 1957? Would Illinoisans embrace an act that would result in them agreeing to have a person of color or someone of another faith live next door, on the same floor, or even in their town? Would such an act genuinely force real estate agents, home builders, landlords, and communities to abide by a fair housing law?Frey and a group from the EHRC—along with local civic and religious leaders and private citizen activists—wrote, published, lectured, and began thinking anew about putting forth local open occupancy legislation.7 This Evanston-based group was interested in whether there were any correlations in the national dialogue that they could use in service of a growing frustration within their own city limits.But what started as a community initiative quickly became an Illinois-wide event. Unlike other “white suburban-led” groups, such as the metropolitan Boston movement described by Lily Geismer, the FOR did not constrict their focus to municipal or dense population areas.8 Instead, they grew to describe themselves as both “a federation of existing organizations . . . and many individuals in various towns and cities of Illinois,” and “a statewide movement with a membership consisting of national, state, and local human relations groups, church and community groups, and individual members subscribing to the thesis that segregation in housing is a basic evil that must be eradicated.”9 This unique perspective allowed the FOR to establish flexibility in their programs, and and to on individual and knew their better than a the of the state, for when the FOR that of live title: Disruptive Means and Radical Ends: Toward an Embodied Understanding of Dewey's Vision of Democracy
abstract: john dewey famously advocated for a vision of democracy as an ethical way of life. Far from viewing democracy as a static institution, Dewey imagined it as a continuous experiment in associated living, collaborative inquiry, cooperation, and adaptation. One of his key tenets was that democracy can only be achieved by democratic means. In his 1937 essay “Democracy Is Radical,” Dewey insisted that “the fundamental principle of democracy is that the ends of freedom and individuality for all can be attained only by means that accord with those ends” (22). At the time, he was writing to critique growing global movements that were justifying violent, militant, and authoritarian means in the supposed name of democracy. He aimed to counter this instrumental use by reminding us that democracy must be embodied in its methods rather than presented as a distant, disembodied goal. For Dewey, the very essence of democracy requires methods rooted in equality, participation, and adaptability. His radical insight was that democracy's transformative potential lies in maintaining a dynamic interplay between means and ends and, further, that “[t]he end of democracy is a radical end. . . . It is radical because it requires great change in existing social institutions, economic, legal, and cultural. A democratic liberalism that does not recognize these things in thought and action is not awake to its own meaning and to what that meaning demands” (22).When taken apart from the context of his radical vision of democracy, Dewey's notion of democratic means loses much of its original meaning. Too often in dominant political and philosophical discourse, “democratic means” has come to act as a shorthand for a type of watered-down deliberative democracy—an act of “coming to the table” for a pre-programmed debate of ideas. In many of these deliberative frameworks, democracy is reduced to formalized arenas of rational argumentation—calm, orderly spaces where disembodied, idealized participants reason together free from any messiness of their embodied realities. Richard Bernstein has argued that Dewey was not a fan of accounts of deliberative democracy that overemphasized rational argumentation. He writes: Some versions of ‘deliberative democracy’ tend to exaggerate the role of rational persuasion in democratic politics. There is a tendency to overemphasize the role and potential power of rational argumentation. Dewey was never happy with the way in which philosophers and political theorists characterized reason—especially when they sharply distinguished reason from emotion, desire, and passion. He preferred to speak about intelligence and intelligent action. Intelligence is not the name of a special faculty. Rather, it designates a cluster of habits and dispositions that includes attentiveness to details, imagination, and passionate commitment. What is most essential for Dewey is the embodiment of intelligence in everyday practices. (Bernstein 85; emphasis added)An impoverished understanding of democratic means not only distorts Dewey's project, but risks reinforcing existing injustices by silencing those whose anger, pain, and lived experiences defy the neat boundaries of “reasonable” debate, and by dismissing “disruptive means” such as people taking to the streets, occupying public spaces, or anything that spills out from the carefully corralled boundaries of where democracy should happen. It further overlooks the generative role of social movements, protests, and these acts of disruption that bring new voices into the public sphere. On this view, for example, the sole purpose of social movements is to bring issues to the table for discussion. As political theorist Deva Woodly notes in her introduction to Reckoning: Black Lives Matter and the Democratic Necessity of Social Movements, in 2016, President Barack Obama criticized the Black Lives Matter movement along these lines. In an article in The New York Times, he is quoted as saying that the movement was “really effective at bringing attention to problems,” but that “once you've highlighted an issue and brought it to people's attention . . . then you can't just keep on yelling at them. . . . The value of social movements and activism is to get you at the table, get you in the room, and then to start trying to figure out how the problem is to be solved.”3 Woodly turns this view on its head. She suggests that the value of social movements is not in bringing issues to the table, but rather that they offer something vital in themselves. She writes: Movements are a pragmatic politics in process; they are the performance of the political. They remind members of the polity that there is a public sphere where politics can and must take place if democracy is to be both authorized by and responsive to the people. In this way, social movements are not only instrumental, but institutionally important in themselves. They teach us how to reclaim citizenship in times when public life has become anemic or repressive, and many have forgotten that their political action is both necessary and beneficial. (Woodly 17)In this paper, I argue that realizing Dewey's radical vision of democracy requires embracing a more robust understanding of democratic means—one that invites disruption and centers the lived experiences of marginalized communities. To support this claim, I first contrast two interpretations of democratic means—the rational, deliberative model epitomized by Jürgen Habermas and an embodied, disruptive model that I will argue aligns with Dewey's pragmatism. Next, I introduce Jacques Rancière's concept of dissensus to elucidate the role of disruption in revealing and challenging systemic inequalities and Claude Lefort's conception of democracy as the “empty place of power” to strengthen our understanding of the necessity of such disruption. Finally, I engage Deva Woodly's analysis of the Movement for Black Lives (M4BL) and its development of Radical Black Feminist Pragmatism (RBFP), a political philosophy that I argue offers a necessary framework for actualizing Dewey's ethical vision.As previously stated, for Dewey, democracy is not a stable endpoint, but an evolving experiment rooted in social intelligence and collective problem solving. His conception of democracy extends well beyond electoral systems and formal institutions, requiring “the full range of human experience” to thrive (Bernstein 86). Bernstein reminds us thatAs Bernstein rightly calls out, after the linguistic turn, philosophers sought to ground democratic legitimacy in rational-discursive procedures. Jürgen Habermas, in particular, developed a robust theory of communicative rationality, positing that democratic legitimacy emerges from the “unforced force of better arguments” within an ideal speech situation (306). While Habermas's model aimed to prevent power from distorting political discourse, it inadvertently risked placing a premium on a particular mode of rationality—one often abstracted from lived experience, emotion, and historical injustice. In this idealized public sphere, participants present and evaluate reasons as if free from material constraints and social hierarchies. Critics, including Bernstein, have noted that such a model often fails to recognize that structural inequalities shape who gets to speak, who is heard, and whose experiences are deemed “rational.” As a result, rather than neutralizing power, the insistence on reason-giving can subtly reinforce it, privileging the groups already coded as rational and dismissing emotional appeals or embodied testimonies as disruptive or irrational.This limitation becomes evident in real-world contexts where structural inequalities shape who is heard and whose experiences are deemed legitimate. Consider the 2024 New Zealand parliamentary protest against a bill that threatened Māori rights under the Treaty of Waitangi—a 184-year-old treaty between the British Crown and the Māori people. Māori MP Hana-Rāwhiti Maipi-Clarke stood up, tearing up the bill and leading a group of fellow MPs and supporters in a haka—a traditional Māori ceremonial dance historically performed before a battle to demonstrate strength and unity—disrupting the parliamentary session.4 Viewed through a narrow lens of procedural deliberation, it can be seen as (and has been characterized as) disorderly, disruptive, even “childish.” Yet, from an embodied perspective, it can be understood as a powerful assertion of democratic agency that galvanized public protests across New Zealand.5With the New Zealand example in view, we can begin to see that by focusing on “reasoned consensus,” Habermas's framework seems less equipped to handle deep forms of social discord—those rooted in colonial legacies, racial oppression, and gender hierarchies that do not simply vanish because participants agree to speak “rationally.” Power structures shape who feels entitled to speak and who is asked to “translate” their demands into a language recognizable as rational to those in power. This can render invisible the moral force of anger, pain, and the urgent claims raised by social movements. Such movements confront systemic injustices that cannot be fully addressed by calm deliberation alone. Their disruptive tactics challenge the very frameworks that treat their demands as issues for neutral debate rather than immediate moral crises.Revisiting Dewey's emphasis on the embodied and experimental aspects of democracy can help to highlight the limitations of procedural models. In the next section, I take this critique further, examining Jacques Rancière's theory of dissensus, which challenges the structural exclusions embedded in democratic norms.Jacques Rancière's work can provide a useful theoretical vocabulary through which to understand these issues. Framing tinnitus-correlated distress as a brain disorder may contribute to the very distress it seeks to explain
abstract: The Nature Reviews Disease Primer by Vanneste and colleagues is an accomplished synthesis of tinnitus research (Vanneste et al., 2026): a state-of-the-field review covering epidemiology, mechanisms, diagnosis, management, quality of life and future directions. It traces the tinnitus percept to cochlear injury and deafferentation followed by maladaptive plasticity, increased central gain and thalamocortical dysrhythmia, "modulated by limbic and salience networks", and distinguishes the symptom from an accompanying "distress component" hypothesised to be encoded by a "medial, extra-lemniscal pathway that projects to the anterior cingulate cortex, the insula and other regions of the limbic system". Tinnitus accompanied by such distress is termed "bothersome tinnitus" or, in reflection of previous work (De Ridder et al., 2021), "tinnitus disorder". The Primer recommends de-catastrophising psychoeducation ("counselling") and cognitive behavioural therapy as first-line care, and its Outlook locates future progress in research concerning biomarkers, gene and regenerative therapies, neuromodulation and the digital delivery of psychological treatment.Contemporaneously, nine of the Primer's ten authors published a Perspective built on the same conceptual framework (De Ridder et al., 2026). Whereas the Primer synthesises the available evidence, the Perspective extends it into a set of more explicit clinical claims, arguing that the currently descriptive, operational definition of "tinnitus disorder" should also be understood as a theoretical one, identifying a distinct disorder entity with its own presumed aetiology and pathophysiology (De Ridder et al., 2026).Neurophysiologically, three pathways are distinguished: "a lateral 'loudness' pathway, a descending 'inhibitory' pathway, and a medial 'distress' that is specifically activated in tinnitus disorder, providing a neural basis for tinnitus related suffering." On this basis, the Perspective argues that tinnitus disorder should be diagnosed and graded as a distinct clinical entity using standardised diagnostic criteria and severity thresholds based on anxiety and depression questionnaire cut-offs.Taken together, the two publications may be understood as offering a unified account of tinnitus that is likely to shape both research funding and clinical practice, and to determine what the scientific and clinical community might take the field's current position to be.The account presented in these papers is necessarily broad. Our concern focuses on how tinnitus-related distress is defined, described, explained, classified and putatively addressed within this framework.Both the Primer and Perspective acknowledge psychological stress as a mechanism of symptom chronification including roles of catastrophising, threat magnification, helplessness and rumination as processes linking psychological vulnerability to suffering. In addition, we do not dispute that tinnitus may be accompanied by substantial distress, cognitive difficulties and functional impairment, nor the importance of the mechanistic research the Primer synthethises. Rather, we argue that the framework progressively shifts the explanatory centre of gravity from the psychological content and meaning of distress towards its presumed neurophysiological correlates. This shift proceeds through a series of moves which are cumulatively consequential. First, distress associated with tinnitus is constituted as a disorder in its own right (Perspective; adopted by the Primer under the heading "bothersome tinnitus" and "tinnitus disorder"). Second, domain-general neural correlates of stimulus processing are hypothesised as encoders of that distress (Primer) and subsequently elevated to putative pathophysiological substrates of "tinnitus disorder" (Perspective). Third, those same correlates are proposed as targets for neuromodulation (Primer).Fourth, the distress defining the construct is redescribed through psychiatric comorbidity nomenclature (Primer, Perspective) and then used to anchor a severity classification (Perspective). Fifth, psychological interventions, although acknowledged as first-line treatments, risk being recast as transferable packages of techniques suited to standardised or digital delivery (Primer). Across these transitions, five conceptual distinctions are repeatedly collapsed: correlation and causation; description and explanation; neural implementation and psychological meaning; the pragmatic function of diagnostic categories and their transformation into explanatory disorder constructs; and standardised symptom-focused treatment protocols versus individualised psychological formulations that may include, but are not limited to, tinnitus as index symptom.Table 1 provides a structured reconstruction of this inferential sequence. For each move, we contrast the claims advanced in the Primer or Perspective with what the cited evidence appears to support, and with the interpretations that would follow if neural correlates were not assumed to constitute the primary explanatory level. Overall, we argue that emotional, cognitive, behavioural, interpersonal and social contexts, as well as the related meaning of the tinnitus stimulus contribute to clinical presentations in their own right rather than as mere downstream consequences of neural events. A framework that implies neurophysiological findings to be inherently explanatory risks decontextualising the processes through which distress is experienced, and maintained in lived experience and changed in clinical practice.Throughout the paper, we use "tinnitus-correlated distress" wherever we advance a claim of our own about the relation between percept and distress, since "related" risks being heard as "caused by", which is the inference the available evidence does not license. We retain "tinnitus-related distress" only when quoting the source texts verbatim or reporting findings under the label used by their authors. et al., 2026;Vanneste et al., 2026); loudness measures are unreliable and unsuitable as trial endpoints.
