title: Women, the arts, and music making in Melbourne’s Austral Salon, 1890–1915
abstract: Melbourne’s Austral Salon was founded in January 1890 by a small group of enterprising and unconventional women for the promulgation of literature, the arts, and music. The Austral Salon was enormously successful and remains one of the oldest, continuously operating musical institutions in Australia. It is older than any of the state of Victoria’s tertiary-level music schools and national philanthropic institutions and predates the establishment of two other major institutes for women, the Alexandra Club, founded in 1903, and the Lyceum Club, founded in 1912. Clubs for men had been founded earlier: in 1855 (Garrick Club, closed 1866), 1875 (Bohemian Club), 1878 (Australian Club), 1886 (Beefsteak Club), and 1894 (Savage Club). Except for the Garrick Club, these clubs survived the short but brutal economic collapse of the state of Victoria in the 1890s and most survive in some form today.1 In this article, I aim to reconstruct the history of the Austral Salon from its founding to 1915, a time which coincides with an especially aspirational phase in Melbourne’s history. The article is the first study of a salon in the southern hemisphere and seeks to complement existing studies on salons in Europe and Britain. I will also explore the ways in which the salon’s female founders created and made use of various other social, cultural, and musical networks in Melbourne and beyond. Indeed, the 1890s were ripe for broad female participation in the arts and civic life, as Melbourne had long been a city encouraging women’s interests and their agency in its cultural life. Suzanne Robinson’s work on the promotion of women in music in Melbourne in the late nineteenth to early twentieth century is a useful backdrop to situate the emergence of the Austral Salon. Her study of Melbourne’s Marshall-Hall Orchestra (MHO) from 1892–1912 provides a detailed illustration of musical life in Melbourne in the 1890s and 1900s during a period of “exceptional wealth and cultivated aspirations,” notwithstanding the economic crises of the time.2 Robinson’s article gives important context to my work because it highlights the elevated status and success of female classical musicians—and women generally—of the period; it is also biographical, not only in terms of an individual per se but of a group of people who, in the sum of their parts across multiple roles, comprise an institution. By the 1890s, as recorded by Robinson, Melburnians were used to seeing female musical stars on stage: among the touring violin virtuosi who visited Australia were Jenny Claus (1873), Camilla Urso (1879–80), and Lady Hallé (Wilma Norman-Neruda) in 1890 and Terese Liebe in 1891.3 Moreover, of 370 instrumentalists engaged by the Marshall-Hall Orchestra over the years, fifty-eight, or 16 percent, were women averaging just under twenty-five years of age.4 In 1899, the inclusion of women in the orchestra “was a remarkable accomplishment, fully 14 years before women were drafted into one of the London symphony orchestras.” Robinson goes on to write that “at least half of the women in the MHO attended a conservatorium and more than a fifth of them had the means to study in London, Leipzig, Dresden, Prague or Vienna.”5 My account of the Austral Salon’s history is situated in the context of “Marvellous Melbourne,” a term used to describe the cultural wonders of the city in the late nineteenth century, especially for women.6 At first blush, the salon presents itself as a conventional salon akin to the kind found in Paris, for example. But the Austral Salon, while holding musical salons, was a ladies’ club, requiring the payment of membership fees, and was run on commercial lines, which set it apart from most other salons in Australia and abroad. The Austral Salon was a meeting place for affluent and artisan white women interested not only in music but in arts of all kinds. It exploited its many social, philanthropic, and business connections for the pursuit of culture but also, through myriad philanthropic activities, for the benefit of people in Melbourne less fortunate than themselves. Men could join the salon but did not have voting rights.7 The intersection of the salon’s identity and activities found expression in its cultural exchange with other nations, including Britain, France, and Germany. Just as the Marshall-Hall Orchestra was populated with immigrants, some of the musicians and supporters of the Austral Salon were immigrants too. These musicians and supporters had ties to Britain because they were born there, or it was the country to which they would return after living in Melbourne temporarily. Associations with France came via the Charbonnet-Kellermann family, for example, but also through singers who gained experience performing at the salon before leaving to study in Paris.8 A German connection was formed via the association of Hamburg-born violinist Franz Shieblich to the salon. The article is arranged in five parts, which provide a basis for a discussion of the Austral Salon during its foundational years as well as for other scholars who, I hope, will write about the salon’s later history. Doing things with Thucydides: a global approach
venue: Bulletin of the Institute of Classical Studies
abstract: This introduction explores Thucydides’ reception in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries, combining theoretical and more creative and experiential approaches, examining the dynamic relationship between the two. ‘Doing things with Thucydides’ is used as a conceptual framework which reflects the emphasis on active engagement with the text. The five articles included in this collection concentrate on politics, education, and performance as three interconnected areas of the text's reception and are associated with the international workshop ‘Thucydides Global: Teaching, Researching, and Performing Thucydides’, which took place at the Institute of Classical Studies in London in 2019. In addition to the five articles published in this cluster, further presentations were delivered at the workshop, some of which were creative and practical in character, while others were experimental or work-in-progress, at early stages of research. This introduction situates the five articles in the ‘Doing Things with Thucydides’ conceptual framework, also expanding on themes and questions investigated at the workshop as a meaningful context. Additional research material is provided selectively, aiming to supplement and illuminate further key questions addressed in both the articles and the workshop: Why is ‘doing things with Thucydides’ a suitable conceptual framework for exploring the text's modern reception? How is it differentiated from ‘reading’ or ‘thinking with’ Thucydides, which have been the more dominant forms of engagement with this historical text? The letter and the spirit of Thucydides’ text have occupied ancient authors such as Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Plutarch, and Sallust, in more or less traceable ways, have shaped school curricula from the Byzantine period until today, and have intrigued translators and scholars since the Renaissance.1 The consistent authorial flagging of Thucydides’ History of the Peloponnesian War as a written account (1.1; cf. 2.70, 2.103, 3.25) or other statements about method and aims, the handling of causes, observations about human nature, might vs right, national security, leadership and characterization, along with the narratological and rhetorical intricacies of the text have influenced the way human history is understood and written as least in the Western tradition. Thucydides has had a formative influence on modern disciplines such as political theory and philosophy, history of ideas, international relations, and war studies. In turn our understanding of Thucydides has been shaped by the evolution of these disciplines in the modern era.2 The role of Thucydides in these areas has been studied extensively, whereas cultural, creative and practical environments of the text's reception remain underexplored. This introduction offers a reappraisal of the current field of research, aiming to redress the imbalance and bridge the distance between theoretical and practical approaches. ‘Doing things with Thucydides’ alludes to ‘Doing Things with Words’, a seminal study by the philosopher and classicist J. L. Austin, written over half a century ago. Austin theorized ‘action’ and ‘performance’, by arguing that utterances do not only say things or provide information, but also perform actions (‘speech acts’).3 Austin's book has spurred a range of ‘Doing things’ discussions in performative linguistics and translation studies, literary criticism, philosophy and intellectual history, material culture, game and play theory (ludo-literacy, ludology), and last but not least classics and ancient history.4 ‘Doing Things with Thucydides’ calls for active reception, that is, an exploration of not just how Thucydides has been read, but how it has been used, repurposed, and made to speak to new audiences, genres, ideological, cultural, and political moments. It underscores the importance of experience in the process of reception and the need for interaction among different disciplines, groups, and individuals; political scientists and philosophers, sociologists, translators, playwrights, novelists, artists, digital medialists, public discourse analysts, and so on. It broadens the scope by creating a dynamic space, where academic disciplines and creative industries can meet and share knowledge, skills, experiences, and methods. Crossing boundaries and an ‘anarchic’5 intermingling of academic and non-academic environments inspired ‘Thucydides Global: Teaching, Researching, and Performing Thucydides’, the international workshop from which the present collection of articles arises. The workshop took a global or decompartmentalized approach, allowing for fresh and unexpected encounters, meanings and forms to emerge by not only readers and theoreticians, but also by listeners, viewers, translators, and theatrical practitioners of Thucydides’ text.6 ‘Global’ and ‘globalism’ have entered popular discourse since the 1990s and have been associated with both negative and positive connotations and values.7 In the context of Thucydides’ reception, where connections matter, they underscore chronological and geographical coverage, dialogue across disciplines, comparative discussion, a multicentric, non-hierarchical, and decolonizing approach to the classics and humanities at large.8 ‘Thucydides Global’ and ‘Doing Things with Thucydides’ are inspired by the same holistic and active mindset, and in this discussion they are treated as two associated concepts. The workshop brought together academics and non-academics from different disciplines and backgrounds, who came together to share knowledge, skills, experiences, and methods and to explore questions such as: Why is Thucydides’ so present today?’9 Why does Thucydides matter so much? Why and how does this text continue to invite dialogues between past, present and future? How do different societies, educational systems, groups and individuals respond to it and receive its historical lessons? Does Thucydides’ History owe its lasting value and relevance to its ability to resonate with global and local crises? Concentrating on politics, education and performance the five articles published in this collection explore these questions and reception environments of Thucydides, which repurpose, reshape, and reinvent the text for twentieth and twenty-first century audiences and historical circumstances. The articles by Christian Wendt, Hans Kopp and Carlotta Voss sit in the wider area of active political and ideological readings. Wendt challenges the validity of ‘Thucydides’ Trap’, a notion from the field of International Relations, which has used, and misused as Wendt argues, Thucydides’ intellectual capital to explain the shifts in global power dynamics between USA (as classical Sparta, an established power) and China (as classical Athens, a rising power). Kopp probes into the power of Thucydides as an all-time model, and the text's ability to inspire historical analogies, concentrating on Hartvig Frisch, a Danish politician and man of letters, operative in the Second World War. Voss turns the focus to Hannah Arendt, a political philosopher, and her framing of an active—and performative—life in politics (Vita Activa) through a political, philosophical, and poetical reading of Thucydides. title: Introduction
abstract: This Handbook is an attempt to define ‘archaeolinguistics’ as a new scientific discipline by combining recent trends with basic frameworks. It aims at presenting a methodological apparatus, exploring the archaeology–language interface across time and space, and illustrating the extent to which linguistic, archaeological, and genetic histories align or differ. In pursuit of this objective, the Handbook attempts to go beyond the level of ‘broad brush’ and ‘one-man’ approaches by engaging specialists from different disciplines as co-authors in ‘tandem’ approaches. The incentive for this Handbook came from an online workshop, ‘Archaeology and Language’, organized by the editors at the former Max Planck Institute for the Science of Human History in Jena from 16 to 18 November 2021, in the midst of the Covid-19 pandemic. With only twenty vaccinated or recovered persons allowed in the meeting room, it was a feat to allow all sixty-five speakers from around the world to take the virtual floor in a structured programme. Participants from a range of different time zones had to get up in the middle of the night to triangulate language with culture and genes, but they all did it with a great deal of positivity, commitment, and humour. And so, from that surreal setting, the current Handbook was born. Apart from a strong will to move science forward in our fight against the coronavirus and the drive to make the impossible possible, there were other, more objective reasons why the timing of this project was favourable. Over the last decades, genetics has been leapfrogging archaeology and linguistics to become a reliable source of knowledge on human prehistory. However, now that the major patterns of human migration in the Neolithic and Bronze Age are taking shape, at least in certain regions, we also come to realize that although genetics can provide us with detailed descriptions of where and when people moved, it cannot tell us why these people moved. So, to gain better insight into the causalities of human prehistory, the need arose for a more inclusive approach, integrating linguistics, archaeology, and genetics in a single Handbook. The initiative for the Handbook also came at a time when the ‘Big Data’ movement and ‘Third Science Revolution’ in genetics and archaeology were starting to make inroads into linguistics. The combination of large quantitative data sets with powerful analytical tools is an emerging trend in linguistics, making it easier to align the results with evidence from archaeology and genetics in a meaningful way. The emergence of an explicit field of ‘archaeolinguistics’ can perhaps be dated to the late 1980s and early 1990s. During this period, several archaeologists began to examine—and often critique—models of language dispersal proposed by historical linguists. The new research was sometimes discussed in terms of the role of Neolithic farming dispersals in the spread of languages (Renfrew 1987; Bellwood 1991), an interest which drew on earlier suggestions in that respect (see below). What was new was an attempt to model the connections in a much more theoretical way than had previously been attempted (Renfrew 1989, 1992). This new theoretical concern enabled archaeologists to enter the debates in historical linguistics with more confidence (Hudson 1992, 1994). The great diversity of interest in the field was on display at the third World Archaeology Congress, held in New Delhi in 1994 where some eighty papers were presented over five days at a session on language and archaeology. Many of these papers, together with others specially commissioned, were later published in four volumes under the general title Archaeology and Language (Blench and Spriggs 1997–1999). The growth of interest in archaeolinguistics occurred during a period of great transformation in world affairs. The end of the Cold War, the fall of the Soviet Union, and the reunification of Europe had far-reaching impacts on understandings of ethnicity and identity. Previously constrained within the East–West dichotomy of the Cold War, social identities now became diversified, a trend which sometimes led to the revival of earlier nationalisms, most viscerally in the conflicts in the former Yugoslavia (Renfrew 1994; Chernykh 1995; Graves-Brown et al. 1996; McCormack 1996). This was also the time for new synthetic analyses of human genetic data, notably by Cavalli-Sforza and colleagues (1994), as well as the first successful attempts at the extraction of DNA from ancient human remains (e.g. Pääbo 1985; Horai et al. 1989; Hagelberg and Clegg 1991). The new genetic work generated an excitement about future possibilities (Oota and Hudson 1998) and stimulated attempts at modelling broad processes in human prehistory in terms of a combination of language, culture, and biology (e.g. Greenberg et al. 1987; Cavalli-Sforza and Cavalli-Sforza 1995). Paralleling Greenberg’s work on Eurasiatic, the Russian tradition of research on the Nostratic hypothesis also provided a stimulus for archaeologists such as Renfrew (1992). Yet, if archaeolinguistics as presently understood owes a great deal to ideas and approaches that gained traction from the late 1980s, it also draws on much deeper traditions within anthropology. In fact, the relationship between people, culture, and language has always been a key question firing the anthropological imagination. For archaeologists, understanding the distribution of artefacts—and, by extension, of people and their languages—in time and space has been a key objective. Such issues connect to broader debates over ethnic identity and the formation of modern nations. The national awakenings of the nineteenth century grew from Romantic ideas about language and culture. Based in Weimar, the early Romantic philosopher Johann Gottfried Herder (1744–1803) argued that it was the German language that united the German nation. By the early twentieth century, archaeologists began to consider in earnest the prehistory of ethnolinguistic units. German philologist and prehistorian Gustaf Kossinna (1859–1931) developed his Siedlungsarchäologische Methode wherein he linked archaeological cultures with ethnic groups and their languages (Kossinna 1911). Already in 1902, Kossinna had published an article proposing that Corded Ware pottery could be linked with the spread of Indo-European speakers. Australian-born archaeologist Vere Gordon Childe took up this approach, publishing a book titled The Aryans, A Study of Indo-European Origins in 1926. In this work, however, Childe was unsure how to explain the ‘success’ of the Indo-Europeans, continually shifting between critiques of racism and support for other factors such as superior ‘mentality’ that today seem far-fetched. His opposition to misuse of the concept of race was already clear. Ideas linking skull shape with intellectual ability were, he wrote, not only ‘worthless’ but ‘positively mischievous’. As a result of such thinking, ‘the word “Aryan” has become the watchword of dangerous factions and especially of the more brutal and blatant forms of anti-Semitism’. Childe even suggested that the neglect of Indo-European studies in England at the time could be ‘very largely attributable to a legitimate reaction against the extravagancies of Houston Stewart Chamberlain and his ilk’. The spread of the Indo-Europeans could not be put down to a superior skull shape or material culture; instead, Childe proposed, it was due to ‘a more excellent language and the mentality it generated’. Yet the book ends on the contradictory note that, because the first Aryans were ‘Nordics’, the ‘physical qualities of that stock did enable them by the bare fact of superior strength to conquer even more advanced peoples and so to impose their language’ (Childe 1926: 164, 211–212). After the Second World War, the anthropological community went beyond Childe and developed a strong negative reaction to any consideration of questions of race, ethnicity, or large-scale migrations. The horrors of the Holocaust had shown how the idea of ‘race’ could lead to the murder of people deemed inferior or indeed ‘sub-human’ (Untermensch) in Nazi terminology. Scholars such as Montagu (1942) had started to critique the biological basis of racial classifications, and, by the onset of the post-war era, race was no longer a major analytical concept in archaeology. The reaction against past misuse of such concepts was, however, associated with a much broader movement away from questions of ethnicity and migration, even an aversion to explicit theory building, especially of the type associated with the American ‘New Archaeology’ (Veit 1989; Härke 1991; Tsude 1995). Many German archaeologists and institutions had struck a ‘Faustian bargain’ with the National Socialist regime, which had provided support for their work, and were now excessively cautious about potential political misuse of their discipline (Arnold and Hassmann 1995). While noting the rather different history of archaeology in Britain as compared to Germany, Grahame Clark (1966) explored how migrations had become less and less invoked to explain British prehistory since the Second World War. A similar trend was found in Japan where, in reaction to the ethnic nationalism of the wartime era, archaeologists became focused on the minutiae of ceramic and stone tool typologies at the expense of broader questions of population history (Hudson 2006). For these reasons, Renfrew (1987: 288) emphasized that his own approach placed ‘less emphasis on specific ethnic groups and their supposed migrations, and rather more upon the underlying economic and social processes at work’. There were exceptions to the post-war archaeological rejection of migration and ethnicity. In Chapter 9 of this volume, Iversen and Riede discuss the work of Glob (1945, 1971) in Scandinavia. Rouse (1986) extended his earlier research on the Caribbean to examine prehistoric migrations in Polynesia, the Arctic, and Japan. Korean archaeology continued to be based on models of ethnic migration, an approach that was partly a reaction to the colonial interpretations of Korea’s past enforced during the Japanese occupation (1910–1945) (Nelson 1995). As discussed by Hudson and Robbeets (2020), these ideas still throw a significant shadow over Korean archaeolinguistics. In Japan, Egami’s (1964) ‘Horserider’ thesis proposed an invasion by mounted nomads in the fourth century AD but was quickly critiqued by archaeologists on both empirical and ideological grounds (Edwards 1983). In the Soviet Union, research on ethnogenesis continued to consider links between archaeology and past languages (Shnirelman 1995, 1997). title: Public Memory in the USSR and Soviet Myths about World War II
abstract: Jonathan Brunstedt, The Soviet Myth of World War II: Patriotic Memory and the Russian Question in the USSR, Cambridge, UK: Cambridge University Press, 2021. Editor's Introduction: This book by Jonathan Brunstedt of Texas A&M University, looking at changing notions of patriotism and national identity in the Soviet Union as reflected in public commemorations of the USSR's role in the Second World War, raises a host of intriguing issues regarding Soviet history and the Cold War. We asked three distinguished experts to offer appraisals of Brunstedt's book. Their assessments are published here seriatim, along with a reply by Brunstedt.Jonathan Brunstedt's The Soviet Myth of World War II: Patriotic Memory and the Russian Question in the USSR offers an unusually nuanced approach to understanding the striking power of the myth of the war in the USSR after 1945.1 Beginning with a thorough overview of the relevant historiography, Brunstedt analyzes how Soviet officialdom characterized the USSR's wartime experience through two legends that seem at first glance to be mutually exclusive. The first of these—the myth of Soviet Russocentrism—dwells on the pivotal leadership role the Russian people supposedly played in the war, combining centuries of historical experience with acumen, altruism, and self-sacrifice. The second myth—that of the pan-Soviet people—celebrates how a restive and divided young society mustered the ideological unity necessary to win a brutal war of attrition.Perhaps the greatest contribution of The Soviet Myth of World War II is the way Brunstedt treats the contradictions inherent to this mythology. In his telling, Soviet wartime propaganda and postwar commemorative practices varied widely in place, space, and time. This variation allowed a variety of agitators and propagandists to highlight a variety of issues in front of a variety of audiences. Although this complex approach to propaganda sometimes created a cacophony of competing rallying calls, Brunstedt argues that party leaders not only tolerated the contradictions but at times even cultivated them.An intriguing model of deliberate ideological dynamism, the book avoids many of the pitfalls of more static propaganda paradigms. It outlines a type of mobilizational realism in the USSR in which state and society operated in dialogue with each other. It suggests that Soviet ideologists were aware of both the diversity of their society and the limitations of their agitprop outreach. Brunstedt rejects the tall tales of a truly monolithic model of Soviet ideological messaging that were told by the party and then mythologized thereafter by several generations of analysts.Brunstedt posits three elements of this heretofore underappreciated ideological dynamism. First, he takes a close look at the eternal “Russian question.” Here, Brunstedt follows other recent scholars to argue that, particularly under Stalin, Soviet party leaders embraced an inherently non-nationalist sense of Russocentrism. This Russocentrism allowed them to endorse a sense of Russian linguistic, cultural, and historical primacy in Soviet society without allowing the Russian nation sovereignty, self-rule, or any of the privileges that might go with true nationalism. Instead, the Russians were cast as the ever-altruistic primus inter pares on account of their generosity in regard to the broader Soviet family of nations.2Second, Brunstedt examines the nature of the “pan-Soviet people”—a rather artificial and sometimes awkward construct that was simultaneously not only supra-ethnic and multiethnic but also federal and centrally led. Continuously formulated and reformulated after the introduction of the concept in the mid-1930s, the phrase remained subject to constant modulation and renegotiation even after it was formally defined by Nikita Khrushchev in 1961.3 Such semantic dynamism, according to Brunstedt, kept Soviet wartime propaganda and postwar commemorative messaging flexible and inclusive.Third, Brunstedt points to the existence of an unusually multivalent sort of Soviet internationalism. title: Rock Music and Masculinity in Ireland, 1970–85
abstract: From public sculptures and gig venues to a dedicated museum, it is easy to find the traces of Ireland’s rock culture in the city of Dublin today. Rock music is now packaged as an integral part of the country’s heritage and an important chapter of the story that modern Ireland likes to tell of itself, something that speaks not just to the music’s popularity but also to the efficacy with which its longstanding advocates have championed its cause. Early surveys were keen to emphasize the achievements of Ireland’s rock musicians.1 More recent popular music scholars like Gerry Smyth, Noel McLaughlin, and Martin McLoone speak variously of “Ireland’s amazing success in the sphere of modern popular music,” or the music’s “real cultural achievements that have so often been denied a space in the national narratives of Irishness.”2 And the historian Diarmaid Ferriter, in his expansive study of twentieth-century Ireland, has nothing but praise for the likes of Van Morrison, “one of the world’s leading rock stars,” and U2, “the greatest rock band in the world in the 1980s and 1990s.”3 But for a cultural phenomenon so widely celebrated, it is chronically under-historicized, though perhaps that is no coincidence. In this article, I develop an approach to Irish popular music that works more from the basis of social history and gender studies than the mode of cultural studies that has most often been deployed to understand this music, which revolves around a hermeneutics of “Irishness.” I focus on rock music in the years 1970–85, and instead of treating popular musicians and their performances, personas, songs, lyrics and so on as the primary cultural texts to be interpreted, I seek a bottom-up approach to the larger social emergence and discursive circulation of this music in Ireland, a process in which questions of national identity were far less central than they are to the disciplinary norms of the study of Irish popular music.4 I also build considerations of gender into my approach from the beginning, not just because these have often been evacuated in the study of Irish rock music (or addressed only when women are discussed) but because the recent work of scholars such as Aileen Dillane, Laura Watson, and Ann-Marie Hanlon has pointed to a larger need to rethink the history of Irish popular music in terms of gender.5 The conventional story of the emergence of Irish rock music charts a succession of groups that broke with the showband tradition first established in the 1950s (on which more below), beginning with groups like Them and Taste in the beat scene of the 1960s, blossoming with the solo careers of Van Morrison and Rory Gallagher and the emergence of groups like Thin Lizzy, Horslips, and the Boomtown Rats in the 1970s, and culminating with U2’s international success in the 1980s and beyond. Many of these artists and acts remain in place in this article, but as part of an otherwise quite different, three-pronged historical analysis. First, I examine rock music’s emerging social practices. To do this is to ask: what did it mean, in an immediately corporeal sense, to engage with Irish rock culture in the 1970s? I answer this question both by comparing the norms of rock gigs with those of the showband tradition—explicitly rejected by Irish rock musicians in these years—and by mapping the growth of rock venues title: Not Peace but Victory: Hanoi and the Exploitation of Western Protest Activists
abstract: In popular discourse the Vietnam War protest movement is portrayed as a morally laudable rebellion of the young against the old and a heroic attempt to bring a cruel and senseless war to a halt. The Vietnam War protesters, the argument goes, were pacifists with a conscience, who turned against a belligerent and racist imperialism that belonged in the dustbin of history.1 Certainly related to this canonization, academic literature on the protests is both laudatory and abundant.2 Although interest in the protests has changed over time, most recently focusing on issues of gender and race, the view that the protest movement was selflessly trying to end the war still dominates.3Although most scholarship on the protest movements has focused on the United States, things look different from the other side.4 Because the Vietnamese Communists sought through their “diplomatic front” to present the war as a global affair, they needed friends in what their main ally, the People's Republic of China (PRC), at the time referred to as “intermediate countries”—those that could credibly agitate against U.S. intervention and change the global discourse in terms transcending the Cold War paradigm. Sweden was such a country, neutral and amenable to both East-West and North-South exchanges on its territory. Under pressure from the domestic Vietnam movement, Sweden soon turned into the West's most vocal critic of the war and was the first Western country to establish diplomatic relations with the Communist-ruled Democratic Republic of Vietnam (DRV).5 Sweden also hosted the so-called International War Crimes Tribunal (the Russell Tribunal) in 1967, a huge propaganda triumph for Hanoi. It was followed by a series of ten Stockholm International Conferences for Vietnam, during which the DRV arranged important contacts for antiwar activists from all over the world while successfully spreading pro-Hanoi propaganda.6The highly popular writer Sara Lidman arguably was instrumental in bringing forward this broad Swedish political movement against the war.7 Already a beloved Swedish writer with a flair for public speaking, she visited the People's Republic of China (PRC) and then North Vietnam in the autumn of 1965. The trip lasted a full month and included meetings with the highest leaders such as Ho Chi Minh. Afterward, she began ardently promoting the cause of the National Front for the Liberation of the South (NLF), which grouped together the Communist insurgents in the South.8 This article shows that her visit to Beijing and Hanoi was conducted with financial and logistical assistance from the PRC—through its embassy in Stockholm—to foster a protest movement against U.S. involvement in Vietnam, clandestinely led by Maoists.From 1965 until the late 1970s, Lidman continued to cooperate almost full time with the Vietnamese Communists. Having been the first Swede to visit wartime Hanoi, she became a sought-after authority to reflect the DRV's perspective on the war. title: Lessons from the Past that Apply to the Present: On the 110th Anniversary of the Founding of the Mexican Consulate in Salt Lake City, Utah
abstract: Since their respective foundings, the relationship between Mexico and the United States has been one of the most complex between countries of the Americas. The economic, social, and cultural histories of the two nations are intertwined. The United States and Mexico first established diplomatic relations on December 12, 1822, and with time, different particularities developed on either side of the border.The twentieth century ushered in a new era in the relationship between Mexico and the United States, as the end of the Civil War and the beginning of the Mexican Revolution created continuous changes in the development of diplomacy. On the one hand, the United States grew in its position as an economic power. This spurred the migration of Mexicans in search of better working conditions. In Mexico, meanwhile, political instability led to ups and downs in terms of the quality of response by the Mexican Foreign Service (Servicio Exterior Mexicano, SEM).1In 2022, the Mexican Consulate in Salt Lake City, Utah, marked its 110th anniversary. Within the framework of that celebration, we review the beginnings of the Salt Lake City Consulate in order to understand some of the lessons about consular work this diplomatic corps can pass on to others. This article, which is based on documents kept in the Genaro Estrada Diplomatic Historical Archives of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, is divided into three sections. The first contains a brief description of the binational historical context that characterized both countries; the second section discusses the first three decades of the establishment of the consulate in Salt Lake City, to understand its evolution and the contribution it makes to consular diplomacy; and the third section presents our final thoughts.Beginning in the second half of the nineteenth century and through the start of the twentieth century, once the expansion to the Pacific had been completed and the Civil War had come to its conclusion, the United States underwent a period of internal transformation prior to its emergence as a world power. One of the key developments was its accelerated progress toward industrialization, which changed US production to the detriment of some sectors, such as agriculture, whose contribution to the country's total production fell from 70 percent to 30 percent between 1839 and 1900.2Alongside this process, new transportation routes for raw materials and goods were developed, leading to an increase in railroads and the use of river transport. Likewise, the country underwent a demographic shift, which allowed access to an abundant and cheap pool of labor in the main productive centers. The United States’ own growing population met this need, as well as migration and the transition from a rural to an urban society. The process culminated in 1920, the year in which, for the first time, a greater number of people lived in cities than in the countryside.3This transformation of the United States strengthened its business sector, which began to have greater influence on politics. The elite consolidated large monopolies and expanded their businesses abroad, with the support and backing, in most cases, of the government. In the years leading up to World War I, the United States positioned itself as the leading producer of manufactured goods, accounting for 36 percent of global production and outpacing the United Kingdom, which accounted for 14 percent of production, and Germany, which accounted for 15.7 percent.4This impacted both the United States itself and nations abroad. One of the important results at home was the emergence of the Progressive movement, which included public criticism of economic monopolies, corruption in state and municipal governments, and the lack of protection for women and children, all of which affected the political climate of the time.5In terms of international relations, the expansion of the US economy brought about a shift in the execution of foreign policy. The most notable actions include the Spanish-American War of 1898, through which the United States obtained control of former Spanish islands in the Caribbean and the Philippines; the enactment of the Platt Amendment, which legitimized its intervention in Cuba; the implementation of Theodore Roosevelt's Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine, which sought to position the United States as an “international police force” to preserve the stability and interests of its investors (above all, in Latin America); and the emergence of “dollar diplomacy,” promoted by President William H. Taft between 1909 and 1912, which aimed to promote the use of the currency as a means of furthering American commercial interests abroad.6This transformation of the United States coincided with two key moments in Mexican history: the Porfiriato and the Mexican Revolution. During the years of General Porfirio Díaz's dictatorial rule, from the late 1870s to 1911, Mexico experienced much modernization—at the cost of liberties. Then, beginning with the political challenge to Díaz posed by Francisco I. Madero (1909–1910) and continuing through the decade-long Mexican Revolution, the nation went through great upheavals. During these years, economic issues stood out on the agenda as one of the most important factors in the binational relationship. In the first decade of the twentieth century, foreign direct investment (FDI) increased in Mexico, as did the number of companies with a presence in the territory. By 1910, most of the FDI inflow (60 percent) was composed of US capital; in terms of that country's outflows, Mexico was the destination for one-quarter of its investments.7American financial capital in Mexico increased considerably and was concentrated in different sectors throughout the country: in the north, it went mainly to the railroad system and the mining and smelting complex; in the center of the country, investments were made in the mining and energy industries; in the Gulf of Mexico, capital was directed at the incipient oil industry; and in the south, it went to the tropical rubber plantations. Likewise, the trade relationship accounted for three-quarters of Mexican exports and half of its imports.8Financial and credit factors presented new dynamics for the development of the binational relationship. In 1899, the New York Stock Exchange issued loans for foreign debt swaps and thus paved the way for the first debt issuance by a Latin American country. In 1900, a money order system was established that allowed money to be transferred and exchanged between the two countries. The most significant change came with the reform of the Mexican monetary system, which led to the adoption of the gold standard and allowed an exchange rate to be established between the currencies of the two countries. All of these changes strengthened financial and business relations between the nations.At the beginning of the twentieth century, significant migration occurred in both directions, although a larger number of people flowed from Mexico into the United States. An estimated 125,000 Mexicans lived in the United States in 1900; by 1910, that figure had increased to 230,000. The migrants were mainly agricultural and railroad workers and cowboys. More than half were located in Texas, followed by California, Arizona, Kansas, and New Mexico. The rest of the states were home to less than 5 percent of the total Mexican migrant population.9As the relationship between Mexico and the United States developed, a strengthening of diplomatic ties took place both at the binational and multilateral levels. The United States government sought to increase its influence on the continent and saw Mexico as providing a strategic position to connect with Latin America. It was in line with this that, in 1900, it proposed that the second Pan American Conference take place in Mexico City and, three years later, Colombia asked the United States to mediate the conflict over the separation of Panama. All of this suggests that, despite Mexico taking an autonomous position on the international scene, American influence and interest were beginning to permeate the Mexican agenda.10During the revolutionary period, the relationship between the nations began to experience ups and downs. First of all, the critical US media in Mexico influenced public opinion, highlighting, above all, the movements against President Porfirio Díaz, which were organized in the north of the country and in border states such as Texas. In spite of the Mexican government's requests to Washington that it put a stop to the organization of these groups in its territory, Madero's influence in some areas of the United States prevented any halt of this movement.11 Second, Díaz's resignation was well received by the Taft administration; what's more, the appointment of Francisco León de la Barra (the former Mexican ambassador to the United States) as interim president contributed to the recognition of his government by the United States.During Madero's short term in office, he stressed support for arms control in order to prevent weapons from reaching insurgent groups. The Taft administration had such confidence in the revolutionary process that it ignored Ambassador Henry Wilson's insistence that it intervene in Mexican territory against the elected government of Madero. President Taft maintained his stance even after the event known as the Ten Tragic Days (la Decena Trágica).12The Mexican Revolution had significant consequences for the relationship between Mexico and the United States. First and foremost, the outbreak of the armed conflict led to the displacement of those Mexicans who were fleeing the guerrillas. Gilberto Loyo reported that between 1926 and 1927, of sixty-one migrants surveyed, seventeen said they had migrated to the United States due to the revolution.13 All of the above suggests that Mexico and the United States underwent periods of conflict and reconciliation, mainly due to the instability of the Mexican government.The increase in the Mexican population in the United States introduced new challenges. From an economic standpoint, the United States experienced an increase in its labor force that enabled development in California and Texas.14 The settlement of people of Mexican origin in the country can be categorized according to birthrate and migration. Regarding birthrates, the number of Mexican-born children in the United States began to increase in 1880 and reached a peak in 1940. In terms of migration, it is estimated that the Mexican Revolution became a motivating factor in the migration of Mexicans to the United States from 1920 onwards.15The increase in the Mexican population in the United States constituted a major shift in binational diplomatic relations, since the Mexican government not only had to assist Americans who had business interests in Mexico but also had to develop mechanisms to defend the rights of Mexican migrants. As a result, Mexican diplomacy focused on the actions of its consulates, essential players in Mexican foreign policy, who used both creativity and common sense to reach out to their Mexican compatriots.16The growing number of undocumented migrants in the United States led to the creation of mechanisms such as the Immigration and Naturalization Service (INS) in 1922 and the border patrol in 1924. In response, consular diplomats had to specialize in a new issue: advocating for the dignity of their fellow countrymen. Since the beginning, the consulates had been conceived as centers that specialized in the US-Mexican relationship and aimed to address trade and political issues. However, the increase in the Mexican population and their treatment by the American authorities required the development of consular agents, inspectors, and chancellors for protection, and bilateral meetings focused on the regulation of migratory flows.17In short, these events not only provide the historical backdrop against which the relationship between Mexico and the United States shifted beginning in the twentieth century, but they also indicate a new series of challenges that needed to be addressed at the time, some of which persist today. Against this backdrop, Mexican consular work can be seen to have adapted to the historical development needs in the interest of preserving its work of promoting Mexico abroad while, at the same time, protecting Mexican nationals who migrate north.At the beginning of the twentieth century, the relationship between Mexico and the United States began to increase in importance on the agendas of these nations. The Mexican Revolution necessitated US recognition to validate the plans for government of the revolutionary campaigns. At the same time, the United States needed to reach out to the Mexican governments to attract and regulate the entry of Mexican workers into the country, especially since the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 stemmed the migration of laborers from China.18The entry of Mexican migrants into the United States marked the beginning of a complex relationship that is so closely connected on many levels. Mexican migration focused mainly on the borders of California and Texas. The Mexican communities that settled there had visions of opportunities for development and a future for their families.19While it is understandable that Mexicans focused on settling in border areas to maintain their family relationships across the border, there are also records of settlements in other states, such as Utah. Mexican migration to Utah was concentrated mainly in mining areas and specifically in the Salt Lake Valley, home to the Kennecott Copper Company. title: Narco-Legitimacy in Latin America as a Radical Expression of Syncretism Between Religious and Populist Narratives
venue: Journal for the Study of Radicalism
abstract: Government discourses and public policy approaches to drug trafficking in Latin America often adopt a prohibitionist and economic tone that may be understood as a normalization process related to the presence of an enemy and that justifies errors or covers up complicity within state institutions.1 Normalization takes place since, differing from other illegal criminal practices such as kidnapping, extortion, and human trafficking,2 drug trafficking has managed to transform itself, to adapt3 and blend within the cultural ethos so as to become part of the social system.4 Within this framework, drug traffickers (narcos) have found legitimate spaces that allow them to exert sovereignty in parallel with the state.5 To do so, among other strategies, they confront and interact with religious institutions and instrumentalize their practices and rites.This article proposes that in territories where there is drug trafficking, the guarantees of minimum coexistence parameters are met without formalizing any norm. Drug traffickers make use of emotional narratives and identity bonds such as religion and populism to generate cohesion and earn credibility; that is, they take hold of tools and strategies that have allowed their legitimization in the social order.Drug traffickers thus become a tolerated sociocultural product, 6 and a source to impose axiological structures:7Drug traffickers and addicts are not marginalized from culture. Not only are they formless shadows that are never present in society, but their world is wrapped in by a complete lattice of patterns, values, music, partying, films, religiosity, clothing, and linguistic patterns. This universe is often described as “narco-culture.”8In addition, narcos’ conceptions have become naturalized, popularized and sophisticated. Culture and aesthetics surging from drug trafficking have flourished through the artistic, journalistic, and television fields, among others. A system of values and traditions has set in that leads to the creation of an ideal to wish for.9This ideal is reinforced in settings where conditions of poverty and inequality pave the way for drug trafficking development, turning it into a profitable and desirable economic activity for various types of people. Palacios and Safford10 refer to this phenomenon as of the 1990s in Colombia thus: “Poor youths found new opportunities getting hired as hitmen within a context where death was trivialized.”This way, even though they do not stop exercising violence and projecting themselves as forces that intimidate local populations and state institutions, illegal drug dealers have tried to preserve consensual spaces,11 thus projecting an image of benefactors in the face of everyday needs such as health, infrastructure, and housing and as protectors of local traditions. Through such guarantees they aim to exert power over communities and gain spaces to negotiate and set up alliances with those who stand out as friends/enemies.These negotiation spaces are important when considering the structure underlying organized crime and drug trafficking through their flexible exchange networks that respond to market needs.12 Thus, networks bent on personal relationships, social traditions, and socioeconomic conditions, inherent in the surroundings where they operate, determine the way they carry out their activities and how they connect with communities.Within the Latin American and Caribbean context, according to the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, there are two conditions within the surroundings that facilitate the insertion and adaptation of organized crime. First, in the region there persist high levels of income inequality and little access to services such as education and health; a high percentage of homicides and nonlethal violence derived from organized crime; and high unemployment rates among the youth that “place the youth under a condition of vulnerability in the face of victimization, violent and criminal conflicts, and even to their being recruited by organized criminal structures.”13Second, in cultural terms, the region is characterized by a broad dominance of the Christian faith (76%).14 Hence, in the exercise of structuring flexible exchange networks, drug trafficking usually resorts jointly to the promise of better living conditions and narratives of appropriation of religion's symbols and cultural elements.15 These narratives are understood as identity and emotional links—from a Weberian perspective16—that allow drug traffickers to forge communities of meaning and challenge the modern state's pretensions of order. In the Latin American case (extending to countries such as Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay, and Argentina),17 these links have been strengthened through religious syncretism,18 and stand out as a source of hope in political contexts where precarious democracies predominate and there is an erosion of the public sphere, and social mistrust toward institutionality.19Based on the preceding descriptions, the objective of this article is to analyze how the appropriation of religious practices and modes of semiotization by drug traffickers has engendered a narrative that legitimizes an illegal structure and adapts itself to popular culture. The success of this strategy has led to different radicalization scenarios of territories where drug trafficking has an impact, and to the increase of drug traffickers’ negotiating power.Thus, drug traffickers manage to become guiding axes of social order in the territories where they hold dominion, as well as becoming spiritual leaders with the power of forgiveness, atonement for guilt, punishment, and pointing out sinners–offenders. As a consequence, religious institutions and the political regime are forced to grant spaces for co-governance20 to preserve their image of influential players in civil society and in the formal representation of democracy.This article is structured into four sections. The section that follows this introduction discusses the role of religion within the social order, the concept of legitimacy and legality, and the appropriation of populist and religious narratives by drug traffickers. The second section addresses the methodological design based on digital ethnography techniques and the method of prototypical narratives as schemes that build up sense and meaning of the social environment through the assignment of actantial roles, discursive intentions, and strategic interactions.The third section shows that although religious and populist narratives cannot generalize the dynamics of cultural incidence of drug traffickers as a non-monolithic group in the territories, they can describe trends in the struggle for meaning and social control through narrative programs.In this way, it is proposed that the drug traffickers’ strategy is closely aligned to Weberian types of domination (charismatic, traditional, and legal) and creates its own forms of legitimacy, which we call narco-legitimacy. As a prospective reflection, four research scenarios are proposed to analyze whether the incorporation of these narratives by drug traffickers is part of a radical and para-institutional expression that is presented as an unintended consequence of drug trafficking organizations, or whether it is a deliberate and planned strategy for political and territorial incidence purposes.The role played by religion in society transcends the scope of the individuals’ spiritual life; for authors like Marx, it is an expression of class struggle, an instrument used by those who exercise power and impose injustice and a popular reaction to oppression.21 Durkheim,22 for his part, sees in religion a unified system of beliefs and practices related to the sacred that come together in a moral community called the church; even in recent decades it has been associated with the recovery of democratic orders in the Latin American context.23 This structuring role that religion plays in societies such as the Latin American ones allows us to anticipate that the study of individuals who practice religion, popular practices, and signs of religiosity will provide clues about the ways of social
